chapters.book0-p01:
Start Here How This Course Works

Welcome, Jacob. This box of paper is a complete six-month path from zero to comfortable everyday Delhi Hindi — built for exactly your situation: classes for structure, a Delhi partner for reality, and self-study to do the actual heavy lifting. Here's the machine and how to run it at 45–60 minutes a day.

The six pieces

Book 0 · Master PlanThis book: the 26-week schedule, trackers, and operating instructions. Keep it on top of the pile.
Book 1 · Pronunciation & ScriptThe mouth-first pronunciation course (tongue positions, diagrams, drills) plus the complete Devanagari reading & writing course. Chapters 1–7 are your first-month backbone; Chapters 8–13 are reference and drills you'll revisit all six months.
Book 2 · Grammar Workbook24 units, one core pattern each, with exercises and full answer keys. One unit per week after week 1 (two pivot units get two).
Book 3 · Vocabulary20 themed chapters, ~1,100 words, every entry with script + roman + phonetics + gender. Feeds the flashcards.
Book 4 · Practice24 Delhi-situation dialogues with drills and translations, plus 6 monthly tests with keys. This is where grammar and vocab become speech.
Flashcards · 17 decks~800 print-and-cut cards (3 PDFs). Devanagari on the front — always try to read before flipping.

The daily hour (45–60 min)

10 minFlashcards — run today's Leitner boxes (below). Non-negotiable; this is the compound interest.
20–25 minMain work — this week's Book 2 unit or Book 1 chapter, per the weekly plan. Do exercises in pencil; check against the key immediately (wrong answers are the curriculum).
10 minMouth & hand — alternate days: pronunciation drills (Book 1 Ch. 3–5, 12) / writing practice (Book 1 Ch. 10–11), then always 2 minutes reading the current dialogue aloud.
10 minPartner time — one game from Book 1 Ch. 13 or the current lesson's roleplay box. No partner around? Shadow a voice note instead.
5 minClose the loop — tick the tracker, glance at tomorrow, add any word you needed today but didn't have to the "hit list" page.

Six days a week; day seven is catch-up or rest. Test weeks replace the main work with the monthly test + review of everything it exposed.

The Leitner system (your card engine)

Get five envelopes or a 5-slot box, labeled 1–5. New cards enter Box 1. Any card you answer correctly moves one box right; any miss sends it back to Box 1. The boxes run on different clocks:

BoxReviewMeaning
1every daynew + missed cards
2every 2nd day (Mon/Wed/Fri)getting there
3weekly (Saturdays)known
4every 2nd Saturdaysolid
51st of the monthowned — three straight rights here and the card retires

Feed rate: ~10 new cards a day from the decks the weekly plan activates. A card counts as "right" only if you got the pronunciation right too — say every answer out loud. For verbs, name the transitivity (vt/vi) after Unit 14 makes you care; for nouns, gender counts: kitaab without "(f)" is a miss.

Using your classes

This plan doesn't compete with your classes — it feeds them. Three habits: (1) Bring a question list. Anything marked "ask a native/teacher" in your week, plus every exercise you got wrong twice. (2) Request pronunciation audits. Once a month, read your current Gauntlet sentences (Book 1, Ch. 13) to the teacher and ask for brutal honesty — teachers rarely volunteer pronunciation correction unless asked. (3) Map, don't march. If class order differs from this plan (most start with script, some with phrases), keep this plan as your spine and treat class topics as free reinforcement — every unit here is self-contained, and the index-by-topic means you can pull a unit forward the week your class covers it.

Using your partner (the house rules)

A partner from Delhi is a superpower with one failure mode: turning every dinner into a grammar exam ruins both the dinner and the grammar. The rules that work: ten scheduled minutes a day (the games are designed to be fun — pointing games, candle tests, vendor roleplay), a standing "Hindi window" (e.g., making chai = Hindi-only), and voice notes — ask them to send one WhatsApp voice note a day at normal speed; it becomes your shadowing material (Ch. 7). Let them teach you the family's own words — every Delhi household has its own slang — and write those in the blank pages of Book 3. What they should not have to do: explain WHY grammar works (that's Book 2's job and your teacher's job), or slow down their family dinner for you. Around their parents: आप forms, always — Book 4 Lesson 14 is your training camp.

What "done" looks like

By the end of Month 6, per the final test and capstone: you can hold a ten-minute everyday conversation, survive Delhi transactions (metro, auto, market, dhaba) in Hindi, read Devanagari at a careful pace, write notes in a fair hand, follow slowish family conversation, and — the real graduation — spend an evening with your in-laws where the Hindi parts of the evening include you. Fluency is a years-long road, but this is the part where the road gets fun.

Printing & assembly: print Books 0–4 double-sided and drop them in three-ring binders (Book 1 gets opened most — give it the good binder). Flashcards: print single deck at a time, double-sided, "flip on long edge," 100% scale, on cardstock if your printer takes it. Cut on the dashed lines (a $10 paper trimmer beats scissors by a mile). The first page of the flashcard PDFs is an alignment tester — print that one sheet first, check front/back line up, then commit.
chapters.book0-p02:
The Plan Months 1–3, Week by Week

Every week below lists exactly what to open. "B1 Ch. 3" = Book 1 Chapter 3; "U7" = Book 2 Unit 7; "c06" = Book 3 Chapter 6; "L11" = Book 4 Lesson 11; "D05" = flashcard deck 5. Weekly rhythm stays the same throughout: cards daily, main work 5 days, one partner game most days, tracker every night.

Month 1 — Sounds & Script Boot Camp

Goal: mouth retrained, alphabet read and written, first phrases alive. Grammar starts gently in week 1 — the heavy lifting this month is Book 1.

Week 1 — Your mouth, the map

Main workB1 Ch. 1 (the map — do every "feel it"), Ch. 2 (vowels — the freeze drill daily). B2 U1 (sentence shape). Start B1 Ch. 10 writing: vowel rows.
Vocabulary & cardsBuild your Leitner box. Start D01 (vowels & matras): 10/day. From B4 L1, learn the greeting lines by ear (roman is fine this week).
Speak & listenPartner: pointing game with haan/saans-type nasal pairs + length pairs (kam/kaam). Ask them to send your first daily voice note.
You can nowSay namaste with a real dental t, hold a pure ए for 3 seconds, read the 13 vowels, say "main Jacob hoon."

Week 2 — The Big One (dental vs. retroflex)

Main workB1 Ch. 3 — the week's centerpiece; alternation ladder every day. B1 Ch. 8: rows क–ङ, च–ञ, ट–ण, त–न (read WITH the mouth instructions). B2 U2 (honaa + aap/tum/tu). Writing: Ch. 10 rows 1–2.
Vocabulary & cardsStart D02 (consonants), first ~20 cards. B3 c01 first half (greetings — say each aloud twice).
Speak & listenB4 L1 dialogue: read aloud daily, roleplay with partner by Friday. Pointing game: त/ट papers, every day, 2 minutes.
You can nowIntroduce yourself politely, ask "aap kaise hain?", produce distinct त vs ट in isolation, read 20+ letters.

Week 3 — The puff

Main workB1 Ch. 4 (aspiration — palm/candle daily), Ch. 8 remaining rows (प–म, य–व, श–ह, nukta letters). B2 U3 (gender). Writing: Ch. 11 rows 3–5.
Vocabulary & cardsFinish D02. B3 c01 second half + c02 first half (immediate family — the words that matter most in your life).
Speak & listenB4 L2 (chai stall!) — this is your first "real Delhi" script; get bhaiyaa, do chaay denaa partner-certified. Candle night (Ch. 4 box).
You can nowOrder chai, pass the palm test on all five rows, name your partner's immediate family in Hindi, read any single letter.

Week 4 — Matras: the script clicks

Main workB1 Ch. 9 (matras & conjuncts — take two passes; the ि-writes-left surprise needs reps). B1 Ch. 5 (tricky customers — the flap!). B2 U4 (plurals). Writing: Ch. 11 matra rows + first words.
Vocabulary & cardsStart D05 (family & people). B3 c02 second half (the full in-law map — yes, all of it; it's a love language).
Speak & listenB4 L3 (meeting the family). B1 Ch. 12 minimal pairs: Sets 1–2 with partner. Daily: read one L1–L3 dialogue line in pure Devanagari, no roman peeking.
You can nowSound out real written words (धन्यवाद!), do the ड़ flap, say who everyone at the dinner table is.

Month 2 — First Grammar Engine

Week 5 — The invisible vowel · TEST 1

Main workB1 Ch. 6 (schwa deletion). B2 U5 (kaa/ke/kee + apnaa). Weekend: Test 1 (B4 t1) closed-book, grade with key at1, then Month-1 milestones (B1 Ch. 13).
Vocabulary & cardsStart D03 (numbers 0–30 this week). B3 c03 (pronouns & little words).
Speak & listenB4 L4 (around the house — narrate your own place room by room). Voice-note shadowing 3×.
You can nowSay whose everything is (meree chaay!), read words the Delhi way (kamraa not ka-ma-raa), count to 30.

Week 6 — Adjectives & the sound of Delhi

Main workB2 U6 (adjectives & agreement). B1 Ch. 7 (rhythm & the Delhi accent — start daily shadowing habit for good). B3 c04 first half (numbers chapter: patterns + 0–50).
Vocabulary & cardsD03 to 60. B1 Ch. 12 Sets 3–4 (vowel length, nasals) into rotation.
Speak & listenRe-run L4 roleplay with adjectives everywhere (baRaa kamraa, chhoTee balcony). Melody game (Ch. 7 box).
You can nowCompliment things convincingly (kitnaa achchhaa hai!), say है as [heh] like a Delhiite, count to 60.

Week 7 — The oblique week (the pivot)

Main workB2 U7 (postpositions & oblique case) — two main-work sessions; this unit unlocks everything after it. B3 c05 (time — days, months, DeRh/Dhaaee!).
Vocabulary & cardsFinish D03 (to 100); start D11 (time & calendar). Numbers game with partner nightly (c04 partner box).
Speak & listenLocation sentences about your real life: mez par, ghar mein, dillee se. Re-read L1–L4 in Devanagari only.
You can nowSay where anything is, tell the time (saaRhe saat!), give today/tomorrow plans a timestamp, count anything.

Week 8 — The present tense arrives

Main workB2 U8 (present habitual). B3 c06 (food, Delhi style — the joy chapter).
Vocabulary & cardsStart D06 (food & drink). Hit-list page: add every food word your household actually uses.
Speak & listenB4 L5 (daily routine — tell yours for real). Partner: "aap roz kyaa karte hain?" interview, both directions.
You can nowDescribe your day, your habits, your chai order and your golgappa loyalty in real sentences.

Week 9 — Right now · TEST 2

Main workB2 U9 (present continuous). B3 c07 (home). Weekend: Test 2 (t2/at2) + Month-2 milestones.
Vocabulary & cardsStart D07 (home & daily objects).
Speak & listenB4 L6 (on the phone). New standing habit: one real "kyaa kar rahe ho?" phone/text exchange with partner daily, in Hindi.
You can nowNarrate the present moment, hold a 60-second phone check-in, pass Test 2's reading passage without the roman line.

Month 3 — Wants, Pasts & Futures

Week 10 — The ko-construction (how Hindi feels)

Main workB2 U10 (mujhe pasand hai / chaahiye / lagnaa — Hindi's emotional engine). B3 c14 (feelings & small talk).
Vocabulary & cardsStart D04 (survival phrases — many will already feel like old friends).
Speak & listenB4 L7 (ordering & likes) and L8 (prices & time — light, mostly numbers you own now). Nightly: three genuine mujhe-pasand sentences at dinner.
You can nowWant things, like things, feel hungry/cold/happy out loud, order for two, ask what things cost.

Week 11 — Yesterday exists now

Main workB2 U11 (thaa + past habitual/continuous). B3 c13 (weather — instant small-talk fuel, Delhi edition).
Vocabulary & cardsStart D16 (weather & nature). Ch. 12 Sets 5–7 into rotation.
Speak & listenB4 L9 (talking about yesterday). Partner: "kal kaisaa thaa?" becomes the new daily question.
You can nowCompare today's weather to yesterday's, tell where you were and what life was like "back then."

Week 12 — Tomorrow too

Main workB2 U12 (future). B3 c08 (body & health — vocabulary you want BEFORE you need it).
Vocabulary & cardsStart D08 (body & health).
Speak & listenB4 L10 (weekend plans — make real ones and then keep them). The kal-means-both joke will happen this week; enjoy it.
You can nowPlan a weekend, promise things (milenge!), handle past-present-future in one conversation.

Week 13 — Politely bossy · TEST 3

Main workB2 U13 (imperatives & requests — the keejiye class). B3 c10 (Delhi city & transport). Weekend: Test 3 (t3/at3) + Month-3 milestones.
Vocabulary & cardsStart D10 (city & transport).
Speak & listenB4 L11 (auto bargaining — the rite of passage) and L12 (metro & directions). Vendor drill (Ch. 13 game 4) makes its debut.
You can nowDirect an auto, buy a metro token, bargain without offending, request politely at three politeness levels. Halfway there.
chapters.book0-p03:
The Plan Months 4–6, Week by Week

Month 4 — The Ergative Mountain (and the view from the top)

Week 14 — ne, part one

Main workB2 U14 (simple past & the ergative) — two main-work sessions, exercises spread across the week. This is Hindi's famous hard turn; the unit takes it slowly, so should you. B3 c11 (money & bargaining).
Vocabulary & cardsVerbs matter now: start D12 (core verbs) at 10/day — the (vt)/(vi) tags are your ne-compass.
Speak & listenB4 L12 consolidation + L13 (what happened?! — your first past-tense storytelling). Nightly: one true "aaj maine…" sentence.
You can nowSay what you did today without fear: maine chaay banaaee. (Check that agreement — you just did the hard thing.)

Week 15 — ne, part two + perfects

Main workB2 U14 exercises finished cold; B2 U15 (perfect tenses). B3 c09 (clothing & colors).
Vocabulary & cardsStart D09 (clothing & colors). D12 continues.
Speak & listenB4 L13 mastered; partner tells you their day in past tense, you relay it back third-person.
You can nowHandle "have you eaten?" — khaanaa khaayaa? — and answer it like family: haan, khaa liyaa (the compound sneaks in as a set phrase; Unit 19 explains it later).

Week 16 — The in-law dinner (the boss level)

Main workB2 U15 consolidation. B3 c19 (love & affection — because the partner deserves vocabulary too). Review c02 in-law terms until instant.
Vocabulary & cardsStart D17 (love & sweet nothings — deploy responsibly). D05 back into daily rotation for a refresher week.
Speak & listenB4 L14 (dinner at the in-laws') — rehearse until the aap-forms are automatic; then, if geography allows, DO it (video call counts; the letter of thanks in Devanagari is extra credit).
You can nowSurvive — no, shine at — a family dinner: compliment the cooking, take seconds correctly, use aap without slipping once.

Week 17 — Can-do

Main workB2 U16 (saknaa/paanaa/chuknaa). B3 c12 (work & study — talk about your actual job).
Vocabulary & cardsD12 continues (aim: 60+ verbs in rotation). Hit-list: your job's ten key words, partner-translated.
Speak & listenB4 L15 (Sarojini shopping). "main … kar saktaa hoon" inventory game with partner: trade five true sentences each.
You can nowAsk permission, offer help, shop for clothes, explain what you do for a living in two sentences.

Week 18 — Should, must, gotta · TEST 4

Main workB2 U17 (obligation: chaahiye/hai/paRnaa). Weekend: Test 4 (t4/at4 — the ne gauntlet) + Month-4 milestones.
Vocabulary & cardsc08 health words refreshed (D08 rotation) — they pair with obligation ("mujhe aaraam karnaa chaahiye").
Speak & listenB4 L16 (not feeling well — doctor roleplay with partner; let them play the strict Delhi doctor AND the haldee-doodh dispensing parent).
You can nowSay what you should, have to, and were forced to do — and fend off home remedies in grammatical Hindi.

Month 5 — Sounding Like a Person, Not a Textbook

Week 19 — Maybes & ifs

Main workB2 U18 (subjunctive + agar…to). B3 c17 (adverbs, postpositions & connectors — the glue chapter).
Vocabulary & cardsStart D14 (little words). These cards are small but they're the ones that make speech flow.
Speak & listenB4 L17 (asking for help). Suggestion game: every plan this week gets proposed in Hindi first — "chalein? … agar time ho to…"
You can nowSuggest, hedge, wonder and bargain with fate: shaayad, agar, chalein — the polite Indian art of the soft plan.

Week 20 — Compound verbs (the native-speaker switch)

Main workB2 U19 (compound verbs) — two sessions; this is the unit that upgrades "correct" Hindi to "real" Hindi. Suddenly half of what your partner says will click retroactively.
Vocabulary & cardsD12 push to complete. Re-listen to old voice notes and count the ho-gayaas — they were there all along.
Speak & listenB4 L18 (making plans with friends). Retell L13's disaster story, now with vectors: kho gayaa, mil gayaa, ho gayaa.
You can nowSay le lo, de do, ho gayaa, aa jaao in the right places — and hear the warmth they carry.

Week 21 — Joining everything

Main workB2 U20 (ki-clauses, kyonki, jab…tab, reported speech, -kar). B3 c16 (core adjectives — sweep what you don't know into the box).
Vocabulary & cardsStart D13 (adjectives & opposites).
Speak & listenB4 L19 (sabzi mandi — quantities + the sacred free dhaniyaa). Relay game: partner tells you something, you report it to the wall: "usne kahaa ki…"
You can nowBuild long sentences without stalling, quote people, explain because-therefore, shop by the paav.

Week 22 — The one who · TEST 5

Main workB2 U21 (jo…voh relatives). Weekend: Test 5 (t5/at5) + Month-5 milestones.
Vocabulary & cardsD13 continues. D04 sweep — anything not in Box 4+ gets drilled.
Speak & listenB4 L20 (telling a story — partner tells a childhood Delhi story; you retell YOUR childhood one). Record both; this recording is gold.
You can nowDescribe people and things with clauses ("the one who…"), tell a whole story with a beginning, middle and ho-gayaa.

Month 6 — Delhi Polish & the Victory Lap

Week 23 — Slang week (the fun one)

Main workB2 U22 (comparisons). B3 c18 (Delhi street talk — yaar, jugaaR, scene, vellaa…).
Vocabulary & cardsStart D15 (slang — mind the register notes; in-law-safe subset only at family dinners).
Speak & listenB4 L21 (describing people). License granted: one yaar per conversation with partner. Ask them which five slang words THEY actually say.
You can nowCompare anything (Dilli sabse achchhee hai), banter a little, hear "kyaa scene hai" and answer it.

Week 24 — Getting things done, Delhi style

Main workB2 U23 (causatives & passive, light). B3 c20 (festivals & occasions — timed for whichever one's next on the calendar).
Vocabulary & cardsFestival greetings into the box the week before any real festival; they're single-use-per-year but high-value.
Speak & listenB4 L22 (jugaaR — the darzee/press-vaalaa economy). Field trip if possible: get one real thing silvaaoed/kaTvaaoed/banvaaoed.
You can nowGet things done through people (karvaanaa), wish anyone a proper festival, explain what pheras are at a wedding.

Week 25 — The finishing touches

Main workB2 U24 (hee/bhee/to/na, vaalaa, tag questions — the seasoning). B1 Ch. 7 full revisit: shadowing daily, one certified line per day this week.
Vocabulary & cardsBox maintenance week: everything below Box 3 gets a decision — drill it or retire it consciously.
Speak & listenB4 L23 (phone call home & gossip). Eavesdrop practice on a real family call: count the to's and hee's you now hear.
You can nowSound like yourself in Hindi — emphasis, warmth, teasing: main to Theek hoon, tum batao na!

Week 26 — Capstone · FINAL TEST

Main workB4 L24 (a full day in Delhi — the everything lesson). Final Test (t6/at6) closed book; the Devanagari letter in Section E is your diploma-in-disguise. Month-6 milestones (B1 Ch. 13) + the full can-do list in the trackers.
Vocabulary & cardsNone new. Victory lap through Box 5.
Speak & listenThe capstone performance: run L24's full day FOR REAL as far as life allows — chai, errands, market, a family call, an evening walk — narrating in Hindi throughout. Partner grades leniently and buys the jalebi.
You can nowHave the ten-minute conversation. Read the letter. Write the reply. Say the thing you couldn't say in January: अब मुझे हिन्दी आती है।

After Month 6 — keeping it alive

The course ends; the Hindi doesn't. The maintenance stack that works: (1) keep the 10-minute card habit but feed it only from real life — words you needed and lacked; (2) graduate your input — Bollywood with Hindi subtitles (not English), Hindi audio + your partner's running commentary, music with lyrics open; (3) upgrade the partner window from ten minutes to whole activities (cooking = Hindi, walks = Hindi); (4) book a Delhi trip milestone if you can — nothing consolidates six months of work like one week of sabzi mandis and family dinners; (5) for grammar beyond this course (contrafactuals, advanced causatives, literary registers), your classes and any standard intermediate text will slot cleanly on top of Units 1–24. And write the in-laws a Divaalee card in your own hand this year. That was always the real final exam.

chapters.book1-s01:
Chapter 1 Your Mouth, the Map: How Hindi Sound Works

Here is the best-kept secret of Hindi pronunciation: the alphabet is a map of your mouth. Devanagari isn't an arbitrary pile of letters the way A–Z is — it's a grid, organized by where your tongue is and what your breath is doing. Learn to feel five tongue positions and two breath switches, and all thirty-odd consonants snap into place like keys on a keyboard. That's why this book starts in your mouth, not on the page.

One promise before we start: you do not need a perfect accent. You need about six contrasts that Hindi ears rely on to tell words apart — miss those and kal (yesterday) becomes khal (villain), or a polite word becomes a rude one. Nail those six and every Delhi aunty will beam at you. Your partner is your secret weapon here: their ear is already perfectly tuned, and Chapter 13 gives you ready-made two-minute games to borrow it.

The map itself

Side view of the mouth, facing left. The numbered dots are the five "home bases" every Hindi consonant lives at — the same five rows you'll meet in the alphabet.

The five home bases (feel each one now)

Say each English word below slowly and notice where your tongue lands. You already own every position except one — Hindi just asks you to use them more precisely.

BaseWhereFeel it withHindi row (preview)
1Soft palate — back of tongue rises to the soft rear roofsay "go", "king" — feel the back hump upk kh g gh (क ख ग घ)
2Front dome — blade of tongue against the front of the hard palatesay "cheese", "jam"ch chh j jh (च छ ज झ)
3Curled back (RETROFLEX) — tip curls up and back; the underside of the tip taps the bumpy ridge behind the teeth. The one new position — Chapter 3 trains it.say "herd" and hold the r — many Americans curl the tip; now tap the roof from that curlT Th D Dh N (ट ठ ड ढ ण)
4Teeth (DENTAL) — tip pressed flat on the back of the upper teeth, farther forward than any English t/dsay "width" — the d slides to the teeth for the th; that forward contact is home base 4t th d dh n (त थ द ध न)
5Lipssay "me", "pie"p ph b bh m (प फ ब भ म)

The trap for English speakers sits between bases 3 and 4. Your everyday English t/d lives on the ridge — exactly halfway between Hindi's dental त and retroflex ट. Stay there and every t you say is a coin-flip to a Hindi ear. The fix is simple to state and takes two weeks of reps: push forward to the teeth for त, curl up and back for ट, and never park on the ridge again.

The genius of the grid

Now watch what the alphabet does with those five bases. Each base gets a row, and each row runs through the same four-step breath pattern, plus its nasal:

voicelessvoiceless + puffvoicedvoiced + breathynasal
1 soft palateक kaख khaग gaघ ghaङ nga
2 front domeच chaछ chhaज jaझ jhaञ nya
3 curled backट Taठ Thaड Daढ Dhaण Na
4 teethत taथ thaद daध dhaन na
5 lipsप paफ phaब baभ bhaम ma

Twenty-five consonants, one pattern. When a Hindi teacher says a letter is "the fourth letter of the ट row," they've told you everything: position 3, voiced, breathy. The leftover letters (य र ल व, the s-sounds, ह, and the Urdu guests ज़ फ़ क़) get their own tour in Chapters 5 and 8.

The two breath switches

Every row above is just one tongue position with two switches flipped on or off:

Switch 1 — Voice. Put two fingers on your throat and say ssss then zzzz. That buzz is voicing. क/ट/त/प are buzz-off; ग/ड/द/ब are buzz-on. English has this switch too, so it's free.

Switch 2 — The puff (aspiration). Hold your palm an inch from your lips. Say "pin" — you'll feel a little explosion of air. Say "spin" — almost none. English flips this switch automatically and never uses it to tell words apart. Hindi uses it to tell words apart constantly, which is why Chapter 4 exists. The h in kh, th, bh… is that puff, not a separate h-sound.

How to practice anything in this book

Use this loop for every new sound, five minutes at a time: (1) Position — read the "in your mouth" instruction, place your tongue silently, hold it, feel it. (2) Slow motion — produce the sound absurdly slowly three times; speed hides errors, slowness exposes them. (3) Contrast — say it against its neighbor (ta–Ta, ka–kha) ten times, exaggerating the difference. (4) Word — drop it into the example words. (5) Ear check — once or twice a week, run a Chapter 13 partner game; being heard correctly is the only score that counts. A phone voice memo is a fine substitute on solo days: record, wait an hour, listen cold.

Triage, Delhi edition: if your bandwidth is limited, spend it in this order — (1) dental vs. retroflex, (2) the puff, (3) vowel length (kam vs kaam), (4) nasal vowels. Delhiites will forgive a soft व or a flat र forever, but ट-vs-त confusions genuinely change words, and aspiration slips can turn innocent words rude. The good news: your partner's family will find a careful dental त more impressive than any amount of vocabulary.

Tonight's two-minute game: have your partner say these four pairs at random while you point — kal/khal · Taal/taal · dam/daam · haan/hah. Then swap roles and let them grade you. Log your score; you'll rerun this in Week 4 and feel like a different person.
chapters.book1-s02:
Chapter 2 The Vowels: Length, Purity & the Nose

Hindi vowels are easier than English vowels — there are fewer of them and they never do the sneaky reductions English loves. But they demand two disciplines English never taught you: length (short vs. long changes the word) and purity (no sliding). Add the nose (nasalization) and you have the whole system.

Discipline 1 — Length is meaning

In English, saying "beeeeach" long or short is just emphasis. In Hindi, length is vocabulary:

कम / काम  ·  दिन / दीन  ·  सुनना / सूना
kam / kaam · din / deen · sunnaa / soonaa [kum / kahm · din / deen · sun-nah / soo-nah]
less / work  ·  day / poor  ·  to listen / deserted

Rule of thumb: a long vowel takes roughly twice the time of a short one. When practicing, exaggerate — make the long ones luxurious. Native speakers never mis-hear an over-long आ, but an under-long one becomes a different word.

Discipline 2 — Freeze the vowel (no glides)

Say English "day" slowly: your mouth starts at "deh" and glides up to "ee" — that's a diphthong. Hindi ए is the starting position only, frozen. Same for ओ: English "go" ends in a little "oo" glide; Hindi ओ holds still. The trick: say the vowel and hold it for three seconds without letting anything move — jaw, lips, tongue all parked. If the sound stays identical from start to finish, it's pure.

The vowel map

Where each vowel lives: height = how high the tongue body sits, left–right = front vs. back, and the back column rounds the lips.

Vowel by vowel

LetterRoman · Say itHow to make itAnchor words
अa · uhTotal relaxation — the vowel of about. Jaw loose, tongue flat. Never the "a" of cat.अब ab [ub] now
आaa · ahDrop the jaw — doctor's "say ahh." Long; give it two beats.आप aap [ahp] you
इi · iShort and light, as in bit. Quick — don't let it grow into "ee."इधर idhar [i-dhur] over here
ईee · eeBig smile, tongue high and forward, held long.जी jee [jee] (respect word)
उu · uShort, as in put — never the "uh" of putt. Lips lightly rounded.सुन sun [sun] listen!
ऊoo · ooStrong lip-rounding, long — the "oo" of food with commitment.दूध doodh [doodh] milk
एe · ayMid-front, FROZEN — say minus the glide. Hold three seconds; nothing may move.एक ek [ayk] one
ऐai · ehIn Delhi: the vowel of bed, held long. Open the ए one notch. (Textbooks from other regions teach "uh-ee" — in Delhi you will simply never hear that.)है hai [heh] is
ओo · ohRounded, mid-back, FROZEN — go minus the glide.दो do [doh] two
औau · awIn Delhi: the vowel of law with round lips. Open the ओ one notch.और aur [awr] and
ऋri · riHistorically a vocalic r; in modern Hindi just say "ri." Rare, Sanskrit-flavored words.ऋषि rishi [ri-shi] sage
ऑo · awThe "office vowel" — invented for English loans; hot/office à l'américaine.ऑफ़िस ofis [aw-fis] office

The two vowels Americans mangle most: अ (they say the "a" of cat — keep it a lazy uh) and ए (they add the glide — freeze it). Test yourself on बेटा beTaa [bay-Tah] "son": both vowels pure, no "bay-tuh," no glide.

The nose: nasalized vowels

Any Hindi vowel can also be said through the nose. In script it's the moon-dot ँ (candrabindu) or, when there's no room above, just the dot ं. In our system it's (n) — and here is the crucial part: your tongue touches nothing. It is not "an," not "ahn," there is no n-contact at the end. The velum (that soft palate from Chapter 1) simply drops and lets half the air exit through your nose while the vowel plays.

How to find it: say a long "ahhhh." Now, without stopping, think about humming — you'll feel a soft switch flip at the back and the sound turn slightly brassy. That's the velum opening. Pinch your nose shut: a plain आ sounds identical pinched or free, but a nasal आँ goes muffled and weird the instant you pinch. That's your self-test.

हाँ  ·  कहाँ  ·  मैं हूँ  ·  सास / साँस
haan · kahaan · main hoon · saas / saans [hah(n) · kuh-hah(n) · meh(n) hoo(n) · sahs / sah(n)s]
yes · where · I am · mother-in-law / breath

That last pair is the classic: सास is your mother-in-law and साँस is breath — "meree saans" vs "meree saas" is a whole different sentence at a family dinner. Delhi humor being what it is, someone will absolutely make this joke at you. Nasalize with confidence and make it first.

Drill 1: partner says haan / haa(no nasal), saas / saans, kahaa / kahaan in random order; you call "nose!" or "no nose!" Drill 2: you say them; partner grades. Drill 3 (length): kam/kaam, din/deen, pul/pool — same game. Two minutes each.
chapters.book1-s03:
Chapter 3 Dental vs. Retroflex: The Big One

If this book could teach you only one thing, it would be this chapter. Hindi has two complete families of t/d/n sounds, and English speakers arrive owning neither — your English t/d sits on the ridge exactly between them. Here are the three positions, side by side:

Hindi dental: the tip presses the back of the upper front teeth — so far forward you almost bite it.
Your English habit: tip on the alveolar ridge — between the two Hindi families. Retire this position.
Hindi retroflex: the tip curls up and back; the underside of the tip taps the bumpy ridge.

Building the dental त द न (base 4)

Step 1. Find the spot: run your tongue tip down the roof of your mouth until it slides off the ridge and lands on the backs of your upper front teeth. Press gently — that's home. Step 2. Seal and release: with the tip pressed there, build a little air pressure and release a clean, crisp t. It should feel lighter and "thinner" than an English t, almost like the t in Spanish taco or the way "th" positions in width. Step 3. Voice it for द, add the nose for न (tip stays glued to the teeth).

Cheat code: put the very edge of the tongue tip between your teeth, like a lazy "th," and say t. Now retract it just behind the teeth. That exaggerated-forward feeling is correct — if it feels too far forward, it's probably right. Dental words to loop: तुम tum [tum], दिन din [din], नमस्ते namaste [nuh-muhs-tay], दाल daal [dahl], तीन teen [teen].

Building the retroflex ट ड ण (base 3)

Step 1. Curl: say American "er" and hold it — feel how the tip lifts and curls back without touching anything. That's the launch position. Step 2. Contact: from that curl, raise the tip until the underside touches the roof just behind the ridge. It's a small motion — you're tapping with the bottom of the tip, fingernail-side up, not the top. Step 3. Pop: build pressure and release. The sound is darker, rounder, more "hollow" than dental त — Indians describe ट as a heavy sound and त as a soft one. Voice it for ड; ण is its nasal (rare alone, automatic in words like बाण).

Cheat code: Americans already say near-retroflex D's around r's. Say "harder" fast — the d after the r comes out curled. Or borrow from Indian-accent English you've heard: the way "time" and "doctor" sound in an Indian accent (Taim, DaakTar) is literally these letters — that accent exists because Hindi ears map English t/d to retroflex. Imitate it shamelessly: टाइम Taim [Tah-im], डॉक्टर DokTar [Dawk-Tur]. Retroflex words to loop: टमाटर TamaaTar [Tuh-mah-Tur], बेटा beTaa [bay-Tah], ठीक Theek [Theek], डर Dar [Dur].

The alternation ladder (do this daily, week 1–4)

Slowly, exaggerating the tongue travel — feel it swing from teeth to curl:

ta – Ta – ta – Ta – ta – Ta  ·  da – Da – da – Da  ·  ata – aTa – ada – aDa  ·  too – Too – doo – Doo

Then words in contrast pairs — read each pair aloud three times:

Dental (teeth)Say itRetroflex (curl)Say it
दाल daal — lentilsdahlडाल Daal — branchDahl
तन tan — bodytunटन Tan — tonTun
तोता totaa — parrottoh-tahटोटा* ToTaa — shortage (colloq.)Toh-Tah
दो do — twodohडो‑ in डोसा Dosaa — dosaDoh-sah
नाता naataa — bond, relationnah-tahनाटा naaTaa — short (person)nah-Tah

*Chapter 12 has the full minimal-pair training sets; this is just your daily warm-up.

The most common failure isn't picking the wrong family — it's drifting back to the English ridge when speaking fast, which makes every t/d ambiguous. Slow sentences down for the first month. And one high-stakes example to motivate you: at dinner, दाल daal gets you lentils; डाल Daal gets you a tree branch. The kitchen will provide daily practice.

Reassurance from the streets of Delhi: nobody expects perfection in week 2. But Delhiites do instinctively rate the dental त as the mark of someone who's really learning Hindi (it's the sound English speakers "can't" make). The first time you produce a clean namaste with a true dental t, someone in your partner's family will visibly light up. That's the whole game.

The pointing game, level 2: write त and ट big on two pieces of paper. Partner says single syllables (ta Ta da Da tee Tee…) at random; you point. Ten in a row right = they flip the table and you say, they point. Track your streak in the Master Plan tracker.
chapters.book1-s04:
Chapter 4 Aspiration: The Puff That Changes Words

Hold your palm one inch from your lips and say "pin." Feel that little explosion? Now say "spin." Almost nothing. English makes both kinds of p automatically and treats them as the same letter. Hindi treats them as different letters that make different words — and it does this at every single tongue position. That's the fourth column of the grid from Chapter 1, and it's why फ exists next to प and ख next to क.

पल / फल  ·  कल / खल  ·  चल / छल
pal / phal · kal / khal · chal / chhal [pul / phul · kul / khul · chul / chhul]
moment / fruit  ·  yesterday / villain  ·  walk! / deceit

The palm test (your permanent referee)

Every aspirated letter — kh, chh, Th, th, ph — should blow out a birthday-candle flame an inch away. Every plain letter — k, ch, T, t, p — should barely flutter it. A strip of paper held in front of your lips works too: aspirated = paper jumps; plain = paper twitches. Calibrate daily for two weeks; after that your mouth knows.

Harvesting what English gave you

You already own both sounds — English just hides them by position. Use these harvests:

Plain (no puff)the p/t/k after s: spin, stop, skip. Say "spin," then say it again without the s — that naked, puff-less "pin" is Hindi प. Same trick: "stop" → त-ish, "skip" → क.
Aspirated (puff)word-initial English p/t/k: pie, tie, kite — those are naturally puffed. Hindi फ/थ/ख just asks for MORE: puff like you're fogging a mirror.

So the discipline is two-directional: train your plain letters DOWN (Americans over-puff everything at the start of words) and train your aspirates UP (make the puff theatrical; native speakers' puffs are genuinely strong).

The four-way switchboard, one row at a time

Work each row slowly with the palm test — this is the complete breath system of Hindi:

Row1 plain2 + puff3 voiced4 voiced + breathy
soft palateक ka [kuh]ख kha [khuh]ग ga [guh]घ gha [ghuh]
front domeच chaछ chhaज jaझ jha
curled backट Taठ Thaड Daढ Dha
teethत taथ thaद daध dha
lipsप paफ phaब baभ bha

Daily ladder (30 seconds, any row): ka – kha – ga – gha, four beats, palm up. The goal is four clearly different sounds from one tongue position.

Column 4 — the breathy voiced sounds (the honest hard part)

घ झ ढ ध भ are the one genuinely new skill in this chapter: voice and breath at the same time. A plain English g stops the breath; an h has no voice. These want both — a g said while sighing.

Technique 1 — the sighing hum. Hum a lazy "uhhh" and, mid-hum, exhale extra air without stopping the voice — you'll hear a breathy, Marilyn-Monroe texture. Keep that texture running and say baa → it becomes bhaa. The voice never stops; it just gets air-soaked.

Technique 2 — the compound-word bridge. Say these English pairs fast and smash the boundary: dog house → gh · club house → bh · mad hatter → dh · hedgehog → jh · hot head (with a curled t) → Dh-ish. Crude but effective launchers.

घर  ·  भाई  ·  धन्यवाद  ·  झूठ  ·  ढाई
ghar · bhaaee · dhanyavaad · jhooTh · Dhaaee [ghur · bhah-ee · dhun-yuh-vahd · jhooTh · Dhah-ee]
house · brother · thank you · a lie · two-and-a-half

Two classic errors. (1) Saying bh as "b-h" — two separate sounds, "ab-haee" — it's ONE sound, a breathy b: [bhah-ee]. (2) Substituting f for फ: फ (ph) is a puffed p — lips fully close and pop — while फ़ (f) is the English f. फल phal "fruit" with an f is a different (and in some regions unfortunate) word — pop the p.

Delhi reality check: the aspirated column is not optional street garnish — Theek hai [Theek heh], khaanaa, bhaaee, ghar, dhanyavaad are hour-one words and every one carries a puff or a breathy voice. The single most Delhi sentence you'll say all month — भैया, ठीक है! bhaiyaa, Theek hai! [bheh-yah Theek heh] — is an aspiration exam all by itself.

Candle night: light a candle, take turns saying kal/khal, pal/phal, taalee/thaalee, Deck? no — Dol/Dhol… any pair from Chapter 12's Set 2, watching the flame. The flame is an incorruptible judge and this is legitimately fun. Partner grades your column-4 breathiness on ghar, bhaaee, dhoop — ask them to demonstrate first and put your palm in front of their mouth to feel the target.
chapters.book1-s05:
Chapter 5 The Tricky Customers

Beyond the grid live a handful of sounds that each need one honest paragraph of attention. None is as important as Chapters 3–4, but each has a trap.

व — the v/w blend

Hindi व is between English v and w: round your lips like w, let the upper teeth barely graze the lower lip, and keep the friction gentle. A hard English v (teeth digging in, motorboat buzz) sounds foreign; a pure w is closer than a hard v. Honestly, anywhere in the middle is fine — Hindi has no v/w contrast, so nothing can go wrong meaning-wise. वह voh [voh], दरवाज़ा darvaazaa [dur-vah-zah], स्वागत svaagat [svah-gut].

र — the tapped r

Hindi र is a single tap: the tongue tip flicks the ridge once, like the tt in American "butter" said fast. It is never the growly American r of "car" (tongue bunched, no contact). Say "butter" → "budder" → feel that quick d-ish flick — that's र. A short Spanish-style trill is also fine and common. रात raat [raht], करना karnaa [kur-nah], अरे arre [uh-ray].

ड़ / ढ़ — the retroflex flap (the coolest sound you'll learn)

Here's the secret: you already make this sound in English. The dd in "ladder" is a flap — the tongue slaps through the ridge without stopping. Hindi ड़ is that exact slap, but starting from the Chapter-3 curl: curl the tip up and back like for ड, then instead of holding contact, fling the tip forward so its underside strikes the ridge on the way past. One clean slap, no stop.

The flap: curl like ड, then fling forward — the underside of the tip strikes the ridge in passing. "Ladder" with a curl.

ड़ never starts a word — it lives in the middles and ends: लड़का laRkaa [luhR-kah] boy, थोड़ा thoRaa [thoh-Rah] a little, सड़क saRak [suh-Ruk] road, पढ़ना paRhnaa [puRh-nah] to read/study (ढ़ = the same flap with breathy release), बड़ा baRaa [buh-Rah] big.

Don't substitute a plain र: laRkaa with a plain r (larkaa) is instantly noticeable, and पड़ना paRnaa (to fall) vs पढ़ना paRhnaa (to study) vs परना? — well, only two of those are words, but your partner "fell a book" jokes write themselves. Curl, then slap.

फ़ vs फ, ज़ vs ज — the Urdu guests

Delhi Hindi is saturated with Persian/Urdu vocabulary, which brought two sounds English already has: f (फ़ — फ़िल्म film, फ़ोन fon, फ़र्क़ farq "difference") and z (ज़: ज़रूर zaroor [zuh-roor] "definitely", ज़्यादा zyaadaa, मज़ा mazaa). The trap runs the other direction: don't let English habits turn every ज into z or every फ into f. जाना is jaanaa with a true j; फल is phal with a popped, puffed p. The dot under the letter (नुक़्ता) is the signal — and yes, Delhiites really do say z and f clearly, even when they drop the other nukta sounds (क़ ख़ ग़ relax toward plain k/kh/g in most mouths, and no one will mind if yours do too).

श / ष / स — the s-family

Two working sounds: sh (श — and ष, which in modern Hindi is pronounced identically; it survives in spelling only) and s (स). English owns both. The only job is reading them correctly: शादी shaadee wedding, साल saal year, शहर shehar [sheh-hur] city, भाषा bhaashaa language.

ह — and the vanishing h

ह at the start of words is a normal English h: हाँ haan. Between vowels, Delhi speech makes it feather-light or drops it entirely, bending the vowels around it: कहना is [keh-nah] not "ka-ha-na", बहुत is [bo-hut], शहर is [sheh-hur], कहाँ often floats out as [kuh-hah(n)] → [k'hah(n)]. Don't fight it — this is why our phonetic line sometimes disagrees with the spelling; trust the phonetic line, it's transcribing Delhi.

Doubled consonants — park and hold

When a consonant doubles (दिल्ली, अच्छा, बच्चा), you don't say it twice — you touch, hold one beat, then release once. English does this across word boundaries: "bookcase" (one long k-hold), "pen-knife". Practice: पता pataa [puh-tah] "address" vs पत्ता pattaa [put-tah] "leaf" — in the second, your tongue parks on the t through a full silent beat. दिल्ली [dil-lee]: lean on that l. It's the difference between a city and a mispronunciation.

ङ ञ — the automatic nasals

These two never stand alone in real words — they're the nasal shadows that appear before their row's consonants: the n in रंग rang (an "ng"), the n in पंजाब panjaab (an "ny-ish n"). English does exactly the same thing automatically (compare the n's in ink vs input). Read the dot, let your tongue copy the following consonant's position, done. Never force a hard "g" into rang.

ल — always the light l

English has two l's: the light l of "leaf" (tip forward) and the dark, swallowed l of "full" (back bunched). Hindi only uses the light one, tip on the teeth like a dental — even at word ends: दाल daal ends bright, not swallowed: [dahl], tip touching teeth on the final l. दिल dil [dil] heart — light l, and now you can pronounce both halves of दिलवाले।

This chapter's partner game is "loanword karaoke": have your partner say ten English-origin words the Delhi way (fon, Taim, DaakTar, skool, glaas, boTal, kampyooTar, peTrol, sTeshan, hoTal) and copy their version exactly — curls, vowels and all. It feels like doing an impression; it is, and it's the fastest accent training that exists.
chapters.book1-s06:
Chapter 6 The Invisible Vowel: Schwa & the Vanishing Act

Every Devanagari consonant letter carries a free vowel inside it: क isn't "k," it's "ka" [kuh]. That built-in uh is called the schwa, and it explains why the script needs no letter between क and म in कम. So far so good. The plot twist is that spoken Hindi deletes many of these built-in vowels — and the spelling never tells you. This chapter is the decoder.

Rule 1 — Word-final schwa is silent. Always.

Written राम is raam, not "raama." दिन is din. बात is baat. If you've heard Sanskrit chanting ("raamaayaNa"), that final -a is exactly what Hindi dropped a few centuries ago. This rule has essentially no exceptions in ordinary words — never voice a final consonant's schwa.

Rule 2 — The middle schwa drops in the __a__ sandwich

When a word runs consonant-a-consonant-a-consonant + vowel, the second schwa quietly disappears:

Spelled (letter by letter)Actually saidWord
कमरा = ka-ma-raakum-rahkamraa — room
नमकीन = na-ma-keennum-keennamkeen — savory snacks
सड़क पर = sa-Ra-k + parsuh-Ruk purfinal schwa silent (Rule 1)
करना = ka-ra-naakur-nahkarnaa — to do
आदमी = aa-da-meeahd-meeaadmee — man
जानवर = jaa-na-varjahn-vurjaanvar — animal

Contrast the same letters when the sandwich doesn't form: नमक "salt" keeps its middle vowel — [nuh-muk] — because dropping it would leave an unsayable word-final cluster (namk). Add a suffix and watch it flip: नमक [nuh-muk] → नमकीन [num-keen]. समझ samajh [suh-mujh] → समझा samjhaa [sum-jhah]. Same letters, dancing schwa.

You do not need to compute this in real time. Two safety nets: (1) every word in this course comes with its phonetic line, schwa-deletion already applied; (2) our Roman spelling also applies it (karnaa, never "karanaa"). After a month of reading pairs of lines, your mouth will generalize the pattern without being told — this chapter just makes the magic visible so the spelling never spooks you.

Why this matters for sounding Delhi

Textbook-taught foreigners are instantly recognizable by their fully-voiced schwas: "sa-ma-jha-naa" for samajhnaa [suh-mujh-nah], "ka-ha-naa" for kehnaa [keh-nah]. Deleting on schedule is half of what makes speech sound native-paced — it's free speed, since you're literally saying less.

The अह special: schwa + h = "eh"

When a schwa sits next to ह, Delhi fuses them into an eh: कहना kehnaa [keh-nah], रहना rehnaa [reh-nah], शहर shehar [sheh-hur], बहन behen [beh-hen]. And the superstar irregular: बहुत "very" comes out [bo-hut] in Delhi mouths. Learn these as sounds, not spellings.

Read-aloud practice

Say each, deleting on schedule (answers in the phonetic line — cover it first):

chapters.book1-s07:
Chapter 7 Rhythm, Melody & Sounding Delhi

Individual sounds are the letters of an accent; rhythm and melody are its handwriting. This chapter is short on rules and long on ear-training instructions, because prosody is caught more than taught — and you live with a native tuning fork.

Even syllables, gentle stress

English crushes unstressed syllables ("photography" = phuh-TOG-ruh-fee). Hindi doesn't. Syllables march out evenly, and "stress" is just a mild lean onto heavy syllables — the ones with long vowels (आ ई ऊ ए ऐ ओ औ) or a doubled consonant. Practice by giving every syllable its full face: dhanyavaad is [dhun-yuh-vahd] with three honest syllables, not "DHUN-yvad." When in doubt, flatten your stress rather than exaggerate it — flat sounds more Hindi than punchy.

The melody of questions

Yes/no questions ride a rising tail, exactly like English: चाय पियोगे? chaay piyoge? [chah-ay pi-yoh-gay ↗]. Question-word questions (kyaa/kab/kahaan…) fall at the end like statements: तुम कहाँ हो? [tum kuh-hah(n) hoh ↘]. The one special melody to steal: the drawn-out Delhi achchhaaaa? [uh-chhaaah ↗] — "ohhh really?" — which does about nine jobs of conversational duty.

Phrases move as blocks

Hindi glues words into little prosodic packets — a noun and its postposition are one breath-unit (dillee-mein, ghar-par), a verb and its auxiliary another (jaa-rahaa-hoon). Pause between packets, never inside them. This is why native speech sounds fast: it isn't more sounds per second, it's fewer pauses in the wrong places.

The Delhi sound, itemized

ऐ = eh, औ = awहै [heh], पैसा [peh-sah], औरत [aw-rut] — never "uh-ee"/"uh-oo." This alone moves you 500 km toward Delhi.
वो and येSpoken Delhi says voh and yeh/ye for वह/यह/वे — the spelling-pronunciations "vah/yah" mark a newsreader, not a neighbor.
बहुत = bohot[bo-hut], often just [boht] at speed. "It's bahut good yaar" is a real Delhi sentence.
Light hBetween vowels h thins out: kahaan → [kuh-hah(n)] with barely a breath on the h.
English everywhereNumbers, days, tech, feelings — Delhi swaps freely: "Friday ko movie chalein?" Don't fight it; matching the mix is part of the dialect.
Softeners on repeatjee for respect, na for warmth (chalo na), yaar for friendship, arre to launch a sentence. Delhi conversation is upholstered with these.

What you'll actually hear at family speed: whole auxiliary verbs melting (kyaa kar rahe ho → [kyah kur-ray oh]), naheen shrinking to [nee/nuh-ee(n)], and everything stitched with matlab… bas… achchhaa… Don't panic and don't imitate the melting yet — comprehension first, compression later. Your clear-but-evenly-paced Hindi is exactly right for year one.

Your listening gym (10 minutes/day, no textbook)

Shadowing: take any 15-second clip of Delhi speech (your partner voice-noting a WhatsApp message counts, and is the ideal source), play one sentence, pause, and repeat it with the melody, even if you don't know all the words yet. You're photocopying music, not translating. Three sentences a day beats thirty minutes of passive listening. Eavesdrop practice: when your partner is on the phone with family, try to catch just the melody — where do sentences rise? where do they land? Which little words repeat? The weekly line: each week, pick one line from Book 4's dialogue and get it to "indistinguishable" — partner-certified. Twenty-six perfect lines in six months is a real accent.

Melody game: partner says the same sentence three ways — statement, yes/no question, surprised exclamation (tum aa rahe ho. / tum aa rahe ho? / tum aa rahe ho?!) — in random order; you name which. Then you perform, they guess. If they laugh, that's data too.
chapters.book1-s08:
Chapter 8 The Complete Alphabet, Letter by Letter

This is your reference chapter: every letter of Devanagari, one entry each, in dictionary order. Each entry gives the letter, its Roman spelling, its "Say it" respelling, its IPA value, what it sounds like, what your mouth is doing, and three real words to practice on. You met the mouth mechanics in earlier chapters — here everything sits in one place so you can look any letter up in two seconds. Read it straight through once, then return whenever a letter wobbles.

Reminder of the two standing rules from the articulation chapters: CAPITAL T D N R in Roman = retroflex (tongue tip curled back; the underside taps the bumpy ridge behind the teeth) and lowercase t d n = dental (tongue tip on the back of the upper teeth). An attached h (kh, th, bh…) = aspiration, a strong puff of air.

The Vowels (स्वर svar [svur])

Vowels are the open, unobstructed sounds — the mouth shapes them with jaw, tongue height, and lips, but nothing blocks the air. Hindi vowels come in short/long pairs and every one is pure: no gliding off the end the way English "say" drifts into a y. Hold the shape steady from start to finish.

अ a · uh · IPA /ə/
Sound: like u in "but" — short, relaxed, central.
In your mouth: jaw slightly open, tongue resting flat in the middle, lips neutral; this is the "default" vowel hiding inside every bare consonant.
Words: अब ab [ub] now · अगर agar [uh-gur] if · अच्छा achchhaa [uch-chhah] good
आ aa · ah · IPA /ɑː/
Sound: like a in "father" — long and open. The doctor's "aah".
In your mouth: jaw drops wide, tongue low and flat, lips relaxed; hold it about twice as long as अ.
Words: आप aap [ahp] you (polite) · आज aaj [ahj] today · आम aam (m) [ahm] mango
इ i · i · IPA /ɪ/
Sound: like i in "bit" — short and light.
In your mouth: tongue high and forward, jaw nearly closed, lips spread just a little; clip it short.
Words: इधर idhar [i-dhur] over here · इतना itnaa [it-nah] this much · इमली imlee (f) [im-lee] tamarind
ई ee · ee · IPA /iː/
Sound: like ee in "feet" — the long partner of इ.
In your mouth: same high-front tongue as इ, lips spread wider, and you hold it; length is the whole difference.
Words: ईद eed (f) [eed] Eid · ईंट eenT (f) [ee(n)T] brick · ईमानदार eemaandaar [ee-mahn-dahr] honest
उ u · u · IPA /ʊ/
Sound: like u in "put" — short, never like the u in "cut".
In your mouth: tongue high and pulled back, lips rounded loosely; quick and light.
Words: उधर udhar [u-dhur] over there · उठना uThnaa [uTh-nah] to get up · उम्मीद ummeed (f) [um-meed] hope
ऊ oo · oo · IPA /uː/
Sound: like oo in "boot" — the long partner of उ.
In your mouth: same high-back tongue as उ, lips rounded tighter, held long.
Words: ऊपर oopar [oo-pur] up, above · ऊन oon (f) [oon] wool · ऊँट oonT (m) [oo(n)T] camel
ऋ ri · ri · IPA /rɪ/
Sound: an old Sanskrit vowel; in modern Hindi simply "ri" as in "rip". Rare — you'll meet it in a handful of Sanskrit loanwords.
In your mouth: a quick tap of the tongue tip plus a short i.
Words: ऋतु ritu (f) [ri-tu] season · ऋषि rishi (m) [ri-shi] sage
ए e · ay · IPA /eː/
Sound: like ay in "say" — but PURE: freeze the first half of the English sound and never let it glide into a y.
In your mouth: tongue mid-high and forward, lips slightly spread, jaw steady from start to finish.
Words: एक ek [ayk] one · एकदम ekdam [ayk-dum] absolutely · एड़ी eRee (f) [ay-Ree] heel
ऐ ai · eh · IPA /ɛː/
Sound: in Delhi, "eh as in bed" — a long open e. (Books that tell you "ai as in aisle" are describing another century.)
In your mouth: tongue mid-low and forward, jaw a touch more open than ए; hold it steady.
Words: ऐसा aisaa [eh-sah] like this · ऐनक ainak (f) [eh-nuk] eyeglasses · है hai [heh] is (the matra form you'll see constantly)
ओ o · oh · IPA /oː/
Sound: like o in "go" — but PURE, with no drift toward w at the end.
In your mouth: tongue mid-high and back, lips rounded and held still; one clean long vowel.
Words: ओर or (f) [ohr] side, direction · ओस os (f) [ohs] dew · ओला olaa (m) [oh-lah] hailstone
औ au · aw · IPA /ɔː/
Sound: in Delhi, like aw in "law" — a long open o. Not "ow" as in "cow".
In your mouth: tongue mid-low and back, lips lightly rounded, jaw more open than ओ.
Words: और aur [awr] and · औरत aurat (f) [aw-rut] woman · औज़ार auzaar (m) [aw-zahr] tool
अं an · u(n) · IPA /əŋ ~ ə̃/
Sound: not a vowel of its own — the dot (anusvar) is the nasal placeholder: it nasalizes the vowel or stands in for an n/m-type sound before a consonant. Full story in Chapter 9.
Words: अंदर andar [un-dur] inside · अंडा anDaa (m) [un-Dah] egg · अंगूर angoor (m) [un-goor] grape
अः ah · uh-h · IPA /əh/
Sound: the visarg — a rare breathy echo of the vowel, kept alive in a few Sanskrit words and prayers; in everyday speech it's usually silent.
Words: दुःख dukh (m) [dukh] sorrow (the ः is silent here in normal speech) · नमः namah [nuh-muh-h] salutation (in prayers)

The Velar Row: क ख ग घ ङ (back of the tongue)

All five velars are made at the same spot: the back of the tongue rises to touch the soft palate — exactly where English k and g live. What changes across the row is only voice and breath: voiceless plain, voiceless with the puff, voiced plain, voiced with the sigh, and the nasal. Keep your palm up in front of your mouth for the whole row.

क ka · kuh · IPA /kə/
Sound: like k in "skip" — NO puff of air.
In your mouth: back of the tongue rises to touch the soft palate; release cleanly with zero breath.
Words: कल kal [kul] yesterday/tomorrow · कमरा kamraa (m) [kum-rah] room · किताब kitaab (f) [ki-tahb] book
ख kha · khuh · IPA /kʰə/
Sound: like k in "kit", exaggerated — with a strong puff of air (palm test!).
In your mouth: same tongue position as क, add the puff; the palm should feel a clear burst.
Words: खाना khaanaa (m) [khah-nah] food; to eat · खिड़की khiRkee (f) [khiR-kee] window · खुश khush [khush] happy
ग ga · guh · IPA /ɡə/
Sound: like g in "go" — voiced, no puff of air.
In your mouth: same spot as क but the vocal cords hum from the start; release clean.
Words: गाना gaanaa (m) [gah-nah] song; to sing · गाड़ी gaaRee (f) [gah-Ree] car, vehicle · गली galee (f) [guh-lee] lane
घ gha · ghuh · IPA /ɡʱə/
Sound: a g that comes out voiced with breathy, sighing release — "g-huh" said as one sound.
In your mouth: same tongue position as ग; keep the voice humming while breath floods out on the release.
Words: घर ghar (m) [ghur] house, home · घड़ी ghaRee (f) [ghuh-Ree] watch, clock · घंटा ghanTaa (m) [ghun-Tah] hour; bell
ङ nga · ng · IPA /ŋ/
Sound: the ng of "sing". It never stands alone in a Hindi word — you'll only ever meet it hiding inside words as the n before a k or g sound, almost always written with the anusvar dot, as in अंक.
Words: अंक ank (m) [unk] digit, mark · पंखा pankhaa (m) [pun-khah] fan

The Palatal Row: च छ ज झ ञ (middle of the tongue)

These five are made where English ch and j live: the middle of the tongue presses up against the hard palate just behind the ridge, and the release gives that ch/j quality. Hindi's versions are a little flatter and tighter than English — no lip rounding, no drawl. Same drill as the velars: plain, puff, voiced, sigh, nasal.

च cha · chuh · IPA /tʃə/
Sound: like ch in "cheese" but tighter — no puff of air (English ch leaks a small puff; pinch it off).
In your mouth: middle of the tongue flat against the hard palate; release cleanly with zero breath.
Words: चाय chaay (f) [chah-ay] tea · चलो chalo [chuh-loh] let's go · चम्मच chammach (m) [chum-much] spoon
छ chha · chhuh · IPA /tʃʰə/
Sound: a ch with a strong puff of air (palm test!).
In your mouth: same tongue position as च, add the puff — a real burst, bigger than any English ch.
Words: छत chhat (f) [chhut] roof · छोटा chhoTaa [chhoh-Tah] small · छुट्टी chhuTTee (f) [chhuT-Tee] holiday, day off
ज ja · juh · IPA /dʒə/
Sound: like j in "jug" — voiced, no puff of air.
In your mouth: same spot as च with the vocal cords humming.
Words: जाना jaanaa [jah-nah] to go · जेब jeb (f) [jayb] pocket · जल्दी jaldee (f) [jul-dee] hurry; quickly
झ jha · jhuh · IPA /dʒʱə/
Sound: a j that is voiced with breathy, sighing release — "j-huh" as one sound.
In your mouth: same tongue position as ज; keep the hum going and let breath pour out as you release.
Words: झूठ jhooTh (m) [jhooTh] lie · झील jheel (f) [jheel] lake · झगड़ा jhagRaa (m) [jhug-Rah] quarrel
ञ nya · ny · IPA /ɲ/
Sound: the ny of "canyon". Like ङ, it never stands alone in modern Hindi — it lives only as the nasal before ch/j sounds, normally written with the anusvar dot.
Words: पंजाब panjaab (m) [pun-jahb] Punjab · चंचल chanchal [chun-chul] restless, playful

The Retroflex Row: ट ठ ड ढ ण + the Flaps ड़ ढ़ (tongue curled back)

Now the sounds that make Hindi sound like Hindi. For all of these the tongue tip is curled back; the underside taps the bumpy ridge behind the teeth. English t and d sit close to this territory, which is exactly why Indians hear an American t as ट — your job is to make the curl deliberate here and keep it OUT of the dental row that follows. The two dotted letters ड़ ढ़ are flaps: the curled tongue doesn't hold its contact but flicks forward, striking the ridge on the way.

ट Ta · Tuh · IPA /ʈə/
Sound: close to the t in "stop", but darker and harder — no puff of air.
In your mouth: tongue tip curled back; the underside taps the bumpy ridge behind the teeth; release with zero breath.
Words: टमाटर TamaaTar (m) [Tuh-mah-Tur] tomato · टोपी Topee (f) [Toh-pee] cap · टाइम Taim (m) [Tah-im] time (the everyday loanword)
ठ Tha · Thuh · IPA /ʈʰə/
Sound: the curled T with a strong puff of air (palm test!). Never the th of "think" — English th does not exist in Hindi.
In your mouth: same tongue position as ट, add the puff.
Words: ठीक Theek [Theek] fine, okay · ठंड ThanD (f) [ThunD] cold (weather) · ठग Thag (m) [Thug] con man (yes — English "thug" is this word)
ड Da · Duh · IPA /ɖə/
Sound: close to the d in "dog" but darker — voiced, no puff of air.
In your mouth: tongue tip curled back; the underside taps the bumpy ridge behind the teeth; vocal cords humming.
Words: डर Dar (m) [Dur] fear · डाल Daal (f) [Dahl] branch · डिब्बा Dibbaa (m) [Dib-bah] box, container
ढ Dha · Dhuh · IPA /ɖʱə/
Sound: the curled D, voiced with breathy, sighing release.
In your mouth: same tongue position as ड; hum plus a flood of breath on release.
Words: ढाई Dhaaee [Dhah-ee] two and a half · ढक्कन Dhakkan (m) [Dhuk-kun] lid · ढाबा Dhaabaa (m) [Dhah-bah] roadside eatery
ण Na · Nuh · IPA /ɳə/
Sound: an n said with the retroflex curl. It appears mostly in Sanskrit loanwords; many Delhi speakers relax it toward a plain n, and no one will blink if you do too.
In your mouth: tongue tip curled back; the underside taps the bumpy ridge behind the teeth while air flows through the nose.
Words: कारण kaaraN (m) [kah-ruN] reason · प्रणाम praNaam (m) [pruh-Nahm] respectful greeting · गुण guN (m) [guN] quality, virtue
ड़ Ra · Ruh · IPA /ɽə/
Sound: the famous retroflex flap — a d and an r colliding. Never starts a word.
In your mouth: tongue curls back as for ड, then FLICKS forward, striking the ridge on the way — one fast brush, no holding.
Words: लड़का laRkaa (m) [luhR-kah] boy · सड़क saRak (f) [suh-Ruk] road · थोड़ा thoRaa [thoh-Rah] a little
ढ़ Rha · Rhuh · IPA /ɽʱə/
Sound: the same flap as ड़, voiced with breathy, sighing release. Also never starts a word.
In your mouth: tongue curls back then FLICKS forward, striking on the way — with a sigh of breath riding the flick.
Words: पढ़ना paRhnaa [puRh-nah] to read, to study · बढ़िया baRhiyaa [buh-Rhi-yah] excellent, first-rate · सीढ़ी seeRhee (f) [see-Rhee] staircase, ladder

The Dental Row: त थ द ध न (tongue on the teeth)

Here the tongue tip is pressed against the back of the upper teeth, like a Spanish or French t — noticeably farther forward than any English t or d. This row is the mirror-image trap of the retroflex row: an English speaker's automatic t/d lands in the middle and gets heard as retroflex, so for these five you must consciously touch the teeth. Feel actual tooth enamel on every one.

त ta · tuh · IPA /t̪ə/
Sound: like the t of Spanish "taco" — flat, forward, no puff of air.
In your mouth: tongue tip on the back of the upper teeth; release cleanly with zero breath.
Words: तीन teen [teen] three · तुम tum [tum] you (informal) · तारा taaraa (m) [tah-rah] star
थ tha · thuh · IPA /t̪ʰə/
Sound: the dental t with a strong puff of air (palm test!). NOT the th of "think" — the tongue touches the back of the teeth, it never pokes between them.
In your mouth: same tongue position as त, add the puff.
Words: थाली thaalee (f) [thah-lee] platter, thali · थकान thakaan (f) [thuh-kahn] tiredness · हाथ haath (m) [hahth] hand
द da · duh · IPA /d̪ə/
Sound: like the d of Spanish "dos" — voiced, forward, no puff of air.
In your mouth: tongue tip on the back of the upper teeth; vocal cords humming.
Words: दिन din (m) [din] day · दाल daal (f) [dahl] lentils · दरवाज़ा darvaazaa (m) [dur-vah-zah] door
ध dha · dhuh · IPA /d̪ʱə/
Sound: the dental d, voiced with breathy, sighing release.
In your mouth: same tongue position as द; keep the hum and let the breath sigh out on release.
Words: धन्यवाद dhanyavaad (m) [dhun-yuh-vahd] thank you (formal) · धूप dhoop (f) [dhoop] sunshine · दूध doodh (m) [doodh] milk
न na · nuh · IPA /n̪ə/
Sound: an n said forward — slightly "brighter" than English n.
In your mouth: tongue tip on the back of the upper teeth while air flows through the nose.
Words: नमस्ते namaste [nuh-muhs-tay] hello, namaste · नाम naam (m) [nahm] name · नया nayaa [nuh-yah] new

The Labial Row: प फ ब भ म (both lips)

Easiest row in the book: both lips press together and release, exactly like English p, b, m. The only work is the breath discipline — keeping प bone-dry, giving फ a real burst, and letting भ sigh. Palm up again.

प pa · puh · IPA /pə/
Sound: like p in "spin" — no puff of air.
In your mouth: lips together, release cleanly with zero breath; the palm feels nothing.
Words: पानी paanee (m) [pah-nee] water · पल pal (m) [pul] moment · पैसा paisaa (m) [peh-sah] money; paisa
फ pha · phuh · IPA /pʰə/
Sound: a p with a strong puff of air (palm test!). It is NOT an f — the lips pop apart; the teeth never touch the lip.
In your mouth: same lip position as प, add the puff.
Words: फल phal (m) [phul] fruit · फूल phool (m) [phool] flower · फिर phir [phir] then, again
ब ba · buh · IPA /bə/
Sound: like b in "big" — voiced, no puff of air.
In your mouth: lips together, vocal cords humming, clean release.
Words: बस bas (f) [bus] bus; enough! · बात baat (f) [baht] talk, matter · बड़ा baRaa [buh-Rah] big
भ bha · bhuh · IPA /bʱə/
Sound: a b that is voiced with breathy, sighing release — "b-huh" as one sound.
In your mouth: same lip position as ब; keep the hum and let breath pour out as the lips open.
Words: भाई bhaaee (m) [bhah-ee] brother · भारत bhaarat (m) [bhah-rut] India · भूख bhookh (f) [bhookh] hunger
म ma · muh · IPA /mə/
Sound: exactly English m.
In your mouth: lips together, air through the nose, voice on.
Words: माँ maan (f) [mah(n)] mom · मैं main [meh(n)] I · मकान makaan (m) [muh-kahn] house (building)

Semivowels & Liquids: य र ल व (glides and flows)

These four sit halfway between consonant and vowel — the air keeps moving; nothing fully closes. Three of them are friendly; only व needs real attention, because it is neither the English v nor the English w but a soft sound in between.

य ya · yuh · IPA /jə/
Sound: like y in "yes".
In your mouth: middle of the tongue rises toward the palate without touching; a smooth glide.
Words: यह yeh [yeh] this (spelled ya-ha, said yeh!) · यहाँ yahaan [yuh-hah(n)] here · यार yaar (m) [yahr] buddy, dude
र ra · ruh · IPA /rə/
Sound: a quick tapped r, like the r in Spanish "pero" or the tt in American "butter". Never the curled-back American r.
In your mouth: tongue tip flicks once against the ridge just behind the upper teeth — one light tap, tip pointing up, not curled.
Words: रात raat (f) [raht] night · रोटी roTee (f) [roh-Tee] flatbread, roti · रहना rehnaa [reh-nah] to live, to stay
ल la · luh · IPA /l̪ə/
Sound: a light, clear l — like the l in "leaf", never the dark l of "full".
In your mouth: tongue tip on the back of the upper teeth; air flows around the sides.
Words: लाल laal [lahl] red · लड़की laRkee (f) [luhR-kee] girl · लेकिन lekin [lay-kin] but
व va · vuh · IPA /ʋə/
Sound: between v and w. Start saying "w", then let the upper teeth drift toward the lower lip — but stop before they bite.
In your mouth: upper teeth LIGHTLY near the lower lip, no hard friction; lips softly rounded. Both an English v and an English w will be understood — the real sound floats between them.
Words: वह voh [voh] that; he/she (spelled va-ha, said voh!) · वहाँ vahaan [vuh-hah(n)] there · वापस vaapas [vah-pus] back (return)

Sibilants & h: श ष स ह (the hissers and the breath)

Three s-type letters plus the breathy h. The tongue makes a narrow channel and the air hisses through it — farther back for श, right behind the teeth for स. Good news: modern Hindi has collapsed श and ष into one sound, so you only have two hisses to learn.

श sha · shuh · IPA /ʃə/
Sound: like sh in "ship".
In your mouth: blade of the tongue raised toward the front of the palate, lips very slightly pushed out; a broad hiss.
Words: शाम shaam (f) [shahm] evening · शहर shehar (m) [sheh-hur] city · शादी shaadee (f) [shah-dee] wedding
ष Sha · shuh · IPA /ʃə/
Sound: in modern Hindi pronounced exactly the same as श — say "sh" and you're done. Historically it was a retroflex sh; today it survives only in spelling, in Sanskrit loanwords.
Words: भाषा bhaaShaa (f) [bhah-shah] language · विशेष visheSh [vi-shaysh] special
स sa · suh · IPA /sə/
Sound: like s in "sun".
In your mouth: tongue tip close behind the upper teeth, thin jet of air — a sharp, forward hiss.
Words: सब sab [sub] all, everyone · साल saal (m) [sahl] year · सस्ता sastaa [sus-tah] cheap
ह ha · huh · IPA /ɦə/
Sound: like h in "ahead" — a soft, voiced breath, warmer than the h in "hat".
In your mouth: nothing moves; the breath itself carries a light hum through an open throat.
Words: हाँ haan [hah(n)] yes · हवा havaa (f) [huh-vah] air, wind · होना honaa [hoh-nah] to be

The Dotted Letters: क़ ख़ ग़ ज़ फ़ (nukta / Urdu sounds)

A dot under a letter (the nukta) marks a sound borrowed through Persian, Arabic, and English — the Urdu side of Delhi's tongue. Two of these are non-negotiable: ज़ z and फ़ f are essential and everywhere — ज़रूर zaroor [zuh-roor], फ़िल्म film [film]. The other three (क़ ख़ ग़) are throat sounds that most Delhi speakers relax to plain k/kh/g in everyday talk; learn to recognize them and don't stress about producing them.

क़ qa · kuh · IPA /qə/
Sound: a k made deeper in the throat (Arabic qaf). In Delhi speech it usually relaxes to a plain k — say k and you're fine.
In your mouth: the very back of the tongue touches the uvula, farther back than क.
Words: क़रीब qareeb [kuh-reeb] near; approximately · क़ानून qaanoon (m) [kah-noon] law
ख़ kha · khuh · IPA /xə/
Sound: the rasping ch of German "Bach" or Scottish "loch". Delhi speakers often soften it to a plain ख — either is fine.
In your mouth: back of the tongue close to the soft palate without sealing; air scrapes through.
Words: ख़त khat (m) [khut] letter (mail) · ख़बर khabar (f) [khuh-bur] news
ग़ ga · guh · IPA /ɣə/
Sound: a gargled g — the voiced twin of ख़, like a French r said with g-color. In Delhi it usually relaxes to plain g.
In your mouth: same near-closure as ख़ with the voice switched on.
Words: ग़लत galat [guh-lut] wrong · ग़रीब gareeb [guh-reeb] poor
ज़ za · zuh · IPA /zə/
Sound: like z in "zoo". Essential — Delhi speech is full of it, and swapping it for j (jaroor for zaroor) is a heavily-mocked mistake.
In your mouth: exactly like स with the voice switched on.
Words: ज़रूर zaroor [zuh-roor] definitely · ज़्यादा zyaadaa [zyah-dah] more · मेज़ mez (f) [mayz] table
फ़ fa · fuh · IPA /fə/
Sound: like f in "fun". Essential — फ़ोन, फ़िल्म, and half the loanwords in Delhi carry it.
In your mouth: upper teeth on the lower lip with real friction — unlike व, here the contact genuinely buzzes.
Words: फ़ोन fon (m) [fohn] phone · फ़िल्म film (f) [film] film, movie · फ़र्क़ farq (m) [furk] difference

Street reality check: on a Delhi shop board you'll see the nukta dropped half the time — जरूर for ज़रूर, फिल्म for फ़िल्म. The dot may vanish in writing, but the z and f sounds do NOT vanish in speech. Read the word, not just the dot: if it's a Persian/Arabic/English loan, it keeps its z and f.

That's the full inventory: 13 vowel entries, 33 core consonants, 2 flaps, and 5 dotted letters. Everything else you will ever read in Hindi is these letters plus the vowel signs and stacking rules of Chapter 9.
chapters.book1-s09:
Chapter 9 Matras, Conjuncts & How Words Assemble

Chapter 8 gave you the letters; this chapter gives you the assembly manual. Devanagari is not really an alphabet of separate letters standing in a row — it's a system of consonant frames that carry vowel signs, stack into clusters, and hang from that headline bar. Master the four mechanisms here — the built-in a, the matras, the vowel-killer, and the conjuncts — and you can read any word in this course.

1. The Inherent 'a': Every Bare Consonant Comes Pre-Loaded

A bare consonant letter is never just a consonant. क is not "k" — it is ka [kuh]: the consonant plus a built-in short a. Every consonant letter in the script works this way. So a word can be spelled with no vowel signs at all and still be full of vowels:

नमक = न + म + क
namak [nuh-muk]
salt (m) — three bare consonants, and the word comes out na-ma-k.
समझ = स + म + झ
samajh [suh-mujh]
understanding (f) — again, the a's are free.

You'll notice the built-in a quietly disappears in certain spots — above all at the end of a word: नमक is namak [nuh-muk], never "namaka". It also drops inside many longer words (कमरा is kamraa [kum-rah], not "ka-ma-raa"). Don't memorize rules for this yet — the Roman column in this course always writes what is actually said, so just copy it. Your ear will absorb the pattern within weeks.

2. Matras: The Vowel Signs

To put any other vowel on a consonant, you don't write the full vowel letter — you attach a small sign, a matra (मात्रा maatraa (f) [maht-rah]), to the consonant frame. The full vowel letters from Chapter 8 are used only when the vowel starts a word or syllable of its own (आम, एक). Here is क wearing every matra:

FormVowel addedRomanSay itWhere the sign sits
क— (inherent a)kakuhnothing to add
काआ aakaakahvertical stroke after
किइ ikikihook BEFORE the letter (!)
कीई eekeekeehook after
कुउ ukukusmall hook below
कूऊ ookookoobigger hook below
कृऋ rikrikrilittle curl below
केए ekekayslash above the bar
कैऐ aikaikehdouble slash above
कोओ okokohstroke after + slash above
कौऔ aukaukawstroke after + double slash
कंं anusvar (nasal)kanku(n)dot above
कःः visargkahkuh-htwo dots after (rare)
काँाँ aa + candrabindukaankah(n)moon-dot above

The #1 reading surprise in all of Devanagari: the इ-matra is written to the LEFT of its consonant but pronounced AFTER it. कि is ki — never "ik". The hook you see first is a flag announcing "an i-vowel follows this letter." So किताब reads kitaab [ki-tahb], दिन reads din [din], फिर reads phir [phir]. Your eye must learn to jump one letter ahead and come back — after a week of reading it becomes automatic.

3. The Same Matras on Different Letters

Matras keep their shape no matter which consonant they ride — learn them once on क and you can read them on everything. Scan these rows out loud:

+ (a)+aa+i+ee+u+oo+e+ai+o+au
ककाकिकीकुकूकेकैकोकौ
बबाबिबीबुबूबेबैबोबौ
ममामिमीमुमूमेमैमोमौ
ससासिसीसुसूसेसैसोसौ
ररारिरीरुरूरेरैरोरौ

One famous exception, bolded above: on र the u-hooks refuse to hang underneath. Instead they swing out from the letter's waist: रु = ru [ru] and रू = roo [roo]. You will meet these constantly:

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
रुपयाrupayaa (m)ru-puh-yahrupee
रूमालroomaal (m)roo-mahlhandkerchief
ज़रूरzaroorzuh-roordefinitely
शुरूshuroo (m)shu-roostart, beginning

4. The Vowel-Killer: Halant ्

What if you need a consonant with NO vowel at all — a bare k, s, t? A small diagonal stroke under the letter, the halant (also called viraam), kills the inherent a:

क = ka, लेकिन क् = k
ka … k [kuh … k]
the stroke under the letter deletes its built-in vowel. (lekin = but)

You will rarely see the halant written out in everyday words, because when a vowel-less consonant runs into the next consonant, the script does something more elegant: it fuses the two letters into a single stacked shape. That is the conjunct — the last big mechanism, and the reason दिल्ली is written with two letters where you might expect three.

5. Conjuncts: When Consonants Stack

Two consonants with no vowel between them fuse into one glyph: usually the first letter drops its vertical stem and welds onto the second. So स + क → स्क, क + य → क्य, च + च → च्च. A few pairs fuse into special shapes you simply memorize (क्ष त्र ज्ञ श्र). Below is your reference wall: the conjuncts that cover nearly everything you'll read in this course, each with one real word. Don't memorize the tables — read the example words aloud, and let the shapes soak in.

Doubled letters (geminates — hold the consonant longer)

ConjunctBuilt fromExampleMeaning
क्कक + कपक्का pakkaa [puk-kah]firm, sure, for-certain
च्चच + चबच्चा bachchaa (m) [buch-chah]child
ज्जज + जसज्जन sajjan (m) [suj-jun]gentleman
त्तत + तपत्ता pattaa (m) [put-tah]leaf
द्दद + दज़िद्दी ziddee [zid-dee]stubborn
द्धद + धशुद्ध shuddh [shud-dh]pure
न्नन + नसुनना sunnaa [sun-nah]to listen, to hear
प्पप + पगप्पें gappen (f) [gup-pay(n)]gossip, idle chat (gappen maarnaa = to shoot the breeze)
ब्बब + बडिब्बा Dibbaa (m) [Dib-bah]box; train car
म्मम + मचम्मच chammach (m) [chum-much]spoon
ल्लल + लदिल्ली dillee (f) [dil-lee]Delhi
स्सस + सरस्सी rassee (f) [rus-see]rope
ट्टट + टछुट्टी chhuTTee (f) [chhuT-Tee]holiday, day off
ट्ठट + ठचिट्ठी chiTThee (f) [chiT-Thee]letter, note
ड्डड + डलड्डू laDDoo (m) [luD-Doo]laddu (the sweet)

Notice how the retroflex letters stack vertically (ट्ट, ड्ड) instead of losing a stem — they have no vertical stem to lose. Say every geminate as a held, doubled consonant: put-tah, not pu-tah. Chapter 12 drills this.

Clusters with y and v

ConjunctBuilt fromExampleMeaning

Clusters with s (the "school-station" set)

ConjunctBuilt fromExampleMeaning

ConjunctBuilt fromExampleMeaning

Nasal + consonant

ConjunctBuilt fromExampleMeaning
न्दन + दबन्द band [bund]closed (also written बंद)
न्द्रन + द + रचन्द्रमा chandrmaa (m) [chun-druh-mah]moon (formal; everyday word is चाँद chaand [chah(n)d])
न्तन + तशान्त shaant [shahnt]calm, quiet (also written शांत)
म्बम + बलम्बा lambaa [lum-bah]long, tall (also written लंबा)
