ंकdot for ङ + कबैंक baink (m) [beh(n)k]bank
ंचdot for ञ + चखींचना kheenchnaa [khee(n)ch-nah]to pull (खींचो on a door = PULL)

The special shapes: क्ष त्र ज्ञ श्र

Four fusions changed so much in the welding that you just learn them as new letters:

ConjunctBuilt fromExampleMeaning
क्षक + ष → "ksh"शिक्षा shikshaa (f) [shik-shah]education
त्रत + र → "tr"यात्रा yaatraa (f) [yaht-rah]journey (metro: "aapkee yaatraa mangalmay ho")
ज्ञज + ञ → said "gy"!ज्ञान gyaan (m) [gyahn]knowledge (never "jn" — modern Hindi says gy)
श्रश + र → "shr"श्री shree [shree]Shri / Mr. (on every wedding card)

Spot-the-conjunct is a great Delhi street game: बच्चा bachchaa [buch-chah] child · सच्चा sachchaa [such-chah] truthful · बिल्ली billee [bil-lee] cat · क्रिकेट krikeT [kri-kayT] cricket · हिन्दी hindee [hin-dee] Hindi · ज़िन्दगी zindagee [zin-duh-gee] life (f). Every auto, every poster, every serial title — conjuncts everywhere. Read them out loud as you ride.

6. The र Special Cases: One Letter, Three Disguises

The letter र refuses to join clusters the normal way. It has costumes for both roles — and one of them breaks the left-to-right rule of the script entirely.

र as the SECOND member: a slash or a knee

When another consonant is followed by r, the र shrinks to a small diagonal slash tucked under that consonant:

ClusterBuilt fromExampleMeaning
क्रक + र = kraक्रिकेट krikeT (m) [kri-kayT]cricket
प्रप + र = praप्रेम prem (m) [praym]love (the formal, poetic word)
ग्रग + र = graग्राहक graahak (m) [grah-huk]customer

On the stemless retroflex letters the slash can't attach, so र becomes a little bent "knee" hanging below:

ClusterBuilt fromExampleMeaning
ट्रट + र = Traट्रेन Tren (f) [Trayn]train
ड्रड + र = Draड्राइवर Draaivar (m) [Drah-i-vur]driver

र as the FIRST member: the reph, written ABOVE — and out of order

When र comes first in a cluster (r + consonant), it leaves the line of writing altogether. It becomes a small curl called the reph, perched on top of the FOLLOWING letter. Read it before the letter it sits on: the r sound comes BEFORE the letter it sits on.

WordReads asRomanSay itMeaning
कर्मक + र्म = ka-r-makarm (m)kurmdeed; karma
धर्मध + र्मdharm (m)dhurmreligion; duty
शर्मश + र्मsharm (f)shurmshyness, shame
गर्मग + र्मgarmgurmhot
मिर्चमि + र्चmirch (f)mirchchili
सिर्फ़सि + र्फ़sirfsirfonly, just

Beginners see गर्म and read "gamr" or "garam-with-something". Work right to left through the stack: the reph on म means the r is pronounced first — garm [gurm]. And note the double illusion in मिर्च: the i-matra is written left but sounds after म, and the reph is written on च but sounds before it. Written order मि-र्च, spoken order m-i-r-ch [mirch]. This one word is the whole chapter in miniature.

7. Spelling Conventions: Anusvar ं and Candrabindu ँ

Hindi has two nasal marks, and Delhi print uses them loosely — so learn what's behind them.

The anusvar dot standing in for a nasal conjunct. Before another consonant, the dot is simply shorthand for the nasal of that consonant's row (n before dentals, m before labials, ng before k/g, and so on). That means many words have two equally correct spellings — full conjunct or dot:

Conjunct spellingDot spellingRomanSay itMeaning
हिन्दीहिंदीhindee (f)hin-deeHindi (this course writes हिन्दी)
बन्दबंदbandbundclosed
लम्बालंबाlambaalum-bahlong, tall — before a labial the dot reads as m
ज़िन्दगीज़िंदगीzindagee (f)zin-duh-geelife

Same word, same sound, two outfits — signboards mix them freely, so recognize both.

The candrabindu (moon-dot) for pure nasal vowels. ँ doesn't stand for any n or m consonant — it sends the vowel itself through the nose, French-style. It lives on the most homely words in the language:

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
हाँhaanhah(n)yes
कहाँkahaankuh-hah(n)where
आँखaankh (f)ah(n)kheye
माँmaan (f)mah(n)mom

When the space above a letter is already occupied by a matra (ी, े, ै…), the moon has no room, so only the dot is printed even for a pure nasal vowel: नहीं naheen [nuh-hee(n)] no, मैं main [meh(n)] I, में mein [may(n)] in. Keep that last pair apart: मैं [meh(n)] vs में [may(n)].

8. Devanagari Digits & the Full Stop

Modern Delhi writes numbers with Western digits almost everywhere, but the Devanagari set still appears on older signs, temple boards, and official Hindi documents. Recognize them:

0123456789
०१२३४५६७८९

Watch for the tricksters: १ is 1 (not 9), ४ is 4 (looks like a fancy 8), and ९ is 9 (looks like an English 3 gone wrong... or a 6 — it's 9).

Finally, punctuation. A Hindi sentence ends not with a period but with the purnviram । — a single vertical bar: मैं ठीक हूँ। main Theek hoon. [meh(n) Theek hoo(n)] I am fine. The question mark ? is used just as in English, and commas and quotation marks are the familiar Western ones.

Full assembly test, Delhi-style. Metro pillar: दिल्ली मेट्रो dillee meTro [dil-lee mayT-roh] — a geminate and a loanword. Dhaba board: शुद्ध शाकाहारी shuddh shaakaahaaree [shud-dh shah-kah-hah-ree] pure vegetarian — conjunct द्ध. Door sign: खींचो kheencho [khee(n)-choh] pull. If you can read those three cold, this chapter has done its job.

Chapter 10 Writing Devanagari I: Vowels & the First Rows

Writing cements reading — hands teach eyes. Ten minutes of tracing a day through weeks 1–4 and the script becomes yours. The general choreography for every letter:

1Body first — draw the letter's curves and bowls, generally left to right, top to bottom.
2Stem next — the vertical bar (if the letter has one) comes after the body.
3Headline (शिरोरेखा) last — the horizontal roof is drawn LAST, in one stroke across the finished letter (across the whole word, once you write words).
4Matras and dots after the roof — vowel signs, bindus and nuktas are the final garnish.

In each row below: copy the solid letter, trace the two gray ones, trace the faint one, then fill the empty boxes freehand. Slow beats pretty; pretty beats fast.

The vowels

अ and आ share a skeleton — आ just adds the tall bar. Master अ's S-curl first; half the alphabet borrows it. इ is one flowing hook; ई adds the overhead loop. उ/ऊ are single graceful curls. ए is a triangle-flag; ऐ adds one flick above.

chapters.book1-s12:
Chapter 12 Minimal-Pair Drills: Train Your Ear & Mouth

A minimal pair is two real words separated by exactly one sound — and Hindi's minimal pairs sit precisely on the contrasts English ignores: tooth-t versus curled-T, puff versus no puff, long vowel versus short, nasal versus plain, single consonant versus held double. If you can hear and produce the pairs in this chapter, you have the whole sound system. If you can't, no amount of vocabulary will save you from ordering a "branch" instead of lentils.

How to use this chapter: five minutes a day, out loud, for the rest of Book 1 — and keep coming back during Books 2–4. For each set: (1) read each pair aloud slowly, exaggerating the difference; (2) read the rows fast, alternating; (3) close your eyes while your partner says ONE word of a pair — point to the one you heard; (4) swap: you say one, your partner tells you which came out of your mouth. Step 4 is the only honest test.

Partner quiz rules: no mercy and no mouthing. Delhi ears will give Jacob no benefit of the doubt at the sabzi stand, so the partner shouldn't either. Mark any pair that gets three passes in a row with a pencil tick; a pair with three ticks on different days is officially yours. The untickable ones — for most Americans that's दाल/डाल and काम/कम — get promoted to daily warm-up.

Set 1 — Dental t/d vs Retroflex T/D (tooth vs curl)

The king of contrasts. Lowercase = tongue tip on the back of the upper teeth; CAPITAL = tongue tip curled back; the underside taps the bumpy ridge behind the teeth. Remember: your automatic American t/d sounds retroflex to Indians, so the real work is forcing the dental.

PairRomanSay itMeanings
दाल / डालdaal (f) / Daal (f)dahl / Dahllentils / tree branch
तन / टनtan (m) / Tan (m)tun / Tunbody / a ton
रोती / रोटीrotee / roTee (f)roh-tee / roh-Tee(she) cries / flatbread
सूत / सूटsoot (m) / sooT (m)soot / sooT(spun) thread / a suit
कातना / काटनाkaatnaa / kaaTnaakaht-nah / kahT-nahto spin (thread) / to cut
नाता / नाटाnaataa (m) / naaTaanah-tah / nah-Tahfamily tie / short-statured
ताला / टालाtaalaa (m) / Taalaatah-lah / Tah-laha lock / put (it) off (past of Taalnaa, to postpone)
तीन / ठीकteen / Theekteen / Theekthree / fine — near pair: dental-plain vs retroflex-aspirated

English t/d live in no-man's-land between the two rows, and Indian ears assign them to the retroflex side. Practical rule: when you're not sure, go DENTAL — touch actual tooth. A too-dental त sounds charmingly careful; a retroflex त turns दाल daal [dahl] into firewood (डाल [Dahl]).

Set 2 — Aspirated vs Unaspirated (the puff)

Palm in front of your mouth for the left word: nothing. For the right word: a real burst. English can't help releasing a small puff on k/p/t at the start of words, so the hard half is the LEFT column — squeezing the puff to zero.

PairRomanSay itMeanings
पल / फलpal (m) / phal (m)pul / phula moment / fruit
पूल / फूलpool (m) / phool (m)pool / phoola (swimming) pool / flower
काना / खानाkaanaa / khaanaa (m)kah-nah / khah-nahone-eyed / food; to eat
कील / खीलkeel (f) / kheel (f)keel / kheela nail / puffed rice (the Diwali offering)
तन / थनtan (m) / than (m)tun / thunbody / udder
बात / भातbaat (f) / bhaat (m)baht / bhahttalk, matter / cooked rice
चल / छलchal / chhal (m)chul / chhulwalk! move! / deceit
बाग़ / भागbaag (m) / bhaagbahg / bhahggarden / run! — near pair (the final g's differ on paper, not in Delhi mouths)

The voiced sighs (घ झ ढ ध भ) hide in that last row: भाग is not "b-hag" but one breathy syllable [bhahg]. If your partner hears two beats, you're adding a vowel — keep the voice humming straight through the release.

Set 3 — Short vs Long Vowels (length does the work)

Hindi has no stressed syllables to lean on; vowel LENGTH carries the meaning. Give long vowels a genuine double count — to an American ear the correct version always feels theatrically slow. The a/aa pairs are the beginner-killers: kam/kaam trips more learners than any retroflex ever will.

PairRomanSay itMeanings
कम / कामkam / kaam (m)kum / kahmless, little / work
दम / दामdam (m) / daam (m)dum / dahmbreath / price
बल / बालbal (m) / baal (m)bul / bahlstrength / hair
दिन / दीनdin (m) / deendin / deenday / poor, wretched
मिल / मीलmil / meel (m)mil / meelmeet! (stem of milnaa) / a mile
पिता / पीताpitaa (m) / peetaapi-tah / pee-tahfather / (he) drinks
चुकना / चूकनाchuknaa / chooknaachuk-nah / chook-nahto be finished, used up / to miss (a chance)
पुल / पूलpul (m) / pool (m)pul / poolbridge / a pool

Bonus triplet for the brave: पुल pul [pul] bridge · पूल pool [pool] pool · फूल phool [phool] flower. Length separates the first two, the puff separates the last two. Delhiites cross the ITO pul daily and will happily quiz you on all three in one breath.

Set 4 — Nasalized vs Plain Vowels (send it through the nose)

The (n) in the phonetics is never a spoken n — the vowel itself hums through the nose, French-style. Pinch your nostrils lightly: on the nasal word you should feel the buzz cut off.

PairRomanSay itMeanings
सास / साँसsaas (f) / saans (f)sahs / sah(n)smother-in-law / breath
कहा / कहाँkahaa / kahaankuh-hah / kuh-hah(n)said / where
है / हैंhai / hainheh / heh(n)is / are — you will say these hundreds of times a day
पूछ / पूँछpoochh / poonchh (f)poochh / poo(n)chhask! (stem of poochhnaa) / tail
गोद / गोंदgod (f) / gond (m)gohd / goh(n)dlap / glue
हँस / हंसhans / hans (m)huh(n)s / hunslaugh! / swan — moon-dot = pure nasal vowel; plain dot here = a real n

The saas/saans pair is a national institution: the mega-hit TV serial Saas Bhi Kabhi Bahu Thi lives on the saas (mother-in-law) side, and every Hindi speaker knows the joke that a bahu meeting her saas needs her saans. Get this pair right before dinner at the in-laws' — asking your सास [sahs] to catch her साँस [sah(n)s] will earn a laugh; mixing them up mid-sentence will earn a bigger one.

Set 5 — Single vs Double Consonants (hold the geminate)

A doubled (conjunct) consonant is genuinely held longer — close the mouth for the consonant, wait a beat, then release: put-tah. English does this across word boundaries ("bus stop", "book case"), never inside a word, so trust the hyphen in the phonetics.

PairRomanSay itMeanings
पता / पत्ताpataa (m) / pattaa (m)puh-tah / put-tahaddress; whereabouts / leaf
बचा / बच्चाbachaa / bachchaa (m)buh-chah / buch-chahsaved, left over / child
पका / पक्काpakaa / pakkaapuh-kah / puk-kahripe, cooked / firm, sure, pukka
गदा / गद्दाgadaa (f) / gaddaa (m)guh-dah / gud-daha mace (Hanuman's weapon) / mattress
दिली / दिल्लीdilee / dillee (f)di-lee / dil-leeheartfelt (dilee khvaahish, a heartfelt wish) / Delhi
सच / सच्चाsuch (m) / sachchaasuch / such-chahtruth / truthful — near pair (the ending differs too)

Set 6 — Loanword Sound Practice: ph vs f, j vs z

These two contrasts separate the native Hindi sounds from the Urdu-Persian-English layer of Delhi speech. Perfect minimal pairs are scarce here, so drill them as lists — left column pops, right column buzzes.

फ (p + puff) vs फ़ (true f)

Lips pop: फ phSay itTeeth buzz: फ़ fSay it
फल phal (m) fruitphulफ़ोन fon (m) phonefohn
फूल phool (m) flowerphoolफ़िल्म film (f) filmfilm
फिर phir againphirसाफ़ saaf cleansahf
फीका pheekaa blandphee-kahफ़र्क़ farq (m) differencefurk

Register note: plenty of Delhiites let native फ slide toward f too — you'll hear fool for फूल in fast speech, and nobody blinks. The reverse (saying philm for फ़िल्म) is heard as small-town. So: keep loanwords firmly f (fon, film, farq), and don't panic about the native words drifting.

ज (j) vs ज़ (z)

Native: ज jSay itLoan: ज़ zSay it
जो jo who, whichjohज़ोर zor (m) forcezohr
जान jaan (f) life; darlingjahnज़मीन zameen (f) ground, landzuh-meen
जेब jeb (f) pocketjaybज़रूर zaroor definitelyzuh-roor
जल्दी jaldee (f) hurryjul-deeज़ुकाम zukaam (m) head coldzu-kahm

And one genuine minimal pair to seal it: सजा sajaa [suh-jah] decorated (from sajnaa) vs सज़ा sazaa (f) [suh-zah] punishment. A wedding hall is sajaa; a jail term is sazaa. Saying jaroor for ज़रूर is the single most-teased pronunciation slip in Hindi — one week with this list buys a lifetime of credibility.

Set 7 — श sh vs स s

Easy for English speakers to SAY — the trap is reading: श and स look nothing like sh and s, and your eye will swap them for months. Two real pairs, then a mixed list to read fast.

PairRomanSay itMeanings
साल / शालsaal (m) / shaal (f)sahl / shahlyear / shawl
सेर / शेरser (m) / sher (m)sayr / shayran old measure of weight / lion; couplet

Read aloud, alternating hisses: शहर shehar (m) [sheh-hur] city · सड़क saRak (f) [suh-Ruk] road · शादी shaadee (f) [shah-dee] wedding · समोसा samosaa (m) [suh-moh-sah] samosa · शीशा sheeshaa (m) [shee-shah] mirror, glass · सस्ता sastaa [sus-tah] cheap · शक shak (m) [shuk] doubt · स्टेशन sTeshan (m) [sTay-shun] station. Proverb-grade combo: सस्ती शादी sastee shaadee [sus-tee shah-dee] — a cheap wedding.

Practice Sentences: All Contrasts, Full Speed

Twelve natural sentences, each loaded with the contrasts above. Read the Devanagari; fall back on the Roman only when stuck. One run-through daily, and once a week have your partner pick three at random for a clean-pronunciation test.

आज काम कम है।
aaj kaam kam hai. [ahj kahm kum heh]
There's not much work today. (kaam vs kam in one breath)
यह दाल है, वह डाल है।
yeh daal hai, voh Daal hai. [yeh dahl heh, voh Dahl heh]
This is daal; that is a branch.
ठंड में गरम दाल अच्छी लगती है।
ThanD mein garam daal achchhee lagtee hai. [ThunD may(n) guh-rum dahl uch-chhee lug-tee heh]
In the cold, hot daal feels wonderful.
बाग़ में फल और फूल हैं।
baag mein phal aur phool hain. [bahg may(n) phul awr phool heh(n)]
There are fruits and flowers in the garden.
सास ने लम्बी साँस ली।
saas ne lambee saans lee. [sahs nay lum-bee sah(n)s lee]
Mother-in-law took a long breath. (the classic — nail it before you meet yours)
बच्चा बड़ा सच्चा है।
bachchaa baRaa sachchaa hai. [buch-chah buh-Rah such-chah heh]
The kid is really truthful. (three geminates and a flap)
बच्ची रोती है क्योंकि रोटी ठंडी है।
bachchee rotee hai kyonki roTee ThanDee hai. [buch-chee roh-tee heh kyoh(n)-ki roh-Tee Thun-Dee heh]
The little girl is crying because the roti is cold. (rotee cries, roTee is bread)
स्टेशन एक मील दूर है।
sTeshan ek meel door hai. [sTay-shun ayk meel door heh]
The station is a mile away.
माँ ने नए साल पर शाल दी।
maan ne nae saal par shaal dee. [mah(n) nay nuh-ay sahl pur shahl dee]
Mom gave a shawl for New Year's. (saal vs shaal, plus a nasal maan)
पिता जी पानी पीते हैं।
pitaa jee paanee peete hain. [pi-tah jee pah-nee pee-tay heh(n)]
Father drinks water. (short i, long ee, back to back)
मुझे ज़रूर फ़ोन करना।
mujhe zaroor fon karnaa. [mu-jhay zuh-roor fohn kur-nah]
Do call me, for sure. (z and f — the Delhi essentials)
तुम्हारा घर कहाँ है?
tumhaaraa ghar kahaan hai? [tum-hah-rah ghur kuh-hah(n) heh]
Where is your house? (breathy gh, nasal kahaan)

Progress check: record yourself reading all twelve sentences on day one of using this chapter, and again a month later. The difference will convince you of the method better than any teacher could. Then keep the daily five minutes going — pronunciation is a muscle, not a fact.
chapters.book1-s13:
Chapter 13 Self-Tests, Partner Games & the Gauntlet

Pronunciation only improves against feedback. This chapter is your feedback machine: a weekly solo protocol, four two-minute partner games, a set of twenty loaded sentences, and a troubleshooting table for when something keeps missing.

The weekly solo check (10 minutes, phone voice memo)

Every weekend: (1) record yourself reading the current week's ten flashcard words plus two gauntlet sentences; (2) do something else for an hour; (3) listen cold, next to the phonetic line. Fresh ears catch what busy ears excuse. Keep the recordings — replaying Week 2 during Week 10 is the single most motivating thing you can do in this course.

The four partner games

1 · Pointing pairs
(trains your EAR)		Write the two target letters big on two papers (start with त/ट). Partner speaks random syllables or pair-words; you point. Ten right in a row = level up to the next pair set from Chapter 12. Two minutes.
2 · Which did I say?
(trains your MOUTH)		Reverse roles: you speak a secretly-chosen item from a pair; partner writes down which they heard. Ten items, compare, score /10 in the tracker. The brutal, beautiful truth-teller.
3 · Shadow karaoke
(trains your MELODY)		Partner voice-notes one natural sentence (their normal speed). You copy it until they certify "indistinguishable-ish." One line per session. These certified lines are your accent's trophy shelf.
4 · The vendor drill
(trains REAL LIFE)		Partner plays a Delhi chai-vaalaa / auto-vaalaa / sabzi-vaalaa at 80% real speed, using this week's Book 4 dialogue as the script but improvising freely. You survive the transaction. Graduation: they go 100% speed and add background heckling.

The Gauntlet — twenty loaded sentences

Each sentence concentrates one target. Read down the list weekly; circle the numbers that still feel wobbly and drill just those. When all twenty pass the partner test, your pronunciation course is functionally complete.

1. भैया, दो कड़क चाय देना।
bhaiyaa, do kaRak chaay denaa. [bheh-yah, doh kuh-Ruk chah-ay day-nah]
Bhaiya, two strong chais. (bh + flap R)
2. ठीक है, थोड़ा ठंडा पानी दो।
Theek hai, thoRaa ThanDaa paanee do. [Theek heh, thoh-Rah Thun-Dah pah-nee doh]
Okay, give a little cold water. (Th vs th in one breath)
3. मैं दिल्ली में रहता हूँ।
main dillee mein rehtaa hoon. [meh(n) dil-lee may(n) reh-tah hoo(n)]
I live in Delhi. (nasals + geminate ll)
4. यह आटा बहुत अच्छा है।
yeh aaTaa bahut achchhaa hai. [yeh ah-Tah bo-hut uch-chhah heh]
This flour is very good. (retroflex T + chh)
5. मेरी सास साँस ले रही हैं।
meree saas saans le rahee hain. [may-ree sahs sah(n)s lay ruh-hee heh(n)]
My mother-in-law is taking a breath. (THE nasal pair)
6. लड़का सड़क पर दौड़ रहा है।
laRkaa saRak par dauR rahaa hai. [luhR-kah suh-Ruk pur dawR ruh-hah heh]
The boy is running on the road. (three flaps)
7. फल और फ़ोन मेज़ पर हैं।
phal aur fon mez par hain. [phul awr fohn mayz pur heh(n)]
The fruit and the phone are on the table. (ph vs f, z)
8. घर में धूप और भाप है।
ghar mein dhoop aur bhaap hai. [ghur may(n) dhoop awr bhahp heh]
There's sunshine and steam in the house. (gh dh bh trio)
9. काका कच्चा केला खाते हैं।
kaakaa kachchaa kelaa khaate hain. [kah-kah kuch-chah kay-lah khah-tay heh(n)]
Uncle eats raw banana. (k vs kh + geminate)
10. दादी दही और डबल रोटी लाईं।
daadee dahee aur Dabal roTee laaeen. [dah-dee duh-hee awr Duh-bul roh-Tee lah-ee(n)]
Grandma brought yogurt and bread. (d vs D vs T)
11. पत्ता कहाँ गिरा, पता नहीं।
pattaa kahaan giraa, pataa naheen. [put-tah kuh-hah(n) gi-rah, puh-tah nuh-hee(n)]
Where the leaf fell, no idea. (geminate vs single t)
12. तुम्हें ज़रूर मज़ा आएगा।
tumhen zaroor mazaa aaegaa. [tum-hay(n) zuh-roor muh-zah ah-ay-gah]
You'll definitely have fun. (true z's)
13. वह लड़की बड़ी समझदार है।
voh laRkee baRee samajhdaar hai. [voh luhR-kee buh-Ree suh-mujh-dahr heh]
That girl is very sensible. (flaps + schwa deletion)
14. क्या आप कल दिल्ली जाएँगे?
kyaa aap kal dillee jaaenge? [kyah ahp kul dil-lee jah-ay(n)-gay ↗]
Will you go to Delhi tomorrow? (ky cluster + rising melody)
15. छोटे बच्चे छत पर हैं।
chhoTe bachche chhat par hain. [chhoh-Tay buch-chay chhut pur heh(n)]
The little kids are on the roof. (chh + geminate chch)
16. भाभी ने भिंडी बनाई है।
bhaabhee ne bhinDee banaaee hai. [bhah-bhee nay bhin-Dee buh-nah-ee heh]
Bhabhi has made okra. (double bh + nD)
17. ये कपड़े महँगे हैं।
ye kapRe mehnge hain. [yay kup-Ray mehn-gay heh(n)]
These clothes are expensive. (flap + nasal)
18. हाँ, मैं यहाँ हूँ ना।
haan, main yahaan hoon naa. [hah(n), meh(n) yuh-hah(n) hoo(n) nah]
Yes, I'm right here, na. (four nasals, one plain naa)
19. ऋषि को थोड़ी ठंड लग रही है।
rishi ko thoRee ThanD lag rahee hai. [ri-shi koh thoh-Ree Thun-D lug ruh-hee heh]
Rishi is feeling a bit cold. (th/Th again — the boss fight)
20. धन्यवाद, फिर मिलेंगे!
dhanyavaad, phir milenge! [dhun-yuh-vahd, phir mi-lay(n)-gay]
Thank you, see you again! (dh + ph, even syllables)

Troubleshooting: if they hear X, fix Y

Symptom (partner's report)DiagnosisThe fix
"Your ट sounds like त"No curl — tip going straight upHold American "er" first, tap from the curl (Ch. 3)
"Your त sounds like ट/English t"Parked on the ridgeTouch the teeth — exaggerate forward till it feels silly
"कल and खल sound the same"Puff too weakCandle test; double the air on ख (Ch. 4)
"Everything sounds slightly puffed"American initial-aspiration habitHarvest the s-words: say "skin," drop the s, keep that क
"भ sounds like b-h, two sounds"Voice stopping between b and hHum through it — one breathy gesture (Ch. 4)
"साँस sounds like सास"Velum staying shutPinch-nose test; hum first, then vowel (Ch. 2)
"काम sounds like कम"Long vowels too shortTwo full beats on every aa/ee/oo — feel greedy about it
"Your ए sounds English ('day')"Glide at the endFreeze-hold 3 seconds, nothing moves (Ch. 2)
"ड़ sounds like र"Flap starting uncurled"Ladder" with a curled tip — slap, don't tap (Ch. 5)
"दिल्ली sounds like दिली"Geminate not heldPark one silent beat on the double letter (Ch. 5)

Monthly milestones

MonthYou can honestly check this when…
1 I read the whole alphabet aloud slowly · my त/ट are different sounds in isolation · palm test passes on all five rows
2 8/10 on pointing-pairs (all Ch. 12 sets) · I read matra words without the roman line · nasal vowels on demand
3 Gauntlet 1–10 partner-passed · schwa deletion automatic in words I know · I read Book 4 dialogue lines cold, slowly
4 Gauntlet 11–20 partner-passed · partner understands new sentences without repeating ~70%
5 5 shadow-karaoke lines certified · I survive the vendor drill at full speed
6 A stranger (real vendor / video call with family) understands me first try · I read a new paragraph aloud and my partner rates it "clearly understandable"
chapters.book2-u01:
Unit 1 How Hindi Sentences Work

What you'll be able to say: introduce yourself, name the things around you, ask simple questions and answer them — with every verb landing where Hindi wants it: at the end.

मैं जैकब हूँ।
main Jacob hoon. [meh(n) jay-kub hoo(n)]
I am Jacob. (lit. I Jacob am)
यह चाय है।
yeh chaay hai. [yeh chah-ay heh]
This is chai. (lit. this chai is)
क्या आप ठीक हैं?
kyaa aap Theek hain? [kyah ahp Theek heh(n)]
Are you okay? (lit. what you okay are?)

The one big rule: the verb goes last

English builds sentences subject – verb – everything else: “I am Jacob.” Hindi keeps the subject first but parks the verb at the very end: subject – everything else – verb. Grammar books call this SOV (subject–object–verb) order. You can think of the verb as the caboose: whatever else the train is carrying, the caboose closes it.

In this unit you learn the habit, not the machinery. Every sentence here is a ready-made, high-frequency phrase you can use today. The little words hoon, hai, hain all mean “am / is / are” — Unit 2 sorts out which is which. For now, copy the patterns whole.

Two more everyday chunks, in both speaker versions — Jacob uses the first of each pair; a female speaker uses the second:

मैं दिल्ली में रहता हूँ।
main dillee mein rehtaa hoon. [meh(n) dil-lee may(n) reh-tah hoo(n)]
I live in Delhi. (male speaker) (lit. I Delhi-in living am)
मैं दिल्ली में रहती हूँ।
main dillee mein rehtee hoon. [meh(n) dil-lee may(n) reh-tee hoo(n)]
I live in Delhi. (female speaker)
मैं हिन्दी सीख रहा हूँ।
main hindee seekh rahaa hoon. [meh(n) hin-dee seekh ruh-hah hoo(n)]
I am learning Hindi. (male speaker) (lit. I Hindi learning am)
मैं हिन्दी सीख रही हूँ।
main hindee seekh rahee hoon. [meh(n) hin-dee seekh ruh-hee hoo(n)]
I am learning Hindi. (female speaker)

Now watch the skeletons side by side. The verb slot is marked in bold:

English — verb in the middleHindi — verb at the END
I am Jacob.मैं जैकब हूँ। main Jacob hoon.
This is chai.यह चाय है। yeh chaay hai.
I live in Delhi.मैं दिल्ली में रहता हूँ। main dillee mein rehtaa hoon.
I am learning Hindi.मैं हिन्दी सीख रहा हूँ। main hindee seekh rahaa hoon.

Two things Hindi simply doesn't have: the words a and the. यह चाय है। (yeh chaay hai.) covers “This is chai”, “This is a chai”, and “This is the chai”. One worry gone. (Devanagari has no capital letters either.)

Don't transplant English word order. Beginners say मैं हूँ जैकब (main hoon Jacob) because it mirrors “I am Jacob”. To a Hindi ear that's Yoda-speak. Verb last, always: मैं जैकब हूँ। (main Jacob hoon.)

The middle of the sandwich

Subject at the front, verb at the back — everything else (places, “from America”, “in Delhi”) sits in the middle. Notice something curious: Hindi says “Delhi in”, “America from” — the little relation words come after their noun. They're called postpositions, and they get their own unit (Unit 7). For now, swallow these as chunks:

हम अमेरिका से हैं।
ham amerikaa se hain. [hum uh-may-ri-kah say heh(n)]
We are from America. (lit. we America-from are)
मैं दिल्ली में हूँ।
main dillee mein hoon. [meh(n) dil-lee may(n) hoo(n)]
I am in Delhi. (lit. I Delhi-in am)

Dropping “I” — Hindi loves shortcuts

Because hoon already means “(I) am”, Hindi happily drops मैं (main) in quick answers. This is completely natural speech, not laziness:

आप कैसे हैं?
aap kaise hain? [ahp keh-say heh(n)]
How are you? (asking a man)
आप कैसी हैं?
aap kaisee hain? [ahp keh-see heh(n)]
How are you? (asking a woman)
ठीक हूँ, शुक्रिया।
Theek hoon, shukriyaa. [Theek hoo(n), shuk-ri-yah]
(I'm) fine, thanks. (lit. fine am, thanks)

Yes/no questions: क्या + a rising tune

English flips the verb to ask a question (“This is chai” → “Is this chai?”). Hindi never reshuffles. Take the statement exactly as it is, drop क्या (kyaa) [kyah] in front, and let your voice rise at the end — that's the whole trick:

क्या यह चाय है?
kyaa yeh chaay hai? [kyah yeh chah-ay heh]
Is this chai? (lit. what this chai is?)
जी हाँ, यह चाय है।
jee haan, yeh chaay hai. [jee hah(n), yeh chah-ay heh]
Yes, this is chai.
क्या यह कॉफ़ी है?
kyaa yeh kofee hai? [kyah yeh kaw-fee heh]
Is this coffee?
जी नहीं, यह चाय है।
jee naheen, yeh chaay hai. [jee nuh-hee(n), yeh chah-ay heh]
No, it's chai.

How Delhi actually asks. In fast speech the kyaa usually vanishes and the rising tune does all the work: आप ठीक हैं? (aap Theek hain?) At the chai stall a single word with raised eyebrows is a full sentence: चाय? (chaay?) [chah-ay] And agreement comes back with a bounce: हाँ जी! (haan jee!) [hah(n) jee] — “yes indeed!”

Question words sit just before the verb

Who/what/where words do not jump to the front like in English. They slide into the sentence right before the verb — usually the second-to-last word you say:

यह क्या है?
yeh kyaa hai? [yeh kyah heh]
What is this? (lit. this what is?)
वह कौन है?
voh kaun hai? [voh kawn heh]
Who is that? (lit. that who is?)
बाथरूम कहाँ है?
baathroom kahaan hai? [bahth-room kuh-hah(n) heh]
Where is the bathroom? (lit. bathroom where is?)

क्या does double duty. At the start of a sentence, kyaa is just an audible question mark: क्या यह चाय है? (kyaa yeh chaay hai?) “Is this chai?” Right before the verb, it means “what”: यह क्या है? (yeh kyaa hai?) “What is this?” Position tells you which one you're hearing.

The Hindi full stop

Hindi statements end with a standing bar । called the purnviram — it does exactly what a period does. Questions keep the familiar ?. You'll see both throughout this book; use । whenever you write a Hindi statement.

Frozen phrases — your survival kit

Memorize these as single blocks. They work in any situation from day one, and every one of them quietly obeys the verb-last rule.

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
नमस्तेnamastenuh-muhs-tayhello / goodbye (all-purpose)
जी हाँjee haanjee hah(n)yes (polite)

मुझे हिन्दी नहीं आतीmujhe hindee naheen aateemu-jhay hin-dee nuh-hee(n) ah-teeI don't know Hindi (yet)

Each noun is tagged (m) or (f). Ignore the tags for now — Unit 3 explains them — but let your eyes get used to seeing them.

नमस्ते (namaste) [nuh-muhs-tay] with feeling. Palms together at the chest, a small nod — that's the classic greeting, and it works for hello and goodbye, for strangers and for your partner's grandmother. In many Delhi families, younger people also bend to touch an elder's feet on big occasions; don't panic, just follow your partner's lead. A warm नमस्ते जी (namaste jee) [nuh-muhs-tay jee] — with the respect-syllable jee — is always safe and always appreciated.

Exercise 1A — Verb at the end

Items 1–5: choose the correct sentence, (a) or (b). Items 6–10: write the missing verb — हूँ (hoon), है (hai), or हैं (hain) — copying from the model sentences in this unit. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 1.

chapters.book2-u02:
Unit 2 Pronouns & honaa (to be)

What you'll be able to say: who you are, who everyone else is, how you're doing — and all of it with the right level of politeness for the right person.

नमस्ते, मैं जैकब हूँ।
namaste, main Jacob hoon. [nuh-muhs-tay, meh(n) jay-kub hoo(n)]
Hello, I'm Jacob.
आप कैसे हैं?
aap kaise hain? [ahp keh-say heh(n)]
How are you? (respectful, to a man)
तुम कहाँ हो?
tum kahaan ho? [tum kuh-hah(n) hoh]
Where are you? (informal — the classic Delhi phone opener)

Meet होना (honaa) — the verb “to be”

The dictionary form is होना (honaa) [hoh-nah], “to be”. In the present it has just four shapes — hoon, hai, ho, hain — and each pronoun has claimed its favourite. Learn the pairings as fixed couples; mixing them is the number-one beginner giveaway.

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
मैं हूँmain hoonmeh(n) hoo(n)I am
तू हैtu haitoo hehyou are (intimate — handle with care, see below)
तुम होtum hotum hohyou are (informal)
आप हैंaap hainahp heh(n)you are (respectful)
यह हैyeh haiyeh hehthis / he / she (nearby) is
वह हैvoh haivoh hehthat / he / she is
हम हैंham hainhum heh(n)we are
ये हैंye hainyay heh(n)these are; also he/she (nearby, respectful) is
वो लोग हैंvoh log hainvoh lohg heh(n)they are (people)

Spelling vs. sound. वह is written that way but everyone says voh [voh] — and in texts and WhatsApp Delhiites simply type वो. Same story with यह (yeh) [yeh]. Formal written Hindi also has a separate “they” pronoun, वे (ve) [vay]; in this course we stick to what Delhi actually says: वो लोग (voh log), literally “those people”.

यह vs. वह — near and far

Hindi has no separate word for “he”, “she”, or “it”. Someone or something close by is यह (yeh); someone farther away — or just not present — is वह (voh). Context does the rest:

यह राहुल है।
yeh Rahul hai. [yeh rah-hul heh]
This is Rahul. (he's right here)
वह नेहा है।
voh Neha hai. [voh nay-hah heh]
That's Neha. (across the room)

The politeness ladder: तू, तुम, आप

English has one “you”; Hindi has three, stacked like rungs. Picking the right rung matters more than any grammar rule in this book:

PronounUse withVerb pairing
तू (tu)small children, God, childhood-close friends. Intimate — and rude if misjudged. Don't initiate it; just recognize it.तू है (tu hai)
तुम (tum)your partner, friends, people your own age you know wellतुम हो (tum ho)
आप (aap)elders, in-laws (always), strangers, shopkeepers, anyone you've just metआप हैं (aap hain)

When in doubt, climb up: aap never offends. Notice that aap takes hain — the plural verb — even for one person. Speaking of someone respectfully in the third person works the same way: use ये (ye) or वो (voh) with hain:

ये शर्मा जी हैं।
ye Sharma jee hain. [yay shur-mah jee heh(n)]
This is Mr. Sharma. (lit. these Sharma-ji are — plural grammar as respect)

The in-law rule, non-negotiable. With your partner's parents it is aap — on day one, in year ten, forever. Between you and your partner, tum is the loving default. Delhi guy-friends hammer each other with tu constantly and affectionately, but let them start it. And sprinkle जी (jee) [jee] generously: after names (Sharma jee), after yes and no (jee haan, jee naheen) — it's the sound of good manners.

Don't mix the couples. आप कैसे हो? (aap kaise ho?) — you will hear this loose aap…ho mix on Delhi streets, and तुम हैं (tum hain) is flatly wrong. The standard, always-safe pairings are tu hai, tum ho, aap hain. With elders and in-laws, stick to aap + hain without exception.

Introducing yourself

Here is the exchange you'll have a hundred times. The chunk आपका नाम (aapkaa naam) means “your name” — possessives get their full story in Unit 5; for now it's a fixed phrase.

आपका नाम क्या है?
aapkaa naam kyaa hai? [ahp-kah nahm kyah heh]
What is your name? (lit. your name what is?)
मेरा नाम राहुल है।
meraa naam Rahul hai. [may-rah nahm rah-hul heh]
My name is Rahul.
आप कैसी हैं?
aap kaisee hain? [ahp keh-see heh(n)]
How are you? (respectful, to a woman — kaisee, not kaise)
मैं ठीक हूँ, और आप?
main Theek hoon, aur aap? [meh(n) Theek hoo(n), awr ahp]
I'm fine, and you?
आपसे मिलकर ख़ुशी हुई।
aap se milkar khushee huee. [ahp say mil-kur khu-shee hu-ee]
Pleased to meet you. (fixed phrase — learn it whole)

Between you and your partner it's the tum versions — and here both listener-genders matter:

तुम कैसे हो?
tum kaise ho? [tum keh-say hoh]
How are you? (to a man — this is what Jacob hears)
तुम कैसी हो?
tum kaisee ho? [tum keh-see hoh]
How are you? (to a woman — this is what Jacob says back)
मैं अमेरिकन हूँ।
main amerikan hoon. [meh(n) uh-may-ri-kun hoo(n)]
I'm American. (same for male and female speakers)
मैं घर पर हूँ।
main ghar par hoon. [meh(n) ghur pur hoo(n)]
I'm at home. (ghar par = at home — a chunk worth stealing)

Saying “not”: नहीं

नहीं (naheen) [nuh-hee(n)] slides in just before the verb — one word, no “do/does” gymnastics:

मैं ठीक नहीं हूँ।
main Theek naheen hoon. [meh(n) Theek nuh-hee(n) hoo(n)]
I'm not okay. (lit. I okay not am)
वह यहाँ नहीं है।
voh yahaan naheen hai. [voh yuh-hah(n) nuh-hee(n) heh]
He/she is not here.
हम दिल्ली से नहीं हैं।
ham dillee se naheen hain. [hum dil-lee say nuh-hee(n) heh(n)]
We are not from Delhi.

In snappy replies the verb often disappears after naheen: पता नहीं। (pataa naheen.) [puh-tah nuh-hee(n)] “No idea.” You already know कोई बात नहीं (koee baat naheen) from Unit 1 — same pattern.

Asking “who?” and “what?”

Both question words take the Unit 1 position: just before the verb.

यह क्या है?
yeh kyaa hai? [yeh kyah heh]
What is this?
वह कौन है?
voh kaun hai? [voh kawn heh]
Who is that?
आप कौन हैं?
aap kaun hain? [ahp kawn heh(n)]
Who are you? (polite — say it with a smile at the door)

Street-real greetings. The textbook opener is aap kaise hain?; the Delhi opener is क्या हाल है? (kyaa haal hai?) [kyah hahl heh] — “how's it going?” Standard replies, in rising order of enthusiasm: ठीक है। (Theek hai.) — सब बढ़िया! (sab baRhiyaa!) [sub buh-Rhi-yah] “all great!” — एकदम मस्त! (ekdam mast!) [ayk-dum must] “totally awesome!” Then bounce it back with और बताओ! (aur bataao!) [awr buh-tah-oh] — “so, what else?”

chapters.book2-u03:
Unit 3 Nouns & Gender

What you'll be able to say: nothing new yet — this unit hands you the secret key that makes everything else in Hindi click into place: every noun is either masculine or feminine, and the whole sentence dresses to match.

यह मेरा घर है।
yeh meraa ghar hai. [yeh may-rah ghur heh]
This is my house. (meraa — because ghar is masculine)
यह मेरी गाड़ी है।
yeh meree gaaRee hai. [yeh may-ree gah-Ree heh]
This is my car. (meree — because gaaRee is feminine)
चाय अच्छी है!
chaay achchhee hai! [chah-ay uch-chhee heh]
The chai is good! (achchhee — chaay is feminine too)

Every noun picks a team

In Hindi there is no “it”. Every single noun — table, water, love, Wi-Fi — is grammatically either masculine (m) or feminine (f). A table is “she”. Water is “he”. This has nothing to do with logic or biology (except for people and animals, where natural gender wins). It's simply each word's team jersey, fixed forever.

Why care? Because Hindi is an agreement language: the words for “my”, “good”, “big”, and most verb forms all change shape to match the gender of the noun they touch. Get the gender right and whole sentences fall into place; get it wrong and everything downstream wobbles. The good news: two rules of thumb cover most nouns, and the exceptions are famous enough to memorize once and keep for life.

Rule of thumb 1: ends in -आ (-aa)? Usually masculine

लड़काlaRkaa (m)luhR-kahboy

The famous traitors

A small gang of everyday -ee words defected to the masculine team. They happen to be words you'll use daily, so drill them now:

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning

आदमीaadmee (m)ahd-meeman

Memory hook: the kitchen liquids are boys — paanee, dahee, ghee, all (m). And aadmee is a man, so of course he's (m). A couple of -aa words jumped the other way and are feminine: हवा (havaa (f)) [huh-vah] “air, wind” and दवा (davaa (f)) [duh-vah] “medicine”.

People trump endings. Words for male people are (m) and words for female people are (f), no matter how they're spelled. भाई (bhaaee (m)) [bhah-ee] “brother” and पिता (pitaa (m)) [pi-tah] “father” are masculine because they're men; माँ (maan (f)) [mah(n)] “mom”, बहन (behen (f)) [beh-hen] “sister”, and औरत (aurat (f)) [aw-rut] “woman” are feminine because they're women — no -aa or -ee ending required. One flexible word: दोस्त (dost) [dohst] “friend” — it agrees (m) for a male friend and (f) for a female friend: meraa dost (he), meree dost (she).

The unmarked crowd: no helpful ending

Thousands of nouns end in a consonant or some other vowel and give you no visual clue. Their gender simply has to travel with the word — this is why every noun in this course is tagged (m) or (f):

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
घरghar (m)ghurhouse, home
मकानmakaan (m)muh-kahnhouse (the building)
नामnaam (m)nahmname
सेबseb (m)saybapple
आमaam (m)ahmmango
दिनdin (m)dinday
हाथhaath (m)hahthhand
कामkaam (m)kahmwork
किताबkitaab (f)ki-tahbbook
मेज़mez (f)mayztable
चायchaay (f)chah-aychai, tea
बातbaat (f)bahtmatter, thing said
चीज़cheez (f)cheezthing
दुकानdukaan (f)du-kahnshop
रातraat (f)rahtnight
आँखaankh (f)ah(n)kheye

Why gender matters: everything agrees

Here is the payoff, previewed. “My” is मेरा (meraa) [may-rah] before a masculine noun and मेरी (meree) [may-ree] before a feminine one (full system in Unit 5). Adjectives like achchhaa “good” and ठंडा (ThanDaa) [Thun-Dah] “cold” do the same dance (Unit 6). Watch the endings flip:

यह मेरा फ़ोन है।
yeh meraa fon hai. [yeh may-rah fohn heh]
This is my phone. (fon m)
यह मेरी मेज़ है।
yeh meree mez hai. [yeh may-ree mayz heh]
This is my table. (mez f)
पानी ठंडा है।
paanee ThanDaa hai. [pah-nee Thun-Dah heh]
The water is cold. (ThanDaa — m form, because paanee is m!)
चाय ठंडी है।
chaay ThanDee hai. [chah-ay Thun-Dee heh]
The chai is cold. (ThanDee — f form for f chaay. Send it back.)
खाना अच्छा है।
khaanaa achchhaa hai. [khah-nah uch-chhah heh]
The food is good. (khaanaa m)
मेरा नाम जैकब है।
meraa naam Jacob hai. [may-rah nahm jay-kub heh]
My name is Jacob. (naam m — now you know why it's meraa naam)
यह मेरा दोस्त राहुल है।
yeh meraa dost Rahul hai. [yeh may-rah dohst rah-hul heh]
This is my friend Rahul. (for a female friend: yeh meree dost Neha hai)
मेरी चाय कहाँ है?
meree chaay kahaan hai? [may-ree chah-ay kuh-hah(n) heh]
Where is my chai? (the most important sentence in this unit)

The classic trap: trusting the -ee. Learners see paanee and dahee, think “ends in -ee, must be feminine”, and produce पानी ठंडी है (paanee ThanDee hai) — wrong, and instantly heard. The traitors are masculine: पानी ठंडा है। (paanee ThanDaa hai.) दही अच्छा है। (dahee achchhaa hai.) [duh-hee uch-chhah heh]

English words get jerseys too. Delhi Hindi is full of English nouns, and every one has quietly been assigned a gender: फ़ोन (fon (m)) [fohn], टीवी (Teevee (m)) [Tee-vee], स्कूल (skool (m)) [skool], ऑटो (auTo (m)) [aw-Toh], but मेट्रो (meTro (f)) [may-Troh], ट्रेन (Tren (f)) [Trayn], कॉफ़ी (kofee (f)) [kaw-fee]. So a Delhiite shrugs: मेट्रो लेट है। (meTro leT hai.) [may-Troh layT heh] — “the metro's late.”

Your strategy from today

Never learn a bare noun again — learn it wearing its jersey. The cheapest trick: memorize each noun inside a meraa/meree phrase, because you already own those two words. meraa ghar, meraa paanee, meraa kamraa — meree chaay, meree kitaab, meree gaaRee. Say the pair out loud once and the gender rides along for free. Every word list and flashcard in this course carries the (m)/(f) tag; treat the tag as part of the word's spelling.

Exercise 3A — Pick the team

  1. घर (ghar)

Exercise 3C — Translate into Hindi

  1. My name is Jacob.
  2. This is my chai.

Exercise 3D — Translate into English

Write the English meaning. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 3.

  1. यह मेरी गाड़ी है। (yeh meree gaaRee hai.)
  2. दही ठंडा है। (dahee ThanDaa hai.)

  5. मेट्रो लेट है। (meTro leT hai.)
chapters.book2-u04:
Unit 4 Plurals

What you'll be able to say: more than one of anything — two chais, four samosas, all the books — plus the politest trick in Hindi: making one person grammatically plural to show respect.

एक लड़का, दो लड़के।
ek laRkaa, do laRke. [ayk luhR-kah, doh luhR-kay]
One boy, two boys.
ये मेरी किताबें हैं।
ye meree kitaaben hain. [yay may-ree ki-tah-bay(n) heh(n)]
These are my books.
भैया, दो चाय देना।
bhaiyaa, do chaay denaa. [bheh-yah, doh chah-ay day-nah]
Bhaiya, two chais please. (lit. brother, two chai give)

Four patterns cover everything

How a noun pluralizes depends on two things you now know how to read: its gender (Unit 3) and whether it wears a “marked” ending (-aa for m, -ee for f). That gives exactly four patterns:

Noun typeSingularPluralRule
masculine in -aaलड़का laRkaa (m) luhR-kahलड़के laRke luhR-kay-aa → -e
masculine, everything elseघर ghar (m) ghurघर ghar ghurno change at all
feminine in -eeलड़की laRkee (f) luhR-keeलड़कियाँ laRkiyaan luhR-ki-yah(n)-ee → -iyaan
feminine, everything elseकिताब kitaab (f) ki-tahbकिताबें kitaaben ki-tah-bay(n)add -en

Masculine -aa → -e

SingularPluralSay the pluralMeaning
कमरा kamraa (m) kum-rahकमरे kamrekum-rayroom → rooms
केला kelaa (m) kay-lahकेले kelekay-laybanana → bananas
समोसा samosaa (m) suh-moh-sahसमोसे samosesuh-moh-saysamosa → samosas
बेटा beTaa (m) bay-Tahबेटे beTebay-Tayson → sons
कुत्ता kuttaa (m) kut-tahकुत्ते kuttekut-taydog → dogs

A few masculine -aa words refuse to change — mostly relationship words and borrowings: पिता (pitaa (m)) [pi-tah] “father”, चाचा (chaachaa (m)) [chah-chah] “uncle”, राजा (raajaa (m)) [rah-jah] “king”, नेता (netaa (m)) [nay-tah] “politician”. So: दो चाचा (do chaachaa), not “do chaache”.

Masculine unchanged — the verb carries the number

All other masculines — ghar, naam, seb, fon, din, dost, haath, and the Unit 3 traitors aadmee and haathee — look identical in singular and plural. Then how do you know how many? Listen to the verb:

आदमी यहाँ है।
aadmee yahaan hai. [ahd-mee yuh-hah(n) heh]
The man is here. (hai = one)
आदमी यहाँ हैं।
aadmee yahaan hain. [ahd-mee yuh-hah(n) heh(n)]
The men are here. (hain = more than one — same noun!)

Feminine -ee → -iyaan

SingularPluralSay the pluralMeaning
कुर्सी kursee (f) kur-seeकुर्सियाँ kursiyaankur-si-yah(n)chair → chairs
सब्ज़ी sabzee (f) sub-zeeसब्ज़ियाँ sabziyaansub-zi-yah(n)vegetable → vegetables
रोटी roTee (f) roh-Teeरोटियाँ roTiyaanroh-Ti-yah(n)roti → rotis
गाड़ी gaaRee (f) gah-Reeगाड़ियाँ gaaRiyaangah-Ri-yah(n)car → cars
बेटी beTee (f) bay-Teeबेटियाँ beTiyaanbay-Ti-yah(n)daughter → daughters
साड़ी saaRee (f) sah-Reeसाड़ियाँ saaRiyaansah-Ri-yah(n)saree → sarees

Feminine unmarked: add -एं (-en)

SingularPluralSay the pluralMeaning
मेज़ mez (f) mayzमेज़ें mezenmay-zay(n)table → tables
बात baat (f) bahtबातें baatenbah-tay(n)matter → matters, talk
चीज़ cheez (f) cheezचीज़ें cheezenchee-zay(n)thing → things
दुकान dukaan (f) du-kahnदुकानें dukaanendu-kah-nay(n)shop → shops
औरत aurat (f) aw-rutऔरतें auratenaw-ru-tay(n)woman → women
बहन behen (f) beh-henबहनें behnenbeh-nay(n)sister → sisters
रात raat (f) rahtरातें raatenrah-tay(n)night → nights

Pointing at many: यह → ये, वह → वो

The pointing words pluralize too: nearby यह (yeh) becomes ये (ye) [yay], and far-away वह (voh) becomes वो (voh) — which in Delhi speech sounds exactly the same as the singular, so once again the verb does the counting.

यह कमरा है।
yeh kamraa hai. [yeh kum-rah heh]
This is a room.
ये कमरे हैं।
ye kamre hain. [yay kum-ray heh(n)]
These are rooms.
ये समोसे गरम हैं।
ye samose garam hain. [yay suh-moh-say guh-rum heh(n)]
These samosas are hot. (garam = hot — more on adjectives in Unit 6)
मेज़ें यहाँ हैं और कुर्सियाँ वहाँ हैं।
mezen yahaan hain aur kursiyaan vahaan hain. [may-zay(n) yuh-hah(n) heh(n) awr kur-si-yah(n) vuh-hah(n) heh(n)]
The tables are here and the chairs are there.
किताबें मेज़ पर हैं।
kitaaben mez par hain. [ki-tah-bay(n) mayz pur heh(n)]
The books are on the table. (mez par = on the table — chunk; the full “on/in” story is Unit 7)
दो रोटियाँ और एक चाय।
do roTiyaan aur ek chaay. [doh roh-Ti-yah(n) awr ayk chah-ay]
Two rotis and one chai. (a complete, polite order all by itself)

The honorific plural — respect by grammar

Here is the most Indian piece of grammar in this book. To show respect, Hindi treats one person as many. You've already met it: aap takes hain even for one listener. The same upgrade applies to anyone respected — parents, in-laws, teachers, elders — whenever you talk about them:

पिताजी आ रहे हैं।
pitaajee aa rahe hain. [pi-tah-jee ah ruh-hay heh(n)]
Father is coming. (lit. father coming are — plural out of respect; “aa rahe hain” is a chunk for now)
मम्मी जी आ रही हैं।
mummy jee aa rahee hain. [mum-mee jee ah ruh-hee heh(n)]
Mom is coming. (feminine form keeps its -ee, but the verb still goes plural: hain)
शर्मा जी ठीक हैं।
Sharma jee Theek hain. [shur-mah jee Theek heh(n)]
Sharma-ji is fine. (one man, plural verb — respect)

Using singular hai about someone's father isn't just casual — it can sound disrespectful. When in doubt about an elder, go plural.

लोग — people, made explicit

लोग (log (m)) [lohg] means “people”, and Delhi bolts it onto pronouns to mean “…and the gang”: हम लोग (ham log) “we all”, तुम लोग (tum log) “you lot”, आप लोग (aap log) “you all (polite)”, वो लोग (voh log) “they”.

आप लोग कैसे हैं?
aap log kaise hain? [ahp lohg keh-say heh(n)]
How are you all? (the standard greeting to a room)
हम लोग ठीक हैं।
ham log Theek hain. [hum lohg Theek heh(n)]
We're (all) fine.

Numbers you need right now

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
एकekaykone
दोdodohtwo
तीनteenteenthree
चारchaarchahrfour

Numbers take the plural noun: दो लड़के (do laRke), तीन किताबें (teen kitaaben), चार समोसे (chaar samose). The full 0–100 lives in Book 3.

Two English habits to unlearn. First, no -s, ever: “do samosas” is Hinglish, not Hindi — say दो समोसे (do samose). Second, don't force endings onto unchanged masculines: घरें (gharen) doesn't exist. Two houses are simply दो घर (do ghar) — the -en ending belongs to feminine nouns only.

Ordering like a local. At a tea stall nobody says “do chaayen”. Drinks ordered by the cup keep the bare noun: भैया, दो चाय देना। (bhaiyaa, do chaay denaa.) — or count the cups: दो कप चाय (do kap chaay) [doh kup chah-ay]. That trailing denaa is the casual “give (us), would you” — friendly, not bossy. Food still pluralizes normally: चार समोसे देना। (chaar samose denaa.)

Everyone is family. भैया (bhaiyaa (m)) [bheh-yah] literally means “older brother”, and दीदी (deedee (f)) [dee-dee] “older sister” — but in Delhi they're how you warmly address any vendor, auto driver, or shop assistant of roughly your age. Kinship words double as street courtesy; Book 3 hands you the whole set, aunty jee and uncle jee included.

Exercise 4A — Write the plural

Exercise 4C — Translate into Hindi

chapters.book2-u05:
Unit 5 Possession: kaa, ke, kee & apnaa

What you'll be able to say: whose everything is — my name, your phone, Rahul's house, my mother-in-law's legendary cooking — with the little linking word dressed to match the right noun.

यह जैकब की किताब है।
yeh Jacob kee kitaab hai. [yeh jay-kub kee ki-tahb heh]
This is Jacob's book.
मेरा नाम जैकब है।
meraa naam Jacob hai. [may-rah nahm jay-kub heh]
My name is Jacob.
ये मेरे ससुर हैं।
ye mere sasur hain. [yay may-ray suh-sur heh(n)]
This is my father-in-law. (plural mere + hain — respect!)

का / के / की — Hindi's apostrophe-s

To say “X's Y”, Hindi puts a linking word between owner and thing: owner + kaa/ke/kee + thing. Now the rule that trips up every English speaker, so read it twice:

The linker agrees with the THING POSSESSED — never with the owner.

The thing possessed is…LinkerExample
masculine, oneका (kaa) kahराहुल का घर Rahul kaa ghar (m) rah-hul kah ghur — Rahul's house
masculine, manyके (ke) kayराहुल के जूते Rahul ke joote (m pl) rah-hul kay joo-tay — Rahul's shoes
feminine, one or manyकी (kee) keeराहुल की किताबें Rahul kee kitaaben (f pl) rah-hul kee ki-tah-bay(n) — Rahul's books

So Jacob — very much a man — still says Jacob kee kitaab, because kitaab is feminine. And Neha's phone takes masculine kaa, because fon is masculine:

वह नेहा का फ़ोन है।
voh Neha kaa fon hai. [voh nay-hah kah fohn heh]
That is Neha's phone. (kaa matches fon (m), not Neha)
यह पूजा की गाड़ी है।
yeh Pooja kee gaaRee hai. [yeh poo-jah kee gah-Ree heh]
This is Pooja's car.
ये शर्मा जी के बेटे हैं।
ye Sharma jee ke beTe hain. [yay shur-mah jee kay bay-Tay heh(n)]
These are Sharma-ji's sons. (ke — beTe is m plural)

Don't match the owner. The instinct is “Pooja is a woman, so… Pooja kee everything”. No: पूजा का घर (Pooja kaa ghar), because ghar is masculine — and जैकब की चाय (Jacob kee chaay), because chaay is feminine. Eyes on the thing, not the owner.

Sharp eyes may protest: signs in Delhi say things like लड़के की किताब (laRke kee kitaab) “the boy's book” — why laRke and not laRkaa? Before a linker like kaa/ke/kee, the owner noun slips into a special form called the oblique. That's Unit 7's whole job. Until then, stick to owners that don't change shape: names, pitaajee, bhaaee, maan.

my, your, his, her, our — the full set

Pronoun owners fuse with the linker into one word, and each has the same three shapes: -aa before an m singular, -e before an m plural (and, as you'll see below, for honorifics), -ee before anything feminine.

Owner+ m thing+ m pl things+ f thing(s)Meaning
मैं mainमेरा meraa may-rahमेरे mere may-rayमेरी meree may-reemy
तू tuतेरा teraa tay-rahतेरे tere tay-rayतेरी teree tay-reeyour (intimate — same cautions as tu)
तुम tumतुम्हारा tumhaaraa tum-hah-rahतुम्हारे tumhaare tum-hah-rayतुम्हारी tumhaaree tum-hah-reeyour (informal)
आप aapआपका aapkaa ahp-kahआपके aapke ahp-kayआपकी aapkee ahp-keeyour (respectful)
यह yehइसका iskaa is-kahइसके iske is-kayइसकी iskee is-keehis / her / its (nearby)
वह vohउसका uskaa us-kahउसके uske us-kayउसकी uskee us-keehis / her / its
हम hamहमारा hamaaraa huh-mah-rahहमारे hamaare huh-mah-rayहमारी hamaaree huh-mah-reeour
वो लोग voh logउनका unkaa un-kahउनके unke un-kayउनकी unkee un-keetheir — and his/her for one respected person

Note the last row: just as respected people get plural verbs (Unit 4), they get the plural possessive. Talking about your father-in-law's car? उनकी गाड़ी (unkee gaaRee), not uskee — uskaa/uskee about an elder sounds blunt.

आपका नाम क्या है?
aapkaa naam kyaa hai? [ahp-kah nahm kyah heh]
What is your name? (Unit 2's chunk — now fully decoded: naam is m, so aapkaa)
तुम्हारा फ़ोन कहाँ है?
tumhaaraa fon kahaan hai? [tum-hah-rah fohn kuh-hah(n) heh]
Where is your phone? (to your partner)
हमारा घर दिल्ली में है।
hamaaraa ghar dillee mein hai. [huh-mah-rah ghur dil-lee may(n) heh]
Our house is in Delhi.
उसकी गाड़ी यहाँ है।
uskee gaaRee yahaan hai. [us-kee gah-Ree yuh-hah(n) heh]
His car is here. — or her car; uskee only marks the car's gender.
उनका नाम अमित शर्मा है।
unkaa naam Amit Sharma hai. [un-kah nahm uh-mit shur-mah heh]
His name is Amit Sharma. (unkaa — speaking respectfully of one man)

Family words — where possession lives

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
माँmaan (f)mah(n)mom, mother
पिताजीpitaajee (m)pi-tah-jeefather (respectful)
भाईbhaaee (m)bhah-eebrother
बहनbehen (f)beh-hensister
दीदीdeedee (f)dee-deeolder sister
पतिpati (m)puh-tihusband
पत्नीpatnee (f)put-neewife
सासsaas (f)sahsmother-in-law
ससुरsasur (m)suh-surfather-in-law
बेटाbeTaa (m)bay-Tahson
बेटीbeTee (f)bay-Teedaughter

Here the honorific plural (Unit 4) meets possession, and it's worth engraving: for elders you respect, the possessive goes plural even for one person — mere sasur, mere pitaajee — and the feminine form, being identical in singular and plural, just takes the plural verb:

ये मेरी सास हैं।
ye meree saas hain. [yay may-ree sahs heh(n)]
This is my mother-in-law. (meree + hain)
ये मेरे ससुर हैं।
ye mere sasur hain. [yay may-ray suh-sur heh(n)]
This is my father-in-law. (mere, never meraa — the plural IS the respect)
मेरे पिताजी दिल्ली में रहते हैं।
mere pitaajee dillee mein rehte hain. [may-ray pi-tah-jee dil-lee may(n) reh-tay heh(n)]
My father lives in Delhi. (“rehte hain” — the respectful-plural chunk of rehnaa)
यह मेरी पत्नी है।
yeh meree patnee hai. [yeh may-ree put-nee heh]
This is my wife.
मेरी सास का खाना बहुत अच्छा है।
meree saas kaa khaanaa bahut achchhaa hai. [may-ree sahs kah khah-nah bo-hut uch-chhah heh]
My mother-in-law's food is very good. (chains happily: meree saas → kaa khaanaa, each linker matching its own noun)

In-law etiquette, Delhi edition. saas and sasur are words you use about your in-laws, never to their faces. To their faces, most Delhi households run on मम्मी जी (mummy jee) [mum-mee jee] and पापा जी (paapaa jee) [pah-pah jee] — yes, you call them Mom and Dad too, and it delights them. Always aap, always plural forms, and praising the khaanaa is the fastest route to their hearts.

अपना — one's own

अपना (apnaa) [up-nah] is a special possessive meaning “belonging to whoever the subject is”. Rule of thumb: when the owner IS the subject of the sentence, Hindi swaps meraa/tumhaaraa/uskaa… for apnaa (which agrees the usual way: apnaa/apne/apnee [up-nah / up-nay / up-nee]). The verbs below are chunks from Unit 1's pattern — the machinery arrives in Unit 9:

मैं अपना खाना खा रहा हूँ।
main apnaa khaanaa khaa rahaa hoon. [meh(n) up-nah khah-nah khah ruh-hah hoo(n)]
I'm eating my (own) food. (male speaker; female: khaa rahee hoon)
वह अपनी चाय पी रहा है।
voh apnee chaay pee rahaa hai. [voh up-nee chah-ay pee ruh-hah heh]
He's drinking his own chai. (a woman: pee rahee hai)
वह उसकी चाय पी रहा है।
voh uskee chaay pee rahaa hai. [voh us-kee chah-ay pee ruh-hah heh]
He's drinking HIS chai — somebody else's! (uskee = another person's; apnee = his own. One word saves a friendship.)
अपना ख़्याल रखना।
apnaa khyaal rakhnaa. [up-nah khyahl rukh-nah]
Take care of yourself. (the classic sign-off — steal it for texts today)

With plain honaa sentences like यह मेरा घर है you don't need apnaa at all — it earns its keep once sentences have action verbs. File the idea now, use it fully from Unit 8 onward.

The double-my error. English says “I'm eating my food”, so learners produce मैं मेरा खाना खा रहा हूँ (main meraa khaanaa…) — instantly foreign. When the subject owns it, it's apnaa: मैं अपना खाना खा रहा हूँ। (main apnaa khaanaa khaa rahaa hoon.)

Possession, Delhi-style. English nouns slide right into the pattern: आपका नंबर क्या है? (aapkaa nambar kyaa hai?) [ahp-kah num-bur kyah heh] “what's your (phone) number?” — the polite way to stay in touch. And everyone's relatives are फ़ैमिली (faimilee (f)) [feh-mi-lee]: आपकी फ़ैमिली कैसी है? (aapkee faimilee kaisee hai?) “how's your family?” — small talk gold at any Delhi gathering.

Exercise 5A — kaa, ke, or kee?

Fill in का (kaa), के (ke), or की (kee). The bracketed hint tells you what the thing is. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 5.

  1. जैकब ___ किताब (Jacob ___ kitaab — Jacob's book)
  2. राहुल ___ घर (Rahul ___ ghar — Rahul's house)
  3. नेहा ___ फ़ोन (Neha ___ fon — Neha's phone)
  4. पूजा ___ गाड़ी (Pooja ___ gaaRee — Pooja's car)
  5. शर्मा जी ___ बेटे (Sharma jee ___ beTe — Sharma-ji's sons)
  6. मेरी सास ___ खाना (meree saas ___ khaanaa — my mother-in-law's food)
  7. भाई ___ कुर्सी (bhaaee ___ kursee — brother's chair)
  8. पिताजी ___ फ़ोन (pitaajee ___ fon — father's phone)
  9. अमित ___ किताबें (Amit ___ kitaaben — Amit's books)
  10. दीदी ___ जूते (deedee ___ joote — older sister's shoes)

Exercise 5B — Build the possessive

Combine the pronoun with the noun: write the correct possessive plus the noun, e.g. (मैं) + चाय → मेरी चाय. Watch item 6! Answers: Answer Key, Unit 5.

  1. (मैं) + किताब ((main) + kitaab)
  2. (आप) + घर ((aap) + ghar)
  3. (तुम) + फ़ोन ((tum) + fon)
  4. (हम) + बेटी ((ham) + beTee)
  5. (वह) + गाड़ी ((voh) + gaaRee)
  6. (मैं) + ससुर ((main) + sasur — careful: respect!)
  7. (आप) + किताबें ((aap) + kitaaben)

Exercise 5C — Translate into Hindi

Write the Hindi sentence — Devanagari on one line, roman on the other. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 5.

  1. My name is Jacob.
  2. What is your name? (respectful)
  3. This is my wife.
  4. This is my father-in-law. (respect!)
  5. Where is your phone? (to your partner)
  6. Our house is in Delhi.
  7. Rahul's car is here.

Exercise 5D — Translate into English

Write the English meaning. Watch for honorific plurals and for apnaa. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 5.

  1. आपका घर कहाँ है? (aapkaa ghar kahaan hai?)
  2. ये मेरी सास हैं। (ye meree saas hain.)
  3. मेरी सास का खाना बहुत अच्छा है। (meree saas kaa khaanaa bahut achchhaa hai.)
  4. यह उसका फ़ोन नहीं है। (yeh uskaa fon naheen hai.)
  5. अपना ख़्याल रखना! (apnaa khyaal rakhnaa!)
  6. तुम्हारी चाय कहाँ है? (tumhaaree chaay kahaan hai?)
chapters.book2-u06:
Unit 6 Adjectives & Agreement

What you'll be able to say: what things are like — good, big, hot, new, red — with the endings dancing in step with gender and number, plus the question that fishes for compliments: kaisaa?

खाना बहुत अच्छा है!
khaanaa bahut achchhaa hai! [khah-nah bo-hut uch-chhah heh]
The food is very good! (your most useful sentence at any Delhi table)
चाय अच्छी है।
chaay achchhee hai. [chah-ay uch-chhee heh]
The chai is good. (same adjective, feminine dress)
दिल्ली बड़ी है!
dillee baRee hai! [dil-lee buh-Ree heh]
Delhi is big! (dillee is f, so baRee)

Two teams of adjectives

Hindi adjectives split into two teams, and the split is easy to see. Marked adjectives end in -aa and change their ending to agree, exactly like meraa/mere/meree did in Unit 5. Unmarked adjectives end in anything else and never change at all — one shape, every situation.

Here is the whole marked pattern, using achchhaa “good”:

Goes with…FormSay itExample
m singularअच्छा achchhaauch-chhahअच्छा लड़का achchhaa laRkaa (m) uch-chhah luhR-kah — good boy
m plural (and honorifics)अच्छे achchheuch-chhayअच्छे लड़के achchhe laRke uch-chhay luhR-kay — good boys
f singular and pluralअच्छी achchheeuch-chheeअच्छी लड़कियाँ achchhee laRkiyaan (f) uch-chhee luhR-ki-yah(n) — good girls

One elegant detail: with unchanging masculine nouns, the adjective is what shows the plural — बड़ा घर (baRaa ghar) [buh-Rah ghur] “big house” but बड़े घर (baRe ghar) [buh-Ray ghur] “big houses”.

The marked team (-aa, they agree)

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
अच्छाachchhaauch-chhahgood
बड़ाbaRaabuh-Rahbig
छोटाchhoTaachhoh-Tahsmall
लंबाlambaalum-bahtall, long
मोटाmoTaamoh-Tahfat, thick
नयाnayaanuh-yahnew (irregular spelling: m pl नए naye, f नई nayee)
पुरानाpuraanaapu-rah-nahold (for things)
ठंडाThanDaaThun-Dahcold
मीठाmeeThaamee-Thahsweet
सस्ताsastaasus-tahcheap
महंगाmehngaamehn-gahexpensive

The unmarked team (one shape, zero fuss)

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
लालlaallahlred
साफ़saafsahfclean
सुंदरsundarsun-durbeautiful
ख़ूबसूरतkhoobsooratkhoob-soo-rutgorgeous
ग़रीबgareebguh-reebpoor
अमीरameeruh-meerrich
गरमgaramguh-rumhot, warm
ख़राबkharaabkhuh-rahbbad, broken
ख़ुशkhushkhushhappy
आसानaasaanah-sahneasy
मुश्किलmushkilmush-kildifficult
मज़ेदारmazedaarmuh-zay-dahrtasty, fun

So: लाल किताब (laal kitaab), लाल किताबें (laal kitaaben), सुंदर लड़की (sundar laRkee), साफ़ कमरा (saaf kamraa) — the adjective never blinks.

Agreement in action

यह कमरा साफ़ है।
yeh kamraa saaf hai. [yeh kum-rah sahf heh]
This room is clean.
चाय गरम है और समोसे भी गरम हैं।
chaay garam hai aur samose bhee garam hain. [chah-ay guh-rum heh awr suh-moh-say bhee guh-rum heh(n)]
The chai is hot and the samosas are hot too. (bhee = also; garam never changes)
लड़के लंबे हैं।
laRke lambe hain. [luhR-kay lum-bay heh(n)]
The boys are tall.
मेरी गाड़ी नई नहीं है, पुरानी है।
meree gaaRee nayee naheen hai, puraanee hai. [may-ree gah-Ree nuh-ee nuh-hee(n) heh, pu-rah-nee heh]
My car isn't new, it's old.
ऑटो महंगा है, मेट्रो सस्ती है।
auTo mehngaa hai, meTro sastee hai. [aw-Toh mehn-gah heh, may-Troh sus-tee heh]
The auto is expensive, the metro is cheap. (a very Delhi observation)
मेरे ससुर बहुत अच्छे हैं।
mere sasur bahut achchhe hain. [may-ray suh-sur bo-hut uch-chhay heh(n)]
My father-in-law is very nice. (honorific plural pulls the adjective plural too: achchhe)
मेरी सास बहुत अच्छी हैं।
meree saas bahut achchhee hain. [may-ree sahs bo-hut uch-chhee heh(n)]
My mother-in-law is very nice. (feminine keeps achchhee; the respect shows in hain)

Before the noun or before the verb — same agreement

An adjective can sit attributively (right before its noun) or predicatively (across the verb “is”). Either way it agrees with the same noun:

यह अच्छी किताब है।
yeh achchhee kitaab hai. [yeh uch-chhee ki-tahb heh]
This is a good book. (attributive: achchhee kitaab)
यह किताब अच्छी है।
yeh kitaab achchhee hai. [yeh ki-tahb uch-chhee heh]
This book is good. (predicative: same achchhee)

He says, she says — speaker gender

When the adjective describes you, your own gender picks the form. Jacob uses masculine forms; his partner uses feminine ones; and unmarked adjectives shrug at the whole question:

मैं अच्छा हूँ।
main achchhaa hoon. [meh(n) uch-chhah hoo(n)]
I'm good. (male speaker — Jacob's line)
मैं अच्छी हूँ।
main achchhee hoon. [meh(n) uch-chhee hoo(n)]
I'm good. (female speaker — his partner's line)
मैं बहुत ख़ुश हूँ।
main bahut khush hoon. [meh(n) bo-hut khush hoo(n)]
I'm very happy. (khush is unmarked — one line for everyone)

Asking “what's it like?” — kaisaa

कैसा (kaisaa) [keh-sah] “how / what like” is itself a marked adjective, so it agrees with whatever you're asking about: kaisaa / kaise / kaisee [keh-sah / keh-say / keh-see]. And now Unit 2's greeting decodes itself: आप कैसे हैं? (aap kaise hain?) is literally “you how are?” with kaise in the honorific plural — kaisee when asking a woman.

खाना कैसा है?
khaanaa kaisaa hai? [khah-nah keh-sah heh]
How's the food?
चाय कैसी है? — एकदम बढ़िया!
chaay kaisee hai? — ekdam baRhiyaa! [chah-ay keh-see heh — ayk-dum buh-Rhi-yah]
How's the chai? — Absolutely first-rate!

The -saa softener: chhoTaa-saa

Bolt -सा (-saa) [sah] onto an adjective and it softens: “-ish, kind of, a cute little”. It agrees just like -aa adjectives (-saa/-se/-see): छोटा-सा घर (chhoTaa-saa ghar) “a cute little house”, प्यारा-सा (pyaaraa-saa) [pyah-rah sah] “adorable little”, थोड़ा-सा खाना (thoRaa-saa khaanaa) [thoh-Rah sah khah-nah] “just a little food”:

थोड़ी-सी चाय, बस।
thoRee-see chaay, bas. [thoh-Ree see chah-ay, bus]
Just a little chai, that's all. (the polite second-cup surrender)

Colors — a preview

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
लालlaallahlred — never changes
पीलाpeelaapee-lahyellow — marked: peele, peelee
नीलाneelaanee-lahblue — marked
हराharaahuh-rahgreen — marked
कालाkaalaakah-lahblack — marked
सफ़ेदsafedsuh-faydwhite — never changes
गुलाबीgulaabeegu-lah-beepink — never changes (-ee adjectives are invariable)
केले पीले हैं।
kele peele hain. [kay-lay pee-lay heh(n)]
The bananas are yellow.
मेरी कमीज़ सफ़ेद है।
meree kameez safed hai. [may-ree kuh-meez suh-fayd heh]
My shirt is white. (kameez (f) = shirt; safed stays safed)

Impostors on both teams. बढ़िया (baRhiyaa) [buh-Rhi-yah] “first-rate” ends in -aa but never changes: baRhiyaa chaay, baRhiyaa samose. Adjectives ending in -ee, like gulaabee, are likewise invariable. The vocab chapters in Book 3 flag every invariable adjective, so you never have to guess.

Two agreement slips to avoid. First, feminine nouns with masculine endings: चाय अच्छा है (chaay achchhaa hai) is wrong — चाय अच्छी है। (chaay achchhee hai.) Second, don't “feminize” unmarked adjectives: there is no laalee or sundaree — it's लाल साड़ी (laal saaRee) and सुंदर लड़की (sundar laRkee). Only the -aa team changes clothes.

Delhi's favourite compliments. Forget plain achchhaa — the street superlatives are मस्त (mast) [must] “awesome”, ज़बरदस्त (zabardast) [zuh-bur-dust] “tremendous”, and the intensifier एकदम (ekdam) [ayk-dum] “totally”. All conveniently invariable: चाय एकदम मस्त है! (chaay ekdam mast hai!) — फ़िल्म ज़बरदस्त है! (film zabardast hai!) [film zuh-bur-dust heh] (फ़िल्म film (f) = movie).

Colors carry meaning. laal is the color of weddings and good luck — brides traditionally wear red, and a लाल साड़ी (laal saaRee) is festive dress, while plain white clothing is traditionally linked with mourning. Complimenting an outfit? बहुत सुंदर! (bahut sundar!) [bo-hut sun-dur] works every time. More on festival colors when होली (holee) [hoh-lee] — the festival of colors itself — shows up in Book 3.

Exercise 6A — Dress the adjective

Write the correct form of the adjective in brackets. Careful — some never change! Answers: Answer Key, Unit 6.

  7. ___ पानी (ThanDaa + paanee)
  8. ___ गाड़ी (nayaa + gaaRee)

  10. ___ मेज़ें (puraanaa + mezen)

  6. मोटा कुत्ता → (कुत्ते) (moTaa kuttaa → kutte)

Exercise 6C — Translate into Hindi

Write the Hindi sentence — Devanagari on one line, roman on the other. Item 7 wants both speaker versions. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 6.

  1. The chai is hot.
  2. The water is cold.
  3. This is a good book.
  4. My house is small.
  5. The boys are tall.
  6. How is the food?
  7. I am good. (male speaker AND female speaker)

Exercise 6D — Translate into English

Write the English meaning. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 6.

  1. चाय बहुत अच्छी है। (chaay bahut achchhee hai.)
  2. यह कमरा साफ़ नहीं है। (yeh kamraa saaf naheen hai.)

  5. थोड़ी-सी चाय, बस। (thoRee-see chaay, bas.)

chapters.book2-u07:
Unit 7 Postpositions & the Oblique Case

What you'll be able to say: where things and people are (in, on, under, behind…), who something is for, who you're with — and "I have…". This is the hinge unit of the whole book: master it and Units 8–24 open up.

मैं दिल्ली में रहता हूँ।
main dillee mein rehtaa hoon. [meh(n) dil-lee may(n) reh-tah hoo(n)]
I live in Delhi. (lit. I Delhi-in living am)
मेरे पास दो टिकट हैं।
mere paas do TikaT hain. [may-ray pahs doh Ti-kuT heh(n)]
I have two tickets. (lit. my near two tickets are)
यह तोहफ़ा तुम्हारे लिए है।
yeh tohfaa tumhaare liye hai. [yeh toh-fah tum-hah-ray li-yeh heh]
This gift is for you. (lit. this gift your-for is)

Postpositions: little words that come AFTER

English puts its little relation words before the noun: in Delhi, on the table, for you. Hindi puts them after — that's why they're called postpositions: दिल्ली में (dillee mein) [dil-lee may(n)], मेज़ पर (mez par) [mayz pur]. First learn the words themselves; then the one big rule about what they do to the noun in front of them.

The simple postpositions

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
मेंmeinmay(n)in, inside
परparpuron, at
सेsesayfrom; by (a vehicle/tool); with (a person you talk to)
कोkokohto (a person); "to-me" phrases (star of Unit 10)
तकtaktukuntil, up to, as far as
का / के / कीkaa / ke / keekah / kay / kee's (possessive — yes, it's a postposition too!)

The compound postpositions (के + word)

These are two-word postpositions built on के (ke) [kay] — one is built on से (se). Learn them as fixed chunks.

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
के लिएke liyekay li-yayfor
के पासke paaskay pahsnear; "have" (see below)
के साथke saathkay sahthwith, together with

पर (par) [pur] = on (touching): किताब मेज़ पर है (kitaab mez par hai) [ki-tahb mayz pur heh] — the book is on the table. के ऊपर (ke oopar) = above (in the air over it): मेज़ के ऊपर पंखा है (mez ke oopar pankhaa hai) [mayz kay oo-pur pun-khah heh] — above the table there's a fan.

The oblique case: nouns change before a postposition

Here is the big rule. Before any postposition, the noun switches from its normal (direct) form to its oblique form. The changes are small and regular:

In words: masculine -aa becomes -e in the singular (लड़का → लड़के को laRke ko [luhR-kay koh]); every plural of every gender ends in -ों (-on) [oh(n)] before a postposition (लड़कों को laRkon ko [luhR-koh(n) koh], घरों में gharon mein [ghuh-roh(n) may(n)], लड़कियों को laRkiyon ko [luhR-ki-yoh(n) koh]). Feminine singulars never change. Masculine nouns not in -aa (घर, दोस्त dost [dohst]) don't change in the singular either.

Yes — oblique singular लड़के looks exactly like direct plural लड़के ("boys"). The postposition is your clue: लड़के अच्छे हैं (laRke achchhe hain) [luhR-kay uch-chhay heh(n)] "the boys are good" (plural, no postposition) vs. लड़के का नाम (laRke kaa naam) [luhR-kay kah nahm] "the boy's name" (singular + postposition). This is also why Unit 5's possessive phrases already used लड़के का — का is a postposition, so the noun before it went oblique all along.

Adjectives (and मेरा, यह, वह) go oblique too

Everything hanging on the noun matches it. An -aa adjective becomes -e before an oblique masculine noun — singular and plural. Feminine adjectives in -ee stay put. यह/वह have their own oblique forms: इस (is) [is] and उस (us) [us]; plural ये → इन (in), वे → उन (un).

Direct phraseOblique (before postposition)
अच्छा लड़का achchhaa laRkaaअच्छे लड़के को achchhe laRke ko
अच्छे लड़के achchhe laRke (pl)अच्छे लड़कों को achchhe laRkon ko

Two errors to hunt down in your own speech. (1) Putting the little word first, English-style: ✗ में दिल्ली — it's always दिल्ली में (dillee mein). (2) Forgetting the oblique: ✗ मेरा घर में, ✗ अच्छा लड़के को. Once the postposition appears, the whole phrase bends: मेरे घर में (mere ghar mein) [may-ray ghur may(n)], अच्छे लड़के को. Say the phrase as one unit and the -e endings start coming automatically.

Pronouns + postpositions

Pronouns have special oblique stems, and with को most of them fuse into a one-word short form — the short forms are what people actually say. In writing, से/को/का attach to the pronoun (मुझसे); पर is usually written separately (मुझ पर mujh par [mujh pur]); "in it/this" is इसमें ismein [is-may(n)], "in that" उसमें usmein [us-may(n)].

Say the short forms until they're reflexes: मुझे [mu-jhay], तुझे [tu-jhay], इसे [i-say], उसे [u-say], हमें [huh-may(n)], तुम्हें [tum-hay(n)], इन्हें [in-hay(n)], उन्हें [un-hay(n)]. Unit 10 runs on them.

On the street, पर (par) shrinks to पे (pe) [pay]: घर पे (ghar pe), छत पे (chhat pe) [chhut pay] "on the roof". And Delhiites constantly say मेरे को (mere ko) [may-ray koh] and तेरे को (tere ko) for मुझे/तुझे — pure Dilli style. Understand it, enjoy it, but say मुझे yourself, especially with the in-laws; मेरे को is very casual and technically "wrong".

के पास = have

Hindi has no verb "to have". For things you own or carry, park them near yourself: X के पास Y है — "near X there is Y".

मेरे पास नया फ़ोन है।
mere paas nayaa fon hai. [may-ray pahs nuh-yah fohn heh]
I have a new phone. (lit. my near new phone is)
क्या तुम्हारे पास टाइम है?
kyaa tumhaare paas Taim hai? [kyah tum-hah-ray pahs Taym heh]
Do you have time?
उसके पास गाड़ी नहीं है।
uske paas gaaRee naheen hai. [us-kay pahs gah-Ree nuh-hee(n) heh]
He/she doesn't have a car.

के पास is for things, money, time — not for people in your family. Relatives use plain possessives from Unit 5: मेरे दो भाई हैं (mere do bhaaee hain) [may-ray doh bhah-ee heh(n)] "I have two brothers", मेरी एक बहन है (meree ek behen hai) [may-ree ayk beh-hen heh]. Saying ✗ मेरे पास दो भाई हैं sounds like you keep two brothers in your pocket.

के पास also keeps its literal meaning "near": घर के पास एक पार्क है (ghar ke paas ek paark hai) [ghur kay pahs ayk pahrk heh] — there's a park near the house.

Saying where things are

किताब मेज़ पर है।
kitaab mez par hai. [ki-tahb mayz pur heh]
The book is on the table.
दूध फ़्रिज में है।
doodh frij mein hai. [doodh frij may(n) heh]
The milk is in the fridge.
बच्चे कमरे के अंदर हैं।
bachche kamre ke andar hain. [buch-chay kum-ray kay un-dur heh(n)]
The children are inside the room.
गाड़ी घर के बाहर है।
gaaRee ghar ke baahar hai. [gah-Ree ghur kay bah-hur heh]
The car is outside the house.
बैंक होटल के सामने है।
baink hoTal ke saamne hai. [behnk hoh-Tul kay sahm-nay heh]
The bank is in front of the hotel.
मंदिर के पीछे एक छोटा बाज़ार है।
mandir ke peechhe ek chhoTaa baazaar hai. [mun-dir kay pee-chhay ayk chhoh-Tah bah-zahr heh]
Behind the temple there's a small market.
मेरा फ़ोन तकिये के नीचे है।
meraa fon takiye ke neeche hai. [may-rah fohn tuh-ki-yay kay nee-chay heh]
My phone is under the pillow. (takiyaa (m) → oblique takiye)
दुकान सुबह से शाम तक खुली है।
dukaan subah se shaam tak khulee hai. [du-kahn su-beh say shahm tuk khu-lee heh]
The shop is open from morning till evening.
क्लास से पहले मैं घर पर हूँ।
klaas se pehle main ghar par hoon. [klahs say peh-lay meh(n) ghur pur hoo(n)]
Before class I'm at home. (ghar par = at home — idiom, not "on the house"!)
खाने के बाद चाय ज़रूरी है।
khaane ke baad chaay zarooree hai. [khah-nay kay bahd chah-ay zuh-roo-ree heh]
After food, chai is essential. (khaanaa (m) → oblique khaane)
जैकब अपने दोस्तों के साथ बाज़ार में है।
jaikab apne doston ke saath baazaar mein hai. [jeh-kub up-nay dohs-toh(n) kay sahth bah-zahr may(n) heh]
Jacob is at the market with his friends. (dost → pl. oblique doston)
लड़कों के पास नई किताबें हैं।
laRkon ke paas naee kitaaben hain. [luhR-koh(n) kay pahs nuh-ee ki-tah-bay(n) heh(n)]
The boys have new books.
मैं मेट्रो से ऑफ़िस जाता हूँ।
main meTro se ofis jaataa hoon. [meh(n) may-Troh say aw-fis jah-tah hoo(n)]
I go to the office by metro. (se = by; jaataa hoon "I go" — full pattern in Unit 8)
यह चाय आपके लिए है, और वह मेरे लिए।
yeh chaay aapke liye hai, aur voh mere liye. [yeh chah-ay ahp-kay li-yeh heh, awr voh may-ray li-yeh]

Delhi life happens on the छत (chhat (f)) [chhut] — the flat rooftop. Winter sun, pigeons, kite-flying, evening chai: छत पर चाय (chhat par chaay) [chhut pur chah-ay]. If your in-laws say चलो, छत पे बैठते हैं (chalo, chhat pe baiThte hain) [chuh-loh, chhut pay behTh-tay heh(n)] "come, let's sit on the roof", that's an invitation into the family's living room.

Exercise 7A — Fill in the postposition

Write the postposition that fits: में, पर, से, तक, or the right part of a compound (लिए, पास, साथ, बाद, पहले, सामने, बाहर…). Answers: Answer Key, Unit 7.

  1. दूध फ़्रिज ___ है। (doodh frij ___ hai.)
  2. किताबें मेज़ ___ हैं। (kitaaben mez ___ hain.)
  3. यह चाय आपके ___ है। (yeh chaay aapke ___ hai.)
  4. मेरे ___ दो टिकट हैं। (mere ___ do TikaT hain.)
  5. दुकान सुबह ___ शाम ___ खुली है। (dukaan subah ___ shaam ___ khulee hai.)
  6. जैकब अपने दोस्तों के ___ है। (jaikab apne doston ke ___ hai.)
  7. खाने के ___ चाय ज़रूरी है। (khaane ke ___ chaay zarooree hai.)
  8. क्लास से ___ मैं घर पर हूँ। (klaas se ___ main ghar par hoon.)
  9. बैंक होटल के ___ है। (baink hoTal ke ___ hai.)
  10. गाड़ी घर के ___ है। (gaaRee ghar ke ___ hai.)

Exercise 7B — Make it oblique

Combine the noun phrase with the postposition, changing everything that must change. Example: लड़का + को → लड़के को.

  1. लड़का + को (laRkaa + ko)
  2. लड़के (pl) + को (laRke pl + ko)
  3. कमरा + में (kamraa + mein)
  4. घर (pl) + में (ghar pl + mein)
  5. लड़की + को (laRkee + ko)
  6. लड़कियाँ + को (laRkiyaan + ko)
  7. अच्छा लड़का + के साथ (achchhaa laRkaa + ke saath)
  8. मेरा भाई + के लिए (meraa bhaaee + ke liye)

Exercise 7C — Translate into Hindi

Write the Hindi in Devanagari (roman too if you like). Watch the obliques!

  1. The book is on the table.
  2. I have two brothers. (careful!)
  3. I have a new phone.
  4. The children are in the room.
  5. This gift is for my sister.
  6. The bank is in front of the hotel.
  7. Jacob is with his friends.

Unit 8 The Present Habitual

What you'll be able to say: what you do every day — where you live and work, what you eat and drink, when you get up and sleep — and ask the same about anyone else.

मैं रोज़ सुबह छह बजे उठता हूँ।
main roz subah chheh baje uThtaa hoon. [meh(n) rohz su-beh chheh buh-jay uTh-tah hoo(n)]
I get up at six every morning.
वह ऑफ़िस में काम करती है।
voh ofis mein kaam kartee hai. [voh aw-fis may(n) kahm kur-tee heh]
She works in an office.
हम रात को हिन्दी सीखते हैं।
ham raat ko hindee seekhte hain. [hum raht koh hin-dee seekh-tay heh(n)]
We study Hindi at night.

The pattern: stem + -ता/-ते/-ती + present of होना

The habitual describes what happens regularly or generally — English "I go", "she drinks". Build it in two pieces:

1. The stem. Chop -ना (-naa) off any infinitive: करना (karnaa) [kur-nah] → कर (kar).

2. The endings. Add -ता (-taa) for masculine singular, -ते (-te) for masculine plural, -ती (-tee) for feminine — the same -aa/-e/-ee music as adjectives in Unit 6 — then close the sentence with the matching present form of होना (हूँ / हो / है / हैं).

Say the two backbones aloud until they're automatic: करता हूँ [kur-tah hoo(n)], करते हो [kur-tay hoh], करते हैं [kur-tay heh(n)]; करती हूँ [kur-tee hoo(n)], करती हो [kur-tee hoh], करती हैं [kur-tee heh(n)]. Jacob uses the -ता column; his partner uses -ती. One respected person (आप, or a parent-in-law) gets the plural verb.
