हमेशाhameshaahuh-may-shahalways
कभी-कभीkabhee-kabheekuh-bhee kuh-bheesometimes
कभी नहींkabhee naheenkuh-bhee nuh-hee(n)never (verb stays negative too)
हर हफ़्तेhar hafte (haftaa m)hur huf-tayevery week
सुबह / शाम को / रात कोsubah (f) / shaam (f) ko / raat (f) kosu-beh / shahm koh / raht kohin the morning / evening / at night

Saying "don't": the habitual negative

Put नहीं (naheen) before the verb — and here's the twist: in the negative, the हूँ/है/हैं is usually dropped.

मैं गोश्त नहीं खाता।
main gosht naheen khaataa. [meh(n) gohsht nuh-hee(n) khah-tah]
I don't eat meat. (gosht (m)) (no hoon — dropped after naheen)
वह ज़्यादा टीवी नहीं देखती।
voh zyaadaa TeeVee naheen dekhtee. [voh zyah-dah Tee-Vee nuh-hee(n) daykh-tee]
She doesn't watch much TV.

Keeping the auxiliary (मैं गोश्त नहीं खाता हूँ) isn't wrong — just heavier. One real subtlety: when the auxiliary drops, a feminine plural verb takes the nasal itself: वे लोग नहीं जातीं (voh log naheen jaateen) [voh lohg nuh-hee(n) jah-tee(n)] "they (women) don't go". Recognize it; with the auxiliary it's plain जाती हैं.

Asking about habits

Yes/no questions: hang क्या on the front, voice rises at the end. Question words (कब, कहाँ, कितने बजे…) sit just before the verb phrase.

क्या आप गोश्त खाते हैं? — जी नहीं, मैं गोश्त नहीं खाता।
kyaa aap gosht khaate hain? — jee naheen, main gosht naheen khaataa. [kyah ahp gohsht khah-tay heh(n) — jee nuh-hee(n), meh(n) gohsht nuh-hee(n) khah-tah]
Do you eat meat? — No (politely), I don't eat meat.
तुम कब उठते हो?
tum kab uThte ho? [tum kub uTh-tay hoh]
When do you get up?

English speakers love to drop the auxiliary everywhere: ✗ मैं रोज़ जाता. In the affirmative the auxiliary is compulsory: मैं रोज़ जाता हूँ (main roz jaataa hoon). It disappears only in the negative (मैं नहीं जाता). And keep your gender on: Jacob says जाता हूँ, his partner says जाती हूँ — one mixed-up ending and the whole family will (lovingly) correct you.

Real Delhi habitual speech is half English nouns: मैं जिम जाता हूँ (main jim jaataa hoon) [meh(n) jim jah-tah hoo(n)], वह ऑफ़िस में काम करती है, वीकेंड पे मूवी देखते हैं (veekenD pe moovee dekhte hain) [vee-kenD pay moo-vee daykh-tay heh(n)]. And Delhiites seal statements with न? (na?) [nah]: तुम चाय पीते हो न? — "you drink chai, right?"

Morning-walk culture: every Delhi park at 6 a.m. is full of uncles and aunties on their सैर (sair (f)) [sehr] — brisk walking, louder gossip. मेरे ससुर रोज़ पार्क में सैर करते हैं (mere sasur roz paark mein sair karte hain) [may-ray suh-sur rohz pahrk may(n) sehr kur-tay heh(n)] "my father-in-law walks in the park daily" — note the respectful plural verb for one respected person; a respected lady gets करती हैं (kartee hain).

Exercise 8A — Fill in the habitual form

Put the bracketed verb into the correct habitual form (watch gender and number). Answers: Answer Key, Unit 8.

  5. आप कहाँ ___ (रहना)? — asking your father-in-law (aap kahaan ___ ?)
  6. मेरी बहन स्कूल में ___ (पढ़ना)। (meree behen skool mein ___ .)
  7. वे लोग हर हफ़्ते फ़िल्म ___ (देखना)। (voh log har hafte film ___ .)
  8. जैकब गोश्त नहीं ___ (खाना)। (jaikab gosht naheen ___ .)
  9. मेरे ससुर रोज़ पार्क में सैर ___ (करना)। (mere sasur roz paark mein sair ___ .)

Exercise 8C — Translate into Hindi

Exercise 8D — Translate into English

chapters.book2-u09:
Unit 9 The Present Continuous

What you'll be able to say: what's happening right now — what you're doing, what's cooking, who's sleeping — and hold the world's most common Hindi phone conversation.

मैं अभी खाना बना रहा हूँ।
main abhee khaanaa banaa rahaa hoon. [meh(n) uh-bhee khah-nah buh-nah ruh-hah hoo(n)]
I'm cooking right now.
क्या कर रहे हो?
kyaa kar rahe ho? [kyah kur ruh-hay hoh]
What are you doing? (THE phone-opener)
बारिश हो रही है।
baarish ho rahee hai. [bah-rish hoh ruh-hee heh]
It's raining. (baarish (f)) (lit. rain happening is)

The pattern: stem + रहा/रहे/रही + present of होना

For actions in progress, Hindi slips रहा between the stem and the auxiliary. रहा agrees in gender and number exactly like an -aa adjective: रहा (rahaa) [ruh-hah] m sg, रहे (rahe) [ruh-hay] m pl, रही (rahee) [ruh-hee] f. The auxiliary is the same हूँ/हो/है/हैं you already own.

SubjectMaleFemale
मैं mainकर रहा हूँ kar rahaa hoonकर रही हूँ kar rahee hoon
तू tuकर रहा है kar rahaa haiकर रही है kar rahee hai
यह / वह yeh / vohकर रहा है kar rahaa haiकर रही है kar rahee hai
तुम tumकर रहे हो kar rahe hoकर रही हो kar rahee ho
आप aapकर रहे हैं kar rahe hainकर रही हैं kar rahee hain
हम hamकर रहे हैं kar rahe hainकर रही हैं kar rahee hain
ये / वे लोग ye / voh logकर रहे हैं kar rahe hainकर रही हैं kar rahee hain

Habit vs. right now

English "I drink chai" vs. "I'm drinking chai" — Hindi makes exactly the same cut:

मैं चाय पीता हूँ।
main chaay peetaa hoon. [meh(n) chah-ay pee-tah hoo(n)]
I drink chai. (in general — it's my habit)
मैं चाय पी रहा हूँ।
main chaay pee rahaa hoon. [meh(n) chah-ay pee ruh-hah hoo(n)]
I'm drinking chai. (right now, cup in hand)
वह दिल्ली में रहती है। / वह आजकल दिल्ली में रह रही है।
voh dillee mein rehtee hai. / voh aajkal dillee mein reh rahee hai. [voh dil-lee may(n) reh-tee heh / voh ahj-kul dil-lee may(n) reh ruh-hee heh]
She lives in Delhi. / She's staying in Delhi these days (temporarily).

Right-now words

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
अभीabheeuh-bheeright now
इस वक़्तis vaqt (vaqt m)is vuktat this moment
इस समयis samay (samay m)is suh-mayat this time (slightly formal)
आजकलaajkalahj-kulthese days — for the stretched-out present
फ़िलहालfilhaalfil-hahlfor now, at present

आजकल (aajkal) [ahj-kul] "these days" loves the continuous for temporary situations: आजकल मैं हिन्दी सीख रहा हूँ (aajkal main hindee seekh rahaa hoon) — the learning is ongoing this season of life, not this minute. With a true permanent habit, आजकल takes the habitual instead.

Examples: Delhi in motion

मैं हिन्दी सीख रहा हूँ।
main hindee seekh rahaa hoon. [meh(n) hin-dee seekh ruh-hah hoo(n)]
I am learning Hindi.
चाय बन रही है।
chaay ban rahee hai. [chah-ay bun ruh-hee heh]
The chai is brewing. (bannaa = to get made — things "make themselves" in Hindi kitchens)
वह अभी नहा रही है।
voh abhee nahaa rahee hai. [voh uh-bhee nuh-hah ruh-hee heh]
She's showering right now.
बच्चे सो रहे हैं।
bachche so rahe hain. [buch-chay soh ruh-hay heh(n)]
The children are sleeping.
पापा अख़बार पढ़ रहे हैं।
paapaa akhbaar paRh rahe hain. [pah-pah ukh-bahr puRh ruh-hay heh(n)]
Papa is reading the newspaper. (akhbaar (m)) (one respected man → plural रहे हैं)
माँ खाना बना रही हैं।
maan khaanaa banaa rahee hain. [mah(n) khah-nah buh-nah ruh-hee heh(n)]
Mom is cooking. (respected woman: rahee stays feminine, auxiliary goes plural — banaa rahee HAIN)
हम अभी मेट्रो से आ रहे हैं।
ham abhee meTro se aa rahe hain. [hum uh-bhee may-Troh say ah ruh-hay heh(n)]
We're on our way by metro right now.
वे लोग आजकल गुड़गाँव में रह रहे हैं।
voh log aajkal guRgaanv mein reh rahe hain. [voh lohg ahj-kul guR-gah(n)v may(n) reh ruh-hay heh(n)]
They're living in Gurgaon these days.
क्या तुम सुन रहे हो?
kyaa tum sun rahe ho? [kyah tum sun ruh-hay hoh]
Are you listening?
मैं नहीं सुन रहा।
main naheen sun rahaa. [meh(n) nuh-hee(n) sun ruh-hah]
I'm not listening. (as in Unit 8, the auxiliary often drops after naheen)
मेरी सास मंदिर जा रही हैं।
meree saas mandir jaa rahee hain. [may-ree sahs mun-dir jah ruh-hee heh(n)]
My mother-in-law is going to the temple. (saas (f))

On the phone

The continuous is the engine of every Hindi phone call. A typical exchange between Jacob and his wife:

हैलो? क्या कर रहे हो?
hailo? kyaa kar rahe ho? [heh-loh — kyah kur ruh-hay hoh]
Hello? What are you doing?
कुछ नहीं, टीवी देख रहा हूँ। तुम कहाँ हो?
kuchh naheen, TeeVee dekh rahaa hoon. tum kahaan ho? [kuchh nuh-hee(n), Tee-Vee daykh ruh-hah hoo(n) — tum kuh-hah(n) hoh]
Nothing much, I'm watching TV. Where are you?
मैं आ रही हूँ, बस पाँच मिनट!
main aa rahee hoon, bas paanch minaT! [meh(n) ah ruh-hee hoo(n), bus pah(n)ch mi-nuT]
I'm coming — just five minutes! (minaT (m))
अच्छा, मैं बाद में फ़ोन करता हूँ।
achchhaa, main baad mein fon kartaa hoon. [uch-chhah, meh(n) bahd may(n) fohn kur-tah hoo(n)]
Okay, I'll call (you) later. (lit. I call later — habitual used for an immediate plan; more in Unit 12)

Don't let English's plain present fool you into the wrong direction: for something happening now, habitual is wrong — ✗ मैं अभी चाय पीता हूँ → ✓ मैं अभी चाय पी रहा हूँ (main abhee chaay pee rahaa hoon). And रहा carries your gender: Jacob says पी रहा हूँ, his wife says पी रही हूँ — रहे/रही slips are the number-one giveaway of a beginner.

Three Delhi essentials. (1) क्या चल रहा है? (kyaa chal rahaa hai?) [kyah chul ruh-hah heh] — "what's going on?", the standard what's-up. (2) बस पहुँच रहा हूँ (bas pahunch rahaa hoon) [bus puh-hu(n)ch ruh-hah hoo(n)] — "almost there!" Official meaning: arriving. Delhi meaning: has just left home. (3) In June: गर्मी पड़ रही है यार (garmee paR rahee hai yaar) [gur-mee puR ruh-hee heh yahr] — "it's roasting, yaar" (set phrase — learn it whole).

States don't like the continuous, same as English "I am knowing" is off. Being, knowing, liking use other patterns: मुझे पता है (mujhe pataa hai) [mu-jhay puh-tah heh] "I know" — that's Unit 10's machinery, coming next.

Exercise 9A — Fill in the continuous form

Put the bracketed verb into the present continuous. Watch gender, number, and respect. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 9.

chapters.book2-u10:
Unit 10 ko-Constructions: Liking, Wanting, Feeling, Knowing

What you'll be able to say: I like it, I want it, I'm hungry, I'm cold, I know, my head hurts, I can speak Hindi — the everyday inner life, which Hindi frames as things happening to you.

मुझे मोमोज़ पसंद हैं।
mujhe momos pasand hain. [mu-jhay moh-mohz puh-sund heh(n)]
I like momos. (lit. to-me momos pleasing are)
मुझे भूख लगी है।
mujhe bhookh lagee hai. [mu-jhay bhookh luh-gee heh]
I'm hungry. (lit. to-me hunger has stuck)
मुझे हिन्दी आती है!
mujhe hindee aatee hai! [mu-jhay hin-dee ah-tee heh]
I know Hindi! (lit. to-me Hindi comes)

The "to-me" idea

English says I like chai — "I" is the subject. Hindi flips the camera: चाय मुझे पसंद है — "chai is pleasing to me". The person feeling gets को (usually as the short forms from Unit 7: मुझे, तुम्हें, उसे…), and the thing liked/wanted/known is the grammatical subject — so the verb agrees with IT, not with you. That one sentence is the whole unit; everything below is practice.

Feeler (+ को)RomanSay it
मुझे (मैं)mujhemu-jhay
तुझे (तू)tujhetu-jhay
तुम्हें (तुम)tumhentum-hay(n)
आपको (आप)aapkoahp-koh
इसे / उसे (यह / वह)ise / usei-say / u-say
हमें (हम)hamenhuh-may(n)
इन्हें / उन्हें (ये / वे)inhen / unhenin-hay(n) / un-hay(n)
जैकब को / माँ को (names, nouns)jaikab ko / maan kojeh-kub koh / mah(n) koh

पसंद है — liking

मुझे चाय पसंद है।
mujhe chaay pasand hai. [mu-jhay chah-ay puh-sund heh]
I like chai. (chaay f sg → hai)
मुझे मोमोज़ पसंद हैं, समोसे भी पसंद हैं।
mujhe momos pasand hain, samose bhee pasand hain. [mu-jhay moh-mohz puh-sund heh(n), suh-moh-say bhee puh-sund heh(n)]
I like momos, and samosas too. (plural things → hain!) (samosaa (m))
क्या तुम्हें दिल्ली पसंद है? — हाँ, बहुत पसंद है।
kyaa tumhen dillee pasand hai? — haan, bahut pasand hai. [kyah tum-hay(n) dil-lee puh-sund heh — hah(n), bo-hut puh-sund heh]
Do you like Delhi? — Yes, I like it a lot.
उसे यह गाना पसंद है, मुझे यह रंग पसंद नहीं।
use yeh gaanaa pasand hai, mujhe yeh rang pasand naheen. [u-say yeh gah-nah puh-sund heh, mu-jhay yeh rung puh-sund nuh-hee(n)]
She likes this song; I don't like this colour. (gaanaa (m), rang (m))

The classic beginner sentence: ✗ मैं मोमोज़ पसंद हूँ — "I am pleasing to momos." The feeler is never मैं here. Say मुझे मोमोज़ पसंद हैं (mujhe momos pasand hain) — and note हैं, because the momos (plural) are the subject. One liked thing → है; several → हैं. पसंद itself never changes.

चाहिए — want / need

चाहिए (chaahiye) [chah-hi-yay] means "is wanted/needed (by me)". No हूँ/है after it in the present — चाहिए stands alone.

मुझे पानी चाहिए।
mujhe paanee chaahiye. [mu-jhay pah-nee chah-hi-yay]
I want/need water.
आपको क्या चाहिए?
aapko kyaa chaahiye? [ahp-koh kyah chah-hi-yay]
What would you like? (what every shopkeeper asks you)
हमें दो कमरे चाहिए।
hamen do kamre chaahiye. [huh-may(n) doh kum-ray chah-hi-yay]
We need two rooms.
मुझे कुछ नहीं चाहिए, बस चाय।
mujhe kuchh naheen chaahiye, bas chaay. [mu-jhay kuchh nuh-hee(n) chah-hi-yay, bus chah-ay]
I don't need anything — just chai.

With plurals some speakers say चाहिएँ (chaahiyen) [chah-hi-yay(n)] (हमें दो कमरे चाहिएँ). Invariable चाहिए is what you'll mostly hear in Delhi and is always safe. चाहिए also does polite requests better than "I want": मुझे एक किलो टमाटर चाहिए (mujhe ek kilo TamaaTar chaahiye) [mu-jhay ayk ki-loh Tuh-mah-Tur chah-hi-yay] — "I'd like a kilo of tomatoes." (TamaaTar (m))

लगना — feelings that "strike" you

Hunger, thirst, heat, cold, fear, sleepiness: in Hindi these attach themselves to you with the verb लगना (lagnaa) [lug-nah]. The feeling-noun is the subject, so the verb takes its gender:

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
भूखbhookh (f)bhookhhunger
प्यासpyaas (f)pyahsthirst
ठंडThanD (f)ThunDcold
गर्मीgarmee (f)gur-meeheat
नींदneend (f)neendsleep(iness) — uses आना
डरDar (m)Durfear (डर से = of sth.)
मुझे भूख लगी है। — मुझे भी प्यास लगी है।
mujhe bhookh lagee hai. — mujhe bhee pyaas lagee hai. [mu-jhay bhookh luh-gee heh — mu-jhay bhee pyahs luh-gee heh]
I'm hungry. — And I'm thirsty.
मुझे ठंड लग रही है, और उसे गर्मी लग रही है।
mujhe ThanD lag rahee hai, aur use garmee lag rahee hai. [mu-jhay ThunD lug ruh-hee heh, awr u-say gur-mee lug ruh-hee heh]
I'm feeling cold, and she's feeling hot. (continuous: the feeling is happening now)
मुझे नींद आ रही है।
mujhe neend aa rahee hai. [mu-jhay neend ah ruh-hee heh]
I'm getting sleepy. (lit. sleep is coming to me)
उसे कुत्तों से डर लगता है।
use kutton se Dar lagtaa hai. [u-say kut-toh(n) say Dur lug-tah heh]
He's afraid of dogs. (kuttaa (m) → oblique pl. kutton)

लगना also gives opinions — "it seems/feels to me":

मुझे यह गाना अच्छा लगता है।
mujhe yeh gaanaa achchhaa lagtaa hai. [mu-jhay yeh gah-nah uch-chhah lug-tah heh]
I like this song. (lit. this song strikes me as good — gaanaa m → achchhaa lagtaa)
मुझे दिल्ली अच्छी लगती है।
mujhe dillee achchhee lagtee hai. [mu-jhay dil-lee uch-chhee lug-tee heh]
I like Delhi. (dillee f → achchhee lagtee — the adjective and verb both follow Delhi, not you)
पहले यह खाना अजीब लगा, अब पसंद है।
pehle yeh khaanaa ajeeb lagaa, ab pasand hai. [peh-lay yeh khah-nah uh-jeeb luh-gah, ub puh-sund heh]
At first this food seemed strange; now I like it. (lagaa = past "it struck me" — a set form for now; the full past comes in Unit 14)

पता है / मालूम है — knowing

मुझे पता है।
mujhe pataa hai. [mu-jhay puh-tah heh]
I know.
मुझे नहीं पता।
mujhe naheen pataa. [mu-jhay nuh-hee(n) puh-tah]
I don't know. (note the order: naheen before pataa; "pataa naheen" also heard)
क्या आपको मालूम है?
kyaa aapko maaloom hai? [kyah ahp-koh mah-loom heh]
Do you know? (maaloom = pataa; pataa is the everyday Delhi choice)

दर्द — aches and pains

मेरे सिर में दर्द है।
mere sir mein dard hai. [may-ray sir may(n) durd heh]
My head aches. (lit. in my head pain is) (sir (m), dard (m))
मुझे सिरदर्द है।
mujhe sirdard hai. [mu-jhay sir-durd heh]
I have a headache. (same thing, ko-style)
उसके पेट में दर्द है।
uske peT mein dard hai. [us-kay payT may(n) durd heh]
His/her stomach hurts. (peT (m))

आना — skills: what you "know how to"

Skills come to you in Hindi. The skill is the subject; the verb agrees with it.

मुझे थोड़ी-थोड़ी हिन्दी आती है।
mujhe thoRee-thoRee hindee aatee hai. [mu-jhay thoh-Ree thoh-Ree hin-dee ah-tee heh]
I know a little Hindi. (hindee f → thoRee, aatee — your most charming sentence; use it everywhere)
क्या आपको अंग्रेज़ी आती है?
kyaa aapko angrezee aatee hai? [kyah ahp-koh un-gray-zee ah-tee heh]
Do you know English? (angrezee (f))
मुझे खाना बनाना आता है।
mujhe khaanaa banaanaa aataa hai. [mu-jhay khah-nah buh-nah-nah ah-tah heh]
I know how to cook. (a whole infinitive phrase counts as masculine singular → aataa)
उसे गाड़ी चलाना आता है।
use gaaRee chalaanaa aataa hai. [u-say gah-Ree chuh-lah-nah ah-tah heh]
She knows how to drive. (chalaanaa = to drive/operate)

"I'm cold" is not about what you are: ✗ मैं ठंडा हूँ describes your body temperature — alarming news for the family. Feelings happen TO you: मुझे ठंड लग रही है (mujhe ThanD lag rahee hai). Same trap with hunger: ✗ मैं भूखा हूँ is grammatical but blunt; the natural line is मुझे भूख लगी है.

Delhi's dative is मेरे को (mere ko) [may-ray koh]: मेरे को मोमोज़ फ़ुल पसंद हैं (mere ko momos full pasand hain) — with English "full" as an intensifier, very Dilli. You'll also hear the softener न (na) mid-sentence: मुझे न, बहुत भूख लगी है (mujhe na, bahut bhookh lagee hai) "so listen, I'm really hungry." Stick to मुझे in your own speech — but understand मेरे को instantly.

भूख लगी है? (bhookh lagee hai?) is how Indian homes say "I love you". Expect it within minutes of arriving at your in-laws'. Protocol: refuse lightly once — बस, ठीक है (bas, Theek hai) — the food arrives anyway, and that's the point. A flat "no" to food reads colder in Delhi than it does in America.

Exercise 10A — Agreement drill

Fill the blank with the right form: है/हैं, लगा/लगी, लगता/लगती, रही, चाहिए, में. The verb agrees with the thing, not the person! Answers: Answer Key, Unit 10.

  1. मुझे चाय पसंद ___। (mujhe chaay pasand ___ .)
  2. मुझे मोमोज़ पसंद ___। (mujhe momos pasand ___ .)
  3. उसे यह गाना पसंद ___। (use yeh gaanaa pasand ___ .)
  4. क्या आपको हिन्दी आती ___? (kyaa aapko hindee aatee ___ ?)
  5. मुझे भूख ___ है। (mujhe bhookh ___ hai.)
  6. मुझे ठंड लग ___ है। (mujhe ThanD lag ___ hai.)
  7. हमें दो कमरे ___। (hamen do kamre ___ .)
  8. मुझे दिल्ली अच्छी ___ है। (mujhe dillee achchhee ___ hai.)
  9. मुझे यह शहर अच्छा ___ है। (mujhe yeh shehar achchhaa ___ hai.)
  10. मेरे सिर ___ दर्द है। (mere sir ___ dard hai.)

Exercise 10B — Change the feeler

Rewrite for the new experiencer in brackets; keep everything else agreeing correctly.

  1. मुझे चाय पसंद है। (आप — as a question) (mujhe chaay pasand hai. → aap?)
  2. मुझे पानी चाहिए। (हम) (mujhe paanee chaahiye. → ham)
  3. उसे ठंड लग रही है। (मैं) (use ThanD lag rahee hai. → main)
  4. मुझे हिन्दी आती है। (मेरी पत्नी) (mujhe hindee aatee hai. → meree patnee)
  5. मुझे पता है। (वे लोग — negative) (mujhe pataa hai. → voh log, negative)
  6. मुझे मोमोज़ पसंद हैं। (जैकब) (mujhe momos pasand hain. → jaikab)
  7. मुझे सिरदर्द है। (वह) (mujhe sirdard hai. → voh)

Exercise 10C — Translate into Hindi

Think "to-me" first, then check what the verb must agree with.

  1. I like chai.
  2. I like momos. (watch the verb!)
  3. I'm hungry.
  4. I'm feeling cold.
  5. We need two rooms.
  6. I have a headache.
  7. Do you (आप) know Hindi?
  8. I don't know.

Exercise 10D — Translate into English

Write natural English — not the literal "to-me" version.

  1. मुझे नींद आ रही है। (mujhe neend aa rahee hai.)
  2. क्या तुम्हें यह गाना पसंद है? (kyaa tumhen yeh gaanaa pasand hai?)
  3. उसे कुत्तों से डर लगता है। (use kutton se Dar lagtaa hai.)
  4. पहले यह खाना अजीब लगा, अब पसंद है। (pehle yeh khaanaa ajeeb lagaa, ab pasand hai.)
  5. आपको क्या चाहिए? (aapko kyaa chaahiye?)
  6. मुझे थोड़ी-थोड़ी हिन्दी आती है। (mujhe thoRee-thoRee hindee aatee hai.)
chapters.book2-u11:
Unit 11 The Past with था — and Past Habits & Ongoing Past

What you'll be able to say: how things were — where you were yesterday, what there used to be, what you did as a kid, and what was happening when the phone rang.

कल मौसम अच्छा था।
kal mausam achchhaa thaa. [kul maw-sum uch-chhah thah]
Yesterday the weather was nice. (mausam (m))
जब मैं छोटा था, मैं बहुत क्रिकेट खेलता था।
jab main chhoTaa thaa, main bahut krikeT kheltaa thaa. [jub meh(n) chhoh-Tah thah, meh(n) bo-hut kri-kayT khayl-tah thah]
When I was little, I played a lot of cricket. (krikeT (m))
रात को बारिश हो रही थी।
raat ko baarish ho rahee thee. [raht koh bah-rish hoh ruh-hee thee]
It was raining at night.

था / थी / थे / थीं — "was" and "were"

The past of होना has exactly four forms, and they agree like adjectives — by gender and number, not by person:

SubjectMaleFemale
मैं mainथा thaaथी thee
तू tuथा thaaथी thee
यह / वह yeh / vohथा thaaथी thee
तुम tumथे theथीं theen
आप aapथे theथीं theen
हम hamथे theथीं theen
ये / वे लोग ye / voh logथे theथीं theen

Say them: था [thah], थी [thee], थे [thay], थीं [thee(n)] — dental t plus a puff of air. थीं is the feminine plural (and feminine respect) form; in fast speech you may hear plain थी for तुम, but थीं is the standard.

कल मैं घर पर था।
kal main ghar par thaa. [kul meh(n) ghur pur thah]
Yesterday I was at home. (kal = yesterday here; the past verb tells you so — see Unit 12)
वह बहुत ख़ुश थी।
voh bahut khush thee. [voh bo-hut khush thee]
She was very happy.
तुम कल शाम को कहाँ थे?
tum kal shaam ko kahaan the? [tum kul shahm koh kuh-hah(n) thay]
Where were you yesterday evening?

"There was / there were"

कमरे में एक पलंग था।
kamre mein ek palang thaa. [kum-ray may(n) ayk puh-lung thah]
There was a bed in the room. (palang (m))
घर के सामने एक पेड़ था।
ghar ke saamne ek peR thaa. [ghur kay sahm-nay ayk payR thah]
There was a tree in front of the house. (peR (m))
वहाँ बहुत लोग थे।
vahaan bahut log the. [vuh-hah(n) bo-hut lohg thay]
There were a lot of people there.
कल रात बिजली नहीं थी।
kal raat bijlee naheen thee. [kul raht bij-lee nuh-hee(n) thee]
There was no electricity last night. (bijlee (f)) (a very Delhi sentence in June)
मेरी दादी बहुत अच्छी थीं।
meree daadee bahut achchhee theen. [may-ree dah-dee bo-hut uch-chhee thee(n)]
My grandmother was very kind. (daadee (f)) (one respected lady → theen)

Past habits: -ता था "used to"

Take the Unit 8 habitual and swap the present auxiliary for the past one. Both parts agree: जाता था, जाते थे, जाती थी, जाती थीं (jaataa thaa, jaate the, jaatee thee, jaatee theen) [jah-tah thah, jah-tay thay, jah-tee thee, jah-tee thee(n)].

जब मैं छोटा था, हम शिकागो में रहते थे।
jab main chhoTaa thaa, ham shikaago mein rehte the. [jub meh(n) chhoh-Tah thah, hum shi-kah-goh may(n) reh-tay thay]
When I was little, we lived in Chicago. (jab = when — starts the clause)
जब मेरी पत्नी छोटी थी, वह पुरानी दिल्ली में रहती थी।
jab meree patnee chhoTee thee, voh puraanee dillee mein rehtee thee. [jub may-ree put-nee chhoh-Tee thee, voh pu-rah-nee dil-lee may(n) reh-tee thee]
When my wife was little, she lived in Old Delhi.
वह बहुत चाय पीती थी।
voh bahut chaay peetee thee. [voh bo-hut chah-ay pee-tee thee]
She used to drink a lot of chai.
मेरे दादा जी रोज़ सैर करते थे।
mere daadaa jee roz sair karte the. [may-ray dah-dah jee rohz sehr kur-tay thay]
My grandfather used to take a walk every day. (daadaa (m))
पहले मैं हिन्दी नहीं समझता था।
pehle main hindee naheen samajhtaa thaa. [peh-lay meh(n) hin-dee nuh-hee(n) suh-mujh-tah thah]
Earlier I didn't understand Hindi. (note: thaa is NOT dropped after naheen)

Ongoing past: रहा था "was …-ing"

Same trick with Unit 9: कर रहा हूँ → कर रहा था. What was in mid-flow when something else happened:

मैं सो रहा था।
main so rahaa thaa. [meh(n) soh ruh-hah thah]
I was sleeping.
तुम क्या कर रहे थे?
tum kyaa kar rahe the? [tum kyah kur ruh-hay thay]
What were you doing?
वह खाना बना रही थी।
voh khaanaa banaa rahee thee. [voh khah-nah buh-nah ruh-hee thee]
She was cooking.
कल रात तुम कहाँ थे? मैं फ़ोन कर रही थी!
kal raat tum kahaan the? main fon kar rahee thee! [kul raht tum kuh-hah(n) thay — meh(n) fohn kur ruh-hee thee]
Where were you last night? I was calling (you)! (she speaking — kar rahee thee)
हम टीवी देख रहे थे।
ham TeeVee dekh rahe the. [hum Tee-Vee daykh ruh-hay thay]
We were watching TV.

Time words for the past

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
कलkalkulyesterday (and tomorrow! — Unit 12)
परसोंparsonpur-soh(n)day before yesterday (and day after tomorrow)
पहलेpehlepeh-layearlier, in the past
पिछले हफ़्तेpichhle hafte (haftaa m)pichh-lay huf-taylast week
पिछले महीनेpichhle maheene (maheenaa m)pichh-lay muh-hee-naylast month
पिछले सालpichhle saal (saal m)pichh-lay sahllast year
उस वक़्त / उस समयus vaqt (m) / us samay (m)us vukt / us suh-mayat that time
बचपन मेंbachpan (m) meinbuch-pun may(n)in childhood

Notice पिछले (pichhle): पिछला bends to -e before हफ़्ते/महीने/साल because a time expression like this sits in the oblique — Unit 7 quietly at work again.

In the present you learned to drop the auxiliary after नहीं (मैं नहीं जाता). Never drop था: past negatives keep it — मैं नहीं जाता था (main naheen jaataa thaa), बिजली नहीं थी. Without था the sentence snaps back to the present. And keep the four-way agreement honest: दादी थीं (respect), दादा जी थे, बहनें थीं (behnen theen) [beh-nay(n) thee(n)] "the sisters were".

Every Delhi uncle has this speech ready: पहले यहाँ कुछ नहीं था (pehle yahaan kuchh naheen thaa) [peh-lay yuh-hah(n) kuchh nuh-hee(n) thah] "there used to be nothing here" — followed by अब मॉल है (ab mol hai) [ub mawl heh] "now there's a mall." The in-law version opens with हमारे ज़माने में… (hamaare zamaane mein) [huh-mah-ray zuh-mah-nay may(n)] "in our day…" (zamaanaa (m)). Nod along; it's a love language.

पुरानी दिल्ली (puraanee dillee) [pu-rah-nee dil-lee] — Old Delhi — is the walled Mughal city: Chandni Chowk चाँदनी चौक (chaandnee chauk) [chahnd-nee chawk], parathas, wedding-lehenga lanes. If the family has roots there, asking आप पहले कहाँ रहते थे? (aap pehle kahaan rehte the?) "where did you live before?" opens an evening of stories.

Exercise 11A — था, थी, थे or थीं?

Fill in the right past form of होना. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 11.

  1. कल मैं घर पर ___। — Jacob speaking (kal main ghar par ___ .)
  2. वह बहुत ख़ुश ___। — a woman (voh bahut khush ___ .)
  3. वहाँ बहुत लोग ___। (vahaan bahut log ___ .)
  4. पानी नहीं ___। (paanee naheen ___ .)
  5. कल रात बिजली नहीं ___। (kal raat bijlee naheen ___ .)
  6. मेरी दादी बहुत अच्छी ___। (meree daadee bahut achchhee ___ .)
  7. कमरे में दो पलंग ___। (kamre mein do palang ___ .)
  8. तुम कहाँ ___? — to a man (tum kahaan ___ ?)
  9. आप कहाँ ___? — to your mother-in-law (aap kahaan ___ ?)
  10. शादी से पहले हम पड़ोसी ___। (shaadee se pehle ham paRosee ___ .)

Exercise 11B — Push it into the past

Rewrite each present sentence in the past (habitual → used to; continuous → was …-ing).

  1. मैं दिल्ली में रहता हूँ। (main dillee mein rehtaa hoon.)
  2. वह चाय पीती है। (voh chaay peetee hai.)
  3. हम साथ पढ़ते हैं। (ham saath paRhte hain.)
  4. मैं सो रहा हूँ। (main so rahaa hoon.)
  5. वह खाना बना रही है। (voh khaanaa banaa rahee hai.)
  6. तुम क्या कर रहे हो? (tum kyaa kar rahe ho?)
  7. मेरे दादा जी रोज़ सैर करते हैं। (mere daadaa jee roz sair karte hain.)

Exercise 11C — Translate into Hindi

Watch gender agreement on था — and remember नहीं keeps था.

  1. Yesterday the weather was nice.
  2. There was no electricity last night.
  3. When I was little, we lived in Chicago.
  4. She used to drink a lot of chai.
  5. I was sleeping.
  6. What were you (तुम, to a man) doing?
  7. It was raining at night.

Exercise 11D — Translate into English

Write natural English.

  1. शादी से पहले हम पड़ोसी थे। (shaadee se pehle ham paRosee the.)
  2. पहले मैं हिन्दी नहीं समझता था। (pehle main hindee naheen samajhtaa thaa.)
  3. मेरी दादी रोज़ मंदिर जाती थीं। (meree daadee roz mandir jaatee theen.)
  4. कल रात तुम कहाँ थे? मैं फ़ोन कर रही थी! (kal raat tum kahaan the? main fon kar rahee thee!)
  5. पहले यहाँ कुछ नहीं था, अब मॉल है। (pehle yahaan kuchh naheen thaa, ab mol hai.)
  6. बचपन में वह बहुत क्रिकेट खेलता था। (bachpan mein voh bahut krikeT kheltaa thaa.)
chapters.book2-u12:
Unit 12 The Future Tense

What you'll be able to say: plans and promises — I'll call you, we'll meet tomorrow, she won't come, there will be a lot of people — plus the famous double life of कल.

मैं कल तुम्हें फ़ोन करूँगा।
main kal tumhen fon karoongaa. [meh(n) kul tum-hay(n) fohn kuh-roo(n)-gah]
I'll call you tomorrow.
हम अगले हफ़्ते आगरा जाएँगे।
ham agle hafte aagraa jaaenge. [hum ug-lay huf-tay ahg-rah jah-ay(n)-gay]
Next week we'll go to Agra. (aglaa "next" → oblique agle)
आप क्या लेंगे? — मैं चाय लूँगा।
aap kyaa lenge? — main chaay loongaa. [ahp kyah lay(n)-gay — meh(n) chah-ay loo(n)-gah]
What will you have? — I'll have chai. (the politest offer in any Delhi home)

The pattern: stem + person ending + गा/गे/गी

The future is two agreements stacked. First a person ending on the stem: -ऊँ (-oon) for मैं, -ए (-e) for तू/यह/वह, -ओ (-o) for तुम, -एँ (-en) for आप/हम/plurals. Then a gender tail that agrees like an adjective: गा (gaa) m sg, गे (ge) m pl, गी (gee) f. No auxiliary at all.

SubjectMaleFemale
मैं mainकरूँगा karoongaaकरूँगी karoongee
तू tuकरेगा karegaaकरेगी karegee
यह / वह yeh / vohकरेगा karegaaकरेगी karegee
तुम tumकरोगे karogeकरोगी karogee
आप aapकरेंगे karengeकरेंगी karengee
हम hamकरेंगे karengeकरेंगी karengee
ये / वे लोग ye / voh logकरेंगे karengeकरेंगी karengee

Sound check: करूँगा [kuh-roo(n)-gah], करेगा [kuh-ray-gah], करोगे [kuh-roh-gay], करेंगे [kuh-ray(n)-gay], करूँगी [kuh-roo(n)-gee], करेंगी [kuh-ray(n)-gee].

होना in the future

होना follows the same pattern on the stem हो: मैं हूँगा/हूँगी (hoongaa/hoongee) [hoo(n)-gah / hoo(n)-gee] · वह होगा/होगी (hogaa/hogee) [hoh-gah / hoh-gee] · तुम होगे/होगी (hoge/hogee) [hoh-gay] · आप/हम/वे होंगे/होंगी (honge/hongee) [hoh(n)-gay / hoh(n)-gee].

होगा also does educated guessing — the "presumptive": वह घर पर होगा (voh ghar par hogaa) [voh ghur pur hoh-gah] can mean "he'll be home" or "he's probably home (right now)". Delhi runs on this: फ़ोन बंद है? मेट्रो में होगा। (fon band hai? meTro mein hogaa.) [fohn bund heh — may-Troh may(n) hoh-gah] "Phone off? He must be on the metro."

Vowel-ending stems: जा, आ, ले, दे

Stems ending in a vowel take a glue-letter before some endings. Learn these four as a set (feminine: swap final गा/गे for गी):

Verbमैंतू / वहतुमआप / हम / वे
जाना jaanaaजाऊँगा jaaoongaaजाएगा jaaegaaजाओगे jaaogeजाएँगे jaaenge
आना aanaaआऊँगा aaoongaaआएगा aaegaaआओगे aaogeआएँगे aaenge
लेना lenaaलूँगा loongaaलेगा legaaलोगे logeलेंगे lenge
देना denaaदूँगा doongaaदेगा degaaदोगे dogeदेंगे denge

Say them: जाऊँगा [jah-oo(n)-gah], जाएगा [jah-ay-gah], जाएँगे [jah-ay(n)-gay], लूँगा [loo(n)-gah], देंगे [day(n)-gay].

कल is two-faced (so is परसों)

कल (kal) [kul] means yesterday AND tomorrow — one day away from today, in either direction. परसों (parson) [pur-soh(n)] is two days away, both directions. The verb settles which one:

कल मैं दिल्ली में था।
kal main dillee mein thaa. [kul meh(n) dil-lee may(n) thah]
Yesterday I was in Delhi. (thaa = past → kal means yesterday)
कल मैं दिल्ली जाऊँगा।
kal main dillee jaaoongaa. [kul meh(n) dil-lee jah-oo(n)-gah]
Tomorrow I'll go to Delhi. (jaaoongaa = future → kal means tomorrow)
परसों छुट्टी होगी।
parson chhuTTee hogee. [pur-soh(n) chhuT-Tee hoh-gee]
The day after tomorrow is a holiday. (chhuTTee (f))

Plans and promises

वह नहीं आएगी।
voh naheen aaegee. [voh nuh-hee(n) ah-ay-gee]
She won't come.
तुम कब आओगे?
tum kab aaoge? [tum kub ah-oh-gay]
When will you come?
मैं देर से नहीं आऊँगा, वादा!
main der se naheen aaoongaa, vaadaa! [meh(n) dayr say nuh-hee(n) ah-oo(n)-gah, vah-dah]
I won't be late — promise! (vaadaa (m))
शादी में बहुत लोग होंगे।
shaadee mein bahut log honge. [shah-dee may(n) bo-hut lohg hoh(n)-gay]
There will be a lot of people at the wedding.
पार्टी कल रात को होगी।
paarTee kal raat ko hogee. [pahr-Tee kul raht koh hoh-gee]
The party will be tomorrow night. (paarTee (f))
मैं तुम्हारे लिए मोमोज़ लाऊँगा।
main tumhaare liye momos laaoongaa. [meh(n) tum-hah-ray li-yay moh-mohz lah-oo(n)-gah]
I'll bring momos for you. (laanaa = to bring — the fastest route to anyone's heart)
अगले साल हम अमेरिका जाएँगे।
agle saal ham amreekaa jaaenge. [ug-lay sahl hum um-ree-kah jah-ay(n)-gay]
Next year we'll go to America.
ठीक है, मैं आपको बताऊँगा।
Theek hai, main aapko bataaoongaa. [Theek heh, meh(n) ahp-koh buh-tah-oo(n)-gah]
Okay, I'll let you know.

मिलते हैं vs. मिलेंगे

Two ways to say "see you", and the difference is warmth vs. commitment. The habitual फिर मिलते हैं (phir milte hain) [phir mil-tay heh(n)] — literally "so, we meet again" — is the breezy sign-off, like "catch you later". The future कल मिलेंगे (kal milenge) [kul mi-lay(n)-gay] pins an actual plan: we WILL meet tomorrow.

चलो, फिर मिलते हैं!
chalo, phir milte hain! [chuh-loh, phir mil-tay heh(n)]
Okay then, see you around!
कल शाम को मिलेंगे, पक्का।
kal shaam ko milenge, pakkaa. [kul shahm koh mi-lay(n)-gay, puk-kah]
We'll meet tomorrow evening — for sure. (pakkaa = fixed, confirmed; Delhi's favourite seal)

The future carries your gender in its tail. Jacob: मैं करूँगा, जाऊँगा; his wife: मैं करूँगी, जाऊँगी. Read the गा/गी off your own gender, not your listener's. And ✗ मैं करेंगे mixes "I" with the हम ending — "I" is always करूँगा/करूँगी; करेंगे belongs to हम/आप/वे. A mixed or all-male "we" says करेंगे; an all-female "we" says करेंगी.

The most Delhi verb form of all: हो जाएगा (ho jaaegaa) [hoh jah-ay-gah] — "it'll get done." The electrician says it, the tailor says it, the ministry clerk says it. कल आना, हो जाएगा (kal aanaa, ho jaaegaa) "come tomorrow, it'll be done" — in which कल is gloriously elastic. Its cousin देखेंगे (dekhenge) [day-khay(n)-gay] "we'll see" usually means "probably not, but let's not fight about it."

Delhi's wedding season runs November to February, on dates astrologers approve — so some nights the whole city is a बारात (baaraat (f)) [bah-raht], the groom's procession, brass band and all. दिसंबर में हर वीकेंड शादी होगी (disambar mein har veekenD shaadee hogee) [di-sum-bur may(n) hur vee-kenD shah-dee hoh-gee] "in December there'll be a wedding every weekend" — and you WILL be invited.

Exercise 12A — Fill in the future form

Put the bracketed verb into the future. Watch person and gender. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 12.

Exercise 12C — Translate into Hindi

  2. Yesterday I was at home. Tomorrow I will be in the office.

Unit 13 Imperatives & Requests

What you'll be able to say: ask people to do things at exactly the right level of politeness — from a blunt कर kar [kur] with your closest people to a gracious कीजिए keejiye [kee-ji-yay] with your in-laws — and soften any request so it sounds warm, not bossy.

ज़रा सुनिए।
zaraa suniye. [zuh-rah su-ni-yay]
Excuse me — could you listen a moment? (lit. a-little listen)
यहाँ बैठो न।
yahaan baiTho na. [yuh-hah(n) beh-Thoh nuh]
Sit here, won't you?
चलिए, चाय पीते हैं।
chaliye, chaay peete hain. [chuh-li-yay, chah-ay pee-tay heh(n)]
Come, let's have chai.

One command, three levels

You already know Hindi has three words for "you": तू tu [too] (intimate), तुम tum [tum] (familiar), आप aap [ahp] (respectful). Commands come in the same three levels, and they're wonderfully regular. Take the verb stem (infinitive minus -naa) and:

LevelFormSounds likeUse with
तू tubare stem: बोल bolbohlvery close people only — intimate or blunt
तुम tumstem + -ओ -o: बोलो boloboh-lohpartner, friends, kids
आप aapstem + -इए -iye: बोलिए boliyeboh-li-yayelders, in-laws, strangers

The endings are easy to hear: -o [oh] for tum, -iye [i-yay] for aap. Regular verbs:

Infinitiveतू tuतुम tumआप aap
बोलना bolnaa speakबोल bolबोलो boloबोलिए boliye
सुनना sunnaa listenसुन sunसुनो sunoसुनिए suniye
बैठना baiThnaa sitबैठ baiThबैठो baiThoबैठिए baiThiye
लिखना likhnaa writeलिख likhलिखो likhoलिखिए likhiye
खोलना kholnaa openखोल kholखोलो kholoखोलिए kholiye
रुकना ruknaa stop, waitरुक rukरुको rukoरुकिए rukiye
चलना chalnaa move, goचल chalचलो chaloचलिए chaliye

The famous irregulars

Five very common verbs replace their vowel in the aap-form with a long ee + -jiye [jee-ji-yay pattern]; पीना peenaa also changes its tum-form. Learn these as words:

Infinitiveतू tuतुम tumआप aap
करना karnaa doकर karकरो karoकीजिए keejiye
देना denaa giveदे deदो doदीजिए deejiye
लेना lenaa takeले leलो loलीजिए leejiye
पीना peenaa drinkपी peeपियो piyoपीजिए peejiye
आना aanaa comeआ aaआओ aaoआइए aaiye
जाना jaanaa goजा jaaजाओ jaaoजाइए jaaiye
कहना kehnaa sayकह kehकहो kahoकहिए kahiye

Say them: keejiye [kee-ji-yay], deejiye [dee-ji-yay], leejiye [lee-ji-yay], peejiye [pee-ji-yay], aaiye [ah-i-yay], jaaiye [jah-i-yay], piyo [pi-yoh], kahiye [kuh-hi-yay].

About तू tu: the bare-stem command (kar, jaa, de) is for lovers, small children, God — and fights. Delhiites even have a word for rude tu-talk: तू-तड़ाक tu-taRaak [too-tuh-Rahk]. Your partner may use it with you affectionately; never use it with anyone else until they use it with you first. When in doubt, tum-forms with friends, aap-forms with everyone older.

Keep the pronoun and the verb form at the SAME level. Learners love to mix: आप बैठो aap baiTho or तुम बैठिए tum baiThiye. Match them: तुम बैठो tum baiTho · आप बैठिए aap baiThiye. (Delhiites themselves sometimes say aap baiTho in relaxed speech — but from a learner it just sounds like an error. Stay matched.)

The gentle instruction: infinitive as command

Hindi has a fourth, very handy level: use the bare infinitive (-naa form) as a soft instruction for something to be done later. It feels like "do make sure you…" between equals — friendlier than karo, less formal than keejiye.

कल मुझे फ़ोन करना।
kal mujhe fon karnaa. [kul mu-jhay fohn kur-nah]
Call me tomorrow, okay?
यहाँ अपना नाम लिखना।
yahaan apnaa naam likhnaa. [yuh-hah(n) up-nah nahm likh-nah]
Write your name here.
भैया, दो चाय देना।
bhaiyaa, do chaay denaa. [bheh-yah, doh chah-ay day-nah]
Bhaiya, give (us) two chais. (the classic chai-stall order)

Saying "don't": मत mat and न na

मत mat [mut] is the strong "don't" — it goes right before the verb, with tu-, tum- and infinitive commands. न na [nuh] is the gentler "don't", preferred with aap-forms.

देर मत करो।
der mat karo. [dayr mut kuh-roh]
Don't be late. (lit. don't do lateness)
चिंता न कीजिए।
chintaa na keejiye. [chin-tah nuh kee-ji-yay]
Please don't worry.
अभी मत जाओ।
abhee mat jaao. [uh-bhee mut jah-oh]
Don't go yet.

In relaxed Delhi speech you'll also hear mat with aap-forms (मत कीजिए mat keejiye) — fine to understand, but na keejiye is the polished choice.

Softeners: how not to sound bossy

A bare command is fine in Hindi between equals — पानी दो paanee do is normal, not rude. But these little words add warmth:

SoftenerSay itEffect
ज़रा zaraazuh-rah"just / a moment" — the all-purpose politener: ज़रा सुनिए zaraa suniye
थोड़ा thoRaathoh-Rah"a little": थोड़ा धीरे बोलिए thoRaa dheere boliye
न na (tagged after)nuhcoaxing "won't you": आओ न aao na
प्लीज़ pleezpleezEnglish "please", totally at home in Delhi: प्लीज़ रुको pleez ruko
जी jeejeerespect particle: जी, बैठिए jee, baiThiye

You may see कृपया kripayaa [kri-puh-yah] ("please") on signs and metro announcements. In conversation it sounds like an announcement — use zaraa, pleez or simply the -iye form instead.

चलो chalo, चलिए chaliye, चलें chalen

The little family of "let's":

चलो chalo chuh-loh"come on / let's go / fine then" — with friends, and as an all-purpose "okay, moving on"
चलिए chaliye chuh-li-yaypolite "let's go / after you / very well"
चलें? chalen? chuh-lay(n)"shall we go?" — a polite proposal (this is the subjunctive; full grammar in Unit 18)
चलो, देर हो रही है।
chalo, der ho rahee hai. [chuh-loh, dayr hoh ruh-hee heh]
Come on, it's getting late.

Asking, not ordering

For real requests to strangers and elders, stack politeness: attention-getter + -iye form. And here's a preview of the pattern you'll master in Unit 16 — "can you…":

माफ़ कीजिए, ज़रा सुनिए।
maaf keejiye, zaraa suniye. [mahf kee-ji-yay, zuh-rah su-ni-yay]
Excuse me — could I have a moment?
क्या आप धीरे बोल सकते हैं?
kyaa aap dheere bol sakte hain? [kyah ahp dhee-ray bohl suk-tay heh(n)]
Can you speak slowly? (preview of saknaa, Unit 16)
एक मिनट रुकिए।
ek minaT rukiye. [ayk mi-nuT ru-ki-yay]
Please wait one minute.

More examples, Delhi-real

दरवाज़ा खोलो।
darvaazaa kholo. [dur-vah-zah khoh-loh]
Open the door.
खिड़की बंद करो, बाहर शोर है।
khiRkee band karo, baahar shor hai. [khiR-kee bund kuh-roh, bah-hur shohr heh]
Close the window, it's noisy outside.
अंदर आइए, बैठिए।
andar aaiye, baiThiye. [un-dur ah-i-yay, beh-Thi-yay]
Come in, please sit. (the standard welcome)
यह लीजिए।
yeh leejiye. [yeh lee-ji-yeh]
Here you are. (lit. take this — said when handing anything over)
थोड़ा और लीजिए न।
thoRaa aur leejiye na. [thoh-Rah awr lee-ji-yay nuh]
Do take a little more. (what your saas will say at dinner)
मुझे बताओ, क्या बनाऊँ?
mujhe bataao, kyaa banaaoon? [mu-jhay buh-tah-oh, kyah buh-nah-oo(n)]
Tell me — what should I make? (banaaoon = "should I make", Unit 18)

Delhi tags न na and यार yaar [yahr] onto everything: चल न यार chal na yaar [chul nuh yahr] "come ooon, man". Stress-management, Delhi style: टेंशन मत लो Tenshan mat lo [Ten-shun mut loh] "don't take tension" and रहने दो rehne do [reh-nay doh] "let it be". You'll hear aap mixed with tum-forms (aap aa jaao) constantly — understand it, don't copy it yet.

At your in-laws', the -iye forms plus जी jee are your uniform: बैठिए जी, खाना लीजिए. Meanwhile your elders will call you बेटा beTaa [bay-Tah] ("son") and command you with tum- or even tu-forms — बैठो बेटा. That's affection and seniority, not rudeness; you still answer with aap. Refusing seconds? Say बस, बहुत है bas, bahut hai [bus, bo-hut heh] — and expect to be served anyway.

Exercise 13B — Make it polite

  1. यहाँ बैठो। (yahaan baiTho.)

chapters.book2-u14:
Unit 14 Simple Past & the Ergative ने ne

What you'll be able to say: what happened — I went, she came, we ate, who did it. This unit contains the single most famous rule in Hindi grammar, the little word ने ne [nay]. Take it slowly; we'll build it in three small steps.

मैं कल बाज़ार गया।
main kal baazaar gayaa. [meh(n) kul bah-zahr guh-yah]
I went to the market yesterday.
मैंने चाय पी।
maine chaay pee. [meh(n)-nay chah-ay pee]
I drank tea. (lit. I-ne tea drank-f — wait for Step 3!)
तुमने क्या खाया?
tumne kyaa khaayaa? [tum-nay kyah khah-yah]
What did you eat?

Step 1 — The shape of the past: the perfective participle

The simple past ("did/went/ate" — done, over) uses the perfective participle: verb stem + an ending that changes for gender and number, exactly like the adjective endings you know from achchhaa / achchhe / achchhee:

 m sgm plf sgf pl
ending-आ -aa-ए -e-ई -ee-ईं -een
बैठना baiThnaa sitबैठा baiThaaबैठे baiTheबैठी baiTheeबैठीं baiTheen
उठना uThnaa get upउठा uThaaउठे uTheउठी uTheeउठीं uTheen
आना aanaa comeआया aayaaआए aaeआई aaeeआईं aaeen
सोना sonaa sleepसोया soyaaसोए soeसोई soeeसोईं soeen

Say the endings: -aa [ah], -e [ay], -ee [ee], -een [ee(n)]. Note the glide: stems ending in a vowel (aa-, so-) slip in a y before -aa: aayaa [ah-yah], soyaa [soh-yah] — but not in the feminine: aaee [ah-ee], soee [soh-ee].

Step 2 — Movement & change verbs: NO ne, agree with the subject

With intransitive verbs (vi) — going, coming, arriving, sitting, sleeping, happening — the past is beautifully simple: subject + participle, and the participle agrees with the subject. No ne anywhere.

मेरी बहन कल दिल्ली गई।
meree behen kal dillee gaee. [may-ree beh-hen kul dil-lee guh-ee]
My sister went to Delhi yesterday. (gaee f, matching behen)
हम शाम को घर आए।
ham shaam ko ghar aae. [hum shahm koh ghur ah-ay]
We came home in the evening.
आप कब पहुँचे?
aap kab pahunche? [ahp kub puh-hun-chay]
When did you arrive? (to a woman: आप कब पहुँचीं? aap kab pahuncheen? [ahp kub puh-hun-chee(n)])
वह देर से उठी।
voh der se uThee. [voh dayr say u-Thee]
She got up late.
क्या हुआ?
kyaa huaa? [kyah hu-ah]
What happened? (huaa = past of honaa)

Note the two star irregulars here: जाना jaanaa becomes गया gayaa [guh-yah] (not *jaayaa), and होना honaa becomes हुआ huaa [hu-ah]. Full forms below in Step 3's table.

Step 3 — Doing-verbs: subject + ने ne, verb agrees with the OBJECT

Now the famous part. With transitive verbs (vt) — verbs that act on something: eat, drink, read, see, make — the past works differently:

The ne rule. 1) Mark the doer with ने ne. 2) The verb then ignores the doer completely and agrees with the object in gender and number. 3) This happens ONLY in perfective (did/have done/had done) tenses — never in present, continuous or future.

मैंने चाय पी।
maine chaay pee. [meh(n)-nay chah-ay pee]
I drank tea. (chaay is f — so pee, even though Jacob is m)
मैंने खाना खाया।
maine khaanaa khaayaa. [meh(n)-nay khah-nah khah-yah]
I ate food. (khaanaa m → khaayaa)
उसने किताब पढ़ी।
usne kitaab paRhee. [us-nay ki-tahb puh-Rhee]
He/she read a book. (kitaab f → paRhee)
हमने समोसे खाए।
hamne samose khaae. [hum-nay suh-moh-say khah-ay]
We ate samosas. (samose m pl → khaae)
उन्होंने दो रोटियाँ खाईं।
unhonne do roTiyaan khaaeen. [un-hoh(n)-nay doh roh-Ti-yah(n) khah-ee(n)]
They ate two rotis. (roTiyaan f pl → khaaeen)

Whether the doer is a man, a woman, or a crowd, the verb doesn't budge — it's locked onto the object. राज ने चाय पी। दीपा ने चाय पी। raaj ne chaay pee. deepaa ne chaay pee. [rahj nay chah-ay pee · dee-pah nay chah-ay pee] Both pee.

The ne-forms of the pronouns

Pronouns fuse with ne into single words; nouns just add ne separately (राज ने raaj ne).

Pronoun+ neSay it Pronoun+ neSay it
मैं mainमैंने mainemeh(n)-nayहम hamहमने hamnehum-nay
तू tuतूने tunetoo-nayतुम tumतुमने tumnetum-nay
यह yehइसने isneis-nayआप aapआपने aapneahp-nay
वह vohउसने usneus-nayवे / वो लोग voh logउन्होंने unhonneun-hoh(n)-nay
कौन kaunकिसने kisnekis-nay

The irregular participles — learn these six cold

Verbm sgm plf sgf pl
करना karnaa (vt) doकिया kiyaaकिए kiyeकी keeकीं keen
देना denaa (vt) giveदिया diyaaदिए diyeदी deeदीं deen
लेना lenaa (vt) takeलिया liyaaलिए liyeली leeलीं leen
पीना peenaa (vt) drinkपिया piyaaपिए piyeपी peeपीं peen
जाना jaanaa (vi — no ne) goगया gayaaगए gaeगई gaeeगईं gaeen
होना honaa (vi — no ne) happen, beहुआ huaaहुए hueहुई hueeहुईं hueen

Say them: kiyaa [ki-yah], kee [kee], diyaa [di-yah], liyaa [li-yah], piyaa [pi-yah], gae [guh-ay], gaeen [guh-ee(n)], hue [hu-ay], huee [hu-ee].

When the object has को ko: verb goes to default (m sg)

If the object carries को ko — as person-objects and definite objects do — the verb can't agree with it anymore. It falls back to the default form: masculine singular.

मैंने अपनी बहन को देखा।
maine apnee behen ko dekhaa. [meh(n)-nay up-nee beh-hen koh day-khah]
I saw my sister. (behen f, but behen KO → dekhaa, default m sg)
उसने मुझे नहीं देखा।
usne mujhe naheen dekhaa. [us-nay mu-jhay nuh-hee(n) day-khah]
He/she didn't see me. (mujhe = mujh + ko in disguise)
हमने बच्चों को बुलाया।
hamne bachchon ko bulaayaa. [hum-nay buch-choh(n) koh bu-lah-yah]
We called the kids (over).

Compare: मैंने किताब पढ़ी maine kitaab paRhee (no ko → agree with kitaab) vs मैंने इस किताब को पढ़ा maine is kitaab ko paRhaa [meh(n)-nay is ki-tahb koh puh-Rhah] (with ko → default). Both correct; the first is more common for things.

Two rebels: लाना laanaa and बोलना bolnaa

Two everyday verbs look transitive but take no ne: लाना laanaa "bring" and बोलना bolnaa "speak". मैं मिठाई लाया। main miThaaee laayaa. [meh(n) mi-Thah-ee lah-yah] "I brought sweets" — verb agrees with the (male) speaker; a woman says मैं मिठाई लाई। main miThaaee laaee. Likewise वह बोला / वह बोली voh bolaa / voh bolee "he said / she said".

Negatives and questions

Nothing new to learn: नहीं naheen before the verb, question words in place.

मैंने कुछ नहीं किया।
maine kuchh naheen kiyaa. [meh(n)-nay kuchh nuh-hee(n) ki-yah]
I didn't do anything.
किसने दरवाज़ा खोला?
kisne darvaazaa kholaa? [kis-nay dur-vah-zah khoh-lah]
Who opened the door?
तुमने क्या कहा?
tumne kyaa kahaa? [tum-nay kyah kuh-hah]
What did you say?
आपने बहुत अच्छा खाना बनाया।
aapne bahut achchhaa khaanaa banaayaa. [ahp-nay bo-hut uch-chhah khah-nah buh-nah-yah]
You made really good food. (say this to your saas; watch the smile)
शादी में बहुत मज़ा आया।
shaadee mein bahut mazaa aayaa. [shah-dee may(n) bo-hut muh-zah ah-yah]
The wedding was great fun. (lit. much fun came — mazaa m, aanaa: no ne)

The three classic ne disasters — and their fixes:

1. Putting ne on go/come/be verbs: *मैंने गया *maine gayaa and *मैं गया ने *main gayaa ne are both impossible. Going verbs never see ne: मैं गया। main gayaa.

2. Letting the verb agree with the doer: *मैंने चाय पिया *maine chaay piyaa. With ne, the doer is invisible to the verb — chaay is feminine, so: मैंने चाय पी। maine chaay pee.

3. Using ne outside the perfective: *मैंने चाय पीता हूँ *maine chaay peetaa hoon. Present, continuous and future keep the plain subject: मैं चाय पीता हूँ। main chaay peetaa hoon.

The all-purpose Delhi catch-up opener: और बताओ, कल क्या किया? aur bataao, kal kyaa kiyaa? [awr buh-tah-oh, kul kyah ki-yah] "So tell me, what did you do yesterday?" You'll also constantly hear हो गया? ho gayaa? [hoh guh-yah] "done?" (that two-verb trick is Unit 19). And Delhiites often say मैंने बोला maine bolaa for "I said" even though the standard is main bolaa — understand it; in your own speech, मैंने कहा maine kahaa is always safe.

Exercise 14A — ne or no ne?

Fill the blank: items 1–2, 4, 8 need the right past form of the verb in brackets; items 3, 5, 9 need the right subject form (with or without ne); the rest need both thinking steps. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 14.

  1. मैं कल बाज़ार ___। (main kal baazaar ___.) (जाना jaanaa; Jacob speaking)
  2. मेरी बहन कल दिल्ली ___। (meree behen kal dillee ___.) (जाना jaanaa)

  4. हम शाम को घर ___। (ham shaam ko ghar ___.) (आना aanaa)
  5. ___ यह किताब पढ़ी। (___ yeh kitaab paRhee.) (वह voh)

Exercise 14B — Yesterday, not every day

  1. I drank tea.
  2. She went home.
  3. What did you (tum) eat?

  5. They made food.
  6. Who took my phone?

chapters.book2-u15:
Unit 15 Perfect Tenses: "has done" & "had done"

What you'll be able to say: the difference between "she went", "she has gone" and "she had gone" — plus the very Delhi habit of using "had gone" for plain old "went". Good news: this unit is Unit 14 plus one small word. All the ne and agreement rules carry over unchanged.

वह अभी आया है।
voh abhee aayaa hai. [voh uh-bhee ah-yah heh]
He has just come — he's here now.
मैंने खाना खाया है।
maine khaanaa khaayaa hai. [meh(n)-nay khah-nah khah-yah heh]
I've eaten. (so no need to feed me — the result matters now)
हम पिछले साल दिल्ली गए थे।
ham pichhle saal dillee gae the. [hum pichh-lay sahl dil-lee guh-ay thay]
We went to Delhi last year. (lit. gone were — remote past)

The recipe

Take the perfective participle from Unit 14 and add a form of honaa after it:

participle aloneवह गया। voh gayaa.he went — simple past (Unit 14)
+ है/हैं hai/hainवह गया है। voh gayaa hai.he has gone — present perfect: done, and it matters right now
+ था/थी/थे/थीं thaa…वह गया था। voh gayaa thaa.he had gone / he went (back then) — past perfect

Everything you sweated over in Unit 14 still applies. No-ne verbs (go, come, arrive…): participle and auxiliary agree with the subject. Ne-verbs: both agree with the object — and ne stays on the doer.

Present perfect of आना aanaa (no ne) — both genders

 malefemale
मैं mainआया हूँ aayaa hoonआई हूँ aaee hoon
तुम tumआए हो aae hoआई हो aaee ho
आप aapआए हैं aae hainआई हैं aaee hain
वह vohआया है aayaa haiआई है aaee hai
हम hamआए हैं aae hainआई हैं aaee hain
वे लोग voh logआए हैं aae hainआई हैं aaee hain

For the past perfect, swap in thaa / the / thee / theen: आया था, आए थे, आई थी, आई थीं aayaa thaa, aae the, aaee thee, aaee theen [ah-yah thah · ah-ay thay · ah-ee thee · ah-ee thee(n)].

Where did the nasal go? In Unit 14 the feminine plural was आईं aaeen: लड़कियाँ आईं। laRkiyaan aaeen. [luhR-ki-yah(n) ah-ee(n)] When an auxiliary follows, the nasal jumps onto the LAST word only: लड़कियाँ आई हैं। laRkiyaan aaee hain. · लड़कियाँ आई थीं। laRkiyaan aaee theen. Same with objects: मैंने रोटियाँ खाईं maine roTiyaan khaaeen but मैंने रोटियाँ खाई हैं maine roTiyaan khaaee hain.

Present perfect: done — and it matters now

मम्मी आई हैं।
mummy aaee hain. [mum-mee ah-ee heh(n)]
Mom's come (she's here). (respect plural hain for an elder)
मैंने दो किताबें पढ़ी हैं।
maine do kitaaben paRhee hain. [meh(n)-nay doh ki-tah-bay(n) puh-Rhee heh(n)]
I've read two books. (kitaaben f pl → paRhee + hain)
क्या तुमने मेरी चाबी देखी है?
kyaa tumne meree chaabee dekhee hai? [kyah tum-nay may-ree chah-bee day-khee heh]
Have you seen my key? (I need it right now)
मैंने यह फ़िल्म दो बार देखी है।
maine yeh film do baar dekhee hai. [meh(n)-nay yeh film doh bahr day-khee heh]
I've seen this film twice.
क्या आपने कभी दिल्ली की सर्दी देखी है?
kyaa aapne kabhee dillee kee sardee dekhee hai? [kyah ahp-nay kuh-bhee dil-lee kee sur-dee day-khee heh]
Have you ever seen a Delhi winter? (kabhee = ever — loves the present perfect)
वह अभी-अभी गया है।
voh abhee-abhee gayaa hai. [voh uh-bhee uh-bhee guh-yah heh]
He's just this minute left.

Negatives usually drop the hai — the plain past does the job, often with अभी तक abhee tak [uh-bhee tuk] "yet":

मैंने अभी तक खाना नहीं खाया।
maine abhee tak khaanaa naheen khaayaa. [meh(n)-nay uh-bhee tuk khah-nah nuh-hee(n) khah-yah]
I haven't eaten yet.

Past perfect: before then, or just "back then"

Textbook use: an event completed before another past moment. Delhi use: any event you're placing at a distance — last week, last year, that one time. English says "went"; Delhi very often says "had gone". Both of these are everyday sentences:

मैंने वह फ़िल्म पहले देखी थी।
maine voh film pehle dekhee thee. [meh(n)-nay voh film peh-lay day-khee thee]
I had seen that film before.
हम 2020 में मिले थे।
ham 2020 mein mile the. [hum doh huh-zahr bees may(n) mi-lay thay]
We (first) met in 2020. (milnaa: no ne)
आपने मुझे पैसे दिए थे।
aapne mujhe paise diye the. [ahp-nay mu-jhay peh-say di-yay thay]
You had given me money. (paise m pl → diye + the)
कल मैं सरोजिनी नगर गया था।
kal main sarojinee nagar gayaa thaa. [kul meh(n) suh-roh-ji-nee nuh-gur guh-yah thah]
I went to Sarojini Nagar yesterday. (Delhi-style plain past — see box)
मेरी बहन पिछले हफ़्ते आई थी।
meree behen pichhle hafte aaee thee. [may-ree beh-hen pichh-lay huf-tay ah-ee thee]
My sister came last week. (she's gone back now — thee adds that distance)

Which past do I pick?

SituationTenseExample
Event, plainly reportedsimple pastमैंने चाय पी। maine chaay pee.
Done + the result matters this minutepresent perfectमैंने चाय पी है। maine chaay pee hai. (I'm good, thanks)
Before another past event, or held at a distance ("that was then")past perfectमैंने चाय पी थी। maine chaay pee thee. (back then / already)

English lets you say "I have seen it yesterday" — no wait, it doesn't! Hindi has the same allergy. With a stated past time (kal, pichhle saal, 2020 mein), don't use …hai: *कल मैंने खाना खाया है *kal maine khaanaa khaayaa hai sounds off. Say कल मैंने खाना खाया kal maine khaanaa khaayaa or, very Delhi, …खाया था …khaayaa thaa. The hai-perfect lives in the present moment: abhee, aaj, kabhee, abhee tak.

Delhi keeps thaa/thee/the busy. "What did you do on the weekend?" gets answered in past perfect even with zero "before" meaning: हम मूवी देखने गए थे। ham moovee dekhne gae the. [hum moo-vee daykh-nay guh-ay thay] "We went to (see) a movie." मैंने तुझे बताया था न! maine tujhe bataayaa thaa na! [meh(n)-nay tu-jhay buh-tah-yah thah nuh] "I TOLD you, didn't I!" — the past perfect adds that told-you-so distance. Feel free to copy this one; it's core Delhi.

Walk into any Delhi home and within a minute someone will ask: कुछ खाया है? kuchh khaayaa hai? [kuchh khah-yah heh] "Have you eaten anything?" It's care, not curiosity — and "yes" will not stop the snacks. The polite play: जी हाँ, खाया है। jee haan, khaayaa hai. — then accept the chai anyway.

chapters.book2-u16:
Unit 16 Can, Manage, Already Done: सकना · पाना · चुकना

What you'll be able to say: what you can and can't do, ask permission, make polite "can you…?" requests, admit what you didn't manage, and announce that something's already done. All three helpers work the same way: verb STEM + helper, and — mark this now — never, ever with ने ne.

मैं हिन्दी बोल सकता हूँ।
main hindee bol saktaa hoon. [meh(n) hin-dee bohl suk-tah hoon]
I can speak Hindi.
क्या मैं अंदर आ सकता हूँ?
kyaa main andar aa saktaa hoon? [kyah meh(n) un-dur ah suk-tah hoon]
May I come in?
मैं खा चुका हूँ।
main khaa chukaa hoon. [meh(n) khah chu-kah hoon]
I've already eaten.

सकना saknaa — can, be able

Formula: bare stem + a conjugated form of saknaa. The stem never changes; saknaa conjugates like any verb and agrees with the subject.

 malefemale
मैं mainकर सकता हूँ kar saktaa hoonकर सकती हूँ kar saktee hoon
तुम tumकर सकते हो kar sakte hoकर सकती हो kar saktee ho
आप aapकर सकते हैं kar sakte hainकर सकती हैं kar saktee hain
वह vohकर सकता है kar saktaa haiकर सकती है kar saktee hai
हम / वे लोग ham / voh logकर सकते हैं kar sakte hainकर सकती हैं kar saktee hain

Say it: saktaa [suk-tah], sakte [suk-tay], saktee [suk-tee]. Past ("could/couldn't", nearly always negative): सका / सके / सकी sakaa / sake / sakee [suh-kah · suh-kay · suh-kee]. Future: सकूँगा / सकेगी / सकेंगे sakoongaa / sakegee / sakenge [suh-koo(n)-gah · suh-kay-gee · suh-kay(n)-gay].

वह हिन्दी और अंग्रेज़ी बोल सकती है।
voh hindee aur angrezee bol saktee hai. [voh hin-dee awr un-gray-zee bohl suk-tee heh]
She can speak Hindi and English.
क्या तुम गाड़ी चला सकते हो?
kyaa tum gaaRee chalaa sakte ho? [kyah tum gah-Ree chuh-lah suk-tay hoh]
Can you drive? (lit. make-the-car-move)
मैं तैर नहीं सकता।
main tair naheen saktaa. [meh(n) tehr nuh-hee(n) suk-tah]
I can't swim. (naheen likes to sit inside the cluster: tair naheen saktaa)
कल मैं नहीं सो सका।
kal main naheen so sakaa. [kul meh(n) nuh-hee(n) soh suh-kah]
I couldn't sleep last night.

Permission and polite requests

Ask permission with kyaa main … saktaa hoon?; make requests with kyaa aap … kar sakte hain? — the polished version of Unit 13's commands. Expect warm answers: हाँ, बिल्कुल। haan, bilkul. [hah(n), bil-kul] · ज़रूर। zaroor. [zuh-roor]

क्या आप मेरी मदद कर सकते हैं?
kyaa aap meree madad kar sakte hain? [kyah ahp may-ree muh-dud kur suk-tay heh(n)]
Can you help me?
क्या मैं आपसे एक सवाल पूछ सकता हूँ?
kyaa main aapse ek savaal poochh saktaa hoon? [kyah meh(n) ahp-say ayk suh-vahl poochh suk-tah hoon]
May I ask you a question?

पाना paanaa — manage to, get to

पाना paanaa [pah-nah] as a helper means "manage to / get the chance to". It lives mostly in negatives and apologies — where saknaa states inability, paanaa sighs "it just didn't work out":

मैं कल नहीं आ पाया।
main kal naheen aa paayaa. [meh(n) kul nuh-hee(n) ah pah-yah]
I couldn't make it yesterday.
वह रात को सो नहीं पाई।
voh raat ko so naheen paaee. [voh raht koh soh nuh-hee(n) pah-ee]
She couldn't get to sleep at night.
माफ़ कीजिए, मैं कल नहीं आ पाऊँगा।
maaf keejiye, main kal naheen aa paaoongaa. [mahf kee-ji-yay, meh(n) kul nuh-hee(n) ah pah-oo(n)-gah]
Sorry, I won't be able to come tomorrow. (the standard polite decline)
मैं जवाब नहीं दे पाया।
main javaab naheen de paayaa. [meh(n) juh-vahb nuh-hee(n) day pah-yah]
I couldn't (manage to) answer.

On its own, paanaa is a normal transitive verb meaning "get, obtain" (and that one does take ne in the past). As a helper after a stem — aa paayaa, kar paayaa — it never does.

चुकना chuknaa — already done

चुकना chuknaa [chuk-nah] after a stem means the action is finished — "already". It usually appears in the perfect: stem + chukaa/chuke/chukee + hoon/ho/hai/hain.

मैं खाना खा चुका हूँ।
main khaanaa khaa chukaa hoon. [meh(n) khah-nah khah chu-kah hoon]
I've already eaten. (note: main, not maine — see the box!)
वे लोग जा चुके हैं।
voh log jaa chuke hain. [voh lohg jah chu-kay heh(n)]
They've already left.
चाय बन चुकी है।
chaay ban chukee hai. [chah-ay bun chu-kee heh]
The tea's already made. (bannaa vi = to get made)
मैं यह फ़िल्म देख चुका हूँ।
main yeh film dekh chukaa hoon. [meh(n) yeh film daykh chu-kah hoon]
I've already seen this film.

The iron rule of this unit: no ne. Ever. Even when the main verb is a ne-verb, the helper wins and ne is banned — and the verb goes back to agreeing with the subject:

*मैंने यह काम नहीं कर सका *maine yeh kaam naheen kar sakaa → मैं यह काम नहीं कर सका। main yeh kaam naheen kar sakaa.

*मैंने खा चुका हूँ *maine khaa chukaa hoon → मैं खा चुका हूँ। main khaa chukaa hoon.

Watch the agreement flip too: वह चिट्ठी नहीं पढ़ सकी। voh chiTThee naheen paRh sakee. [voh chiT-Thee nuh-hee(n) puRh suh-kee] "She couldn't read the letter" — sakee agrees with her, not the letter. Unit 14's object-agreement applies only when ne is present, and ne is never present here.

Delhi's favourite maybe: हो सकता है। ho saktaa hai. [hoh suk-tah heh] "could be / maybe" — an entire conversation move by itself. Its pessimist twin: नहीं हो पाएगा यार। naheen ho paaegaa yaar. [nuh-hee(n) hoh pah-ay-gah yahr] "it's not going to happen, yaar." And for "already done", street Delhi usually reaches for हो गया ho gayaa / कर लिया kar liyaa (Unit 19) — chuknaa reads a touch neutral-formal, which makes it perfect for the in-laws.

The guest's magic sentence at your in-laws': क्या मैं कुछ मदद कर सकता हूँ? kyaa main kuchh madad kar saktaa hoon? [kyah meh(n) kuchh muh-dud kur suk-tah hoon] "Can I help with anything?" The answer will be a scandalized नहीं-नहीं, आप बैठिए! naheen-naheen, aap baiThiye! — guests don't work. Offer anyway, every time; the offering is the point. After a meal, deploy बस, मैं खा चुका हूँ। bas, main khaa chukaa hoon. — it may buy you mercy from the third helping.

chapters.book2-u17:
Unit 17 Must & Should: Obligation

What you'll be able to say: I should go, I have to work, I had no choice — three strengths of obligation, all built on one frame you already half-know from Unit 10: person + को ko + infinitive + a strength word. Plus "I need…" with zaroorat.

मुझे अब जाना चाहिए।
mujhe ab jaanaa chaahiye. [mu-jhay ub jah-nah chah-hi-yay]
I should go now.
मुझे कल काम पर जाना है।
mujhe kal kaam par jaanaa hai. [mu-jhay kul kahm pur jah-nah heh]
I have to go to work tomorrow.
कल मुझे जल्दी उठना पड़ेगा।
kal mujhe jaldee uThnaa paRegaa. [kul mu-jhay jul-dee uTh-nah puh-Ray-gah]
Tomorrow I'll have to get up early — no way around it.

The frame: person-को + infinitive + strength word

In obligation sentences the person is not a plain subject — they're marked with ko, using the same dative forms as pasand hai and chaahiye in Unit 10:

Pronounko-formSay it Pronounko-formSay it
मैं mainमुझे mujhemu-jhayहम hamहमें hamenhuh-may(n)
तू tuतुझे tujhetu-jhayतुम tumतुम्हें tumhentum-hay(n)
यह yehइसे isei-sayआप aapआपको aapkoahp-koh
वह vohउसे useu-sayवे लोग voh logउन्हें unhenun-hay(n)

Strength 1 — चाहिए chaahiye: should (advice)

आपको आराम करना चाहिए।
aapko aaraam karnaa chaahiye. [ahp-koh ah-rahm kur-nah chah-hi-yay]
You should rest.
तुम्हें ज़्यादा पानी पीना चाहिए।
tumhen zyaadaa paanee peenaa chaahiye. [tum-hay(n) zyah-dah pah-nee pee-nah chah-hi-yay]
You should drink more water.

Past "should have": add thaa — मुझे पहले सोचना चाहिए था। mujhe pehle sochnaa chaahiye thaa. [mu-jhay peh-lay sohch-nah chah-hi-yay thah] "I should have thought earlier."

Don't mix this up with Unit 10's chaahiye-of-wanting. मुझे चाय चाहिए mujhe chaay chaahiye = "I want/need tea" (noun before chaahiye). मुझे चाय पीनी चाहिए mujhe chaay peenee chaahiye = "I should drink tea" (infinitive before chaahiye). Same skeleton, different creature.

Strength 2 — होना honaa: have to / that's the plan

Infinitive + hai: a duty or a firm plan. In Delhi speech it shades into "want to" — मुझे जाना है often just means "I want to go / I'm off".

हमें आज घर जाना है।
hamen aaj ghar jaanaa hai. [huh-may(n) ahj ghur jah-nah heh]
We have to go home today.
मुझे सब्ज़ी ख़रीदनी है।
mujhe sabzee khareednee hai. [mu-jhay sub-zee khuh-reed-nee heh]
I have to buy vegetables. (khareedNEE — see the agreement rule below!)

Past plan: मुझे कल जाना था। mujhe kal jaanaa thaa. "I was supposed to go yesterday." Future: jaanaa hogaa "will have to" — close to paRegaa but a shade softer.

Strength 3 — पड़ना paRnaa: compulsion, no choice

पड़ना paRnaa [puR-nah] literally "to fall (on you)". Outside pressure, often with a sigh:

recurringपड़ता है paRtaa hai puR-tah hehमुझे रोज़ जल्दी उठना पड़ता है। mujhe roz jaldee uThnaa paRtaa hai. I have to get up early every day.
one-time pastपड़ा paRaa puh-Rahमुझे कल देर तक काम करना पड़ा। mujhe kal der tak kaam karnaa paRaa. I had to work late yesterday.
futureपड़ेगा paRegaa puh-Ray-gahमुझे कल ऑफ़िस जाना पड़ेगा। mujhe kal ofis jaanaa paRegaa. I'll have to go to the office tomorrow.

The agreement rule: the infinitive watches the object

Here is the part to learn slowly. When the verb has an object, the infinitive — and hai/thaa/paRaa/paRegaa after it — agree with that object, just like ne-sentences in Unit 14. chaahiye itself stays fixed in Delhi speech; the infinitive still agrees.

ObjectSentenceWhy
काम kaam (m sg)मुझे काम करना है। mujhe kaam karnaa hai.karnaa + hai, m sg
किताब kitaab (f sg)मुझे किताब पढ़नी है। mujhe kitaab paRhnee hai.paRhNEE + hai, f sg
किताबें kitaaben (f pl)मुझे दो किताबें पढ़नी हैं। mujhe do kitaaben paRhnee hain.paRhnee + HAIN, f pl
कपड़े kapRe (m pl)मुझे कपड़े धोने हैं। mujhe kapRe dhone hain.dhoNE + hain, m pl
तुम्हें यह फ़िल्म देखनी चाहिए।

You should watch this film. (film f → dekhnee)
कल मुझे दवाई लेनी पड़ी।
kal mujhe davaaee lenee paRee. [kul mu-jhay duh-vah-ee lay-nee puh-Ree]
Yesterday I had to take medicine. (davaaee f → lenee paRee, both feminine)

No object, or just a destination? Then there's nothing to agree with and everything stays masculine singular: मुझे घर जाना है। mujhe ghar jaanaa hai. — ghar is where you're going, not an object.

ज़रूरत zaroorat — need

ज़रूरत zaroorat (f) [zuh-roo-rut] "need": person-ko + thing + की ज़रूरत है kee zaroorat hai. The thing goes oblique before kee (Unit 7): paise → paison.

मुझे पैसों की ज़रूरत है।
mujhe paison kee zaroorat hai. [mu-jhay peh-soh(n) kee zuh-roo-rut heh]
I need money.
मुझे आपकी मदद की ज़रूरत है।
mujhe aapkee madad kee zaroorat hai. [mu-jhay ahp-kee muh-dud kee zuh-roo-rut heh]
I need your help.
ज़रूरत नहीं है, शुक्रिया।
zaroorat naheen hai, shukriyaa. [zuh-roo-rut nuh-hee(n) heh, shuk-ri-yah]
No need, thanks.

Two traps, one unit:

1. The person must be in the ko-form. *मैं जाना चाहिए *main jaanaa chaahiye is the classic English-speaker sentence — Hindi needs मुझे जाना चाहिए। mujhe jaanaa chaahiye. Same for all three strengths: mujhe … hai, mujhe … paRegaa.

2. Don't freeze the infinitive. *मुझे किताब पढ़ना है *mujhe kitaab paRhnaa hai misses the agreement: kitaab is feminine, so मुझे किताब पढ़नी है। mujhe kitaab paRhnee hai. Check the object's gender every time.

In Delhi, मुझे जाना है mujhe jaanaa hai is how you announce you want to leave, and जाना पड़ेगा jaanaa paRegaa comes with a theatrical sigh — duty calls. The all-purpose shrug of the working world: क्या करें, करना पड़ता है। kyaa karen, karnaa paRtaa hai. [kyah kuh-ray(n), kur-nah puR-tah heh] "What can you do — it's got to be done." (That karen is the subjunctive — next unit.)

Prepare for a steady stream of loving chaahiye from elders: बेटा, तुम्हें ज़्यादा खाना चाहिए। beTaa, tumhen zyaadaa khaanaa chaahiye. "Son, you should eat more." Advice about food, sweaters and marriage timing is affection, not interference. The correct response is a smiling जी। jee. — then do as you like.

chapters.book2-u18:
Unit 18 If & Maybe: the Subjunctive + अगर…तो agar…to

What you'll be able to say: "shall we…?", "what should I do?", "maybe", "so that", "if… then…" — the gentle, might-happen mood of Hindi. The subjunctive looks scary in grammar books and turns out to be the friendliest form in the language: it's just the future with its tail cut off.

चलें?
chalen? [chuh-lay(n)]
Shall we go?
शायद वह कल आए।
shaayad voh kal aae. [shah-yud voh kul ah-ay]
He might come tomorrow.
अगर बारिश होगी तो हम घर पर रहेंगे।
agar baarish hogee to ham ghar par rahenge. [uh-gur bah-rish hoh-gee toh hum ghur pur ruh-hay(n)-gay]
If it rains, we'll stay home.

Making it: future minus -गा/-गे/-गी

Take the Unit 12 future and delete the -gaa/-ge/-gee tail. What's left is the subjunctive — the "may/might/should-I" form. And notice: no gender at all. Men and women use identical forms.

 Future (u12)SubjunctiveSay it
मैं mainकरूँगा karoongaaकरूँ karoonkuh-roo(n)
तू / वह tu / vohकरेगा karegaaकरे karekuh-ray
तुम tumकरोगे karogeकरो karokuh-roh
आप / हम / वे लोग aap / ham / voh logकरेंगे karengeकरें karenkuh-ray(n)

(Yes — the tum subjunctive karo looks exactly like the tum command from Unit 13. Context sorts it out.) The usual suspects with vowel stems:

Verbमैं mainवह vohतुम tumआप/हम aap/ham
जाना jaanaaजाऊँ jaaoonजाए jaaeजाओ jaaoजाएँ jaaen

देना denaaदूँ doonदे deदो doदें den
लेना lenaaलूँ loonले leलो loलें len
पीना peenaaपियूँ piyoonपिए piyeपियो piyoपिएँ piyen
होना honaaहोऊँ hooon (rare)हो hoहो hoहों hon

Say them: jaaoon [jah-oo(n)], jaaen [jah-ay(n)], doon [doo(n)], den [day(n)], piyen [pi-yay(n)], hon [hoh(n)].

Use 1 — Shall we? (suggestions)

The ham-form with a question tune is Hindi's "shall we":

बैठें?
baiThen? [beh-Thay(n)]
Shall we sit?
खाना खाएँ?
khaanaa khaaen? [khah-nah khah-ay(n)]
Shall we eat?
हम थोड़ा इंतज़ार करें?
ham thoRaa intazaar karen? [hum thoh-Rah in-tuh-zahr kuh-ray(n)]
Shall we wait a bit?

Use 2 — What should I do? (asking for instructions)

मैं क्या करूँ?
main kyaa karoon? [meh(n) kyah kuh-roo(n)]
What should I do?
यह कहाँ रखूँ?
yeh kahaan rakhoon? [yeh kuh-hah(n) ruh-khoo(n)]
Where should I put this? (ask this in the kitchen and win hearts)
मैं चाय बनाऊँ?
main chaay banaaoon? [meh(n) chah-ay buh-nah-oo(n)]
Should I make tea?

Use 3 — शायद shaayad + subjunctive: maybe

shaayad + subjunctive = a genuine maybe. (shaayad + future = "probably" — noticeably more confident.)

शायद बारिश हो।
shaayad baarish ho. [shah-yud bah-rish hoh]
It might rain.
शायद वे लोग देर से पहुँचें।
shaayad voh log der se pahunchen. [shah-yud voh lohg dayr say puh-hun-chay(n)]
They might arrive late.

Use 4 — ताकि taaki: so that

धीरे बोलिए ताकि मैं समझ सकूँ।
dheere boliye taaki main samajh sakoon. [dhee-ray boh-li-yay tah-ki meh(n) suh-mujh suh-koo(n)]
Please speak slowly so that I can understand. (taaki always takes the subjunctive)

Use 5 — Wishes and blessings

भगवान करे, सब ठीक हो।
bhagvaan kare, sab Theek ho. [bhug-vahn kuh-ray, sub Theek hoh]
God grant that everything be all right.
भगवान करे, तुम्हारा दिन अच्छा हो।
bhagvaan kare, tumhaaraa din achchhaa ho. [bhug-vahn kuh-ray, tum-hah-rah din uch-chhah hoh]
May your day be good.

अगर…तो agar…to: if… then…

Real, likely conditions take agar + future, then to + future. Hindi keeps the to even where English drops "then" — treat it as non-negotiable glue.

अगर मौसम अच्छा होगा तो हम बाहर खाएँगे।
agar mausam achchhaa hogaa to ham baahar khaaenge. [uh-gur maw-sum uch-chhah hoh-gah toh hum bah-hur khah-ay(n)-gay]
If the weather's good, we'll eat out.
अगर टाइम होगा तो मैं ज़रूर आऊँगा।
agar Taim hogaa to main zaroor aaoongaa. [uh-gur Tah-im hoh-gah toh meh(n) zuh-roor ah-oo(n)-gah]
If there's time, I'll definitely come.

When the if-part is less certain, put it in the subjunctive — and notice how nicely this stacks with Unit 13's gentle infinitive command:

अगर वह आए तो मुझे बताना।
agar voh aae to mujhe bataanaa. [uh-gur voh ah-ay toh mu-jhay buh-tah-nah]
If he comes (should he come), let me know.

Advanced preview — the if-only past. For unreal, contrary-to-fact ifs ("if I were rich…"), Hindi uses the bare -taa form in both halves: अगर मैं अमीर होता तो बड़ा घर ख़रीदता। agar main ameer hotaa to baRaa ghar khareedtaa. [uh-gur meh(n) uh-meer hoh-tah toh buh-Rah ghur khuh-reed-tah] "If I were rich I'd buy a big house." Just learn to recognize it for now — it gets proper treatment later.

English "then" tempts learners into फिर phir: *अगर बारिश होगी, फिर हम नहीं जाएँगे *agar baarish hogee, phir ham naheen jaaenge. Wrong "then"! phir means "afterwards / next". The if-partner is always तो to: अगर बारिश होगी तो हम नहीं जाएँगे। agar baarish hogee to ham naheen jaaenge. You can drop agar in speech — but never drop to.

Delhi suggestions come in three flavours: subjunctive चलें? chalen?, the buddy version चल, चलते हैं chal, chalte hain [chul, chul-tay heh(n)] "c'mon, we're going", and full Hinglish: कल का प्लान बनाएँ? kal kaa plaan banaaen? [kul kah plahn buh-nah-ay(n)] "shall we make a plan for tomorrow?" You'll also hear inshaallah [in-shah-lah] alongside bhagvaan kare — Delhi's Urdu side talking; both mean "here's hoping".

Blessings are the subjunctive's home turf. Greet elders respectfully — a namaste, or touching their feet at festivals — and blessings come back: खुश रहो। khush raho. [khush ruh-hoh] "stay happy", जीते रहो। jeete raho. [jee-tay ruh-hoh] "long may you live". And for hopes about the future, the template is exactly what you learned above: भगवान करे… bhagvaan kare… + subjunctive.

chapters.book2-u19:
Unit 19 Compound Verbs — the Flavor System

What you'll be able to say: finish things off the way Delhi actually does — eat up, hand it over, it's done, it'll get done — by snapping a second "flavor" verb onto the verbs you already know.

खाना खा लो।
khaanaa khaa lo. [khah-nah khah loh]
Eat up (your food). (lit. food eat take)
मुझे अपना नंबर दे दो।
mujhe apnaa nambar de do. [mu-jhay up-nah num-bur day doh]
Give me your number. (lit. give give — the second "give" is pure flavor)
टेंशन मत लो — हो जाएगा।
Tenshan mat lo — ho jaaegaa. [Ten-shun mut loh — hoh jah-ay-gah]
Don't stress — it'll get done.

1. The big idea: stem + flavor verb

Up to now you have used verbs "bare": मैंने खाया (maine khaayaa) [meh(n)-nay khah-yah] — I ate. Grammatical, yes. But real Delhi speech constantly welds two verbs together: the stem of the main verb (the meaning) plus a fully conjugated vector verb (the flavor). The vector loses its dictionary meaning and instead adds a shade: done and dusted, for me, for you, oops, with force.

The stem is just the infinitive minus -naa — the same stem you already use for rahaa hai and for commands:

InfinitiveStemInfinitiveStem
खानाkhaaकरनाkar
सीखनाseekhबतानाbataa
देनाdeलेनाle
होनाhoसोनाso

Only the vector conjugates; the stem never changes. You already know how to conjugate every vector in this unit — lenaa, denaa, jaanaa are old friends. So this unit is not new machinery. It is new seasoning.

Why bother? Because bare verbs often sound stiff or unfinished to Indian ears — like saying "I did eat" when everyone else says "I ate it up." मैंने खाया (maine khaayaa) reports an event; मैंने खा लिया (maine khaa liyaa) [meh(n)-nay khah li-yah] says done, finished, box ticked. In everyday completed-action sentences, Delhi reaches for the compound almost every time.

2. लेना — doing it for yourself

लेना lenaa [lay-nah] "take" as a vector means the action folds back toward the doer: for your own benefit, into your own possession, quietly taking care of your own business.
