3. देना — doing it for someone else

देना denaa [day-nah] "give" points the action outward, away from the doer — done for someone else's benefit, handed over, passed along. le and de are mirror twins:

तुम अपना खाना खा लो, बाक़ी मुझे दे दो।
tum apnaa khaanaa khaa lo, baaqee mujhe de do. [tum up-nah khah-nah khah loh, bah-qee mu-jhay day doh]
You eat (up) your food; give me the rest. (baaqee (f) = the remainder)
पापा को बता दो।
paapaa ko bataa do. [pah-pah koh buh-tah doh]
Tell Dad (let him know).
मैंने पैसे दे दिए।
maine paise de diye. [meh(n)-nay peh-say day di-yay]
I handed the money over. (paisaa (m), plural paise → diye)

The polite forms: दे दीजिए (de deejiye) [day dee-ji-yay], बता दीजिए (bataa deejiye) [buh-tah dee-ji-yay]. With in-laws, a request with a vector sounds warmer and more complete than the bare verb — bataa deejiye feels like "do please let me know," not "inform me."

4. जाना — completion and change of state

जाना jaanaa [jah-nah] "go" is the vector of things tipping over into a new state — finished, changed, arrived, asleep. It pairs mostly with intransitive verbs (honaa, aanaa, sonaa, baiThnaa), and it is everywhere:

दूध ख़त्म हो गया।
doodh khatam ho gayaa. [doodh khuh-tum hoh guh-yah]
The milk is finished. (doodh (m); khatam ho jaanaa = to run out)
ट्रेन आ गई!
Tren aa gaee! [Trayn ah guh-ee]
The train's here! (Tren (f) → gaee)
बच्चा सो गया।
bachchaa so gayaa. [buch-chah soh guh-yah]
The kid's fallen asleep. (bachchaa (m) child)
आप बैठ जाइए।
aap baiTh jaaiye. [ahp behTh jah-i-yay]
Please sit down. (baiTh jaanaa = to sit down, settle into sitting)

Learn the state-change set as a family: हो गया (ho gayaa) it's done · आ गया (aa gayaa) arrived · सो गया (so gayaa) fell asleep · ठीक हो गया (Theek ho gayaa) [Theek hoh guh-yah] it got fixed · देर हो गई (der ho gaee) [dayr hoh guh-ee] it got late (der (f)).

हो जाएगा। (ho jaaegaa.) [hoh jah-ay-gah] — the great Delhi promise. It will happen, it will get done, somehow, by someone, at some point. Plumber, landlord, cousin with a "contact" — everyone says it. Its siblings run the whole day: हो गया? (ho gayaa?) "done?" · चल, हो गया। (chal, ho gayaa.) [chul, hoh guh-yah] "right, that's that" · ले लो यार। (le lo yaar.) [lay loh yahr] "just take it, yaar." Master these four and you sound local.

5. The strong flavors: डालना, बैठना, उठना

Three more vectors, used less often but with vivid color:

VectorFlavorExampleMeaning
डालना Daalnaa Dahl-nahvigorous, decisive, in one goपढ़ डाला paRh Daalaa puRh Dah-lahread it right through
बैठना baiThnaa behTh-nahregrettable, foolish, "went and did it"कर बैठा kar baiThaa kur beh-Thahwent and did (something dumb)
उठना uThnaa uTh-nahsudden, involuntary burstबोल उठा bol uThaa bohl u-Thahblurted out
मैंने एक ही रात में पूरी किताब पढ़ डाली।
maine ek hee raat mein pooree kitaab paRh Daalee. [meh(n)-nay ayk hee raht may(n) poo-ree ki-tahb puRh Dah-lee]
I tore through the whole book in a single night. (kitaab (f) → Daalee)
वह ग़ुस्से में सब कुछ कह बैठा।
voh gusse mein sab kuchh keh baiThaa. [voh gus-say may(n) sub kuchh keh beh-Thah]
In anger he went and said everything (and regretted it). (gussaa (m) anger)
बच्चा अचानक हँस उठा।
bachchaa achaanak hans uThaa. [buch-chah uh-chah-nuk huh(n)s u-Thah]
The child suddenly burst out laughing.

A cousin of uThnaa: sudden bursts also use पड़ना (paRnaa) [puR-nah] — वह रो पड़ी (voh ro paRee) [voh roh puh-Ree] "she burst into tears." Recognize it; you don't have to produce it yet.

6. The ने rule: follow the vector

Here is the rule that trips everyone up. In perfective (simple past / perfect) sentences, whether you use ne depends on the vector, not the main verb:

VectorTransitivityने?Example
lenaa, denaa, Daalnaatransitive (vt)yesमैंने खा लिया। maine khaa liyaa.
jaanaa, baiThnaa, uThnaaintransitive (vi)noवह खा गया। voh khaa gayaa. [voh khah guh-yah] he ate it all up / devoured it

So the same main verb flips depending on the flavor: उसने सब मिठाई खा ली (usne sab miThaaee khaa lee) [us-nay sub mi-Thah-ee khah lee] — with ne; but वह सब मिठाई खा गया (voh sab miThaaee khaa gayaa) — no ne, and the verb now agrees with he, not with the sweets (miThaaee (f)). And वह ग़लती कर बैठा (voh galtee kar baiThaa) [voh gul-tee kur beh-Thah] — no ne, even though karnaa itself is transitive, because baiThnaa is not (galtee (f) mistake).

Don't compute ne from the main verb. English speakers see "he ate," remember khaanaa is transitive, and produce ✗ उसने आ गया (✗ usne aa gayaa) or ✗ मैंने सो गया (✗ maine so gayaa). Wrong: jaanaa is intransitive, so वह आ गया (voh aa gayaa), मैं सो गया (main so gayaa) [meh(n) soh guh-yah]. One glance at the vector settles it every time.

Compounds mostly vanish under negation. "I didn't eat" is मैंने नहीं खाया (maine naheen khaayaa) — not ✗ maine naheen khaa liyaa. Flavor belongs to things that actually happened (or that you're telling someone to do).

7. Delhi reps

मैंने नया फ़ोन ले लिया।
maine nayaa fon le liyaa. [meh(n)-nay nuh-yah fohn lay li-yah]
I've bought (gotten myself) a new phone. (fon (m))
रुको, मैं पूछ लेता हूँ।
ruko, main poochh letaa hoon. [ru-koh, meh(n) poochh lay-tah hoo(n)]
Hang on, I'll just ask (and find out for us). (habitual + vector = "I'll just…")
ऑटो आ गया — चलो, बैठ जाओ।
auTo aa gayaa — chalo, baiTh jaao. [aw-Toh ah guh-yah — chuh-loh, behTh jah-oh]
The auto's here — come on, get in. (auTo (m))
ले लो यार, अच्छी चीज़ है।
le lo yaar, achchhee cheez hai. [lay loh yahr, uch-chhee cheez heh]
Just take it, yaar — it's good stuff. (cheez (f) thing)
कल तक हो जाएगा, भाई।
kal tak ho jaaegaa, bhaaee. [kul tuk hoh jah-ay-gah, bhah-ee]
It'll be done by tomorrow, bhai. (bhaaee (m) brother — Delhi filler)
देर हो गई, अब सो जाओ।
der ho gaee, ab so jaao. [dayr hoh guh-ee, ub soh jah-oh]
It's gotten late — go to sleep now.

At the in-laws' table, compounds carry the hospitality: थोड़ा और ले लो। (thoRaa aur le lo.) [thoh-Rah awr lay loh] "take a little more." Refusing once is polite ritual, not refusal; your plate will be refilled. The graceful out: बस, मैंने बहुत खा लिया। (bas, maine bahut khaa liyaa.) [bus, meh(n)-nay buh-hut khah li-yah] "enough — I've eaten plenty." The compound makes it sound final and satisfied, not rude.

Exercise 19A — Pick the vector

chapters.book2-u20:
Unit 20 Joining Ideas & Reported Speech

What you'll be able to say: sentences with more than one moving part — I think that…, she said that…, because…, when…, before…, after…, having done X… — the glue that turns phrases into conversation.

मुझे लगता है कि यह ठीक है।
mujhe lagtaa hai ki yeh Theek hai. [mu-jhay lug-tah heh ki yeh Theek heh]
I think (it seems to me) that this is fine.
उसने कहा कि वह आ रहा है।
usne kahaa ki voh aa rahaa hai. [us-nay kuh-hah ki voh ah ruh-hah heh]
He said (that) he was coming. (lit. …that he IS coming — see §2!)
खाना खाके सो जाओ।
khaanaa khaake so jaao. [khah-nah khah-kay soh jah-oh]
Eat and (then) go to sleep. (lit. food having-eaten sleep-go)

1. कि — the all-purpose "that"

कि ki [ki] links a verb of thinking, knowing, saying, or feeling to a full clause. English often drops "that"; Hindi almost never drops ki.

OpenerRomanSay itMeaning
मुझे लगता है कि…mujhe lagtaa hai ki…mu-jhay lug-tah heh kiI think / it seems to me that…
मुझे पता है कि…mujhe pataa hai ki…mu-jhay puh-tah heh kiI know that…
उसने कहा कि…usne kahaa ki…us-nay kuh-hah kihe/she said that…
उसने पूछा कि…usne poochhaa ki…us-nay poo-chhah kihe/she asked (whether/what)…
अच्छा है कि…achchhaa hai ki…uch-chhah heh kiit's good that…
मुझे पता है कि तुम थके हो।
mujhe pataa hai ki tum thake ho. [mu-jhay puh-tah heh ki tum thuh-kay hoh]
I know (that) you're tired.
मुझे लगता है कि बारिश होगी।
mujhe lagtaa hai ki baarish hogee. [mu-jhay lug-tah heh ki bah-rish hoh-gee]
I think it'll rain. (baarish (f) rain)

Spelling alert: कि (ki) "that" has the short i; की (kee) is the possessive "of." One matra apart, totally different words. Your eye will learn to catch it; your ear already can — [ki] is clipped, [kee] is long.

2. Reported speech keeps the original tense

This is the star rule of the unit. English backshifts: "I am coming" becomes "he said he was coming." Hindi does not. You freeze the speaker's words in their original tense, swap the pronouns, and pipe them through ki:

They said…You report…English feel
"मैं आ रहा हूँ।" main aa rahaa hoon.उसने कहा कि वह आ रहा है। usne kahaa ki voh aa rahaa hai.He said he was coming.
"मैं कल आऊँगा।" main kal aaoongaa. ah-oo(n)-gahउसने कहा कि वह कल आएगा। usne kahaa ki voh kal aaegaa. ah-ay-gahHe said he'd come tomorrow.
"मुझे भूख लगी है।" mujhe bhookh lagee hai. bhookh luh-gee hehउसने कहा कि उसे भूख लगी है। usne kahaa ki use bhookh lagee hai. u-sayShe said she was hungry.
"तुम कब आओगे?" tum kab aaoge?उसने पूछा कि तुम कब आओगे। usne poochhaa ki tum kab aaoge.She asked when you'd come.

Resist the English backshift. Learners hear "he said he was coming" and produce ✗ उसने कहा कि वह आ रहा था (✗ usne kahaa ki voh aa rahaa thaa) — but in Hindi that means he said he was coming at some earlier time (and probably isn't anymore). If his words were "I'm coming," report …ki voh aa rahaa hai. Keep the tense the speaker used. Every time.

On the street, "said" is usually bolnaa, not kehnaa — and colloquially it skips ne: वह बोला कि पैसे कल मिलेंगे। (voh bolaa ki paise kal milenge.) [voh boh-lah ki peh-say kul mi-lay(n)-gay] "He said (lit. he spoke that) the money will come tomorrow." Feminine: वह बोली कि… (voh bolee ki…) [voh boh-lee ki]. You'll hear main bolaa, voh bolaa all day in Delhi; use usne kahaa when you want to sound a touch more careful.

3. Because and therefore: क्योंकि, इसलिए

मैं देर से उठा क्योंकि कल रात देर से सोया।
main der se uThaa kyonki kal raat der se soyaa. [meh(n) dayr say u-Thah kyoh(n)-ki kul raht dayr say soh-yah]
I got up late because I went to sleep late last night. (der (f) lateness; raat (f) night)
बारिश हो रही थी, इसलिए हम घर पर रहे।
baarish ho rahee thee, isliye ham ghar par rahe. [bah-rish hoh ruh-hee thee, is-li-yay hum ghur pur ruh-hay]
It was raining, so (therefore) we stayed home.

kyonki introduces the reason after the fact; isliye introduces the result. Same logic as English "because" and "so," and they sit in the same places.

4. When…then: जब…तब / तो

Hindi loves paired connectors. A jab ("when") clause is answered by tab ("then") or — far more often in speech — plain to:

जब मैं दिल्ली आया, तब मुझे हिन्दी नहीं आती थी।
jab main dillee aayaa, tab mujhe hindee naheen aatee thee. [jub meh(n) dil-lee ah-yah, tub mu-jhay hin-dee nuh-hee(n) ah-tee thee]
When I came to Delhi, I didn't know Hindi. (hindee aanaa = to know Hindi, u10 pattern)
जब तुम आओगे, तो हम खाएँगे।
jab tum aaoge, to ham khaaenge. [jub tum ah-oh-gay, toh hum khah-ay(n)-gay]
When you come, (then) we'll eat. (note: future in BOTH halves, unlike English)

Until / as long as uses the pair जब तक…तब तक jab tak…tab tak [jub tuk…tub tuk]:

जब तक मैं यहाँ हूँ, तब तक कोई टेंशन नहीं।
jab tak main yahaan hoon, tab tak koee Tenshan naheen. [jub tuk meh(n) yuh-hah(n) hoo(n), tub tuk koh-ee Ten-shun nuh-hee(n)]
As long as I'm here, no tension.
जब तक तुम नहीं आओगे, मैं नहीं खाऊँगा।
jab tak tum naheen aaoge, main naheen khaaoongaa. [jub tuk tum nuh-hee(n) ah-oh-gay, meh(n) nuh-hee(n) khah-oo(n)-gah]
Until you come, I won't eat.

Spot the odd little naheen in the "until" clause: jab tak tum naheen aaoge… is literally "as long as you will not come." When jab tak means "until (something happens)," Hindi puts the clause in the negative. It feels backwards to an English eye; it is completely standard.

5. Before and after: से पहले, के बाद

Take the infinitive, put it in the oblique (-naa → -ne), and add the postposition — exactly the oblique machinery from Unit 7:

PatternExampleMeaning
…ne se pehleजाने से पहले jaane se pehle jah-nay say peh-laybefore going
…ne ke baadखाने के बाद khaane ke baad khah-nay kay bahdafter eating
सोने से पहले फ़ोन मत देखो।
sone se pehle fon mat dekho. [soh-nay say peh-lay fohn mut day-khoh]
Don't look at your phone before sleeping.
जाने से पहले मुझे बता देना।
jaane se pehle mujhe bataa denaa. [jah-nay say peh-lay mu-jhay buh-tah day-nah]
Let me know before you leave. (Unit 19 vector riding along)
खाने के बाद हम टीवी देखते हैं।
khaane ke baad ham Teevee dekhte hain. [khah-nay kay bahd hum Tee-vee daykh-tay heh(n)]
After dinner we watch TV. (Teevee (m))

6. Having done X: the -कर / -के chain

To string actions in sequence — "having eaten, he left" — Hindi glues -कर -kar [kur] or colloquial -के -ke [kay] onto the bare stem. The chained verb never conjugates; only the final verb of the sentence does.

StemFormal-ishDelhi defaultMeaning
khaaखाकर khaakar khah-kurखाके khaake khah-kayhaving eaten
leलेकर lekar lay-kurलेके leke lay-kayhaving taken / with
karकरके karke kur-kay — never ✗ karkarhaving done
वह नहा-धोकर ऑफ़िस चला गया।
voh nahaa-dhokar ofis chalaa gayaa. [voh nuh-hah-dhoh-kur aw-fis chuh-lah guh-yah]
He bathed-and-washed and went off to the office. (nahaa-dhokar — a set phrase; ofis (m))
मैं मेट्रो में बैठकर किताब पढ़ता हूँ।
main meTro mein baiThkar kitaab paRhtaa hoon. [meh(n) may-Troh may(n) behTh-kur ki-tahb puRh-tah hoo(n)]
I read (a book) sitting in the metro. (meTro (f))
चाय पीके बताओ, कैसी बनी है?
chaay peeke bataao, kaisee banee hai? [chah-ay pee-kay buh-tah-oh, keh-see buh-nee heh]
Drink the chai and tell me — how did it turn out?

7. Quick recap: अगर…तो

From Unit 18, the conditional pair sits in the same family: अगर तुम चाहो, तो हम चलें। (agar tum chaaho, to ham chalen.) [uh-gur tum chah-hoh, toh hum chuh-lay(n)] "If you like, let's go." Notice the habit: Hindi marks both halves — agar…to, jab…tab, jab tak…tab tak. Where English drops "then," Hindi keeps it. Lean on the pairs; they hold the sentence up.

Family phone calls run on reported speech. Expect a nightly relay: मम्मी ने पूछा कि तुम कब आ रहे हो। (mummy ne poochhaa ki tum kab aa rahe ho.) [mum-mee nay poo-chhah ki tum kub ah ruh-hay hoh] "Mummy asked when you're coming." Pass a message back with bataa denaa ki… — "do tell (them) that…" — and you're an instant favorite.

Exercise 20B — Report it / chain it

1–4: turn the direct quote into reported speech (keep the tense!). 5–8: join the two actions with -के/-कर.

  1. राहुल: "मैं आ रहा हूँ।" → राहुल ने कहा कि… (raahul ne kahaa ki…)
  2. प्रिया: "मैं कल आऊँगी।" → प्रिया ने कहा कि… (priyaa ne kahaa ki…)
  3. मम्मी: "मुझे भूख लगी है।" → मम्मी ने कहा कि… (mummy ne kahaa ki…)
  4. उसने पूछा: "तुम कहाँ हो?" → उसने पूछा कि… (usne poochhaa ki…)
  5. मैं चाय पीता हूँ + फिर काम करता हूँ → (main chaay peetaa hoon + phir kaam kartaa hoon)
  6. वह खाना खाता है + फिर सो जाता है → (voh khaanaa khaataa hai + phir so jaataa hai)
  7. हम मेट्रो में बैठते हैं + बातें करते हैं → (ham meTro mein baiThte hain + baaten karte hain)
  8. वह नहाता है + ऑफ़िस जाता है → (voh nahaataa hai + ofis jaataa hai)

Exercise 20C — Translate into Hindi

Write Devanagari or roman (or both).

  1. I think (that) the food is very good.
  2. She said (that) she is coming. [keep Hindi tense!]
  3. I stayed home because it was raining.
  4. When you come, we'll eat.
  5. Call me before leaving. (tum; "phone karnaa")
  6. After eating, we'll watch TV.
  7. Having drunk chai, he went to the office.

Exercise 20D — Translate into English

Watch the tense in 1 and the negative in 4.

  1. उसने कहा कि वह दिल्ली में रहता है। (usne kahaa ki voh dillee mein rehtaa hai.)
  2. मुझे पता है कि तुम व्यस्त हो। (mujhe pataa hai ki tum vyast ho.)
  3. जब मैं छोटी थी, तब मैं मुंबई में रहती थी। (jab main chhoTee thee, tab main mumbaee mein rehtee thee.)
  4. जब तक तुम नहीं बोलोगे, कुछ नहीं होगा। (jab tak tum naheen bologe, kuchh naheen hogaa.)
  5. वह बोली कि खाना बन गया है। (voh bolee ki khaanaa ban gayaa hai.)
  6. नहा-धोके तैयार हो जाओ, मेहमान आ रहे हैं। (nahaa-dhoke taiyaar ho jaao, mehmaan aa rahe hain.)
chapters.book2-u21:
Unit 21 Relative Clauses: जो…वह

What you'll be able to say: point at people, things, and places with a whole clause — the boy who's standing there, the shop we buy vegetables from, whoever wants some — using Hindi's paired जो…वह system.

जो लड़का वहाँ खड़ा है, वह मेरा दोस्त है।
jo laRkaa vahaan khaRaa hai, voh meraa dost hai. [joh luhR-kah vuh-hah(n) khuh-Rah heh, voh may-rah dohst heh]
The boy who's standing there is my friend. (lit. which boy there standing is, he my friend is)
जो चाहिए, ले लो।
jo chaahiye, le lo. [joh chah-hi-yay, lay loh]
Take whatever you need.
जो होगा, देखा जाएगा।
jo hogaa, dekhaa jaaegaa. [joh hoh-gah, day-khah jah-ay-gah]
Whatever happens, we'll deal with it then. (the Delhi shrug, in grammar form)

1. The correlative habit: Hindi answers its own clause

English tucks a relative clause inside the sentence: "The boy [who is standing there] is my friend." Hindi almost never does that. It sets the clause up front with जो jo [joh] "which/who," then starts over with वह voh to deliver the main sentence:

English orderHindi order
The boy [who is standing there] is my friend.[जो लड़का वहाँ खड़ा है], वह मेरा दोस्त है।
one interlocking sentencetwo matched halves: a jo-half, answered by a voh-half

You have seen this pairing habit before — agar…to, jab…tab. It runs on a beautiful three-way system. The k- words ask, the j- words relate, and the v-/u- words answer:

Question (k-)Relative (j-)Answer (v-/u-)
कौन kaun who?जो jo who/whichवह voh that one
किस kis which? (obl.)जिस jis jisउस us
कहाँ kahaan where?जहाँ jahaan juh-hah(n)वहाँ vahaan
कब kab when?जब jabतब tab

Never build a relative clause with kaun. English "who" does double duty (question and relative), so learners produce ✗ वह लड़का, कौन वहाँ खड़ा है… (✗ voh laRkaa, kaun vahaan khaRaa hai…). In Hindi kaun only asks questions. The relative "who/which/that" is always jo (oblique jis/jin).

2. जो…वह with people and things

जो लड़की गा रही है, वह मेरी बहन है।
jo laRkee gaa rahee hai, voh meree behen hai. [joh luhR-kee gah ruh-hee heh, voh may-ree beh-hen heh]
The girl who's singing is my sister. (behen (f) sister)
जो चाय तुमने बनाई, वह बहुत अच्छी थी।
jo chaay tumne banaaee, voh bahut achchhee thee. [joh chah-ay tum-nay buh-nah-ee, voh buh-hut uch-chhee thee]
The chai you made was really good. (no "who/that" in the English — Hindi still needs jo)
जो सब्ज़ी ताज़ी है, वही लेना।
jo sabzee taazee hai, vahee lenaa. [joh sub-zee tah-zee heh, vuh-hee lay-nah]
Buy only the vegetables that are fresh. (vahee = voh + hee "exactly that" — more in Unit 24; sabzee (f))

Word order note: the jo-half usually comes first, but speech happily flips it — वह लड़का मेरा दोस्त है जो वहाँ खड़ा है। (voh laRkaa meraa dost hai jo vahaan khaRaa hai.) Both are correct; lead with jo until the flipped version comes naturally.

3. Oblique: जिस / जिन

The moment a postposition touches the relative word, jo obeys the oblique rule you know from Unit 7: singular जिस jis, plural जिन jin [jin]. Its answering pronoun shifts the same way (us/un):

DirectOblique (before a postposition)+ को shortcut
singularजो joजिस jis jisजिसे jise ji-say (= jisko)
pluralजो joजिन jin jinजिन्हें jinhen jin-hay(n) (= jinko)
जिस आदमी से तुम मिले, वह हमारा पड़ोसी है।
jis aadmee se tum mile, voh hamaaraa paRosee hai. [jis ahd-mee say tum mi-lay, voh huh-mah-rah puh-Roh-see heh]
The man you met is our neighbor. (lit. which man-with you met…; paRosee (m))
जिस दुकान से हम सब्ज़ी लेते हैं, वह आज बंद है।
jis dukaan se ham sabzee lete hain, voh aaj band hai. [jis du-kahn say hum sub-zee lay-tay heh(n), voh ahj bund heh]
The shop we buy vegetables from is closed today. (dukaan (f) shop)
जिन लोगों को तुमने बुलाया, वे लोग आ गए।
jin logon ko tumne bulaayaa, voh log aa gae. [jin loh-goh(n) koh tum-nay bu-lah-yah, voh lohg ah guh-ay]
The people you invited have arrived.
जिसे हिन्दी नहीं आती, उसके लिए दिल्ली थोड़ी मुश्किल है।
jise hindee naheen aatee, uske liye dillee thoRee mushkil hai. [ji-say hin-dee nuh-hee(n) ah-tee, us-kay li-yay dil-lee thoh-Ree mush-kil heh]
For someone who doesn't know Hindi, Delhi is a bit tough. (jise ↔ uske: the pair keeps matching in the oblique)

4. जो भी — whoever, whatever

Add bhee and the net widens to "any at all":

जो भी चाहिए, बोल दो।
jo bhee chaahiye, bol do. [joh bhee chah-hi-yay, bohl doh]
Whatever you need, just say (it).
जो भी आएगा, उसे चाय मिलेगी।
jo bhee aaegaa, use chaay milegee. [joh bhee ah-ay-gah, u-say chah-ay mi-lay-gee]
Whoever comes will get chai.

5. Places: जहाँ…वहाँ

जहाँ हम रहते हैं, वहाँ बहुत शोर है।
jahaan ham rehte hain, vahaan bahut shor hai. [juh-hah(n) hum reh-tay heh(n), vuh-hah(n) buh-hut shohr heh]
Where we live, there's a lot of noise. (shor (m) noise)
जहाँ अच्छे छोले भटूरे मिलते हैं, वहीं चलते हैं।
jahaan achchhe chhole bhaToore milte hain, vaheen chalte hain. [juh-hah(n) uch-chhay chhoh-lay bhuh-Too-ray mil-tay heh(n), vuh-hee(n) chul-tay heh(n)]
Let's go exactly where the good chhole bhature are. (chhole bhaToore (m pl); vaheen = right there)

Delhi philosophy comes pre-packaged in jo-pairs. जो होगा, देखा जाएगा। (jo hogaa, dekhaa jaaegaa.) "Whatever happens, we'll see about it then." जो है सो है। (jo hai so hai.) [joh heh soh heh] "It is what it is." Traffic, landlords, cricket scores — one of these two covers it.

For simple descriptions, Delhi often skips the full relative clause and grabs vaalaa instead: लाल वाली कमीज़ (laal vaalee kameez) [lahl vah-lee kuh-meez] "the red one (shirt)" rather than "the shirt which is red." You'll get the full vaalaa toolkit in Unit 24; jo…voh is for when there's a real clause to say.

Introductions at family gatherings run on jo…voh: जो अंकल सोफ़े पर बैठे हैं, वे पापा के बड़े भाई हैं। (jo ankal sofe par baiThe hain, voh paapaa ke baRe bhaaee hain.) [joh un-kul soh-fay pur beh-Thay heh(n), voh pah-pah kay buh-Ray bhah-ee heh(n)] "The uncle sitting on the sofa is Dad's older brother." Note the respectful plurals (baiThe hain… hain) for elders even though he's one person — and yes, every older man is "uncle."

Exercise 21A — jo, jis, jin, jise?

Fill the blank with the right relative word. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 21.

  1. ___ लड़का वहाँ खड़ा है, वह मेरा दोस्त है। (___ laRkaa vahaan khaRaa hai, voh meraa dost hai.)
  2. ___ आदमी से तुम मिले, वह डॉक्टर है। (___ aadmee se tum mile, voh DaukTar hai.)
  3. ___ किताब तुमने दी, वह बहुत अच्छी है। (___ kitaab tumne dee, voh bahut achchhee hai.)
  4. ___ लोगों को मैंने बुलाया, वे नहीं आए। (___ logon ko maine bulaayaa, voh naheen aae.)
  5. ___ घर में हम रहते हैं, वह पुराना है। (___ ghar mein ham rehte hain, voh puraanaa hai.)
  6. ___ भी आएगा, उसे खाना मिलेगा। (___ bhee aaegaa, use khaanaa milegaa.)
  7. ___ हिन्दी नहीं आती, उसके लिए यह किताब है। (___ hindee naheen aatee, uske liye yeh kitaab hai.)
  8. ___ हम कल गए थे, वहाँ की चाय अच्छी थी। (___ ham kal gae the, vahaan kee chaay achchhee thee.)
  9. ___ ऑटो वाले से मैंने बात की, वह ठीक आदमी था। (___ auTo vaale se maine baat kee, voh Theek aadmee thaa.)
  10. ___ सब्ज़ी ताज़ी है, वही लो। (___ sabzee taazee hai, vahee lo.)

Exercise 21B — Two sentences into one

Join with jo…voh (or jis/jin…us/un). Model: वह लड़का मेरा दोस्त है + वह वहाँ खड़ा है → जो लड़का वहाँ खड़ा है, वह मेरा दोस्त है।

  1. वह लड़की मेरी बहन है + वह गाना गा रही है (voh laRkee meree behen hai + voh gaanaa gaa rahee hai)
  2. वह फ़िल्म अच्छी थी + हमने वह फ़िल्म कल देखी (voh film achchhee thee + hamne voh film kal dekhee)
  3. वह दुकान बंद है + उस दुकान से हम दूध लेते हैं (voh dukaan band hai + us dukaan se ham doodh lete hain)
  4. वह आदमी मेरे ससुर हैं + वह आदमी सोफ़े पर बैठे हैं (voh aadmee mere sasur hain + voh aadmee sofe par baiThe hain)
  5. वे लोग अच्छे हैं + उन लोगों के साथ हम काम करते हैं (voh log achchhe hain + un logon ke saath ham kaam karte hain)
  6. वह जगह मुझे पसंद है + वहाँ शांति है (voh jagah mujhe pasand hai + vahaan shaanti hai) [use jahaan…voh/vahaan]

Exercise 21C — Translate into Hindi

Lead with the jo-half. Write Devanagari or roman (or both).

  1. The boy who is standing there is my friend.
  2. The chai (that) you made is very good.
  3. The man (whom) you met yesterday is my father-in-law. [respectful]
  4. Whoever comes will get chai.
  5. The house we live in is old.
  6. Take whatever you need.

Exercise 21D — Translate into English

Turn the two Hindi halves into one smooth English sentence.

  1. जो औरत दरवाज़े पर है, वह मेरी सास हैं। (jo aurat darvaaze par hai, voh meree saas hain.)
  2. जिस होटल में हम रुके, वह सस्ता था। (jis hoTal mein ham ruke, voh sastaa thaa.)
  3. जो काम आज हो सकता है, उसे कल पर मत छोड़ो। (jo kaam aaj ho saktaa hai, use kal par mat chhoRo.)
  4. जो भी बोलोगे, मैं सुनूँगा। (jo bhee bologe, main sunoongaa.)
  5. जहाँ मेरी पत्नी बड़ी हुई, वहाँ हम अगले साल जाएँगे। (jahaan meree patnee baRee huee, vahaan ham agle saal jaaenge.)
chapters.book2-u22:
Unit 22 Comparisons & Superlatives

What you'll be able to say: bigger, cheaper, the best in Delhi, the more the merrier — plus the exclamations (how beautiful!) that run on the same little words.

दिल्ली मुंबई से पुरानी है।
dillee mumbaee se puraanee hai. [dil-lee mum-buh-ee say pu-rah-nee heh]
Delhi is older than Mumbai. (lit. Delhi Mumbai-than old is)
यह दिल्ली की सबसे अच्छी चाय है।
yeh dillee kee sabse achchhee chaay hai. [yeh dil-lee kee sub-say uch-chhee chah-ay heh]
This is the best chai in Delhi.
कितना सुंदर है!
kitnaa sundar hai! [kit-nah sun-dur heh]
How beautiful (it is)!

1. No "-er" in Hindi: the से pattern

Hindi has no equivalent of "-er/-est." An adjective never changes to make a comparison. Instead you name the loser of the comparison with se — literally "compared to" — and keep the plain adjective:

Slot 1: winnerSlot 2: loser + सेSlot 3: plain adjective + verb
दिल्ली dilleeमुंबई से mumbaee seपुरानी है। puraanee hai.
मेट्रो meTro (f)ऑटो से auTo seतेज़ है। tez hai. tayz heh

The adjective still agrees with the subject — the winner: dillee (f) → puraanee. And "than what?" as a question is किससे? (kisse?) [kis-say].

यह कमरा उस कमरे से बड़ा है।
yeh kamraa us kamre se baRaa hai. [yeh kum-rah us kum-ray say buh-Rah heh]
This room is bigger than that room. (kamraa (m); note oblique us kamre before se)
चाय कॉफ़ी से सस्ती है।
chaay kofee se sastee hai. [chah-ay kaw-fee say sus-tee heh]
Chai is cheaper than coffee. (kofee (f))
तुम्हारी हिन्दी मेरी हिन्दी से अच्छी है।
tumhaaree hindee meree hindee se achchhee hai. [tum-hah-ree hin-dee may-ree hin-dee say uch-chhee heh]
Your Hindi is better than my Hindi. (good flattery for the in-laws' house)

Don't hang se on the wrong noun. ✗ दिल्ली से मुंबई पुरानी है (✗ dillee se mumbaee puraanee hai) says "Mumbai is older than Delhi" — you've flipped the ranking. se glues to the one being beaten. Check yourself by reading X se as "compared to X": Delhi, compared-to-Mumbai, is old.

2. Turning it up and down: ज़्यादा and कम

You can add ज़्यादा zyaadaa [zyah-dah] "more" before the adjective — it's optional and doesn't change the meaning, just adds weight. कम kam [kum] "less" is its opposite and is not optional when you mean "less":

आज कल से ज़्यादा गरमी है।
aaj kal se zyaadaa garmee hai. [ahj kul say zyah-dah gur-mee heh]
It's hotter today than yesterday. (garmee (f) heat; lit. today, compared to yesterday, more heat is)
यह होटल उस होटल से कम महँगा है।
yeh hoTal us hoTal se kam mehngaa hai. [yeh hoh-Tul us hoh-Tul say kum meh(n)-gah heh]
This hotel is less expensive than that one. (hoTal (m))

3. The superlative: सबसे

"Best, biggest, most" = beat everyone: सबसे sabse [sub-say], literally "than all," parked right before the adjective:

भारत में सबसे बड़ा शहर कौन-सा है?
bhaarat mein sabse baRaa sheher kaun-saa hai? [bhah-rut may(n) sub-say buh-Rah sheh-hur kawn-sah heh]
Which is the biggest city in India? (sheher (m) city)
मेरे लिए परिवार सबसे ज़रूरी है।
mere liye parivaar sabse zarooree hai. [may-ray li-yay puh-ri-vahr sub-say zuh-roo-ree heh]
For me, family is the most important thing. (parivaar (m))
मुझे चाय सबसे ज़्यादा पसंद है।
mujhe chaay sabse zyaadaa pasand hai. [mu-jhay chah-ay sub-say zyah-dah puh-sund heh]
I like chai the most (of all). (sabse zyaadaa works with verbs too)

4. Degree words: the volume knob

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
बहुतbahutbuh-hutvery
काफ़ीkaafeekah-feequite, pretty (a lot)
थोड़ाthoRaathoh-Raha little
ज़राzaraazuh-rahjust a touch (softens requests)
इतनाitnaait-nahthis much, so
उतनाutnaaut-nahthat much
कितनाkitnaakit-nahhow much? / how…!
आज इतनी गरमी क्यों है?
aaj itnee garmee kyon hai? [ahj it-nee gur-mee kyoh(n) heh]
Why is it so hot today? (itnaa agrees: garmee (f) → itnee)
खाना काफ़ी अच्छा था, बस थोड़ा तीखा था।
khaanaa kaafee achchhaa thaa, bas thoRaa teekhaa thaa. [khah-nah kah-fee uch-chhah thah, bus thoh-Rah tee-khah thah]
The food was quite good — just a little spicy.

5. The more…the more: जितना…उतना

Meet the correlative family again (Unit 21): question kitnaa, relative jitnaa [jit-nah], answer itnaa/utnaa. Pair jitnaa…utnaa for "the X-er, the Y-er" — and remember both agree like adjectives:

जितना गुड़ डालोगे, उतना मीठा होगा।
jitnaa guR Daaloge, utnaa meeThaa hogaa. [jit-nah guR Dah-loh-gay, ut-nah mee-Thah hoh-gah]
The more jaggery you add, the sweeter it'll be. (a real proverb; guR (m) jaggery)
जितनी जल्दी, उतना अच्छा।
jitnee jaldee, utnaa achchhaa. [jit-nee jul-dee, ut-nah uch-chhah]
The sooner, the better. (jaldee (f) → jitnee)

6. Exclamations: कितना…! क्या…!

kitnaa flips from question to exclamation exactly like English "how":

कितनी सुंदर जगह है!
kitnee sundar jagah hai! [kit-nee sun-dur juh-guh heh]
What a beautiful place! (jagah (f) place → kitnee)
यह तो उससे कहीं बेहतर है!
yeh to usse kaheen behtar hai! [yeh toh us-say kuh-hee(n) beh-tur heh]
This is way better than that one! (kaheen behtar = "far better"; behtar = better, straight from Urdu)

Delhi's compliment kit: क्या बात है! (kyaa baat hai!) [kyah baht heh] "wow, superb!" (lit. what a thing!) · एक नंबर! (ek nambar!) [ayk num-bur] "top class!" · सबसे बढ़िया (sabse baRhiyaa) [sub-say buh-Rhi-yah] "the absolute best" — baRhiyaa never changes for gender. And Urdu-flavored behtar (better) / बेहतरीन behtareen [beh-tuh-reen] (finest) will earn you style points at any chai stall.

Comparing is a national sport, and mangoes are the championship. Summer conversation will demand a position: is Delhi's beloved dasheree better, or Mumbai's alfaanso? A safe, crowd-pleasing answer: मेरे लिए तो दशहरी सबसे अच्छा आम है। (mere liye to dasheree sabse achchhaa aam hai.) [may-ray li-yay toh duh-sheh-ree sub-say uch-chhah ahm heh] "For me, dasheri is the best mango." (aam (m) mango.) Bonus points in a Delhi household.

Exercise 22A — Fill the comparison

Fill each blank with one of: से (se) · सबसे (sabse) · ज़्यादा (zyaadaa) · कम (kam) · जितना/जितनी (jitnaa/jitnee) · उतना (utnaa) · कितनी (kitnee). Answers: Answer Key, Unit 22.

  1. दिल्ली मुंबई ___ पुरानी है। (dillee mumbaee ___ puraanee hai.)
  2. यह ___ अच्छा रेस्टोरेंट है। (yeh ___ achchhaa resTorenT hai.) [best of all]
  3. मेट्रो ऑटो से ___ तेज़ है। (meTro auTo se ___ tez hai.) [more]
  4. यह कमीज़ उस कमीज़ से ___ महँगी है। (yeh kameez us kameez se ___ mehngee hai.) [less]
  5. ___ जल्दी, उतना अच्छा। (___ jaldee, utnaa achchhaa.)
  6. जितना पढ़ोगे, ___ सीखोगे। (jitnaa paRhoge, ___ seekhoge.)
  7. ___ सुंदर साड़ी है! (___ sundar saaRee hai!) [how…!]
  8. मुझे चाय कॉफ़ी ___ ज़्यादा पसंद है। (mujhe chaay kofee ___ zyaadaa pasand hai.)
  9. भारत में ___ बड़ा शहर कौन-सा है? (bhaarat mein ___ baRaa sheher kaun-saa hai?)
  10. आज कल से ___ गरमी है। (aaj kal se ___ garmee hai.) [more]

Exercise 22B — Build the comparison

1–4: combine the two facts into one X-se-Y sentence (make the FIRST item the winner). 5–7: turn the sentence into a superlative with sabse.

  1. यह कमरा बड़ा है। वह कमरा छोटा है। (yeh kamraa baRaa hai. voh kamraa chhoTaa hai.)
  2. चाय सस्ती है। कॉफ़ी महँगी है। (chaay sastee hai. kofee mehngee hai.)
  3. मेरा फ़ोन पुराना है। तुम्हारा फ़ोन नया है। (meraa fon puraanaa hai. tumhaaraa fon nayaa hai.) [start with tumhaaraa fon]
  4. दिसंबर ठंडा है। नवंबर कम ठंडा है। (disambar ThanDaa hai. navambar kam ThanDaa hai.)
  5. यह चाय अच्छी है। → [the best chai in Delhi]
  6. वह लड़का लंबा है। → [the tallest boy in the class — class = klaas (f)]
  7. यह रास्ता छोटा है। → [the shortest way — raastaa (m)]

Exercise 22C — Translate into Hindi

Write Devanagari or roman (or both).

  1. Delhi is bigger than my city.
  2. Chai is cheaper than coffee.
  3. This is the best food.
  4. I like mangoes the most.
  5. The sooner, the better.
  6. How beautiful this place is!
  7. Today is hotter than yesterday.

Exercise 22D — Translate into English

Mind who wins each comparison.

  1. मेरी हिन्दी तुम्हारी अंग्रेज़ी से ख़राब है। (meree hindee tumhaaree angrezee se kharaab hai.)
  2. यह दुकान उस दुकान से सस्ती है। (yeh dukaan us dukaan se sastee hai.)
  3. दशहरी सबसे बढ़िया आम है। (dasheree sabse baRhiyaa aam hai.)
  4. जितना बोलोगे, उतना सीखोगे। (jitnaa bologe, utnaa seekhoge.)
  5. कितनी अच्छी ख़बर है! (kitnee achchhee khabar hai!)
  6. यह वाला उससे कहीं बेहतर है। (yeh vaalaa usse kaheen behtar hai.)
chapters.book2-u23:
Unit 23 Causatives & Passive (light touch)

What you'll be able to say: the difference between doing, making, and getting it done — feed someone, show someone, get your hair cut, have a kurta stitched — plus a first look at the passive you'll see on signs.

मैं हर महीने बाल कटवाता हूँ।
main har maheene baal kaTvaataa hoon. [meh(n) hur muh-hee-nay bahl kuT-vah-tah hoo(n)]
I get my hair cut every month. (lit. I hair cause-to-be-cut; baal (m pl) hair)
मेरी पत्नी मुझे हिन्दी सिखाती है।
meree patnee mujhe hindee sikhaatee hai. [may-ree put-nee mu-jhay hin-dee si-khah-tee heh]
My wife teaches me Hindi. (patnee (f) wife; sikhaanaa = make-learn)
यहाँ हिन्दी बोली जाती है।
yahaan hindee bolee jaatee hai. [yuh-hah(n) hin-dee boh-lee jah-tee heh]
Hindi is spoken here.

1. One root, three sizes

Hindi verbs come in families built on one root. The smallest just happens (intransitive), the middle one is done by you (transitive), and the biggest means you make it happen — usually through someone else (causative, with -aanaa or -vaanaa):

Happens (vi)You do it (vt)You get it done
बनना bannaa (vi) bun-nah get madeबनाना banaanaa (vt) buh-nah-nah makeबनवाना banvaanaa bun-vah-nah have made
— करना karnaa (vt) doकराना / करवाना karaanaa / karvaanaa kuh-rah-nah / kur-vah-nah get done
कटना kaTnaa (vi) kuT-nah get cutकाटना kaaTnaa (vt) kahT-nah cutकटवाना kaTvaanaa kuT-vah-nah have cut
धुलना dhulnaa (vi) dhul-nah get washedधोना dhonaa (vt) dhoh-nah washधुलवाना dhulvaanaa dhul-vah-nah have washed
सिलना silnaa (vi) sil-nah get stitchedसीना seenaa (vt) see-nah stitchसिलवाना silvaanaa sil-vah-nah have stitched

You met bannaa long ago in खाना बन गया (khaanaa ban gayaa) [khah-nah bun guh-yah] "the food is ready (got made)." Now you can climb the whole ladder: khaanaa banaa (it got made) → maine khaanaa banaayaa (I made it) → maine khaanaa banvaayaa (I had it made).

Spot the sound pattern in causatives: the root vowel shortens. seekhnaa → sikhaanaa, dekhnaa → dikhaanaa, kaaTnaa → kaTvaanaa, dhonaa → dhulvaanaa. Long vowel in the plain verb, short in the causative — your ear will start predicting it.

2. Feed, show, teach: the -आना causatives

These everyday verbs are "make someone experience X," and the person is marked with ko:

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
खिलानाkhilaanaa (vt)khi-lah-nahto feed (make eat)
पिलानाpilaanaa (vt)pi-lah-nahto give (someone) a drink
दिखानाdikhaanaa (vt)di-khah-nahto show (make see)
सिखानाsikhaanaa (vt)si-khah-nahto teach (make learn)
सुनानाsunaanaa (vt)su-nah-nahto tell/recite (make hear)
उसने मुझे अपनी नई कार दिखाई।
usne mujhe apnee naee kaar dikhaaee. [us-nay mu-jhay up-nee nuh-ee kahr di-khah-ee]
He showed me his new car. (kaar (f) → dikhaaee)
पहले बच्चों को खिलाओ, फिर ख़ुद खाओ।
pehle bachchon ko khilaao, phir khud khaao. [peh-lay buch-choh(n) koh khi-lah-oh, phir khud khah-oh]
Feed the kids first, then eat yourself.
मेहमानों को चाय पिलाओ।
mehmaanon ko chaay pilaao. [meh-mah-noh(n) koh chah-ay pi-lah-oh]
Give the guests some chai. (mehmaan (m) guest)
दादी हमें कहानियाँ सुनाती हैं।
daadee hamen kahaaniyaan sunaatee hain. [dah-dee huh-may(n) kuh-hah-ni-yah(n) su-nah-tee heh(n)]
Grandma tells us stories. (kahaanee (f) story; daadee (f) paternal grandmother)

"Teach" is sikhaanaa, never seekhnaa. Learners map "I'll teach you" onto the verb they already know and say ✗ मैं तुम्हें अंग्रेज़ी सीखूँगा (✗ main tumhen angrezee seekhoongaa) — which means "I'll learn English (to your address?)" — nonsense. Say मैं तुम्हें अंग्रेज़ी सिखाऊँगा। (main tumhen angrezee sikhaaoongaa.) [meh(n) tum-hay(n) un-gray-zee si-khah-oo(n)-gah] Learn = seekhnaa, teach = sikhaanaa; the short i does the teaching.

3. Getting it done: -वाना and the से agent

The -vaanaa forms mean you arranged for it; someone else's hands did it. Name that someone with se:

मैंने दर्ज़ी से कुर्ता सिलवाया।
maine darzee se kurtaa silvaayaa. [meh(n)-nay dur-zee say kur-tah sil-vah-yah]
I had a kurta stitched by the tailor. (darzee (m) tailor; kurtaa (m))
हम शादी का खाना हलवाई से बनवाते हैं।
ham shaadee kaa khaanaa halvaaee se banvaate hain. [hum shah-dee kah khah-nah hul-vah-ee say bun-vah-tay heh(n)]
We have the wedding food made by the halvai (caterer). (shaadee (f) wedding; halvaaee (m))
सर्दियों में मैं कपड़े धुलवाता हूँ।
sardiyon mein main kapRe dhulvaataa hoon. [sur-di-yoh(n) may(n) meh(n) kup-Ray dhul-vah-tah hoo(n)]
In winter I get the clothes washed (by someone). (kapRaa (m) cloth/garment; sardee (f) winter)
गाड़ी ख़राब है — कल ठीक करवाऊँगा।
gaaRee kharaab hai — kal Theek karvaaoongaa. [gah-Ree khuh-rahb heh — kul Theek kur-vah-oo(n)-gah]
The car's broken — I'll get it fixed tomorrow. (gaaRee (f) car/vehicle)

Mind the self/other line. मैंने बाल काटे (maine baal kaaTe) means you took the scissors and cut your own hair — your barber will be hurt, your partner alarmed. "I got a haircut" is मैंने बाल कटवाए। (maine baal kaTvaae.) [meh(n)-nay bahl kuT-vah-ay] Whenever a professional's hands were involved, reach for -vaanaa.

Delhi outsources everything, and the sound of errands is -vaa plus a Unit-19 vector: गाड़ी धुलवा लो (gaaRee dhulvaa lo) [gah-Ree dhul-vah loh] get the car washed · बाल कटवा लो (baal kaTvaa lo) get a haircut · इस्त्री करवा लो (istree karvaa lo) [ist-ree kur-vah loh] get the ironing done (istree (f) iron/ironing) · and the all-purpose promise करवा लेंगे। (karvaa lenge.) [kur-vah lay(n)-gay] "we'll get it sorted" — through a guy someone's cousin knows. That sentence IS Delhi.

4. The passive: participle + जाना

You mostly need to recognize the passive — on signs, menus, news. Form: perfective participle + jaanaa, both agreeing with the subject:

यह मिठाई दूध से बनाई जाती है।
yeh miThaaee doodh se banaaee jaatee hai. [yeh mi-Thah-ee doodh say buh-nah-ee jah-tee heh]
This sweet is made from milk. (miThaaee (f) → banaaee jaatee)
15 अगस्त को दिल्ली में पतंगें उड़ाई जाती हैं।
pandrah agast ko dillee mein patangen uRaaee jaatee hain. [pund-ruh uh-gust koh dil-lee may(n) puh-tung-ay(n) u-Rah-ee jah-tee heh(n)]
On August 15th, kites are flown in Delhi. (patang (f) kite)
यहाँ ऑटो नहीं मिलते — मेट्रो ली जाती है।
yahaan auTo naheen milte — meTro lee jaatee hai. [yuh-hah(n) aw-Toh nuh-hee(n) mil-tay — may-Troh lee jah-tee heh]
You don't get autos here — one takes the metro. ("is taken" — how things are done around here)

Everyday speech often dodges the passive. Where English says "chai is being made," a Delhiite says चाय बन रही है (chaay ban rahee hai) [chah-ay bun ruh-hee heh] — the little intransitive family member does the job. Use the vi verbs for happenings, save …jaataa hai passives for signs, rules, and "that's how it's done" statements.

Feeding people is the family love language, so khilaanaa-pilaanaa carries emotional weight. Your mother-in-law saying मैं तुम्हें अपने हाथ का खाना खिलाऊँगी (main tumhen apne haath kaa khaanaa khilaaoongee) [meh(n) tum-hay(n) up-nay hahth kah khah-nah khi-lah-oo(n)-gee] "I'll feed you food made by my own hands" is a declaration of affection. And on any good news, someone will demand sweets: मुँह मीठा करवाओ! (munh meeThaa karvaao!) [moo(n)h mee-Thah kur-vah-oh] "sweeten our mouths!" — you're buying the mithai.

Exercise 23A — Pick the family member

Choose the right verb from the brackets. Answers: Answer Key, Unit 23.

  1. खाना ___ गया — आओ, खा लो। (khaanaa ___ gayaa — aao, khaa lo.) [ban / banaa / banvaa]
  2. मम्मी रोज़ खाना ___ हैं। (mummy roz khaanaa ___ hain.) [bantee / banaatee / banvaatee — she cooks herself]
  3. हमने शादी का खाना हलवाई से ___। (hamne shaadee kaa khaanaa halvaaee se ___.) [banaayaa / banvaayaa]
  4. मैं हर महीने बाल ___ हूँ। (main har maheene baal ___ hoon.) [kaaTtaa / kaTvaataa]
  5. मेरी पत्नी मुझे हिन्दी ___ है। (meree patnee mujhe hindee ___ hai.) [seekhtee / sikhaatee]
  6. मैं हिन्दी ___ हूँ। (main hindee ___ hoon.) [seekhtaa / sikhaataa]
  7. बच्चों को पहले ___। (bachchon ko pehle ___.) [khaao / khilaao]
  8. उसने मुझे फ़ोटो ___। (usne mujhe foTo ___.) [dekhaa / dikhaayaa]
  9. मैंने दर्ज़ी से सूट ___। (maine darzee se sooT ___.) [siyaa / silvaayaa]
  10. मेहमानों को पानी ___। (mehmaanon ko paanee ___.) [piyo / pilaao]

Exercise 23B — From doing to getting done

1–5: rewrite so the subject GETS it done (use -vaanaa; add the se-agent where given). 6–7: rewrite as a passive with jaanaa.

  1. मैं कपड़े धोता हूँ। (main kapRe dhotaa hoon.) → [get them washed]
  2. मैंने कुर्ता सिया। (maine kurtaa siyaa.) → [by the tailor — darzee se]
  3. उसने घर साफ़ किया। (usne ghar saaf kiyaa.) → [had it cleaned]
  4. मैंने बाल काटे। (maine baal kaaTe.) → [got a haircut]
  5. हम खाना बनाते हैं। (ham khaanaa banaate hain.) → [have it made — kuk se (cook)]
  6. लोग यहाँ हिन्दी बोलते हैं। (log yahaan hindee bolte hain.) → [passive: Hindi is spoken here]
  7. लोग यह मिठाई दूध से बनाते हैं। (log yeh miThaaee doodh se banaate hain.) → [passive]

Exercise 23C — Translate into Hindi

Decide each time: do, make, or get done? Write Devanagari or roman (or both).

  1. Mummy feeds the kids.
  2. Show me your photo. (tum)
  3. I get my hair cut every month.
  4. She teaches me Hindi.
  5. I had a kurta stitched by the tailor.
  6. Give Dad some chai. (tum; "make him drink")
  7. Hindi is spoken here.

Exercise 23D — Translate into English

Watch who is actually doing the work.

  1. दादी बच्चों को खाना खिलाती हैं। (daadee bachchon ko khaanaa khilaatee hain.)
  2. मैंने अपनी शादी का कुर्ता दर्ज़ी से सिलवाया। (maine apnee shaadee kaa kurtaa darzee se silvaayaa.)
  3. गाड़ी ठीक करवा लो। (gaaRee Theek karvaa lo.)
  4. मुझे अपनी नई किताब दिखाओ। (mujhe apnee naee kitaab dikhaao.)
  5. दिवाली पर मिठाई बाँटी जाती है। (divaalee par miThaaee baanTee jaatee hai.) [baanTnaa = distribute]
  6. मुँह मीठा करवाओ, ख़ुशख़बरी है! (munh meeThaa karvaao, khushkhabree hai!)
chapters.book2-u24:
Unit 24 The Finishing Touches

What you'll be able to say: the tiny words that make Hindi sound alive — hee, bhee, to, na, the mighty vaalaa, street flavoring like yaar and arre — plus a victory lap over everything Book 2 gave you. No new paradigms today; just polish.

मैं तो ठीक हूँ, तुम सुनाओ।
main to Theek hoon, tum sunaao. [meh(n) toh Theek hoo(n), tum su-nah-oh]
Me, I'm fine — what's your news? (lit. you make-me-hear, from Unit 23)
ट्रेन आने वाली है, जल्दी करो!
Tren aane vaalee hai, jaldee karo! [Trayn ah-nay vah-lee heh, jul-dee kuh-roh]
The train's about to come — hurry!
खाना अच्छा है न?
khaanaa achchhaa hai na? [khah-nah uch-chhah heh nah]
The food's good, isn't it?

1. ही — only, exactly, the very one

ही hee [hee] sits right after a word and puts a spotlight on it: this one and no other.

आज ही करो।
aaj hee karo. [ahj hee kuh-roh]
Do it today — this very day.
यह काम मैं ही करूँगा।
yeh kaam main hee karoongaa. [yeh kahm meh(n) hee kuh-roo(n)-gah]
I'll do this job myself — I and nobody else.
बस एक ही दिक्कत है।
bas ek hee dikkat hai. [bus ayk hee dik-kut heh]
There's just one single problem. (dikkat (f) — Delhi's favorite word for "problem")

hee loves to fuse. You already know some of the children: अभी abhee [uh-bhee] (ab + hee, right now) · यहीं / वहीं yaheen / vaheen [yuh-hee(n) / vuh-hee(n)] (right here / right there) · यही / वही yahee / vahee [yuh-hee / vuh-hee] (this/that very one) · सभी sabhee [suh-bhee] (every single one).

2. भी — also, even

भी bhee [bhee] is hee's twin with the opposite job: it adds the word to the pile. After a negative or ek, it means "even":

मैं भी आऊँगा।
main bhee aaoongaa. [meh(n) bhee ah-oo(n)-gah]
I'll come too.
एक भी ऑटो नहीं मिला।
ek bhee auTo naheen milaa. [ayk bhee aw-Toh nuh-hee(n) mi-lah]
I couldn't find even one auto.
कुछ भी मत बोलो।
kuchh bhee mat bolo. [kuchh bhee mut boh-loh]
Don't say just anything (don't talk nonsense). (kuchh bhee = "anything at all" — and, on its own, Delhi for "nonsense!")

hee and bhee mark the word directly before them, so moving them moves the meaning. मैं भी चाय पी रहा हूँ (main bhee chaay pee rahaa hoon) = "I too am having chai (like you)." मैं चाय भी पी रहा हूँ (main chaay bhee pee rahaa hoon) = "I'm having chai as well (on top of something else)." English "also" floats; Hindi bhee is glued. Park it right behind the word you mean.

3. तो — as for, mind you

You know to as "then" (agar…to, jab…to). Its second life is as a topic-and-contrast particle after a word: "as for X…" — often setting up a lekin:

गरमी तो बहुत है, लेकिन दिल्ली मज़ेदार है।
garmee to bahut hai, lekin dillee mazedaar hai. [gur-mee toh buh-hut heh, lay-kin dil-lee muh-zay-dahr heh]
The heat, sure, is intense — but Delhi is fun.
तुम तो जानते हो।
tum to jaante ho. [tum toh jahn-tay hoh]
You know how it is (you, of all people, know).
अच्छा, तो चलें?
achchhaa, to chalen? [uch-chhah, toh chuh-lay(n)]
Right — shall we head off, then?

4. The tag न? — "isn't it?"

Hang न na [nah] on the end of a statement and it becomes a friendly check. On a request, it becomes a coax:

तुम आओगे न?
tum aaoge na? [tum ah-oh-gay nah]
You'll come, right?
आ जाओ न!
aa jaao na! [ah jah-oh nah]
Oh come on, come! (pleading na — hard to refuse)

5. वाला — one word, three jobs

वाला vaalaa [vah-lah] agrees like an adjective (vaalaa / vaalee / vaale) and does three jobs Delhi could not function without:

JobPatternExample
1. the X-person (occupation)noun + vaalaaचाय वाला chaay vaalaa chah-ay vah-lah chai seller · दूध वाला doodh vaalaa milkman · ऑटो वाला auTo vaalaa auto driver
2. the X one (description)adjective/word + vaalaaलाल वाली कमीज़ laal vaalee kameez lahl vah-lee kuh-meez the red shirt (kameez (f)) · ऊपर वाला कमरा oopar vaalaa kamraa oo-pur vah-lah kum-rah the upstairs room
3. about to Xoblique infinitive + vaalaa + honaaआने वाला है aane vaalaa hai ah-nay vah-lah heh is about to come · फ़िल्म शुरू होने वाली है film shuroo hone vaalee hai shu-roo hoh-nay vah-lee heh the film's about to start
सब्ज़ी वाले से धनिया माँग लो — मुफ़्त मिलता है।
sabzee vaale se dhaniyaa maang lo — muft miltaa hai. [sub-zee vah-lay say dhuh-ni-yah mah(n)g loh — muft mil-tah heh]
Ask the vegetable-seller for cilantro — it comes free. (dhaniyaa (m); note oblique vaale before se)
छोटा वाला नहीं, बड़ा वाला दो।
chhoTaa vaalaa naheen, baRaa vaalaa do. [chhoh-Tah vah-lah nuh-hee(n), buh-Rah vah-lah doh]
Not the small one — give me the big one. (shopping in five words)
मैं निकलने वाला था कि तुम्हारा फ़ोन आ गया।
main nikalne vaalaa thaa ki tumhaaraa fon aa gayaa. [meh(n) ni-kul-nay vah-lah thah ki tum-hah-rah fohn ah guh-yah]
I was just about to leave when your call came. (female speaker: nikalne vaalee thee)

One vaalaa outranks all others: ऊपर वाला (oopar vaalaa) [oo-pur vah-lah], "the One upstairs" — God, in everyday Delhi talk. ऊपर वाला सब देखता है। (oopar vaalaa sab dekhtaa hai.) "The One above sees everything." Said with a sigh about traffic, landlords, and cricket umpires alike.

6. Street rhythm: अरे, यार, भाई — and "हो गया?"

Delhi sentences come seasoned. अरे arre [uh-ray] opens (surprise, protest, hailing); यार yaar [yahr] closes (friend-flavor, mild complaint); भाई bhaaee [bhah-ee] keeps things brotherly with strangers. And the two-word status check हो गया? (ho gayaa?) [hoh guh-yah] asks "done?" about anything — food, homework, haircut, phone call.

अरे यार, फिर से ट्रैफ़िक!
arre yaar, phir se Traifik! [uh-ray yahr, phir say Treh-fik]
Oh man, traffic again! (Traifik (m))
खाना हो गया? — हाँ, हो गया।
khaanaa ho gayaa? — haan, ho gayaa. [khah-nah hoh guh-yah — hah(n), hoh guh-yah]
Eaten? (Is food done?) — Yep, done.

Hear how the particles stack into pure Delhi: चल न यार! (chal na yaar!) [chul nah yahr] "come on, yaar!" · वही तो! (vahee to!) [vuh-hee toh] "exactly! that's what I'm saying!" · बस हो गया, भाई। (bas ho gayaa, bhaaee.) [bus hoh guh-yah, bhah-ee] "that's it, we're done here." · अरे कुछ भी! (arre kuchh bhee!) [uh-ray kuchh bhee] "what nonsense!" Four tiny sentences, zero new grammar, one hundred percent Dilli.

7. Numbers doing grammar: दो-दो, सारा

Two quick patterns. Doubling a number distributes it — "X each"; and सारा saaraa [sah-rah] "the whole/all" agrees like baRaa (saaraa / saaree / saare):

सब बच्चों को दो-दो लड्डू दो।
sab bachchon ko do-do laDDoo do. [sub buch-choh(n) koh doh-doh luD-Doo doh]
Give all the kids two laddus each. (laDDoo (m))
एक-एक करके बोलो।
ek-ek karke bolo. [ayk-ayk kur-kay boh-loh]
Speak one at a time. (karke from Unit 20)
मैंने सारी रात काम किया, सारा दिन सोया।
maine saaree raat kaam kiyaa, saaraa din soyaa. [meh(n)-nay sah-ree raht kahm ki-yah, sah-rah din soh-yah]
I worked all night and slept all day. (raat (f) → saaree; din (m) → saaraa; and no ne on soyaa!)

Adjectives double too, for fresh-and-intense flavor: गरम-गरम समोसे (garam-garam samose) [guh-rum guh-rum suh-moh-say] "piping-hot samosas" (samosaa (m)). And the learner's best friend: हिन्दी? थोड़ी-थोड़ी आती है। (hindee? thoRee-thoRee aatee hai.) [hin-dee? thoh-Ree thoh-Ree ah-tee heh] "Hindi? I know a little-little." Say it with a grin; it always lands.

8. You now have the full toolkit

This is the last grammar unit of Book 2 — because you don't need more grammar to speak. Here is what each unit handed you:

UnitsWhat they gave you
1–7The frame: SOV order, pronouns + honaa, gender, plurals, kaa/ke/kee + apnaa, adjective agreement, postpositions and the oblique case.
8–12Time: habitual (kartaa hoon), continuous (kar rahaa hoon), ko-constructions (pasand / chaahiye / lagnaa), past honaa + past habits, future.
13–15Action: commands and polite requests, simple past with ne, the perfect tenses.
16–18Possibility: saknaa / paanaa / chuknaa, obligation (chaahiye, honaa, paRnaa), subjunctive and agar…to.
19–23Native gear: compound verbs (le lo, ho gayaa), joining ideas + reported speech (ki), relatives (jo…voh), comparisons (se, sabse), causatives (kaTvaanaa) + sign-passives.
24The shine: hee, bhee, to, na, vaalaa, street rhythm, do-do, saaraa.

From here, Book 3 loads the vocabulary and Book 4 puts you in real Delhi situations — the chai stall, the in-laws' dinner table, the auto negotiation. Every sentence in them is built from tools you now own. तुमने हिन्दी की ग्रामर सीख ली — अब बस बोलना है। (tumne hindee kee graamar seekh lee — ab bas bolnaa hai.) [tum-nay hin-dee kee grah-mur seekh lee — ub bus bohl-nah heh] You've learned the grammar — now you just have to speak. हो जाएगा। (ho jaaegaa.)

These particles are heard far more than written formally, and there's no fine you can pay to skip them — a Hindi sentence without an occasional to or hee sounds like a textbook. Cheapest fluency upgrade available: add one na? per conversation, one yaar per complaint.

Exercise 24A — Drop in the particle

Fill each blank with ही (hee), भी (bhee), तो (to), or न (na). Answers: Answer Key, Unit 24.

  1. मैं ___ ठीक हूँ, तुम बताओ। (main ___ Theek hoon, tum bataao.) [as for me]
  2. मैं ___ आऊँगा। (main ___ aaoongaa.) [me too]
  3. आज ___ करो, कल नहीं। (aaj ___ karo, kal naheen.) [this very day]
  4. तुम आओगे ___? (tum aaoge ___?) [right?]
  5. एक ___ ऑटो नहीं मिला। (ek ___ auTo naheen milaa.) [not even one]
  6. चाय ___ अच्छी है, खाना ठंडा है। (chaay ___ achchhee hai, khaanaa ThanDaa hai.) [the chai, at least]
  7. यह काम मैं ___ करूँगा, तुम आराम करो। (yeh kaam main ___ karoongaa, tum aaraam karo.) [I myself]

  9. आ जाओ ___! सब इंतज़ार कर रहे हैं। (aa jaao ___! sab intazaar kar rahe hain.) [come on!]
  10. अच्छा, ___ चलें? (achchhaa, ___ chalen?) [well then]

chapters.book3-c01:
Chapter 1 Greetings & Courtesy

Delhi greets you in layers: a folded-hands नमस्ते (namaste) [nuh-muhs-tay] for the family, an Urdu-flavored आदाब (aadaab) [ah-dahb] in Old Delhi, and a cheerful “hello!” everywhere else. This chapter gives you the hellos, goodbyes, thank-yous and sorrys that carry you through a whole Delhi day — and tells you which ones people actually use.

Saying hello

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning

आदाबaadaab (m)ah-dahbhello (Urdu-flavored; Old Delhi charm)

How are you?

आप कैसी हैं?aap kaisee hain?ahp keh-see heh(n)how are you? (polite, to a woman)

Heard सब चंगा? (sab changaa?) [suhb chun-gah] in a song or from a Punjabi friend? That’s Punjabi, not Hindi. It floats around Delhi because the city is half Punjabi at heart, but in Hindi say सब बढ़िया? (sab baRhiyaa?) or सब ठीक? (sab Theek?).

Saying goodbye

टाटा / बायTaaTaa / baayTah-Tah / bah-eeta-ta / bye (very common, esp. with kids)

शुभ रात्रि (shubh raatri) [shubh raht-ri] lives on greeting cards and TV announcers. At home in Delhi people say “good night” — गुड नाइट — or just सो जाओ (so jaao) [soh jah-oh], “go to sleep.” Learn shubh raatri to read it, say good night to say it.

Please, sorry, thank you

अच्छा (achchhaa) is Delhi’s Swiss-army word. Falling tone = “I see.” Rising tone = “oh really?!” Quick and flat = “okay, fine.” Drawn out — achchhaaaa — = “so THAT’s what’s going on.” Listen for it; you’ll hear it fifty times a day.

Welcoming someone to your home

In action

नमस्ते जी! आप कैसे हैं?
namaste jee! aap kaise hain? [nuh-muhs-tay jee, ahp keh-say heh(n)]
Hello! How are you? (polite, to a man)
मैं ठीक हूँ, शुक्रिया। आप सुनाइए।
main Theek hoon, shukriyaa. aap sunaaiye. [meh(n) Theek hoo(n), shuk-ri-yah. ahp su-nah-i-yay]
I’m fine, thanks. What’s your news? (lit. I fine am, thanks. You tell.)
और भाई, क्या हाल है? — बस बढ़िया!
aur bhaaee, kyaa haal hai? — bas baRhiyaa! [awr bhah-ee, kyah hahl heh — buhs buh-Rhi-yah]
Hey brother, how’s it going? — Just great!
माफ़ कीजिए, ज़रा सुनिए।
maaf keejiye, zaraa suniye. [mahf kee-ji-yay, zuh-rah su-ni-yay]
Excuse me, could I have a moment? (lit. forgive, just listen)
आइए, आइए! बैठिए। पानी लेंगे?
aaiye, aaiye! baiThiye. paanee lenge? [ah-i-yay, ah-i-yay, beh-Thi-yay. pah-nee layn-gay]
Come in, come in! Sit down. Will you have some water?
बहुत-बहुत शुक्रिया! — अरे, कोई बात नहीं।
bahut-bahut shukriyaa! — arre, koee baat naheen. [bo-hut bo-hut shuk-ri-yah — uh-ray, koh-ee baht nuh-hee(n)]
Thank you so much! — Oh, don’t mention it.
अच्छा, मैं चलता हूँ। कल मिलेंगे।
achchhaa, main chaltaa hoon. kal milenge. [uch-chhah, meh(n) chuhl-tah hoo(n). kuhl mi-layn-gay]
Okay, I’ll get going. See you tomorrow. (lit. okay, I moving am. tomorrow will-meet.)
तुमने खाना बनाया? क्या बात है!
tumne khaanaa banaayaa? kyaa baat hai! [tum-nay khah-nah buh-nah-yah? kyah baht heh]
You made dinner? Wonderful!

Delhi’s hellos wear its history. In Old Delhi and anywhere Urdu’s music lingers you’ll hear आदाब (aadaab) [ah-dahb] with a graceful hand raised toward the face, and a breezy सलाम (salaam) [suh-lahm] between friends. South Delhi mixes freely: “helo yaar, kyaa haal hai?” Answer any of them warmly and you’re a local. And कृपया (kripayaa)? You’ll hear it in every Metro announcement — kripayaa dhyaan deejiye, “kindly pay attention” — but in conversation everyone just says pleez or softens the sentence with ज़रा (zaraa).

Here’s a trap for polite Americans: thanking family constantly feels cold in an Indian home. When your partner’s mother refills your plate the third time, a thank you so much! every single time builds a little wall — family is supposed to be beyond accounting. Smile, say बहुत अच्छा है (bahut achchhaa hai) [bo-hut uch-chhah heh] “it’s really good,” and eat. Save शुक्रिया for real favors, and धन्यवाद for speeches. With shopkeepers and strangers, thank away — though even there, a warm ठीक है भैया (Theek hai bhaiyaa) [Theek heh bheh-yah] is more local than a thank-you.

Three quick rounds with your partner this week:

1. Morning hello: greet each other properly for three days — you take नमस्ते! क्या हाल है? (namaste! kyaa haal hai?), they answer, then swap. Sneak in one आदाब for style points.

2. Doorbell drama: your partner is the guest at your door. Welcome them with आइए, बैठिए, पानी लेंगे? — then switch roles. Bonus: offer chai instead.

3. The achchhaa game: your partner tells you three bits of news (one boring, one surprising, one suspicious). You may only respond with अच्छा in different tones — they judge whether your tone matched the news.

In a Delhi living room this vocabulary is the map of who sits where and who gets touched-feet respect — and since your partner’s family is from Delhi, this chapter is your seating chart. Handle साला (saalaa) with care. Used literally — meraa saalaa, my wife’s brother — it’s a normal family word. Shouted at anyone else, it’s a genuine insult (it implies “I’m married to your sister”). Delhiites toss saalaa/saalee around as spicy slang between close friends, but do not copy that until your Hindi — and your friendship — can carry it. When in doubt, say it only about your actual brother-in-law.

प्रेमी / प्रेमिकाpremee (m) / premikaa (f)pray-mee / pray-mi-kahboyfriend / girlfriend (bookish-filmi; songs & novels)

Family for strangers

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning

दीदीdeedee (f)dee-deeelder sister — any woman a bit older

अंकल जीuncle jee (m)un-kul jeeany man of your parents’ age

In action

यह मेरे पापा हैं और यह मेरी मम्मी हैं।
yeh mere paapaa hain aur yeh meree mummy hain. [yeh may-ray pah-pah heh(n) awr yeh may-ree muhm-mee heh(n)]
This is my dad and this is my mom. (lit. this my papa are — parents get respectful plural)
मेरा एक बड़ा भाई और एक छोटी बहन है।
meraa ek baRaa bhaaee aur ek chhoTee behen hai. [may-rah ayk buh-Rah bhah-ee awr ayk chhoh-Tee beh-hen heh]
I have one elder brother and one younger sister.
आपके कितने बच्चे हैं? — दो बेटे और एक बेटी।
aapke kitne bachche hain? — do beTe aur ek beTee. [ahp-kay kit-nay buch-chay heh(n) — doh bay-Tay awr ayk bay-Tee]
How many children do you have? — Two sons and one daughter.
दादी पापा की माँ हैं, और नानी मम्मी की।
daadee paapaa kee maan hain, aur naanee mummy kee. [dah-dee pah-pah kee mah(n) heh(n), awr nah-nee muhm-mee kee]
Daadi is dad’s mother, and naani is mom’s.
मेरे सास-ससुर दिल्ली में रहते हैं।
mere saas-sasur dillee mein rehte hain. [may-ray sahs-suh-sur dil-lee may(n) reh-tay heh(n)]
My parents-in-law live in Delhi.
भाभी, चाय बहुत अच्छी है!
bhaabhee, chaay bahut achchhee hai! [bhah-bhee, chah-ay bo-hut uch-chhee heh]
Bhabhi, the tea is really good!
वह मेरा दोस्त नहीं, मेरा जीजा है।
voh meraa dost naheen, meraa jeejaa hai. [voh may-rah dohst nuh-hee(n), may-rah jee-jah heh]
He’s not my friend — he’s my brother-in-law (my elder sister’s husband).
यह मेरी मंगेतर है। हमारी शादी मार्च में है।
yeh meree mangetar hai. hamaaree shaadee maarch mein hai. [yeh may-ree mun-gay-tur heh. huh-mah-ree shah-dee mahrch may(n) heh]
This is my fiancée. Our wedding is in March.

Delhi families run on Hinglish. Parents are Mummy-Papa even when the kids are fifty; spouses introduce each other with the English words — “ye mere husband hain, ye meree wife hain” — and boyfriend/girlfriend exist only in English, because the Hindi words sound like a 1970s film script. A friend’s wife is warmly called भाभी (bhaabhee) even though she’s no relation — and a chai vendor may call his customer’s wife bhaabhee jee too.

In Delhi nobody respectable is a stranger for long: the auto driver is भैया (bhaiyaa), the vegetable seller’s wife is दीदी (deedee), your partner’s parents’ neighbors are आंटी जी (aunty jee) and अंकल जी (uncle jee). Using family words for non-family isn’t over-familiar — it’s the polite default, and it instantly warms the interaction. The one to avoid: don’t call a young woman bhaiyaa’s feminine equivalent बहन जी (behen jee) [beh-hen jee] — in Delhi it can come off as calling her dowdy. दीदी is the safe warm choice.

Three mini-tasks with your partner:

1. Family tree, out loud: your partner names five relatives (in English); you produce the exact Hindi term — your mom’s sister? मौसी! Then reverse: they say मामी, you say who that is.

2. The introduction drill: point at photos on your partner’s phone and introduce each person: यह मेरी सास हैं। यह मेरा साला है। (yeh meree saas hain. yeh meraa saalaa hai.) Respect-plural for elders!

3. Who am I to them? Work out together what each of her relatives calls you — you’re daamaad to her parents, jeejaa to her younger sister... Say each one aloud: मैं दामाद हूँ। (main daamaad hoon.)

Chapter 3 Pronouns, Question Words & Little Words

These are the fifty smallest words in Hindi and the fifty you will say most: I, you, who, what, where, also, just, absolutely. Delhi conversation is stitched together out of them — kyaa? kaun? achchhaa, voh bhee? Master this chapter and you can already interrogate, agree, refuse and gossip.

Personal pronouns

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
मैंmainmeh(n)I
हमhamhuhmwe
तूtutooyou (super-intimate — or rude; handle with care)
तुमtumtumyou (casual — partner, friends, kids)
आपaapahpyou (polite — elders, in-laws, strangers)
यहyehyehthis; he/she (nearby)
वहvohvohthat; he/she (over there)
येyeyaythese; they (nearby); also respectful he/she
वो लोगvoh log (log m pl)voh lohgthey, those people (spoken plural of voh)

Print and speech disagree here. On the page you’ll see वह and plural वे (ve) [vay]; out of a Delhi mouth both come out voh — and the plural becomes वो लोग (voh log). Same with यह: written yah-style, said yeh. This course romanizes the spoken forms.

Handy possessives & “to me”

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning

हमाराhamaaraahuh-mah-rahour

आपको / तुमकोaapko / tumkoahp-koh / tum-kohto you (polite / casual)

In action

यह क्या है? — कुछ नहीं!
yeh kyaa hai? — kuchh naheen! [yeh kyah heh — kuchh nuh-hee(n)]
What’s this? — Nothing!
तुम कहाँ हो? — मैं यहीं हूँ।
tum kahaan ho? — main yaheen hoon. [tum kuh-hah(n) hoh — meh(n) yuh-hee(n) hoo(n)]
Where are you? — I’m right here.
वह कौन है? — कोई नहीं, मेरा दोस्त है।
voh kaun hai? — koee naheen, meraa dost hai. [voh kawn heh — koh-ee nuh-hee(n), may-rah dohst heh]
Who’s that? — No one, just a friend of mine.
मेट्रो कब है? — शायद दस बजे।
meTro kab hai? — shaayad das baje. [may-Troh kuhb heh — shah-yud duhs buh-jay]
When is the metro? — Maybe at ten.
कौन-सा अच्छा है? — दोनों अच्छे हैं!
kaun-saa achchhaa hai? — donon achchhe hain! [kawn-sah uch-chhah heh — doh-noh(n) uch-chhay heh(n)]
Which one is good? — Both are good!
मुझे भी चाय चाहिए।
mujhe bhee chaay chaahiye. [mu-jhay bhee chah-ay chah-hi-yay]
I want tea too. (lit. to-me also tea wanted)
सिर्फ़ पानी, और कुछ नहीं।
sirf paanee, aur kuchh naheen. [sirf pah-nee, awr kuchh nuh-hee(n)]
Just water, nothing else.
तुम ज़रूर आओगे? — बिल्कुल!
tum zaroor aaoge? — bilkul! [tum zuh-roor ah-oh-gay — bil-kul]
You’ll definitely come? — Absolutely!
सब लोग वहाँ हैं, हम भी चलें?
sab log vahaan hain, ham bhee chalen? [suhb lohg vuh-hah(n) heh(n), huhm bhee chuh-lay(n)]
Everyone’s there — shall we go too?

On the street, Delhi friends run on तू (tu) and yaar: तू कहाँ है यार? (tu kahaan hai yaar?) [too kuh-hah(n) heh yahr] “where are you, man?” It signals total closeness — and from an outsider it signals disrespect. Your safe ladder: aap for elders, in-laws and strangers, tum for your partner and friends, and tu only if a close friend uses it with you first. When Delhiites want to be extra warm AND polite, they stack: आप बताइए न! (aap bataaiye na!) [ahp buh-tah-i-yay nah] “do tell!”

The tu-tum-aap ladder is a map of intimacy, not just politeness. Old friends, small children, and God all get तू — bhajans and Bollywood love songs are full of it — because total intimacy and total surrender sound the same. Meanwhile many Delhi couples keep a lifelong तुम, and some old-school spouses even use आप with each other. Ask your partner what their parents use for each other — the answer usually comes with a story.

Three mini-tasks with your partner:

1. Twenty questions, Delhi style: your partner thinks of a person you both know. You get ten questions using at least five different question words — कौन? कहाँ? कितना? They answer only with हाँ / नहीं / शायद / बिल्कुल.

2. The bhee game: they say what they want — मुझे चाय चाहिए। You always want the same thing: मुझे भी! (mujhe bhee!) Then flip it with सिर्फ़: sirf ek chaay — only one tea, and argue over who gets it.

3. Pronoun audit: together, list five real people (her mom, the chai bhaiyaa, her best friend...) and decide for each: tu, tum, or aap? Say a one-line greeting to each imaginary person with the right pronoun.

Chapter 4 Numbers 0–100 & the Counting System

Here's the honest truth every Hindi learner deserves upfront: Hindi numbers 1–100 are a hundred little words, not a neat system like English "twenty-one, twenty-two." Each decade rhymes internally, and there are patterns worth knowing (below), but at some point you simply befriend all hundred. That's exactly what flashcard Deck D03 is for — ten a day, and in six weeks they're yours for life. Meanwhile, real Delhi shopping runs on numbers, so this chapter earns its keep fast.

The pattern cheat-sheet (read before the big table)

Decade endingsEach decade rhymes: −ees (20s), −tees (30s), −aalees (40s), the 50s end −van, the 60s −saTh, 70s −hattar, 80s −aasee, 90s −aanave.
First digits echoik− (1), baa−/ba− (2), ti−/tir− (3), chau− (4), pach− (5), chha− (6), sat− (7), aTh− (8) — e.g. ik-kees, ik-tees, ik-taalees, ik-yah-van… all start with ik.
The 9s look aheadNumbers ending in 9 say "one-less-than-next-decade": उन्नीस (19, un-BEES-ish), उनतीस (29), उनचास (49), उनसठ (59), उनहत्तर (69), उन्यासी (79). The un− prefix means "just under." (89 breaks the pattern: नवासी.)
Hyphens in our RomanIn words like baa-ees (22) and ik-hattar (71) the hyphen just marks a seam so you don't misread the vowels — it isn't written in Hindi.

सवाsavaasuh-vahplus a quarter — सवा दो = 2¼ (and 2:15 for time)
साढ़ेsaaRhesah-Rhayplus a half — साढ़े तीन = 3½ (3:30) — from 3 up ONLY
पौनेpaunepaw-nayminus a quarter — पौने चार = 3¾ (3:45)
डेढ़DeRhDayRh1½ — its own word; never "saaRhe ek"
ढाईDhaaeeDhah-ee2½ — its own word; never "saaRhe do"

Big numbers — welcome to the lakh system

सौ sau = 100 · हज़ार hazaar = 1,000 · लाख laakh = 100,000 · करोड़ karoR = 10,000,000. India doesn't count in millions: a flat in Delhi costs अस्सी लाख (80 lakh = 8 million rupees), a hit movie earns सौ करोड़. Even the commas move: 12,34,56,789 (twelve crore, thirty-four lakh…). Compose in-between numbers by stacking: दो सौ पचास do sau pachaas = 250; पंद्रह सौ pandrah sau "fifteen hundred" = 1,500 (very common for prices).

Phone numbers are read digit-by-digit, and repeated digits use "Dabal": 98110-22-33 becomes nau aaTh ek ek shoonya, Dabal do, Dabal teen. Delhiites often just switch to English digits mid-number — both are correct Delhi.

Three number games: (1) partner says any 2-digit number in Hindi, you write the digits — ten per round; (2) price quiz: they name a Delhi item (chai, auto ride, movie ticket), you guess the price in Hindi, they correct you with the real one; (3) the DeRh/Dhaaee trap: they ask times — 1:30? 2:30? 3:30? — you must answer DeRh, Dhaaee, saaRhe teen without stumbling.

Chapter 5 Time: Days, Months & the Clock

Delhi keeps two clocks: the official one, and the social one that runs forty minutes behind it. This chapter gives you the words for both — days, months, parts of the day, and the Hindi clock with its two famous specialties, डेढ़ (DeRh) [DayRh] and ढाई (Dhaaee) [Dhah-ee], which trip up every learner exactly once.

Days of the week

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
सोमवारsomvaar (m)sohm-vahrMonday
मंगलवारmangalvaar (m)mun-gul-vahrTuesday
बुधवारbudhvaar (m)budh-vahrWednesday
गुरुवारguruvaar (m)gu-ru-vahrThursday (Delhi also says वीरवार veervaar [veer-vahr])
शुक्रवारshukravaar (m)shuk-ruh-vahrFriday
शनिवारshanivaar (m)shuh-ni-vahrSaturday
रविवारravivaar (m)ruh-vi-vahrSunday (official word)
इतवारitvaar (m)it-vahrSunday — the word Delhi actually says

Months

Hindi’s everyday month names are Hindi-flavored English — and in Delhi speech people usually just say the English names anyway (“March mein shaadee hai”). Learn these to read signs, tickets and wedding cards.

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
जनवरीjanvaree (f)jun-vuh-reeJanuary
फ़रवरीfarvaree (f)fur-vuh-reeFebruary
मार्चmaarch (m)mahrchMarch
अप्रैलaprail (m)up-rehlApril
मईmaee (f)muh-eeMay
जूनjoon (m)joonJune
जुलाईjulaaee (f)ju-lah-eeJuly
अगस्तagast (m)uh-gustAugust
सितंबरsitambar (m)si-tum-burSeptember
अक्टूबरakToobar (m)uk-Too-burOctober
नवंबरnavambar (m)nuh-vum-burNovember
दिसंबरdisambar (m)di-sum-burDecember

Today, tomorrow — and yesterday

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
आजaajahjtoday
कलkalkuhltomorrow AND yesterday (one day away — see box!)
परसोंparsonpuhr-soh(n)day after tomorrow AND day before yesterday

कल (kal) means one day away from today — in either direction, and परसों (parson) means two. The verb tells you which way: कल मैं गया (kal main gayaa) [kuhl meh(n) guh-yah] = yesterday I went; कल मैं जाऊँगा (kal main jaaoongaa) [kuhl meh(n) jah-oo(n)-gah] = tomorrow I’ll go. English speakers panic; Hindi speakers never notice the ambiguity.

Parts of the day

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
सुबहsubah (f)su-behmorning
दोपहरdopahar (f)doh-peh-hurafternoon, midday
शामshaam (f)shahmevening
रातraat (f)rahtnight (aaj raat = tonight)

Now, later, early, late

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
अबabuhbnow
अभीabheeuh-bheeright now, just now
बाद मेंbaad meinbahd may(n)later, afterwards
पहलेpehlepeh-laybefore, earlier, first
जल्दीjaldeejuhl-deeearly; quickly; soon (jaldee karo! = hurry up!)
देर सेder se (der f)dayr saylate (der = delay; der ho gaee = it got late)
हमेशाhameshaahuh-may-shahalways
कभी-कभीkabhee-kabheekuh-bhee kuh-bheesometimes
रोज़ / हर रोज़roz / har rozrohz / huhr rohzdaily / every single day

Telling time

The question is कितने बजे हैं? (kitne baje hain?) [kit-nay buh-jay heh(n)] — literally “how many have struck?” One o’clock is singular — एक बजा है (ek bajaa hai) [ayk buh-jah heh] — and everything from two up is plural: दो बजे हैं (do baje hain) [doh buh-jay heh(n)].

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
कितने बजे हैं?kitne baje hain?kit-nay buh-jay heh(n)what time is it?
दो बजेdo bajedoh buh-jaytwo o’clock / at two
सवा पाँचsavaa paanchsuh-vah pah(n)chquarter past five (5:15)
साढ़े तीनsaaRhe teensah-Rhay teenhalf past three (3:30)
पौने चारpaune chaarpaw-nay chahrquarter to four (3:45)
डेढ़ बजेDeRh bajeDayRh buh-jayhalf past ONE (1:30) — special word
ढाई बजेDhaaee bajeDhah-ee buh-jayhalf past TWO (2:30) — special word

Never say “saaRhe ek” or “saaRhe do.” Hindi has dedicated words for one-and-a-half and two-and-a-half: डेढ़ (DeRh) = 1½ and ढाई (Dhaaee) = 2½. So 1:30 = DeRh baje, 2:30 = Dhaaee baje, and साढ़े (saaRhe) only starts at 3:30 = saaRhe teen. The same words measure everything: DeRh kilo (1½ kg), Dhaaee saal (2½ years), DeRh ghanTaa (an hour and a half). Delhi will grin and correct you on this one — beat them to it.

Minutes, hours, weeks, years

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
मिनटminaT (m)mi-nuTminute (paanch minaT = five minutes)
घंटाghanTaa (m)ghun-Tahhour
दिनdin (m)dinday
हफ़्ताhaftaa (m)huhf-tahweek (formal word: सप्ताह saptaah [sup-tah])
महीनाmaheenaa (m)muh-hee-nahmonth
सालsaal (m)sahlyear
तारीख़taareekh (f)tah-reekhdate (of the month)
पिछला हफ़्ताpichhlaa haftaa (m)pichh-lah huhf-tahlast week (pichhle hafte = last week [adverb])
अगला हफ़्ताaglaa haftaa (m)ug-lah huhf-tahnext week (agle hafte = next week [adverb])
छुट्टीchhuTTee (f)chhuT-Teeholiday, day off
वीकेंडveekenD (m)vee-kenDweekend (yes, in Devanagari — Delhi says it constantly)

In action

आज सोमवार है।
aaj somvaar hai. [ahj sohm-vahr heh]
Today is Monday.
कल इतवार है — छुट्टी!
kal itvaar hai — chhuTTee! [kuhl it-vahr heh — chhuT-Tee]
Tomorrow is Sunday — day off!
कितने बजे हैं? — साढ़े चार बजे हैं।
kitne baje hain? — saaRhe chaar baje hain. [kit-nay buh-jay heh(n) — sah-Rhay chahr buh-jay heh(n)]
What time is it? — It’s half past four.
फ़िल्म डेढ़ बजे है, ढाई बजे नहीं।
film DeRh baje hai, Dhaaee baje naheen. [film DayRh buh-jay heh, Dhah-ee buh-jay nuh-hee(n)]
The movie is at 1:30, not 2:30.
मैं सुबह जल्दी उठता हूँ।
main subah jaldee uThtaa hoon. [meh(n) su-beh juhl-dee uTh-tah hoo(n)]
I get up early in the morning.
वह हमेशा देर से आता है।
voh hameshaa der se aataa hai. [voh huh-may-shah dayr say ah-tah heh]
He always arrives late.
शादी अगले महीने है, पंद्रह तारीख़ को।
shaadee agle maheene hai, pandrah taareekh ko. [shah-dee ug-lay muh-hee-nay heh, pun-druh tah-reekh koh]
The wedding is next month, on the 15th.
हम रोज़ शाम को चाय पीते हैं।
ham roz shaam ko chaay peete hain. [huhm rohz shahm koh chah-ay pee-tay heh(n)]
We drink tea every evening. (lit. we daily evening-at tea drink)
अभी नहीं, बाद में। पाँच मिनट दो!
abhee naheen, baad mein. paanch minaT do! [uh-bhee nuh-hee(n), bahd may(n). pah(n)ch mi-nuT doh]
Not right now — later. Give me five minutes!

Delhi tells time in Hinglish. The commonest way to ask isn’t the textbook question at all — it’s टाइम क्या हुआ? (Taim kyaa huaa?) [Tah-im kyah hu-ah], “what’s the time become?” Days and months flip into English mid-sentence: “Sunday ko milte hain,” “March mein exam hai.” But the half-hours stay stubbornly Hindi — even in an all-English sentence a Delhiite says “meeting DeRh baje hai.” And Sunday is इतवार (itvaar) far more often than the schoolbook रविवार (ravivaar).

Learn the phrase Indian Standard Time with a wink: invitations run soft. A wedding card that says 8 baje means dinner around 10; “paanch minaT” from anyone means fifteen; बस पहुँच रहा हूँ (bas pahunch rahaa hoon) [buhs puh-hunch ruh-hah hoo(n)] “just arriving” means the person may not have left home. But don’t generalize: the Delhi Metro runs to the second, offices keep real hours, and showing up at an aunty’s exactly on time is charmingly foreign. Ask your partner which events in their family run on the clock and which run on IST.

Three mini-tasks with your partner:

1. Clock flash: your partner shows you random times on their phone clock — at least five, always including 1:30 and 2:30. You answer ... बजे हैं out loud. One DeRh/Dhaaee slip = one extra round.

2. Week in Hindi: go through your real week together: सोमवार को काम है, इतवार को छुट्टी है। (somvaar ko kaam hai, itvaar ko chhuTTee hai.) [sohm-vahr koh kahm heh, it-vahr koh chhuT-Tee heh] Every day gets a sentence.

3. Kal detective: your partner says sentences with कल and परसों in mixed tenses; you call out “past!” or “future!” before translating. Five in a row = chai on them.

Chapter 6 Food & Drink, Delhi Style

Nobody goes hungry in Delhi and nobody stops talking about food: breakfast paranthas, office chai at four, chaat on the way home. This chapter feeds you the vocabulary of a Delhi kitchen and a Delhi street corner — and the phrases to order, praise, and ask for water when the mirchi wins.

In action

मुझे भूख लगी है। खाना कब बनेगा?
mujhe bhookh lagee hai. khaanaa kab banegaa? [mu-jhay bhookh luh-gee heh. khah-nah kuhb buh-nay-gah]
I’m hungry. When will the food be ready? (lit. to-me hunger struck is)
भैया, एक प्लेट गोलगप्पे देना।
bhaiyaa, ek pleT golgappe denaa. [bheh-yah, ayk playT gohl-gup-pay day-nah]
Bhaiya, one plate of golgappe, please.
यह बहुत तीखा है! पानी दो!
yeh bahut teekhaa hai! paanee do! [yeh bo-hut tee-khah heh! pah-nee doh]
This is really spicy! Give me water!
दाल मखनी बहुत मज़ेदार है।
daal makhanee bahut mazedaar hai. [dahl mukh-nee bo-hut muh-zay-dahr heh]
The dal makhani is delicious.
आज डिनर में राजमा-चावल है।
aaj Dinar mein raajmaa-chaaval hai. [ahj din-er may(n) rahj-mah chah-vul heh]
Dinner today is rajma-chawal.
मैं रोज़ नाश्ते में पराँठा खाता हूँ।
main roz naashte mein paraanThaa khaataa hoon. [meh(n) rohz nahsh-tay may(n) puh-rah(n)-Thah khah-tah hoo(n)]
I eat a parantha for breakfast every day.
तुमने मोमोज़ चखे? — हाँ, बहुत अच्छे हैं!
tumne momos chakhe? — haan, bahut achchhe hain! [tum-nay moh-mohz chuh-khay — hah(n), bo-hut uch-chhay heh(n)]
Did you try the momos? — Yes, they’re great!
एक कड़क चाय और दो समोसे — बस!
ek kaRak chaay aur do samose — bas! [ayk kuh-Ruk chah-ay awr doh suh-moh-say — buhs]
One strong chai and two samosas — that’s all!
भैया, बिल देना।
bhaiyaa, bil denaa. [bheh-yah, bil day-nah]
Bhaiya, the bill please.

Street ordering has a rhythm: catch the vendor’s eye, call him भैया (bhaiyaa), name the quantity, then soften the command with denaa/banaa do: भैया, एक प्लेट चाट बना दो, तीखा कम। (bhaiyaa, ek pleT chaaT banaa do, teekhaa kam.) [bheh-yah, ayk playT chahT buh-nah doh, tee-khah kum] — “make me a plate of chaat, easy on the spice.” No please needed; bhaiyaa IS the please. And the puri filled with spicy water is गोलगप्पा (golgappaa) in Delhi — say panipuri and you’ve outed yourself as Mumbai, puchka as Kolkata. In Delhi: golgappe, always.

Food is how Indian homes say I-love-you, so the second helping is not a question — it’s a landing. और लो न! (aur lo na!) [awr loh nah] “take more!” will come at you before your plate is empty. A flat “no” reads as rejection; the graceful moves are बस, थोड़ा-सा (bas, thoRaa-saa) [buhs, thoh-Rah sah] “just a little,” or the veteran’s trick: eat slowly and never fully finish the plate until you truly surrender with बस, पेट भर गया! (bas, peT bhar gayaa!) [buhs, payT bhur guh-yah] “enough, my stomach is full!”

Three mini-tasks with your partner:

1. Dinner narration: whoever cooks tonight, name everything on the table in Hindi — यह दाल है, यह चावल है, यह सब्ज़ी है। Then each of you rates it: मीठा? तीखा? मज़ेदार!

2. The order rehearsal: your partner plays a chaat vendor. Order for both of you using the pattern भैया, एक प्लेट ___ देना — three rounds: golgappe, momos, samose. They heckle like a real vendor; you keep your cool and add तीखा कम.

3. Taste-test quiz: partner names five real foods you both eat (pizza, achaar, jalebi...); for each one you shout the right taste word — खट्टा! मीठा! नमकीन! Disagreements settled by actually eating some.

In action

हमारा फ़्लैट छोटा है, लेकिन बालकनी बड़ी है।

अरे, बिजली गई! पंखा बंद है।

चाबी कहाँ है? दरवाज़े पर ताला है।
