मतलब, तुम कल नहीं आ रहे?
matlab, tum kal naheen aa rahe? [mut-lub, tum kul nuh-hee(n) ah ruh-hay]
Meaning… you're not coming tomorrow?
ख़ैर, छोड़ो — पहले चाय पियो।
khair, chhoRo — pehle chaay piyo. [khehr, chhoh-Roh — peh-lay chah-ay pi-yoh]
Anyway, drop it — first have your chai.
काम के बाद हम बाहर खाना खाएँगे।
kaam ke baad ham baahar khaanaa khaaenge. [kahm kay bahd hum bah-hur khah-nah khah-ay(n)-gay]
After work we'll eat out.
यह जगह बिल्कुल घर जैसी है।
yeh jagah bilkul ghar jaisee hai. [yeh juh-guh bil-kul ghur jeh-see heh]
This place is exactly like home. (jaisee agrees with jagah f)

Three connectors run every Delhi conversation. matlab buys thinking time and rephrases: मतलब, कहना ये है कि… (matlab, kehnaa ye hai ki…) [mut-lub, keh-nah yay heh ki] "I mean, the point is that…". vaise pivots to gossip: वैसे, सुना तुमने? (vaise, sunaa tumne?) [veh-say, su-nah tum-nay] "by the way, did you hear?". khair closes a chapter with a sigh: ख़ैर, जो हुआ सो हुआ। (khair, jo huaa so huaa.) [khehr, joh hu-ah soh hu-ah] "anyway, what's done is done." Bonus: Delhi English swallows ki whole — "I told him ki don't be late."

Time words in India are elastic — say hello to Indian Stretchable Time. अभी आया। (abhee aayaa.) [uh-bhee ah-yah] "just coming" can mean twenty minutes; बस पाँच मिनट (bas paanch minaT) [bus pah(n)ch mi-nuT] is a unit of hope, not of time. Remember from Chapter 5 that kal is both yesterday and tomorrow, and parson both two days ago and two days ahead — the verb tense decides. If a Delhi dinner invitation says 8 o'clock, arriving at 8 sharp means helping your hosts set the table.

1) Postposition hunt: describe where five things in the room are, each with a different postposition — फ़ोन तकिये के नीचे है। (fon takiye ke neeche hai.) [fohn tuh-ki-yay kay nee-chay heh] — then let your partner quiz you: chaabee kahaan hai? 2) Habit interview: ask each other about routines and answer only with hameshaa / aksar / kabhee-kabhee / kabhee naheen — do the answers match what your partner thinks? 3) The agar…to game: trade five silly hypotheticals — अगर करोड़ रुपये मिलें, तो? (agar karoR rupaye milen, to?) [uh-gur kuh-rohR ru-puh-yay mi-lay(n), toh] — and answer in Hindi.
chapters.book3-c18:
Chapter 18 Delhi Street Talk — Slang & Fillers

Grammar makes you understood; this chapter makes you sound like you actually live in Delhi. Everything here is current, everyday, and clean — the words friends toss across a chai stall, not anything that will get you in trouble. One rule before you start: all of it is informal. Friends and your partner, yes; elders, in-laws, and your boss, no — the culture box at the end draws the exact line.

Calling people

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning & usage
यारyaar (m)yahrdude, man, buddy — ends half of Delhi's sentences (chalo yaar, naheen yaar)
भाईbhaaee (m)bhah-eebro — friends, cousins, any guy your age (shopkeepers get bhaiyaa)
हाँ भाईhaan bhaaeehah(n) bhah-ee"yes bro" — hello / so, what's up; opens phone calls
बंदाbandaa (m)bun-dahguy (f: बंदी bandee [bun-dee] girl) — achchhaa bandaa hai = he's a good guy
अरेarreuh-rayhey! oh! — grabs attention, starts half of all sentences
ओएoyeoh-ayoi! — CLOSE friends only; never strangers, never elders
ओए होए!oye hoye!oh-ay hoh-ayooh la la! — teasing someone who's dressed up or blushing
पागलpaagalpah-gulsilly, crazy — affectionate between friends and couples (paagal hai tu!)

Yes, right, wow — agreement & praise

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning & usage
हाँ जीhaan jeehah(n) jeewarm yes — the one item here that's safe with absolutely everyone
ठीक है जीTheek hai jeeTheek heh jee"okay then" — warm, slightly wry sign-off
पक्काpakkaapuk-kahfor sure, confirmed — pakkaa na? = promise?
सही है!sahee hai!suh-hee hehnice, right on, fair enough — the all-purpose approval
क्या बात है!kyaa baat hai!kyah baht hehwow, beautiful! — THE compliment reaction
ज़बरदस्तzabardastzuh-bur-dustsmashing, awesome
मस्तmastmustgreat, lovely, chilled — mast hai yaar
कमालkamaal (m)kuh-mahlkamaal hai! = unbelievable; kamaal kaa = amazing (kamaal kaa khaanaa)
ग़ज़बgazab (m)guh-zubgazab! = incredible, killer
एकदमekdumayk-dumtotally, completely — ekdum sahee, ekdum fresh
बिंदासbindaasbin-dahscarefree, bold; also "go right ahead" (poochho? bindaas poochho!)

अच्छा — one word, five meanings

You met अच्छा (achchhaa) [uch-chhah] as "good." In conversation it's a Swiss Army knife — the tone does all the work:

Toneहिन्दीIt meansSituation
flat, shortअच्छा।OK, got itacknowledging an instruction
pitch jumps upअच्छा?!really?!reacting to news
long and slowअच्छा…ohhh, I see…the penny finally drops
sharp, clippedअच्छा!oh right!suddenly remembering (achchhaa! doodh laanaa thaa)
sing-song, eyebrow upअच्छा जी?oh really, is that so?teasing challenge — big with couples

Moving things along

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning & usage
चलोchalochuh-lohlet's go; also "fine, okay then" (chalo, Theek hai)
चलchalchulc'mon; also "yeah right, come off it" (chal, jhooTh mat bol) — very close friends only
चल नाchal naachul nahcome onnn — the wheedle that gets people out of the house
बसbasbusenough, that's it — bas bas! = stop pouring!
हो गयाho gayaahoh guh-yahdone, that's that — ho gayaa? = all done?
और बताओaur bataaoawr buh-tah-oh"so, what else?" — keeps a conversation from ever ending
क्या सीन है?kyaa seen (m) hai?kyah seen hehwhat's the plan? what's happening?

The great Delhi words

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning & usage
जुगाड़jugaaR (m)ju-gahRthe clever workaround — see below, it deserves a paragraph
सेटिंगseTing (f)say-Tingan "arrangement" — inside contact, connection (meree seTing hai = I know a guy)
वेल्लाvellaa (v)vayl-lahidle, loafing — Delhi's proudest state of being (f: vellee)
टाइमपासTaimpaas (m)Tah-im-pahstime-killing fun; light fluff (the classic movie review: Theek hai, Taimpaas hai)
फ़ालतूfaaltoofahl-toouseless, pointless; faaltoo mein = for no reason
फ़ंडाfunDaa (m)fun-Dahconcept, personal theory — simpal funDaa hai…
पंगाpangaa (m)pun-gahtrouble, a run-in; pangaa lenaa = to pick a fight (pangaa mat lo)
बकवासbakvaas (f)buk-vahsnonsense, rubbish — film bakvaas thee; bakvaas band karo (friends only)

जुगाड़ (jugaaR) [ju-gahR] is Delhi's national sport: fixing the problem with whatever is on hand — a phone call, a spare wire, a friend's friend, sheer nerve. A cooler bolted onto a bicycle is jugaaR; sold-out tickets appearing "through a contact" is jugaaR; so is your landlord's TV antenna made from a cooking pot. The verbs are jugaaR karnaa and jugaaR lagaanaa, and the word is half compliment, half national confession — Delhiites say it with real pride.

Chill, Delhi-style

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning & usage
टेंशन मत लो यारTenshan mat lo yaarTayn-shun mut loh yahrrelax, don't stress — the city's unofficial motto
चिल मारchil maarchil mahrchill out — chil maar yaar, sab Theek hai
सब सेट हैsab seT haisub sayT heheverything's sorted, all arranged

In action — the top twelve

यार, बहुत भूख लगी है — कुछ खाते हैं?
yaar, bahut bhookh lagee hai — kuchh khaate hain? [yahr, bo-hut bhookh luh-gee heh — kuchh khah-tay heh(n)]
Yaar, I'm starving — shall we eat something?
हाँ भाई, क्या हाल है? — बस, मस्त।
haan bhaaee, kyaa haal hai? — bas, mast. [hah(n) bhah-ee, kyah hahl heh? — bus, must]
Hey bro, how's it going? — Just great.
अच्छा जी? तो कल रात कहाँ थे आप?
achchhaa jee? to kal raat kahaan the aap? [uch-chhah jee? toh kul raht kuh-hah(n) thay ahp]
Oh really? So where were YOU last night? (the teasing aap — couples' specialty)
पक्का आओगे ना? — हाँ यार, पक्का!
pakkaa aaoge naa? — haan yaar, pakkaa! [puk-kah ah-oh-gay nah? — hah(n) yahr, puk-kah]
You'll definitely come, right? — Yes yaar, hundred percent!
क्या बात है! नई शर्ट में हीरो लग रहे हो!
kyaa baat hai! naee sharT mein heero lag rahe ho! [kyah baht heh! nuh-ee shurT may(n) hee-roh lug ruh-hay hoh]
Look at that! You're looking like a film hero in the new shirt! (sharT f)
कल का डिनर ज़बरदस्त था, एकदम ज़बरदस्त।
kal kaa Dinar zabardast thaa, ekdum zabardast. [kul kah Di-nur zuh-bur-dust thah, ayk-dum zuh-bur-dust]
Yesterday's dinner was awesome, totally awesome. (Dinar m — English loan)
चल ना यार, वहाँ मज़ा आएगा।
chal naa yaar, vahaan mazaa aayegaa. [chul nah yahr, vuh-hah(n) muh-zah ah-ay-gah]
Come onnn yaar, it'll be fun there.
और भाई, वीकेंड का क्या सीन है?
aur bhaaee, veekenD kaa kyaa seen hai? [awr bhah-ee, vee-kaynD kah kyah seen heh]
So bro, what's the scene this weekend? (veekenD m)
कोई जुगाड़ करो यार, टिकट चाहिए ही चाहिए।
koee jugaaR karo yaar, TikaT chaahiye hee chaahiye. [koh-ee ju-gahR kuh-roh yahr, Ti-kuT chah-hi-yay hee chah-hi-yay]
Work some jugaad, yaar — we absolutely have to get tickets.
आज मैं एकदम वेल्ला हूँ — कोई काम नहीं।
aaj main ekdum vellaa hoon — koee kaam naheen. [ahj meh(n) ayk-dum vayl-lah hoo(n) — koh-ee kahm nuh-hee(n)]
I'm completely vella today — nothing to do.
फ़िल्म कैसी थी? — यार, पूरी बकवास।
film kaisee thee? — yaar, pooree bakvaas. [film keh-see thee? — yahr, poo-ree buk-vahs]
How was the movie? — Total rubbish, yaar. (film f, bakvaas f → pooree)
टेंशन मत लो यार, चिल मारो — सब सेट है।
Tenshan mat lo yaar, chil maaro — sab seT hai. [Tayn-shun mut loh yahr, chil mah-roh — sub sayT heh]
Don't stress yaar, chill — it's all sorted.

Delhi slang wears its Punjabi heart openly — oye, vellaa, pangaa all came up the Grand Trunk Road. The other engine is English: Delhi will verb anything — chil maarnaa, bank maarnaa [bunk mahr-nah] (to skip class), seT karnaa, scene banaanaa. And don't fear sounding dated: slang fashion changes, but this chapter is the evergreen core — yaar has been cool since your in-laws were in college.

Slang is a register, not just vocabulary. With friends and your partner, every word here signals warmth; with elders and in-laws, the same words signal disrespect. Hard rules: never oye, never bare chal, never yaar to your saas-sasur; with them it's जी हाँ (jee haan) [jee hah(n)], aap, and full sentences. The one safe crossover is jee itself — haan jee, Theek hai jee — which makes everything respectful. When unsure, listen to your partner's register and stay one notch politer.

1) Watch one scene of a Delhi film or web series together and count the yaars and achchhaas — loser buys chai. 2) The achchhaa drill: your partner says अच्छा five ways (flat, surprised, slow, sharp, teasing); you call out which meaning each one was — then swap. 3) Plan Saturday using only this chapter: kyaa seen hai? — main to vellaa hoon. — chal naa, kaheen chalte hain. — pakkaa? — pakkaa. ho gayaa, seT hai.
chapters.book3-c19:
Chapter 19 Love & Affection

This chapter is for the two of you. Hindi sweet-talk runs from film-song poetry down to the world's most practical love language — खाना खाया? (khaanaa khaayaa?) [khah-nah khah-yah] "have you eaten?" — and Delhi couples mix English into all of it without blinking. Here are the pet names, the compliments, the big sentence, and the two verbs every couple needs: rooThnaa and manaanaa.

Pet names

Private vocabulary — for the two of you, not for the dinner table with elders (see the culture box).

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
जानjaan (f)jahndarling (literally: life)
मेरी जानmeree jaanmay-ree jahnmy love, my life
जानूjaanoojah-noosweetie (jaan, made cuter)
बाबूbaaboobah-boobabe — yes, grown adults; extremely common
बेबीbebeebay-beebaby — English, fully adopted
शोनाshonaashoh-nahsweetie, "goldie" (from sonaa = gold)

Love words

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
प्यारpyaar (m)pyahrlove — the everyday word
मोहब्बतmohabbat (f)moh-hub-butlove — Urdu-Delhi, a shade deeper and more romantic
इश्क़ishq (m)ishqlove — poetic and passionate; lives in ghazals and film songs, use it for effect, not errands
दिलdil (m)dilheart (dil se = from the heart)
यादyaad (f)yahdmemory; the missing of someone
वादाvaadaa (m)vah-dahpromise
रिश्ताrishtaa (m)rish-tahrelationship, bond
नोक-झोंकnok-jhonk (f)nohk-jhoh(n)kplayful bickering — the sign of a healthy Delhi couple
हमेशा के लिएhameshaa ke liyehuh-may-shah kay li-yayforever

Saying it

PatternRomanSay itMeaning
मैं तुमसे प्यार करता हूँ।main tumse pyaar kartaa hoon.meh(n) tum-say pyahr kur-tah hoo(n)I love you (Jacob speaking)
मैं भी तुमसे प्यार करती हूँ।main bhee tumse pyaar kartee hoon.meh(n) bhee tum-say pyahr kur-tee hoo(n)I love you too (her reply — female form)
तुम मुझे बहुत पसंद हो।tum mujhe bahut pasand ho.tum mu-jhay bo-hut puh-sund hohI really like you
तुम्हारी याद आ रही है।tumhaaree yaad aa rahee hai.tum-hah-ree yahd ah ruh-hee hehI miss you (right now) (lit. your memory is coming)
मैं तुम्हें मिस कर रहा था।main tumhen mis kar rahaa thaa.meh(n) tum-hay(n) mis kur ruh-hah thahI was missing you — Delhi happily mixes in English
तुम मेरी जान हो।tum meree jaan ho.tum may-ree jahn hohyou are my life

Compliments

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
तुम बहुत सुंदर लग रही हो।tum bahut sundar lag rahee ho.tum bo-hut sun-dur lug ruh-hee hohyou're looking beautiful (to her)
तुम बहुत अच्छे लग रहे हो।tum bahut achchhe lag rahe ho.tum bo-hut uch-chhay lug ruh-hay hohyou're looking great (to him)
क्या बात है!kyaa baat hai!kyah baht hehwow, look at you! (when your partner dresses up)
यह रंग तुम पर बहुत अच्छा लग रहा है।yeh rang tum par bahut achchhaa lag rahaa hai.yeh rung tum pur bo-hut uch-chhah lug ruh-hah hehthis color looks great on you (rang m)
तुम्हारी मुस्कान बहुत प्यारी है।tumhaaree muskaan (f) bahut pyaaree hai.tum-hah-ree mus-kahn bo-hut pyah-ree hehyour smile is lovely

The real love language

In an Indian relationship, "I love you" is said daily — just usually disguised as food and logistics:

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
खाना खाया?khaanaa khaayaa?khah-nah khah-yahhave you eaten? — functionally "I love you"
घर पहुँच के बताना।ghar pahunch ke bataanaa.ghur puh-hu(n)ch kay buh-tah-nahlet me know when you reach home
ध्यान रखना।dhyaan rakhnaa.dhyahn rukh-nahtake care (of yourself)
आराम करो।aaraam karo.ah-rahm kuh-rohget some rest
मैं हूँ ना।main hoon naa.meh(n) hoo(n) nahI'm here, no? — don't worry, you have me

Couple verbs

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
रूठनाrooThnaa (vi)rooTh-nahto sulk, to be miffed (usually rooTh jaanaa)
मनानाmanaanaa (vt)muh-nah-nahto win (someone) back with sweetness — the cure for rooThnaa
गले लगानाgale lagaanaa (vt)guh-lay luh-gah-nahto hug (गले लग जाओ gale lag jaao = come here, hug)
हाथ पकड़नाhaath (m) pakaRnaa (vt)hahth puh-kuR-nahto hold hands
तारीफ़ करनाtaareef (f) karnaa (vt)tah-reef kur-nahto compliment, to praise

The rooThnaa–manaanaa cycle is the plot of half of Bollywood and most real couples: one sulks charmingly, the other brings chai, compliments, and apologies until peace returns. It's practically a hobby — learn both verbs as a pair.

In action

मैं तुमसे बहुत प्यार करता हूँ।
main tumse bahut pyaar kartaa hoon. [meh(n) tum-say bo-hut pyahr kur-tah hoo(n)]
I love you very much.
मैं भी तुमसे प्यार करती हूँ।
main bhee tumse pyaar kartee hoon. [meh(n) bhee tum-say pyahr kur-tee hoo(n)]
I love you too. (her reply — kartee)
तुम्हारी बहुत याद आ रही है।
tumhaaree bahut yaad aa rahee hai. [tum-hah-ree bo-hut yahd ah ruh-hee heh]
I'm really missing you.
मैं तुम्हें पूरा दिन मिस कर रहा था।
main tumhen pooraa din mis kar rahaa thaa. [meh(n) tum-hay(n) poo-rah din mis kur ruh-hah thah]
I was missing you all day.
तुम आज बहुत सुंदर लग रही हो।
tum aaj bahut sundar lag rahee ho. [tum ahj bo-hut sun-dur lug ruh-hee hoh]
You're looking really beautiful today.
अरे वाह — तुम बहुत अच्छे लग रहे हो!
arre vaah — tum bahut achchhe lag rahe ho! [uh-ray vah — tum bo-hut uch-chhay lug ruh-hay hoh]
Oh wow — you're looking very handsome! (her to him)
खाना खाया? घर पहुँच के बताना।
khaanaa khaayaa? ghar pahunch ke bataanaa. [khah-nah khah-yah? ghur puh-hu(n)ch kay buh-tah-nah]
Did you eat? Text me when you reach home. (= I love you, twice)
जानू रूठ गई है — अब उसे मनाना पड़ेगा।
jaanoo rooTh gaee hai — ab use manaanaa paRegaa. [jah-noo rooTh guh-ee heh — ub u-say muh-nah-nah puh-Ray-gah]
Jaanu is sulking — now I'll have to win her back.
वादा करो, हमेशा साथ रहोगे।
vaadaa karo, hameshaa saath rahoge. [vah-dah kuh-roh, huh-may-shah sahth ruh-hoh-gay]
Promise me you'll always stay with me.
इधर आओ, गले लग जाओ।
idhar aao, gale lag jaao. [i-dhur ah-oh, guh-lay lug jah-oh]
Come here — give me a hug. (idhar = over here)

Delhi couple-speak is Hinglish at its purest: "I love you yaar", mis kar rahaa thaa, "tum cute lag rahee ho", चलो, डेट पे चलते हैं। (chalo, DeT pe chalte hain.) [chuh-loh, DayT pay chul-tay heh(n)] — note Delhi's pe for par. The cheapest sweetness upgrade is tacking naa onto requests: रुको ना… (ruko naa…) [ru-koh nah] "staaay, no?". Even the fights are Hinglish: "pehle tum sorry bolo!"

Public affection in India is modest: hand-holding in malls and parks is normal for couples now, but kissing in public is not done, and in front of parents or in-laws even a hug between partners is unusual — affection there flows through care instead: serving food, khaanaa khaayaa?, dhyaan rakhnaa. Pet names are private too — meree jaan lands beautifully at home and lands you teasing for a decade if the cousins hear it. Traditionally many couples wouldn't even say each other's first names in front of elders; modern Delhi is relaxed, but you'll still hear a spouse summoned with just सुनो! (suno!) [su-noh] "listen!"

1) Pick pet names for each other from the table and use them all evening — first one to slip back to real names makes the chai. 2) Compliment volley: three compliments each from this chapter, with the right endings (lag rahee ho / lag rahe ho) — the listener referees the grammar before saying shukriyaa. 3) Drama practice: one of you pretends to rooTh (arms crossed, face turned); the other has to manaao using at least three lines from this chapter. Swap roles. No laughing — okay, some laughing.
chapters.book3-c20:
Chapter 20 Festivals & Occasions

Delhi's year is a festival relay: दिवाली (divaalee) [di-vah-lee] lights in autumn, colors at होली (holee) [hoh-lee] in spring, Eid crowds at Jama Masjid, and wedding bands blocking traffic all winter. This chapter gives you the words for every big त्योहार (tyohaar) [tyoh-hahr], the greetings people actually say, and the two customs that will make you the favorite son-in-law: the sweets box and touching feet.

दिवाली (divaalee) — the festival of lights

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
त्योहारtyohaar (m)tyoh-hahrfestival
दिवालीdivaalee (f)di-vah-leeDiwali (October–November; cards say दीपावली deepaavalee)
दीयाdeeyaa (m)dee-yahlittle oil lamp (pl. दीये deeye)
मिठाईmiThaaee (f)mi-Thah-eesweets
पटाखाpaTaakhaa (m)puh-Tah-khahfirecracker (pl. पटाखे paTaakhe)
लक्ष्मी पूजाlakshmee poojaa (f)luksh-mee poo-jahthe Lakshmi worship on Diwali night
सफ़ाईsafaaee (f)suh-fah-eecleaning — the great pre-Diwali scrub-down of the whole house
रंगोलीrangolee (f)run-goh-leecolored floor design at the doorway

होली (holee) — the festival of colors

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
होलीholee (f)hoh-leeHoli (March)
रंगrang (m)rungcolor
गुलालgulaal (m)gu-lahlthe dry colored powder
पिचकारीpichkaaree (f)pich-kah-reewater gun
ठंडाईThanDaaee (f)Thun-Dah-eespiced milk-and-almond drink of Holi
बुरा न मानो, होली है!buraa na maano, holee hai!bu-rah nuh mah-noh, hoh-lee heh"don't mind — it's Holi!" (the all-purpose Holi excuse)

राखी और करवा चौथ (raakhee aur karvaa chauth)

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
रक्षाबंधनrakshaabandhan (m)ruk-shah-bun-dhunRakshabandhan (August) — everyone just says राखी
राखीraakhee (f)rah-kheethe thread a sister ties on her brother's wrist
करवा चौथkarvaa chauth (m)kur-vah chawthautumn fast wives keep for their husbands
व्रतvrat (m)vrutfast (vrat rakhnaa = to keep a fast)
चाँदchaand (m)chah(n)dmoon — the karvaa chauth fast opens only at moonrise

Karvaa chauth is a couples' festival at heart — she fasts sunrise to moonrise, dresses up, and the first sip of water comes looking at the moon and then at her husband. Plenty of modern Delhi husbands now keep the fast alongside their wives. If your partner keeps it, मैं भी तुम्हारे साथ व्रत रखूँगा। (main bhee tumhaare saath vrat rakhoongaa.) [meh(n) bhee tum-hah-ray sahth vrut ruh-khoo(n)-gah] is about the most romantic sentence in this book.

ईद (eed)

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
ईदeed (f)eedEid
मस्जिदmasjid (f)mus-jidmosque — Delhi's जामा मस्जिद jaamaa masjid overflows on Eid morning
सेवइयाँsevaiyaan (f pl)say-vai-yah(n)the sweet vermicelli of Eid
ईदीeedee (f)ee-deeEid money/gift for the youngsters
इफ़्तारiftaar (m)if-tahrthe evening fast-breaking meal in the month of ramzaan

नवरात्रे, दशहरा और छठ (navraatre, dashehraa aur chhaTh)

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
नवरात्रेnavraatre (m pl)nuv-raht-rayNavratri, the nine nights of the Goddess (Delhi says navraatre; standard is नवरात्रि navraatri)
दशहराdashehraa (m)duh-sheh-rahDussehra, the day good defeats evil
रावणraavaN (m)rah-vuNRavan — his giant effigies burn at Dussehra
पुतलाputlaa (m)put-laheffigy
रामलीलाraamleelaa (f)rahm-lee-lahthe Ram story staged over ten nights — Old Delhi's is legendary
छठchhaTh (f)chhuThChhath — sun-worship festival Delhi's Purvanchali families celebrate at the Yamuna ghats

जन्मदिन (janmdin) — birthdays

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
जन्मदिनjanmdin (m)juh-num-dinbirthday (Delhi says बर्थडे barthDe just as often)
केक काटनाkek (m) kaaTnaakayk kahT-nahto cut the cake — the centerpiece ritual, cameras out
पार्टीpaarTee (f)pahr-Teeparty (paarTee kab de rahe ho? = so when are you treating us?)
तोहफ़ाtohfaa (m)toh-fahgift, present (Delhi also just says गिफ़्ट gifT)

शादी (shaadee) — the big fat Delhi wedding

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
शादीshaadee (f)shah-deewedding, marriage (vivaah is the formal word on invitation cards)
दूल्हाdoolhaa (m)dool-hahgroom
दुल्हनdulhan (f)dul-hunbride
बारातbaaraat (f)bah-rahtthe groom's procession — brass band, dancing, traffic jam
घोड़ीghoRee (f)ghoh-Reethe mare the groom rides in on
मेहंदीmehndee (f)meh(n)-deehenna; the mehndi ceremony
संगीतsangeet (m)sun-geetthe music-and-dance night before the wedding
फेरेphere (m pl)phay-raythe seven rounds of the sacred fire — the actual "I do"
लहंगाlehngaa (m)leh(n)-gahthe bride's heavy embroidered skirt outfit
शेरवानीshervaanee (f)shayr-vah-neethe groom's long formal coat
कार्डkaarD (m)kahrDthe wedding invitation — shaadee kaa kaarD

मंदिर और पूजा (mandir aur poojaa)

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
पूजाpoojaa (f)poo-jahworship, prayer ritual (also at home)
मंदिरmandir (m)mun-dirtemple
प्रसादprasaad (m)pruh-sahdblessed food shared after worship — accept with the right hand
आरतीaartee (f)ahr-teethe lamp-waving prayer song
भगवानbhagvaan (m)bhug-vahnGod
आशीर्वादaasheervaad (m)ah-sheer-vahdblessing — what elders give when you touch their feet

Greetings people actually say

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
हैप्पी दिवाली!haippee divaalee!heh-pee di-vah-leewhat 90% of Delhi actually says
दिवाली मुबारक!divaalee mubaarak!di-vah-lee mu-bah-rukhappy Diwali! (mubaarak works after any occasion word)
शुभ दीपावलीshubh deepaavaleeshubh dee-pah-vuh-leeformal version — printed on cards and sweet boxes
होली मुबारक!holee mubaarak!hoh-lee mu-bah-rukhappy Holi!
ईद मुबारक!eed mubaarak!eed mu-bah-rukEid Mubarak!
जन्मदिन मुबारक!janmdin mubaarak!juh-num-din mu-bah-rukhappy birthday!
शादी मुबारक!shaadee mubaarak!shah-dee mu-bah-rukcongratulations on the wedding!
नया साल मुबारक!nayaa saal (m) mubaarak!nuh-yah sahl mu-bah-rukhappy new year!
आपको भी!aapko bhee!ahp-koh bheesame to you! — the reply you'll need within seconds

In action

दिवाली पर हम दीये जलाएँगे और मिठाई बाँटेंगे।
divaalee par ham deeye jalaaenge aur miThaaee baanTenge. [di-vah-lee pur hum dee-yay juh-lah-ay(n)-gay awr mi-Thah-ee bah(n)-Tay(n)-gay]
On Diwali we'll light lamps and hand out sweets. (baanTnaa = to distribute)
कल लक्ष्मी पूजा है — आज घर की सफ़ाई करनी है।
kal lakshmee poojaa hai — aaj ghar kee safaaee karnee hai. [kul luksh-mee poo-jah heh — ahj ghur kee suh-fah-ee kur-nee heh]
Tomorrow is the Lakshmi puja — today the house has to be cleaned.
होली पर सब एक-दूसरे को रंग लगाते हैं।
holee par sab ek-doosre ko rang lagaate hain. [hoh-lee pur sub ayk-doos-ray koh rung luh-gah-tay heh(n)]
On Holi everyone puts color on each other.
राखी पर बहन भाई को राखी बाँधती है।
raakhee par behen bhaaee ko raakhee baandhtee hai. [rah-khee pur beh-hen bhah-ee koh rah-khee bah(n)dh-tee heh]
On Rakhi, a sister ties a rakhi on her brother. (baandhnaa = to tie)
मैं भी तुम्हारे साथ व्रत रखूँगा।
main bhee tumhaare saath vrat rakhoongaa. [meh(n) bhee tum-hah-ray sahth vrut ruh-khoo(n)-gah]
I'll keep the fast with you too. (karvaa chauth points: maximum)
ईद पर पुरानी दिल्ली में सेवइयाँ ज़रूर खाना।
eed par puraanee dillee mein sevaiyaan zaroor khaanaa. [eed pur pu-rah-nee dil-lee may(n) say-vai-yah(n) zuh-roor khah-nah]
On Eid, definitely eat sevaiyaan in Old Delhi.
दशहरे पर रावण का पुतला जलता है।
dashehre par raavaN kaa putlaa jaltaa hai. [duh-sheh-ray pur rah-vuN kah put-lah jul-tah heh]
At Dussehra, Ravan's effigy goes up in flames. (jalnaa vi = to burn)
जन्मदिन मुबारक! चलो, केक काटो!
janmdin mubaarak! chalo, kek kaaTo! [juh-num-din mu-bah-ruk! chuh-loh, kayk kah-Toh]
Happy birthday! Come on, cut the cake!
दूल्हा घोड़ी पर आता है और बाराती नाचते हैं।
doolhaa ghoRee par aataa hai aur baaraatee naachte hain. [dool-hah ghoh-Ree pur ah-tah heh awr bah-rah-tee nahch-tay heh(n)]
The groom arrives on a mare and the baraat guests dance. (baaraatee m = procession member)
आंटी जी, आपको और पूरे परिवार को दिवाली मुबारक!
aanTee jee, aapko aur poore parivaar ko divaalee mubaarak! [ahn-Tee jee, ahp-koh awr poo-ray puh-ri-vahr koh di-vah-lee mu-bah-ruk]
Aunty ji, happy Diwali to you and the whole family! (parivaar m)

Festival season runs on miThaaee: nobody crosses a doorstep empty-handed in Diwali week. The standard offering is a डिब्बा (Dibbaa) [Dib-bah] — a box — of sweets or dry fruits, handed over with both hands; काजू कतली (kaajoo katlee) [kah-joo kut-lee] is the undisputed crowd-pleaser. The boxes circulate so vigorously that Delhi jokes the same box of सोन पापड़ी (son paapRee) [sohn pahp-Ree] tours the entire city every year. Bringing a good Dibbaa to the in-laws is basic festival armor — and never return anyone's container empty.

पैर छूना (pair chhoonaa) [pehr chhoo-nah] — touching elders' feet — is the highest-value gesture you can learn: bend and touch (or reach toward) the feet of grandparents, parents, and elder relatives on festivals, first meetings, and goodbyes. The formal name is चरण स्पर्श (charaN sparsh) [chuh-ruN spursh]. The elder blesses you — जीते रहो! (jeete raho!) [jee-tay ruh-hoh] "live long!", ख़ुश रहो! (khush raho!) [khush ruh-hoh] — or pulls you up mid-bend with bas bas, beTaa; the attempt itself is the point. An American son-in-law who does this on Diwali will be discussed admiringly for weeks. Follow your partner's lead on whose feet and when.

Every festival has a Delhi address: Dussehra's burning raavaN at the Ramlila grounds near the Red Fort, Eid morning and iftaar lanes at jaamaa masjid, chhaTh crowds at the Yamuna ghats, and baraats blocking your road all wedding season — give it five minutes and enjoy the band. Two practical notes: firecrackers are heavily restricted in Delhi these days, so Diwali is more lights, card games — ताश (taash) [tahsh] — and food than bombs; and in Holi week, watch for water balloons from balconies. Kids start "practicing" days early.

1) Festival quiz: your partner names a festival, you fire back three words that belong to it — divaalee → deeye, miThaaee, safaaee! Then swap. 2) Ask your partner to walk you through their family's biggest festival day, then retell it back in three Hindi sentences using this chapter's words. 3) Rehearse the in-law entrance for the next occasion, full choreography: Dibbaa in both hands, नमस्ते आंटी जी, दिवाली मुबारक! (namaste aanTee jee, divaalee mubaarak!) [nuh-muhs-tay ahn-Tee jee, di-vah-lee mu-bah-ruk], then the feet-touch — your partner plays the aunty and must bless you properly: jeete raho!
chapters.book4-L01:
Lesson 1 Namaste! First Introductions

Friday evening, a rooftop cafe in Hauz Khas Village. Fairy lights, the smell of rain on dust, a wall of scooter noise from the lane below. Priya's oldest school friend Kabir arrives — and Jacob is about to survive his very first real Hindi conversation. Small sentences. Big moment.

Everything in this lesson runs on just one verb — होना (honaa) [hoh-nah], "to be" — plus a handful of frozen phrases. A frozen phrase is a chunk you memorize whole, like a password. Don't take it apart yet; the grammar inside it arrives in later units. Bonus for beginners: none of today's sentences change for gender. Enjoy the calm.

Dialogue: at the cafe

Priya:
कबीर! यह जैकब है।
Kabir! yeh Jacob hai. [kuh-beer! yeh jay-kub heh]
Kabir! This is Jacob.
Jacob:
नमस्ते! मैं जैकब हूँ।
namaste! main Jacob hoon. [nuh-muhs-tay! meh(n) jay-kub hoo(n)]
Namaste! I am Jacob.
Kabir:
नमस्ते जी! मैं कबीर हूँ। आप कैसे हैं?
namaste jee! main Kabir hoon. aap kaise hain? [nuh-muhs-tay jee! meh(n) kuh-beer hoo(n). ahp keh-say heh(n)]
Namaste! I'm Kabir. How are you?
Jacob:
मैं ठीक हूँ, शुक्रिया। आप कैसे हैं?
main Theek hoon, shukriyaa. aap kaise hain? [meh(n) Theek hoo(n), shuk-ri-yah. ahp keh-say heh(n)]
I'm fine, thanks. How are you?
Kabir:
बस, बढ़िया! आप कहाँ से हैं?
bas, baRhiyaa! aap kahaan se hain? [bus, buh-Rhi-yah! ahp kuh-hah(n) say heh(n)]
Doing great! Where are you from?
Jacob:
मैं अमेरिका से हूँ। और आप?
main amerikaa se hoon. aur aap? [meh(n) uh-may-ri-kah say hoo(n). awr ahp]
I'm from America. And you?
Kabir:
मैं यहीं से हूँ — दिल्ली से।
main yaheen se hoon — dillee se. [meh(n) yuh-hee(n) say hoo(n) — dil-lee say]
I'm from right here — from Delhi.
Priya:
कबीर मेरा दोस्त है। स्कूल से।
Kabir meraa dost hai. school se. [kuh-beer may-rah dohst heh. skool say]
Kabir is my friend. From school.
Kabir:
जी हाँ। और जैकब, आपकी हिन्दी अच्छी है!
jee haan. aur Jacob, aapkee hindee achchhee hai! [jee hah(n). awr jay-kub, ahp-kee hin-dee uch-chhee heh]
Yes indeed. And Jacob, your Hindi is good!
Jacob:
नहीं, नहीं… थोड़ी-थोड़ी।
naheen, naheen… thoRee-thoRee. [nuh-hee(n), nuh-hee(n)… thoh-Ree-thoh-Ree]
No, no… just a little.
Kabir:
अरे, बिल्कुल ठीक है!
arre, bilkul Theek hai! [uh-ray, bil-kul Theek heh]
Hey, it's absolutely fine!
Priya:
चलो — चाय?
chalo — chaay? [chuh-loh — chah-ay]
Come on — chai?
Jacob:
जी हाँ, चाय ज़रूर!
jee haan, chaay zaroor! [jee hah(n), chah-ay zuh-roor]
Yes, chai for sure!
Kabir:
जैकब, आप से मिलकर ख़ुशी हुई।
Jacob, aap se milkar khushee huee. [jay-kub, ahp say mil-kur khu-shee hu-ee]
Jacob, (I'm) happy to have met you.
Jacob:
मुझे भी!
mujhe bhee! [mu-jhay bhee]
Me too!

Almost nobody in Delhi answers आप कैसे हैं? (aap kaise hain?) with a full textbook sentence. You'll hear बस, बढ़िया! (bas, baRhiyaa!) [bus, buh-Rhi-yah] "just great!", सब ठीक! (sab Theek!) [sub Theek] "all good!", or pure Hinglish: "I'm good yaar, aap bataao!" Delhi also flips जी हाँ into हाँ जी (haan jee) [hah(n) jee] — same warmth, street order.

Key phrases

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
नमस्तेnamastenuh-muhs-tayhello / goodbye (all-purpose)
मैं जैकब हूँ।main Jacob hoon.meh(n) jay-kub hoo(n)I am Jacob.
आप कैसे हैं?aap kaise hain?ahp keh-say heh(n)How are you? (to a man)
आप कैसी हैं?aap kaisee hain?ahp keh-see heh(n)How are you? (to a woman)
मैं ठीक हूँ।main Theek hoon.meh(n) Theek hoo(n)I'm fine. (same for men & women)
आप कहाँ से हैं?aap kahaan se hain?ahp kuh-hah(n) say heh(n)Where are you from?
मैं अमेरिका से हूँ।main amerikaa se hoon.meh(n) uh-may-ri-kah say hoo(n)I'm from America.
यह जैकब है।yeh Jacob hai.yay jay-kub hehThis is Jacob.
मेरा दोस्त / मेरी दोस्तmeraa dost / meree dost (m/f)may-rah dohst / may-ree dohstmy friend (male / female) — frozen for now
थोड़ी-थोड़ी हिन्दीthoRee-thoRee hindee (f)thoh-Ree-thoh-Ree hin-deea little bit of Hindi
आप से मिलकर ख़ुशी हुई।aap se milkar khushee huee.ahp say mil-kur khu-shee hu-eeNice to meet you. — frozen phrase
फिर मिलेंगे!phir milenge!phir mi-lay(n)-gaySee you again! — frozen phrase

That little word जी (jee) [jee] is respect in one syllable. Add it to a yes (जी हाँ), to a name (कबीर जी), or use it alone as "yes? / pardon?". With your partner's parents, sprinkle it generously — जी costs nothing and buys everything. The folded-hands namaste plus one जी will carry your first meeting with any elder.

English word order will pull you toward मैं हूँ जैकब (main hoon Jacob) — "I am Jacob." Resist. In Hindi the verb parks at the end: मैं जैकब हूँ। Same with questions: आप कैसे हैं?, never कैसे आप हैं? Verb last. Always verb last.

Did you catch that?

Exercise 1A — Comprehension

Answer in Hindi — short answers are fine. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 1.

  1. जैकब कहाँ से है? (Jacob kahaan se hai?)
  2. कबीर कहाँ से है? (Kabir kahaan se hai?)
  3. क्या कबीर प्रिया का दोस्त है? (kyaa Kabir Priya kaa dost hai?)
  4. जैकब कैसा है? (Jacob kaisaa hai?)
  5. क्या जैकब की हिन्दी अच्छी है? (kyaa Jacob kee hindee achchhee hai?)

Pattern practice

The whole lesson is one machine with three gears. Mix any left column with any middle column — the right column is fixed by the person:

PersonMiddle (anything)Verb (fixed)
मैं (main)जैकब / ठीक / अमेरिका सेहूँ (hoon)
आप (aap)कैसे? / कहाँ से?हैं (hain)
यह (yeh)प्रिया / मेरा दोस्तहै (hai)

Exercise 1B — Build the sentence

The words are scrambled. Write each sentence in the correct order — remember: verb last. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 1.

  1. हूँ / मैं / जैकब (hoon / main / Jacob)
  2. से / मैं / अमेरिका / हूँ (se / main / amerikaa / hoon)
  3. हैं / आप / कैसे ? (hain / aap / kaise ?)
  4. ठीक / मैं / हूँ (Theek / main / hoon)
  5. से / आप / हैं / कहाँ ? (se / aap / hain / kahaan ?)
  6. है / यह / प्रिया (hai / yeh / Priya)
  7. दोस्त / मेरा / है / यह (dost / meraa / hai / yeh)
  8. से / कबीर / है / दिल्ली (se / Kabir / hai / dillee)

Translation practice

Exercise 1C — Into Hindi

Write in Devanagari (roman underneath if you like). Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 1.

  1. Namaste! I am Jacob.
  2. I am from America.
  3. How are you? (to your father-in-law — so: aap)
  4. This is my friend Kabir.

Exercise 1D — Into English

Write the English meaning. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 1.

  1. आप कहाँ से हैं? (aap kahaan se hain?)
  2. मैं दिल्ली से हूँ। (main dillee se hoon.)
  3. आप से मिलकर ख़ुशी हुई। (aap se milkar khushee huee.)
  4. प्रिया मेरी दोस्त है। (Priya meree dost hai.)

Roleplay: you're at a cafe and your partner plays a friend you've never met. Greet, trade names, ask आप कैसे हैं / कैसी हैं? and आप कहाँ से हैं?, answer both yourself, and close with आप से मिलकर ख़ुशी हुई। Then swap roles.

Round two: your partner replays it as three different people — a new friend, an auntie from the colony, an uncle at a wedding. Your आप stays; watch them switch कैसे/कैसी at you. Round three: introduce your partner to an imaginary guest: यह प्रिया है। प्रिया मेरी दोस्त है। — with their real name, of course.
chapters.book4-L02:
Lesson 2 Chai at the Stall

Saturday morning, Lajpat Nagar. A hand-cart chai stall by the market gate: a dented kettle roaring on a gas ring, steel glasses in a wire rack, Parle-G packets strung up like bunting. Priya has decided Jacob will do all the talking today. The chai-vaalaa has seen everything; a nervous American is nothing new.

Still just honaa ("to be") plus frozen phrases. Today's key chunk: …देना (…denaa) [day-nah], tacked on to an order — "give (me)…". It's friendly-casual and standard at stalls. Memorize it whole; the grammar of requests comes in Unit 13. Numbers get their full treatment in Book 3 — today you only need ek (1), do (2) and tees (30).

Dialogue: at the chai stall

Chai-vaalaa:
आइए जी, आइए! चाय, चाय, गरम चाय!
aaiye jee, aaiye! chaay, chaay, garam chaay! [ah-i-yay jee, ah-i-yay! chah-ay, chah-ay, guh-rum chah-ay]
Come, sir, come! Chai, chai, hot chai!
Jacob:
भैया, दो चाय देना।
bhaiyaa, do chaay denaa. [bheh-yah, doh chah-ay day-nah]
Bhaiya, give (us) two chais.
Chai-vaalaa:
जी। छोटी या बड़ी?
jee. chhoTee yaa baRee? [jee. chhoh-Tee yah buh-Ree]
Sure. Small or big?
Jacob:
बड़ी, जी!
baRee, jee! [buh-Ree, jee]
Big, please!
Priya:
और भैया, यह क्या है?
aur bhaiyaa, yeh kyaa hai? [awr bheh-yah, yeh kyah heh]
And bhaiya, what is this?
Chai-vaalaa:
यह? यह मठरी है।
yeh? yeh maThree hai. [yeh? yeh muTh-ree heh]
This? This is mathri (a flaky salted cracker).
Jacob:
और वह क्या है?
aur voh kyaa hai? [awr voh kyah heh]
And what is that?
Chai-vaalaa:
वह पार्ले-जी है! बिस्कुट!
voh paarle-jee hai! biskuT! [voh pahr-lay-jee heh! bis-kuT]
That is Parle-G! Biscuit!
Jacob:
अच्छा! एक पार्ले-जी भी।
achchhaa! ek paarle-jee bhee. [uch-chhah! ayk pahr-lay-jee bhee]
I see! One Parle-G too.
Chai-vaalaa:
लो जी — चाय तैयार! गरम है!
lo jee — chaay taiyaar! garam hai! [loh jee — chah-ay teh-yahr! guh-rum heh]
Here you go — chai ready! It's hot!
Jacob:
अरे! बहुत गरम है!
arre! bahut garam hai! [uh-ray! bo-hut guh-rum heh]
Whoa! It's very hot!
Priya:
आराम से, यार, आराम से!
aaraam se, yaar, aaraam se! [ah-rahm say, yahr, ah-rahm say]
Easy, yaar, take it easy!
Jacob:
वाह… चाय बहुत अच्छी है! भैया, कितने पैसे?
vaah… chaay bahut achchhee hai! bhaiyaa, kitne paise? [vah… chah-ay bo-hut uch-chhee heh! bheh-yah, kit-nay peh-say]
Wow… the chai is really good! Bhaiya, how much (money)?
Chai-vaalaa:
तीस रुपये, जी।
tees rupaye, jee. [tees ru-puh-yay, jee]
Thirty rupees, sir.
Jacob:
यह लीजिए। शुक्रिया!
yeh leejiye. shukriyaa! [yeh lee-ji-yeh. shuk-ri-yah]
Here you are. Thanks!
Chai-vaalaa:
ठीक है जी! फिर आइए!
Theek hai jee! phir aaiye! [Theek heh jee! phir ah-i-yay]
All good, sir! Come again!

भैया (bhaiyaa) [bheh-yah] literally means "big brother", and it's the universal friendly address for chai-vaalaas, auto drivers, shopkeepers — any man providing a service. For a woman at a stall, say दीदी (deedee) [dee-dee], "big sister". And note: Mumbai orders "cutting chai" — in Delhi you just say छोटी or बड़ी. The glass is steel, it WILL burn your fingers, and holding it by the rim like a local is a skill worth practicing.

Key phrases

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
भैयाbhaiyaa (m)bheh-yah"brother" — address for male vendors
एक चाय देना।ek chaay denaa.ayk chah-ay day-nahOne chai, please. (frozen order form)
यह क्या है?yeh kyaa hai?yay kyah hehWhat is this? (near you)
वह क्या है?voh kyaa hai?voh kyah hehWhat is that? (farther away)
गरम है!garam hai!guh-rum hehIt's hot! (temperature, not weather)
ठीक है।Theek hai.Theek hehOkay / fine / all good.
कितने पैसे?kitne paise?kit-nay peh-sayHow much (money)? — frozen for now
तीस रुपयेtees rupaye (m)tees ru-puh-yaythirty rupees
यह लीजिए।yeh leejiye.yay lee-ji-yayHere you are. (handing something over)
पानीpaanee (m)pah-neewater
बिस्कुटbiskuT (m)bis-kuTbiscuit / cookie
फिर आइए!phir aaiye!phir ah-i-yayCome again! (you'll hear it everywhere)

यह (yeh) vs वह (voh): English speakers grab voh for everything because "that" feels safe. Hindi is picky about distance — within reach or under discussion right now: यह; across the stall or across the street: वह. Point at your own glass and say वह क्या है? and the chai-vaalaa will look behind himself.

Chai at a stall is a ritual, not a transaction. You stand, you sip slowly, you watch the street go by — nobody hurries you. Dunking a Parle-G until it nearly collapses is a national sport; losing half of it in the glass is the beginner's tax. When you finish, hand the glass back — the stack by the kettle is the recycling system.

Did you catch that?

Exercise 2A — Comprehension

Answer in Hindi — short answers are fine. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 2.

  1. क्या चाय गरम है? (kyaa chaay garam hai?)
  2. चाय कैसी है? (chaay kaisee hai?)
  3. कितने पैसे? (kitne paise?)
  4. क्या जैकब की चाय छोटी है? (kyaa Jacob kee chaay chhoTee hai?)
  5. पार्ले-जी क्या है? (paarle-jee kyaa hai?)

Pattern practice

Two moves cover the whole stall: asking what something is, and ordering it.

AskAnswerOrder
यह क्या है? (yeh kyaa hai?)यह चाय है। (yeh chaay hai.)भैया, एक चाय देना। (bhaiyaa, ek chaay denaa.)
वह क्या है? (voh kyaa hai?)वह पानी है। (voh paanee hai.)भैया, दो पानी देना। (bhaiyaa, do paanee denaa.)

Exercise 2B — At the stall

Write the full Hindi line for each cue. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 2.

  1. Ask "what is this?" about the thing in front of you (चाय chaay) — then answer it.
  2. Ask "what is this?" (पानी paanee) — then answer it.
  3. Ask "what is that?" about the far shelf (बिस्कुट biskuT) — then answer it.
  4. Ask "what is this?" (मठरी maThree) — then answer it.
  5. Order one chai.
  6. Order two chais.
  7. Order one water.
  8. Ask the price.

Translation practice

Exercise 2C — Into Hindi

Write in Devanagari. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 2.

  1. Bhaiya, one chai please.
  2. What is this?
  3. The chai is very hot!
  4. Okay. How much (money)?

Exercise 2D — Into English

Write the English meaning. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 2.

  1. यह मठरी है। (yeh maThree hai.)
  2. वह क्या है? (voh kyaa hai?)
  3. चाय तैयार है। (chaay taiyaar hai.)
  4. फिर आइए! (phir aaiye!)

Set up a chai stall in your kitchen. Your partner is the chai-vaalaa; the counter is anything with mugs on it. You must: (1) order for both of you — दो चाय देना; (2) point at three real things and ask यह क्या है? / वह क्या है? (partner answers यह … है — new words are free!); (3) react to the first sip: गरम है!; (4) ask कितने पैसे?, pay in imaginary rupees with यह लीजिए. Swap roles — and as chai-vaalaa, don't forget your sales cry: चाय, चाय, गरम चाय!
chapters.book4-L03:
Lesson 3 Meeting the Family

Sunday afternoon on the sofa. Next weekend Jacob meets Priya's parents for the first time, so tonight is homework: Priya scrolls through her phone gallery — Diwali photos, a wedding, one very photogenic dog — and introduces the whole cast. Learn these faces well. They come with grammar attached.

New tools this lesson: meraa / meree / mere "my", tumhaaraa "your", hamaaraa "our", plurals, and one very Indian rule — the respect plural. Parents, grandparents, elder siblings: grammatically plural, always. One mother, but मम्मी हैं (mummy hain), never hai. It isn't bad math; it's good manners.

Dialogue: the phone gallery

Priya:
देखो — यह मेरी मम्मी हैं।
dekho — yeh meree mummy hain. [day-khoh — yeh may-ree mum-mee heh(n)]
Look — this is my mom. (lit. these are my mom — respect plural!)
Jacob:
वाह! और यह कौन हैं?
vaah! aur yeh kaun hain? [vah! awr yeh kawn heh(n)]
Wow! And who is this?
Priya:
यह मेरे पापा हैं।
yeh mere paapaa hain. [yeh may-ray pah-pah heh(n)]
This is my dad.
Jacob:
अच्छा… तुम्हारे कितने भाई-बहन हैं?
achchhaa… tumhaare kitne bhaaee-behen hain? [uch-chhah… tum-hah-ray kit-nay bhah-ee-beh-hen heh(n)]
Okay… how many brothers and sisters do you have?
Priya:
एक भाई और एक बहन। यह मेरा भाई रोहन है।
ek bhaaee aur ek behen. yeh meraa bhaaee Rohan hai. [ayk bhah-ee awr ayk beh-hen. yeh may-rah bhah-ee roh-hun heh]
One brother and one sister. This is my brother Rohan.
Jacob:
और यह?
aur yeh? [awr yeh]
And this?
Priya:
यह मेरी दीदी हैं — नेहा।
yeh meree deedee hain — Neha. [yeh may-ree dee-dee heh(n) — nay-hah]
This is my big sister — Neha.
Jacob:
दीदी बड़ी हैं?
deedee baRee hain? [dee-dee buh-Ree heh(n)]
Didi is older?
Priya:
हाँ। दीदी तीस साल की हैं। रोहन बाईस साल का है।
haan. deedee tees saal kee hain. Rohan baaees saal kaa hai. [hah(n). dee-dee tees sahl kee heh(n). roh-hun bah-ees sahl kah heh]
Yes. Didi is thirty. Rohan is twenty-two. (lit. of thirty years)
Jacob:
और तुम?
aur tum? [awr tum]
And you?
Priya:
मैं सत्ताईस साल की हूँ। और तुम, जैकब जी?
main sattaaees saal kee hoon. aur tum, Jacob jee? [meh(n) sut-tah-ees sahl kee hoo(n). awr tum, jay-kub jee]
I'm twenty-seven. And you, Jacob-ji? (teasing him with the जी)
Jacob:
मैं उनतीस साल का हूँ।
main untees saal kaa hoon. [meh(n) un-tees sahl kah hoo(n)]
I'm twenty-nine.
Priya:
और यह मेरी दादी हैं। दादी बहुत प्यारी हैं।
aur yeh meree daadee hain. daadee bahut pyaaree hain. [awr yeh may-ree dah-dee heh(n). dah-dee bo-hut pyah-ree heh(n)]
And this is my grandma (dad's side). Grandma is very sweet.
Jacob:
तुम्हारा परिवार बहुत सुंदर है!
tumhaaraa parivaar bahut sundar hai! [tum-hah-rah puh-ri-vahr bo-hut sun-dur heh]
Your family is very beautiful!
Priya:
शुक्रिया! और यह हमारा कुत्ता शेरू है!
shukriyaa! aur yeh hamaaraa kuttaa Sheru hai! [shuk-ri-yah! awr yeh huh-mah-rah kut-tah shay-roo heh]
Thanks! And this is our dog, Sheru!
Jacob:
अरे वाह! शेरू भी बहुत प्यारा है!
arre vaah! Sheru bhee bahut pyaaraa hai! [uh-ray vah! shay-roo bhee bo-hut pyah-rah heh]
Oh wow! Sheru is very cute too!

Delhi families say मम्मी and पापा — the shuddh-Hindi maataa-jee / pitaa-jee survives mostly in TV serials and wedding cards. Elder sister is दीदी (or just दी (dee) [dee]: "Neha di"), elder brother भैया — yes, the same word you used for the chai-vaalaa; context does the work. And every second dog in Delhi is named Sheru — "little lion". The full in-law dictionary is in Book 3, Chapter 2; learn saas and sasur before Lesson 14.

Key phrases

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
यह मेरी मम्मी हैं।yeh meree mummy hain. (f)yay may-ree mum-mee heh(n)This is my mom. (respect plural)
यह मेरे पापा हैं।yeh mere paapaa hain. (m)yay may-ray pah-pah heh(n)This is my dad. (respect plural)
भाईbhaaee (m)bhah-eebrother
बहनbehen (f)beh-hensister
दीदीdeedee (f)dee-deeelder sister
दादीdaadee (f)dah-deegrandmother (father's side)
तुम्हारे कितने भाई-बहन हैं?tumhaare kitne bhaaee-behen hain?tum-hah-ray kit-nay bhah-ee-beh-hen heh(n)How many siblings do you have? (casual)
आपके कितने भाई-बहन हैं?aapke kitne bhaaee-behen hain?ahp-kay kit-nay bhah-ee-beh-hen heh(n)same question, polite — for elders
… साल का / साल की… saal kaa / saal keesahl kah / sahl kee… years old (kaa for m, kee for f)
परिवारparivaar (m)puh-ri-vahrfamily
सुंदरsundarsun-durbeautiful (never changes form)
प्यारा / प्यारीpyaaraa / pyaareepyah-rah / pyah-reesweet, cute, dear (m / f)

Two traps in one photo. First: मेरी मम्मी है with singular hai sounds curt, even rude — elders get hain. Second: the possessive goes plural with them too — मेरे पापा (mere paapaa), not मेरा पापा, and adjectives follow along: दादी प्यारी हैं. Younger people stay singular: रोहन प्यारा है. Age flows through the whole sentence.

Within ten minutes of meeting any Indian auntie or uncle, you WILL be asked आपके कितने भाई-बहन हैं? — family is the small talk. Ask it back about siblings and children, freely. But don't ask elders their age; ages are for siblings and kids. And with everyone in your partner's parents' generation: आप, always आप, forever आप.

Did you catch that?

Exercise 3A — Comprehension

Answer in Hindi — short answers are fine. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 3.

  1. प्रिया के कितने भाई-बहन हैं? (Priya ke kitne bhaaee-behen hain?)
  2. रोहन कौन है? (Rohan kaun hai?)
  3. दीदी कितने साल की हैं? (deedee kitne saal kee hain?)
  4. क्या दादी प्यारी हैं? (kyaa daadee pyaaree hain?)
  5. शेरू कौन है? (Sheru kaun hai?)

Pattern practice

"My / your / our" must match the person owned — masculine, feminine, or plural/respect:

+ masculine+ feminine+ plural or respect
myमेरा भाई (meraa bhaaee)मेरी बहन (meree behen)मेरे पापा (mere paapaa)
your (tum)तुम्हारा भाई (tumhaaraa bhaaee)तुम्हारी बहन (tumhaaree behen)तुम्हारे पापा (tumhaare paapaa)
your (aap)आपका भाई (aapkaa bhaaee)आपकी बहन (aapkee behen)आपके पापा (aapke paapaa)
ourहमारा कुत्ता (hamaaraa kuttaa)हमारी दादी (hamaaree daadee)हमारे मम्मी-पापा (hamaare mummy-paapaa)

Exercise 3B — Whose is it?

Fill the blank with the right form of the word in brackets. Watch gender AND respect. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 3.

  1. यह ___ भाई है। (yeh ___ bhaaee hai.) [my]
  2. यह ___ बहन है। (yeh ___ behen hai.) [my]
  3. यह ___ मम्मी हैं। (yeh ___ mummy hain.) [my]
  4. ___ पापा दिल्ली से हैं। (___ paapaa dillee se hain.) [my]
  5. ___ दीदी बहुत सुंदर हैं। (___ deedee bahut sundar hain.) [your — tum]
  6. ___ परिवार बड़ा है। (___ parivaar baRaa hai.) [our]
  7. ___ कुत्ता प्यारा है। (___ kuttaa pyaaraa hai.) [your — aap]
  8. ___ दो बहनें हैं। (___ do behnen hain.) [my]

Translation practice

Exercise 3C — Into Hindi

Write in Devanagari. Mind the respect plural. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 3.

  1. This is my mother.
  2. My sister is twenty-two years old.
  3. How many brothers and sisters do you have? (to your partner — tum)
  4. Your family is very beautiful. (tum)

Exercise 3D — Into English

Write the English meaning. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 3.

  1. यह मेरे पापा हैं। (yeh mere paapaa hain.)
  2. मेरी दो बहनें हैं। (meree do behnen hain.)
  3. हमारा कुत्ता बहुत प्यारा है। (hamaaraa kuttaa bahut pyaaraa hai.)
  4. तुम्हारी दीदी कितने साल की हैं? (tumhaaree deedee kitne saal kee hain?)

Open a real photo album or phone gallery together. Round one: point and ask यह कौन है? (young people) or यह कौन हैं? (elders) — your partner answers, you repeat. Round two: flip it — introduce five of YOUR family members in Hindi: यह मेरी मम्मी हैं। यह मेरा भाई है। Your partner polices the respect plural mercilessly. Round three: siblings' ages only — तुम्हारा भाई कितने साल का है? Wrong kaa/kee costs one pretend rupee per slip.
chapters.book4-L04:
Lesson 4 Around the House

Jacob and Priya have just moved into a 2BHK in Malviya Nagar — second floor, mango tree outside the balcony, landlord downstairs. Kabir arrives with a box of sweets for the new place, and Jacob, gloriously overconfident after three lessons, insists on giving the tour in Hindi.

Two little location words do today's heavy lifting: में (mein) [may(n)] "in" and पर (par) [pur] "on". They come AFTER the place: किचन में = "in the kitchen". And for owning things, Hindi says मेरे पास … है (mere paas … hai) [may-ray pahs] — literally "near me is…" = "I have…". These are postpositions; their full machinery arrives in Unit 7. Today, use them as fixed patterns.

Dialogue: the grand tour

Kabir:
वाह! नया घर!
vaah! nayaa ghar! [vah! nuh-yah ghur]
Wow! New house!
Jacob:
जी हाँ! यह हमारा घर है। आइए!
jee haan! yeh hamaaraa ghar hai. aaiye! [jee hah(n)! yeh huh-mah-rah ghur heh. ah-i-yeh]
Yes! This is our home. Come in!
Kabir:
घर बड़ा है, यार!
ghar baRaa hai, yaar! [ghur buh-Rah heh, yahr]
The house is big, yaar!
Jacob:
यह कमरा बड़ा है। और वह कमरा छोटा है।
yeh kamraa baRaa hai. aur voh kamraa chhoTaa hai. [yeh kum-rah buh-Rah heh. awr voh kum-rah chhoh-Tah heh]
This room is big. And that room is small.
Kabir:
और किचन? किचन में क्या है?
aur kitchen? kitchen mein kyaa hai? [awr ki-chun? ki-chun may(n) kyah heh]
And the kitchen? What's in the kitchen?
Jacob:
किचन में फ़्रिज है, गैस है… और मेरी कॉफ़ी मशीन!
kitchen mein frij hai, gais hai… aur meree coffee machine! [ki-chun may(n) frij heh, gehs heh… awr may-ree kaw-fee muh-sheen]
In the kitchen there's a fridge, a gas stove… and my coffee machine!
Kabir:
कॉफ़ी मशीन! अरे वाह, अमेरिकन स्टाइल!
coffee machine! arre vaah, amerikan sTaail! [kaw-fee muh-sheen! uh-ray vah, uh-may-ri-kun sTah-il]
A coffee machine! Oh wow, American style!
Priya:
और यहाँ बालकनी है।
aur yahaan baalkanee hai. [awr yuh-hah(n) bahl-kuh-nee heh]
And here's the balcony.
Kabir:
बालकनी में क्या है?
baalkanee mein kyaa hai? [bahl-kuh-nee may(n) kyah heh]
What's on the balcony?
Priya:
बालकनी में पौधे हैं। और एक मेज़ और दो कुर्सियाँ।
baalkanee mein paudhe hain. aur ek mez aur do kursiyaan. [bahl-kuh-nee may(n) paw-dhay heh(n). awr ayk mayz awr doh kur-si-yah(n)]
There are plants on the balcony. And a table and two chairs.
Jacob:
और मेरे पास एक ख़ास चीज़ है!
aur mere paas ek khaas cheez hai! [awr may-ray pahs ayk khahs cheez heh]
And I have one special thing!
Kabir:
क्या?
kyaa? [kyah]
What?
Jacob:
टीवी! बहुत बड़ा टीवी!
TV! bahut baRaa TV! [Tee-vee! bo-hut buh-Rah Tee-vee]
A TV! A very big TV!
Kabir:
क्रिकेट के लिए?
krikeT ke liye? [kri-kayT kay li-yay]
For cricket?
Jacob:
जी हाँ! और मैच आज है!
jee haan! aur maich aaj hai! [jee hah(n)! awr mehch ahj heh]
Yes! And the match is today!
Kabir:
यार, तुम्हारा घर बहुत अच्छा है!
yaar, tumhaaraa ghar bahut achchhaa hai! [yahr, tum-hah-rah ghur bo-hut uch-chhah heh]
Yaar, your place is really great! (Notice: Kabir has switched to तुम — you're friends now.)

Delhi flat-speak is its own dialect: a "2BHK" is two Bedrooms, Hall, Kitchen; the hall is the living room even if it's tiny. The kitchen is किचन at least as often as रसोई (rasoee) [ruh-so-ee], and the bathroom is just बाथरूम. Oh — and the balcony isn't only yours: बालकनी में कबूतर है! (baalkanee mein kabootar hai!) [kuh-boo-tur] "there's a pigeon on the balcony!" is a daily Delhi battle cry. The pigeons always win.

Key phrases

नया / पुरानाnayaa / puraanaanuh-yah / pu-rah-nahnew / old (things)
ख़ास चीज़khaas cheez (f)khahs cheezspecial thing

Things vs people. Gadgets, furniture, money: मेरे पास — मेरे पास टीवी है। Family and friends: plain possessives — मेरे दो भाई हैं (mere do bhaaee hain), NOT मेरे पास दो भाई हैं, which sounds like you keep two brothers in a drawer next to the remote.

Shoes off at the door — look for the pile of chappals and add yours. A guest is offered water first, then chai, then more chai; your host will say आइए, बैठिए! (aaiye, baiThiye!) [ah-i-yay, beh-Thi-yay] "come, sit!" — a frozen pair worth recognizing. And Kabir's box of sweets? Never visit a new home empty-handed. मिठाई (miThaaee) [mi-Thah-ee] always fits.

Did you catch that?

Exercise 4A — Comprehension

Answer in Hindi — short answers are fine. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 4.

  1. क्या घर बड़ा है? (kyaa ghar baRaa hai?)
  2. किचन में क्या है? (kitchen mein kyaa hai?)
  3. बालकनी में क्या है? (baalkanee mein kyaa hai?)
  4. जैकब के पास ख़ास चीज़ क्या है? (Jacob ke paas khaas cheez kyaa hai?)
  5. मैच कब है? (maich kab hai?)

Pattern practice

One frame, endless rooms. Slot a place before में, a thing after it, and match hai/hain to the thing:

Place + में/परThingVerb
किचन मेंफ़्रिजहै (hai)
बालकनी मेंपौधेहैं (hain)
मेज़ परकिताबेंहैं (hain)
घर मेंदो कमरेहैं (hain)

Exercise 4B — What's where?

Make a full sentence from each cue pair. Watch है vs हैं. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 4.

  1. किचन / फ़्रिज (kitchen / frij)
  2. बालकनी / पौधे (baalkanee / paudhe)
  3. घर / दो कमरे (ghar / do kamre)
  4. मेज़ / किताबें (mez / kitaaben — on the table!)
  5. फ़्रिज / पानी (frij / paanee)
  6. मेरे पास / टीवी (mere paas / TV)
  7. मेरे पास / कॉफ़ी मशीन (mere paas / coffee machine)
  8. हमारे पास / नया घर (hamaare paas / nayaa ghar)

Translation practice

Exercise 4C — Into Hindi

Write in Devanagari. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 4.

  1. This room is big.
  2. There are plants on the balcony.
  3. I have a new TV.
  4. Our house is small, but very good.

Exercise 4D — Into English

Write the English meaning. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 4.

  1. किचन में फ़्रिज है। (kitchen mein frij hai.)
  2. मेरे पास एक ख़ास चीज़ है। (mere paas ek khaas cheez hai.)
  3. यह कमरा छोटा है, लेकिन अच्छा है। (yeh kamraa chhoTaa hai, lekin achchhaa hai.)
  4. मेज़ पर किताबें हैं। (mez par kitaaben hain.)

Give your partner the tour of your actual home, room by room, in Hindi: यह किचन है। किचन में फ़्रिज है… In each room name two things and one adjective (यह कमरा बड़ा है!). Then play "detective": your partner asks … में क्या है? about a room you're NOT in, and you answer from memory. Finish with show-and-tell: each of you presents one prized possession — मेरे पास … है! — the more dramatic the reveal, the better.

chapters.book4-L05:
Lesson 5 Daily Routine

Sunday breakfast on the Malviya Nagar balcony. Below: the press-vaalaa's cart, a school van honking, the sabzi-vaalaa's morning cry. Priya, second chai in hand, has decided to interview Jacob about his weekday routine — partly for Hindi practice, mostly to build a case in the great chai-versus-coffee war.

This lesson unlocks your first real verbs: the present habitual — things you do regularly. Formula: verb stem + -taa/-tee/-te + the matching form of honaa. A man says मैं उठता हूँ (main uThtaa hoon); a woman says मैं उठती हूँ (main uThtee hoon). Full machinery in Unit 8 — here you get the working kit.

Dialogue: the interview

Priya:
जैकब, तुम रोज़ सुबह क्या करते हो?
Jacob, tum roz subah kyaa karte ho? [jay-kub, tum rohz su-beh kyah kur-tay hoh]
Jacob, what do you do every morning?
Jacob:
मैं सुबह जल्दी उठता हूँ। फिर मैं कॉफ़ी बनाता हूँ।
main subah jaldee uThtaa hoon. phir main coffee banaataa hoon. [meh(n) su-beh jul-dee uTh-tah hoo(n). phir meh(n) kaw-fee buh-nah-tah hoo(n)]
I get up early in the morning. Then I make coffee.
Priya:
कॉफ़ी! छी! मैं चाय पीती हूँ।
coffee! chhee! main chaay peetee hoon. [kaw-fee! chhee! meh(n) chah-ay pee-tee hoo(n)]
Coffee! Yuck! I drink chai.
Jacob:
कॉफ़ी अच्छी है, यार!
coffee achchhee hai, yaar! [kaw-fee uch-chhee heh, yahr]
Coffee is good, yaar!
Priya:
नहीं जी, चाय! अच्छा, फिर क्या करते हो?
naheen jee, chaay! achchhaa, phir kyaa karte ho? [nuh-hee(n) jee, chah-ay! uch-chhah, phir kyah kur-tay hoh]
No sir, chai! Okay — then what do you do?
Jacob:
मैं नहाता हूँ, नाश्ता करता हूँ, और मेट्रो से ऑफ़िस जाता हूँ।
main nahaataa hoon, naashtaa kartaa hoon, aur meTro se ofis jaataa hoon. [meh(n) nuh-hah-tah hoo(n), nahsh-tah kur-tah hoo(n), awr may-troh say aw-fis jah-tah hoo(n)]
I shower, have breakfast, and go to the office by metro.
Priya:
तुम रोज़ मेट्रो से जाते हो?
tum roz meTro se jaate ho? [tum rohz may-troh say jah-tay hoh]
You go by metro every day?
Jacob:
हाँ, रोज़। येलो लाइन।
haan, roz. yelo laain. [hah(n), rohz. yay-loh lah-in]
Yes, every day. The Yellow Line.
Priya:
और ऑफ़िस में?
aur ofis mein? [awr aw-fis may(n)]
And at the office?
Jacob:
मैं काम करता हूँ… और कॉफ़ी पीता हूँ!
main kaam kartaa hoon… aur coffee peetaa hoon! [meh(n) kahm kur-tah hoo(n)… awr kaw-fee pee-tah hoo(n)]
I work… and I drink coffee!
Priya:
फिर कॉफ़ी! तुम बिल्कुल अमेरिकन हो!
phir coffee! tum bilkul amerikan ho! [phir kaw-fee! tum bil-kul uh-may-ri-kun hoh]
Coffee again! You are SUCH an American!
Jacob:
और तुम? तुम दिन में क्या करती हो?
aur tum? tum din mein kyaa kartee ho? [awr tum? tum din may(n) kyah kur-tee hoh]
And you? What do you do during the day?
Priya:
मैं घर से काम करती हूँ। और शाम को हम साथ खाना खाते हैं।
main ghar se kaam kartee hoon. aur shaam ko ham saath khaanaa khaate hain. [meh(n) ghur say kahm kur-tee hoo(n). awr shahm koh hum sahth khah-nah khah-tay heh(n)]
I work from home. And in the evening we eat dinner together.
Jacob:
हाँ! और रात को तुम टीवी देखती हो, और मैं… कॉफ़ी पीता हूँ।
haan! aur raat ko tum TV dekhtee ho, aur main… coffee peetaa hoon. [hah(n)! awr raht koh tum Tee-vee daykh-tee hoh, awr meh(n)… kaw-fee pee-tah hoo(n)]
Yes! And at night you watch TV, and I… drink coffee.
Priya:
अरे यार, बस! ज़्यादा कॉफ़ी अच्छी नहीं है!
arre yaar, bas! zyaadaa coffee achchhee naheen hai! [uh-ray yahr, bus! zyah-dah kaw-fee uch-chhee nuh-hee(n) heh]
Oh come on, enough! Too much coffee is not good!

A Delhi morning has a fixed soundtrack: the doodh-vaalaa's cycle bell, the press-vaalaa setting up his ironing cart, school vans, and the first सुबह की चाय (subah kee chaay) [su-beh kee chah-ay] — which for most households is non-negotiable infrastructure, like electricity. Jacob's cafe-latte generation exists too (Delhi has more coffee bars every year), but at home, the kettle answers to chai. Choose your battles.

Key phrases

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
रोज़rozrohzevery day, daily
सुबहsubah (f)su-behmorning / in the morning
शाम कोshaam ko (f)shahm kohin the evening
रात कोraat ko (f)raht kohat night
जल्दीjaldeejul-deeearly; quickly
मैं जल्दी उठता हूँ।main jaldee uThtaa hoon.meh(n) jul-dee uTh-tah hoo(n)I get up early. (woman: उठती uThtee)
नाश्ता करनाnaashtaa karnaa (m)nahsh-tah kur-nahto have breakfast (lit. do breakfast)
नहानाnahaanaanuh-hah-nahto bathe, shower
मेट्रो से जानाmeTro se jaanaamay-troh say jah-nahto go by metro
काम करनाkaam karnaa (m)kahm kur-nahto work
कभी-कभीkabhee-kabheekuh-bhee-kuh-bheesometimes
हमेशा / अक्सरhameshaa / aksarhuh-may-shah / uk-suralways / often

A hazard of learning Hindi from a partner: you absorb THEIR endings. If Priya says मैं उठती हूँ, Jacob must still say मैं उठता हूँ — swapping them is the single most charming, most common learner giveaway in India. Second hazard: dropping the helper. मैं जाता is half a verb; it needs its हूँ. Stem + -taa/-tee + hoon/ho/hai/hain, every time.

Did you catch that?

Exercise 5A — Comprehension

Answer in Hindi — short answers are fine. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 5.

  1. जैकब सुबह क्या बनाता है? (Jacob subah kyaa banaataa hai?)
  2. प्रिया क्या पीती है? (Priya kyaa peetee hai?)
  3. जैकब ऑफ़िस कैसे जाता है? (Jacob ofis kaise jaataa hai?)
  4. प्रिया कहाँ काम करती है? (Priya kahaan kaam kartee hai?)
  5. शाम को जैकब और प्रिया क्या करते हैं? (shaam ko Jacob aur Priya kyaa karte hain?)

Pattern practice

The habitual machine, all persons, both genders — memorize this grid cold:

PersonMan / masc.Woman / fem.
मैं (main)करता हूँ (kartaa hoon)करती हूँ (kartee hoon)
तुम (tum)करते हो (karte ho)करती हो (kartee ho)
यह/वह (yeh/voh)करता है (kartaa hai)करती है (kartee hai)
हम (ham)करते हैं (karte hain)करती हैं (kartee hain)
आप + eldersकरते हैं (karte hain)करती हैं (kartee hain)

Exercise 5B — Conjugation drill

Complete each sentence with the habitual form of the verb in brackets. You are Jacob (masculine) unless the subject says otherwise. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 5.

  1. मैं रोज़ जल्दी ___ । (main roz jaldee ___ .) [उठना uThnaa]
  2. प्रिया चाय ___ । (Priya chaay ___ .) [पीना peenaa]
  3. तुम सुबह क्या ___ ? (tum subah kyaa ___ ?) [करना karnaa — asking a man]
  4. हम साथ खाना ___ । (ham saath khaanaa ___ .) [खाना khaanaa]
  5. जैकब मेट्रो से ऑफ़िस ___ । (Jacob meTro se ofis ___ .) [जाना jaanaa]
  6. मेरी मम्मी रात को टीवी ___ । (meree mummy raat ko TV ___ .) [देखना dekhnaa — respect!]
  7. आप कहाँ काम ___ ? (aap kahaan kaam ___ ?) [करना karnaa — asking your father-in-law]
  8. मैं रात को जल्दी ___ । (main raat ko jaldee ___ .) [सोना sonaa]

Translation practice

Exercise 5C — Into Hindi

Write in Devanagari. You are Jacob (masculine forms). Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 5.

  1. I get up early every day.
  2. Priya drinks chai.
  3. In the evening we eat dinner together.
  4. Do you watch TV at night? (to a woman — tum)

Exercise 5D — Into English

Write the English meaning. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 5.

  1. मैं मेट्रो से ऑफ़िस जाता हूँ। (main meTro se ofis jaataa hoon.)
  2. तुम सुबह क्या करते हो? (tum subah kyaa karte ho?)
  3. मेरे पापा रोज़ चाय पीते हैं। (mere paapaa roz chaay peete hain.)
  4. हम कभी-कभी बाहर खाते हैं। (ham kabhee-kabhee baahar khaate hain.) [bah-hur = outside]

Interview time, and the microphone is a chai spoon. Ask your partner: तुम रोज़ सुबह क्या करती हो? (or करते हो) — they answer step by step; you repeat each answer back in third person: तुम जल्दी उठती हो? अच्छा — प्रिया जल्दी उठती है! Then they interview you. Finish with the frequency game: each of you makes three true sentences with रोज़ / कभी-कभी / हमेशा — and one scandalous false one for the other to catch: नहीं! झूठ! (naheen! jhooTh!) [jhooTh] "Lies!"
chapters.book4-L06:
Lesson 6 On the Phone Right Now

Priya is at her parents' place in Lajpat Nagar for the weekend; Jacob is home alone in Malviya Nagar with a daal recipe open on YouTube. Eight p.m.: he calls. Down the line come the sounds of a Delhi evening — a pressure cooker mid-whistle, traffic, someone's wedding band warming up three streets away.

New gear: the present continuous — what's happening RIGHT NOW. Formula: verb stem + rahaa / rahee / rahe + hoon / ho / hai / hain. A man: मैं बना रहा हूँ (main banaa rahaa hoon) "I am making". A woman: मैं बना रही हूँ (main banaa rahee hoon). Habitual = every day; continuous = this minute. Full story in Unit 9.

Dialogue: the call

Jacob:
हेलो? प्रिया?
helo? Priya? [hay-loh? pri-yah]
Hello? Priya?
Priya:
हाँ जी! क्या कर रहे हो?
haan jee! kyaa kar rahe ho? [hah(n) jee! kyah kur ruh-hay hoh]
Hi! What are you doing?
Jacob:
मैं अभी खाना बना रहा हूँ।
main abhee khaanaa banaa rahaa hoon. [meh(n) uh-bhee khah-nah buh-nah ruh-hah hoo(n)]
I'm making food right now.
Priya:
अरे वाह! क्या बना रहे हो?
arre vaah! kyaa banaa rahe ho? [uh-ray vah! kyah buh-nah ruh-hay hoh]
Oh wow! What are you making?
Jacob:
दाल! मैं यूट्यूब देख रहा हूँ और दाल बना रहा हूँ।
daal! main yooTyoob dekh rahaa hoon aur daal banaa rahaa hoon. [dahl! meh(n) yoo-Tyoob daykh ruh-hah hoo(n) awr dahl buh-nah ruh-hah hoo(n)]
Daal! I'm watching YouTube and making daal.
Priya:
और यहाँ मम्मी भी खाना बना रही हैं!
aur yahaan mummy bhee khaanaa banaa rahee hain! [awr yuh-hah(n) mum-mee bhee khah-nah buh-nah ruh-hee heh(n)]
And here Mom is making food too! (respect plural, even mid-gossip)
Jacob:
अच्छा… यह क्या आवाज़ है?
achchhaa… yeh kyaa aavaaz hai? [uch-chhah… yeh kyah ah-vahz heh]
Okay… what's that sound?
Priya:
कुकर की सीटी!
kukar kee seeTee! [ku-kur kee see-Tee]
The pressure-cooker whistle!
Jacob:
और वह आवाज़?
aur voh aavaaz? [awr voh ah-vahz]
And THAT sound?
Priya:
हॉर्न बज रहा है, बाबा! दिल्ली है!
horn baj rahaa hai, baabaa! dillee hai! [hawrn buj ruh-hah heh, bah-bah! dil-lee heh]
A horn is honking, dear! It's Delhi!
Jacob:
(laughing) पापा क्या कर रहे हैं?
paapaa kyaa kar rahe hain? [pah-pah kyah kur ruh-hay heh(n)]
What's Papa doing?
Priya:
पापा टीवी देख रहे हैं — क्रिकेट! और रोहन सो रहा है।
paapaa TV dekh rahe hain — krikeT! aur Rohan so rahaa hai. [pah-pah Tee-vee daykh ruh-hay heh(n) — kri-kayT! awr roh-hun soh ruh-hah heh]
Papa's watching TV — cricket! And Rohan is sleeping.
Jacob:
अच्छा, तुम कब आ रही हो?
achchhaa, tum kab aa rahee ho? [uch-chhah, tum kub ah ruh-hee hoh]
So… when are you coming (back)?
Priya:
कल शाम को। क्यों?
kal shaam ko. kyon? [kul shahm koh. kyoh(n)]
Tomorrow evening. Why?
Jacob:
बस… तुम्हारी याद आ रही है।
bas… tumhaaree yaad aa rahee hai. [bus… tum-hah-ree yahd ah ruh-hee heh]
Just… I miss you. (lit. your memory is coming)
Priya:
अरे! मुझे भी तुम्हारी याद आ रही है।
अच्छा चलो, खाना तैयार है — बाय!
arre! mujhe bhee tumhaaree yaad aa rahee hai. achchhaa chalo, khaanaa taiyaar hai — baay! [uh-ray! mu-jhay bhee tum-hah-ree yahd ah ruh-hee heh. uch-chhah chuh-loh, khah-nah teh-yahr heh — bah-ee]
Aww! I miss you too. Okay then, dinner's ready — bye!

Delhi's soundtrack, decoded: one short horn = "I exist", long horn = "I am coming through", continuous horn = wedding season. The pressure cooker is the other city bird — households count whistles like timers: तीन सीटी (teen seeTee) and the daal is done. That बाबा Priya used isn't "father" here — it's an affectionate Delhi filler, roughly "silly / dear", deployable at both ends of any sentence.

Key phrases

हिन्दीRomanSay itMeaning
क्या कर रहे हो?kyaa kar rahe ho?kyah kur ruh-hay hohWhat are you doing? (to a man)
क्या कर रही हो?kyaa kar rahee ho?kyah kur ruh-hee hohWhat are you doing? (to a woman)
मैं खाना बना रहा हूँ।main khaanaa banaa rahaa hoon.meh(n) khah-nah buh-nah ruh-hah hoo(n)I'm making food. (woman: बना रही हूँ)
अभीabheeuh-bheeright now
आवाज़aavaaz (f)ah-vahzsound, voice
यह क्या आवाज़ है?yeh kyaa aavaaz hai?yay kyah ah-vahz hehWhat's that sound?
हॉर्न बज रहा है।horn baj rahaa hai.hawrn buj ruh-hah hehA horn is honking.
कुकर की सीटीkukar kee seeTee (f)ku-kur kee see-Teethe pressure-cooker whistle
तुम कब आ रही हो?tum kab aa rahee ho?tum kub ah ruh-hee hohWhen are you coming? (to a woman)
कलkalkultomorrow (also yesterday — context decides)
तुम्हारी याद आ रही है।tumhaaree yaad aa rahee hai.tum-hah-ree yahd ah ruh-hee hehI miss you.
सो रहा है / सो रही हैso rahaa hai / so rahee haisoh ruh-hah heh / soh ruh-hee hehhe / she is sleeping

English pushes "I AM making" → मैं हूँ बना रहा. No: the whole verb train stays coupled at the end — मैं खाना बना रहा हूँ। And rahaa/rahee/rahe carries gender+number just like -taa/-tee/-te: Papa (respect) gets देख रहे हैं, Mummy (respect, feminine) gets बना रही हैं — feminine rahee stays rahee even in the respect plural; only the hain goes plural.

तुम्हारी याद आ रही है — literally "your memory is coming (to me)". Hindi routes many feelings through this "it comes to me" pattern; you'll meet the full family (missing, liking, knowing) from Lesson 7 onward. For now, learn this one whole. Used on the phone with your partner, it outperforms any imported "I miss you". Daily calls to mummy are also standard issue in Delhi families — if Priya calls her mother every evening, that's not unusual, that's Tuesday.

Did you catch that?

Exercise 6A — Comprehension

Answer in Hindi — short answers are fine. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 6.

  1. जैकब क्या बना रहा है? (Jacob kyaa banaa rahaa hai?)
  2. जैकब क्या देख रहा है? (Jacob kyaa dekh rahaa hai?)
  3. मम्मी क्या कर रही हैं? (mummy kyaa kar rahee hain?)
  4. पापा क्या देख रहे हैं? (paapaa kyaa dekh rahe hain?)
  5. प्रिया कब आ रही है? (Priya kab aa rahee hai?)

Pattern practice

Exercise 6B — Right-now drill

Make a full "right now" sentence from each cue. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 6.

  1. मैं / खाना बनाना (main / khaanaa banaanaa) — you are Jacob
  2. प्रिया / चाय पीना (Priya / chaay peenaa)

  4. पापा / टीवी देखना (paapaa / TV dekhnaa — respect!)
  5. रोहन / सोना (Rohan / sonaa)
  6. हम / हिन्दी सीखना (ham / hindee seekhnaa)

Translation practice

Exercise 6C — Into Hindi

Write in Devanagari. You are Jacob (masculine forms). Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 6.

  1. What are you doing? (to a man — tum)
  2. I am making chai.
  3. Papa is watching TV. (respect)

Exercise 6D — Into English

Write the English meaning. Answers: Answer Key, Lesson 6.

  1. हॉर्न बज रहा है। (horn baj rahaa hai.)
  2. रोहन सो रहा है। (Rohan so rahaa hai.)
